Chinese President Xi Jinping is likely to attend the BRICS summit in New Delhi next month with a large delegation. It will be his first visit in seven years and a new sign of warming relations between the rivals, UNN reports, citing Reuters.
Details
India is hosting the summit on September 12-13, and Xi Jinping’s presence will be assessed not so much in terms of the BRICS agenda as in terms of what it signals about efforts by Beijing and New Delhi to stabilize relations after deadly border clashes in 2020.
"Chinese officials are busy finalizing hotel arrangements and security protocols," one Indian source directly familiar with the situation told Reuters.
Last year, Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi visited China for the first time in seven years, but relations have improved only gradually. Recently, a new border dispute triggered a sharp diplomatic exchange between the two sides.
Two other Indian sources said Xi Jinping would likely be accompanied by a delegation of approximately 400 officials, compared with fewer than 200 officials the last time in 2019.
Officials from both countries are expected to use the summit to explore ways to expand engagement while resolving long-standing differences over border and regional security issues.
Final plans for Xi Jinping’s trip and agenda for any potential bilateral meetings between India and China have not yet been finalized, the sources said.
China’s Ministry of Foreign Affairs said: "China attaches great importance to and actively participates in BRICS cooperation, and supports India, the current chair, in successfully holding this year’s BRICS summit."

India’s Ministry of External Affairs did not comment on the matter.

Washington Post ordered to rehire columnist fired over social media posts on Charlie Kirk
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:10:00 UTC
22:10:00 KST

Washington Post ordered to rehire columnist fired over social media posts on Charlie Kirk
Benjamin Mullin
A private arbitrator has ordered The Washington Post to rehire opinion columnist Karen Attiah, who was fired in September over her social media posts about the assassination of conservative activist Charlie Kirk. It also ordered the company to compensate her with back pay.
Sarah Miller Espinosa, the arbitrator, said in a written decision on Aug 20 that the Post “did not have good and sufficient cause” to terminate Attiah and “violated” its labour agreement, according to a copy of the decision shared with The New York Times by Attiah’s lawyers.
“The Washington Post failed to establish the grievant engaged in gross misconduct,” Espinosa wrote.
In a statement, Attiah said that she hoped the decision “sends a message to journalists and media institutions everywhere that freedom of expression is always worth fighting for.” She said that she was “willing to go back” to her work at the Post, which she called “one of the world’s most storied newspapers”.
“This decision confirms what we’ve said from the start: I was doing my job as an opinion writer, and this was wrongful termination,” she said, adding that she was “relieved to finally have that record set straight”
A spokesperson for the Post said the company respects the arbitration process and declined to comment further.
The decision is the result of a year-long fight between the Post and Attiah, who in 2025 accused the company of violating its labour agreement and social media policy when it fired her for posts she said were within her purview as an opinion columnist. A clause in the agreement allows employees to submit disputes for arbitration.
Arbitration is generally considered binding in most disputes, though courts have occasionally overturned decisions after courtroom findings of fraud or other improprieties. The Post’s labour agreement says arbitration is binding, though both the company and the employee retain their legal rights.
The Washington Post said in its termination letter that Attiah’s posts about Kirk had harmed “the integrity” of the organisation and violated standards requiring employees to use social media with civility and respect.
Attiah’s remarks about Kirk’s assassination, which she posted to the social network Bluesky on Sept 10, the day he was shot, responded to the outpouring of grief after the shooting. “Refusing to tear my clothes and smear ashes on my face in performative mourning for a white man that espoused violence is… not the same as violence,” Attiah wrote in one of the posts.
The Post’s opinion section has been in flux since early 2025, when Jeff Bezos, the newspaper’s owner, moved to reorient the section to focus on “personal liberties and free markets”. Some readers cancelled their subscriptions and accused Bezos of attempting to curry favour with the Trump administration.
Lawyers for The Washington Post and Attiah made their arguments before Espinosa in June during a hearing that included testimony from Attiah; Adam O’Neal, then the opinion editor at The Washington Post; and Wayne Connell, the company’s chief human resources officer. Attiah was represented by Democracy Defenders Action, a progressive nonprofit co-founded by the lawyer Norman Eisen, and by the Washington-Baltimore News Guild.
In his testimony, O’Neal said he saw Attiah’s posts the morning after Kirk died and sent them to Connell, according to a transcript of the hearing obtained by The New York Times. “Karen’s social media feed yesterday and today is beyond the pale, completely unacceptable for someone associated with Opinions,” O’Neal wrote, according to the transcript.
Soon after, O’Neal and Connell met with Will Lewis, then the CEO of The Washington Post, to discuss the posts, according to the transcript. They ultimately decided to fire Attiah.
During her testimony, Attiah defended her social media posts, saying that they were part of her work for The Post, “commenting on our discourse on political violence”, Attiah said, according to the transcript.
In a statement, Eisen called the decision “a landmark victory for one of our nation’s crusading journalists.”
- This article originally appeared in The New York Times.

DR Congo Ebola cases top 5,500 as WHO warns of "defining moment"
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
21:09:41 CST
22:09:41 KST

KINSHASA, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) have surpassed 5,500, with more than 2,600 deaths, government figures showed Monday, as the World Health Organization (WHO) said the outbreak reached a "defining moment" more than 100 days after it was declared.
The latest official tally, with data through Saturday, recorded 5,514 confirmed cases and 2,642 deaths, putting the case fatality rate at 47.9 percent. A total of 1,200 patients have recovered.
The outbreak has spread to 57 health zones in Ituri, North Kivu, South Kivu, Haut-Uele, Bas-Uele and Tshopo provinces.
The WHO said Monday that the epidemic has become the fastest-growing Ebola outbreak ever recorded in the DRC, warning that transmission continues to outpace control efforts.
"This outbreak has reached a defining moment," WHO Regional Director for Africa Mohamed Janabi said in a statement. "The choices we make now will determine how quickly we can bring this outbreak under control, protect and save lives."
Ituri remains the epicenter, accounting for about 85 percent of all cases and 79 percent of deaths, according to the WHO.
Deaths occurring outside Ebola treatment centers remain a major concern. The WHO said community deaths accounted for around 60 percent of fatalities recorded in recent weeks, pointing to persistent problems with early detection, referral and access to treatment.
The organization said insecurity, recurrent conflict, population displacement, attacks on health facilities, community reluctance and difficult access were continuing to hamper operations, particularly in eastern DRC.
"We can bring the Ebola outbreak under control but only through scaled-up action in affected communities," WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus said, calling for sustained resources and stronger cooperation among national and local authorities, affected communities and international partners.
Response capacity has expanded significantly since the outbreak began. The number of laboratories capable of testing for Ebola has risen from one to 19, with capacity to process more than 3,000 samples a day, while treatment capacity has grown from fewer than 10 beds to more than 1,300, according to the WHO.
Clinical trials of potential treatments and evaluations of candidate vaccines are also underway. The WHO said the first emergency-listed molecular diagnostic test for Bundibugyo virus disease has been deployed.
The agency warned that the coming months would be critical to closing remaining gaps and slowing transmission, saying an end to fighting in affected areas was also essential for health teams to reach communities.
The outbreak, caused by the Bundibugyo ebolavirus, was declared by the DRC authorities in May. ■

====================================================================================================

China Focus: China opens exhibition to preserve, bring linguistic diversity to life
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
21:09:36 CST
22:09:36 KST

A visitor listens to dialects of various regions in Hunan at the Exhibition Hall of the Project for the Protection of Language Resources of China in Changsha, central China's Hunan Province, Aug. 24, 2026. A new exhibition hall dedicated to the preservation of China's diverse language resources opened on Monday in Changsha, capital of central China's Hunan Province, bringing a decade-long effort to document languages and dialects to the public through digital and interactive displays. The Exhibition Hall of the Project for the Protection of Language Resources of China, located in the Hunan Museum, brings together recordings and other language materials collected from more than 1,800 field survey sites across China, covering Chinese dialects, ethnic minority languages and related cultural traditions. (Xinhua/Xue Yuge)
CHANGSHA, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Putting on headphones at a new exhibition hall in central China, visitors can hear a chorus of voices from across the country, including regional dialects, traditional songs in ethnic minority languages and field recordings of languages on the verge of extinction.
The Exhibition Hall of the Project for the Protection of Language Resources of China opened Monday in Changsha, capital of central China's Hunan Province, bringing decade-long efforts to document languages and dialects to the public through digital and interactive displays.
Located in the Hunan Museum, the exhibition brings together recordings and other language materials collected from more than 1,800 field survey sites across China. More than 30 language-related cultural relics are also on display.
The recordings represent 10 major Chinese dialects and more than 100 ethnic minority languages, including Mongolian, Tibetan, Uygur and Zhuang, said Chen Xuliang, deputy Party secretary of the Hunan Museum.
"Digital technology is helping bring the results of language preservation research out of databases and into public cultural spaces," he said.
The exhibition draws on materials collected through a national language preservation project launched in 2015 to document and preserve the country's diverse languages and dialects. It is the world's largest project of its kind, according to experts.
Over the past decade, researchers have traveled to remote mountain villages and pastoral areas to find native speakers of different ages. They systematically recorded words, grammatical examples, oral traditions and other language materials, turning oral memories at risk of disappearing in digital records that can be preserved for generations.
The work has become increasingly urgent as the number of native speakers of some languages declines.
China is home to more than 100 languages and numerous dialects. Some languages, including Hezhen and Manchu, now have fewer than 100 speakers.
Economic integration, population mobility and the social changes they bring are making it increasingly difficult to preserve languages and cultural traditions around the world, said Wang Lining, a professor at Beijing Normal University's School of Chinese Language and Literature and a participant in the language preservation project.
Many languages lack well-developed writing systems, Wang said, meaning knowledge and memories passed down orally can be lost when their speakers die.
The new exhibition aims to bring such preservation work closer to the public. It also promotes the principles of the "Yuelu Proclamation," which was officially released in 2019 and described as UNESCO's first permanent document themed on the protection of linguistic diversity.
Experts attending the exhibition's opening said a key challenge is how to use artificial intelligence and digital museum technologies to turn vast collections of field recordings into cultural experiences the public can engage with.
For Wang, documenting endangered languages is only the beginning.
"In the past, the focus was on recording endangered languages and preserving samples of their voices," she said. "In the future, preservation needs to move toward keeping languages alive."
The exhibition hall, Wang said, is part of that shift, taking language resources beyond academic research and bringing them closer to everyday life. ■

Iran Foreign Ministry spokesperson warned Monday that Tehran would respond harshly to expanded U.S. sanctions, including measures against countries it sees as cooperating with Washington.
"Any escalation of this situation will undoubtedly bring about consequences," Esmail Baghaei said. "Our hands are not tied."

The expanded sanctions come after weeks of impasse. The United States has not dislodged Iran’s grip on the Strait of Hormuz, through which a fifth of the world’s traded oil passed before the war started nearly six months ago.
Iran's demands for reopening the strait include lifting the U.S. naval blockade, withdrawing U.S. forces from the region and reparations for damages sustained in the war.

Sanctions have historically raised prices of basic goods in Iran, but after decades of withstanding them, Iran’s economy has adapted through finding new trading partners and building domestic industries.
Ahead of the expected U.S. announcement, the country's currency hit a record low on Monday.
Meanwhile, Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir, who has built a personal rapport with U.S. President Donald Trump, arrived in Iran on Monday for talks, Iranian media said.

The U.S. and Iran have not conducted airstrikes on each other's militaries for weeks, but their last official face-to-face talks to end the six-month-old conflict took place in June and strikes on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz have continued.

They did not say who had launched the projectile. Iran's Houthi allies last month said they would block Saudi oil exports diverted to the Red Sea to avoid Hormuz.
Thousands of people have died, most of them in Iran and Lebanon, since the U.S. and Israel began strikes on Feb. 28, degrading much of Iran's conventional military capacity and inflicting economic pain while killing Iran's then-Supreme Leader Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.
Yet Iran has preserved enough missile and drone capability to attack its Gulf neighbors and bring shipping in the Strait of Hormuz to a near standstill, pushing up world fuel prices. The exact state of Iran's nuclear program, which the Americans and Israelis aim to wipe out, remains unknown.
Oil prices eased Monday after two weeks of gains as investors took profits ahead of the expected U.S. announcement.
Without detailing specific measures, Bessent signaled the U.S. would target "fearful nations" that practice "appeasement" by engaging with Iran's economy and financial system.
"They would do well to consider the consequences of sustaining it," he wrote in the Financial Times.
Iran has been bracing for the sanctions for days, issuing a series of statements hinting at a major military response.

Source: Kremlin-aligned Russian news agency Interfax
Details: Under the decree titled On Measures to Ensure the Security of Critical Infrastructure Facilities of the Russian Federation, the measures may be introduced if attempts to prevent drone attacks are deemed ineffective or if a business fails to restore critical infrastructure facilities to operational status in a timely manner.
Critical infrastructure facilities are defined as those in the fuel and energy sector, industrial facilities, communications, utilities, transport and logistics infrastructure (including transport and logistics complexes), energy facilities (including nuclear facilities), facilities providing essential services, critically important and potentially hazardous facilities, "and other facilities deemed essential to Russia's security, economic stability and the livelihoods of its population".
According to the document, the decree has been signed "due to the increased threats to the security of critical infrastructure facilities during the special military operation" [as Russia refers to its war against Ukraine – ed.].
Temporary management can be imposed on all or part of a business entity's movable or immovable property located in Russia. The entity may be a Russian legal entity or individual, or a foreign organisation or citizen. The measure can also apply to securities, shares in the capital of legal entities and property rights belonging to the entity.
By default, the Federal Agency for State Property Management will act as the temporary manager, although the government may, on the instruction of the Russian leader, assign these functions to another entity.
The costs of temporary management will be financed from the income generated by the use of the property.

Meloni made migrant 'returns' popular in the EU. Now the policy is backfiring on her
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:03:50 UTC
22:03:50 KST

Meloni championed irregular migrant “returns” in a hardline push to externalise EU borders. Now, more member states are asking Italy to take back migrants under the first-arrival principle.
Giorgia Meloni was one of the main political sponsors of a policy of “returns” for irregular migrants. Now, as a growing number of EU countries push Rome to take back migrants who entered the bloc through Italy, she is getting a taste of her own medicine.
On Sunday, Ireland became the latest in a growing number of member states to call on Italy, as a country of first entry into the EU, to take back asylum seekers.
It joins Germany, Switzerland, Austria, Finland, Sweden and the Netherlands.
The requests stem from the new EU Pact on Asylum and Migration, which reaffirms a key principle of the Dublin system: the EU country where a non-EU national first enters the bloc and applies for protection should handle their asylum claim.
A few weeks after Meloni took office in 2022, Italy unilaterally suspended the reception of Dublin transfers, citing practical and capacity constraints. The European Commission has considered the move a breach of Italy’s Dublin obligations, a position also upheld by the EU Court of Justice in several rulings.
New Pact on Asylum and Migration
Since the Dublin Convention entered into force in 1997, some European governments have tried to scrap this principle, arguing it overwhelms countries geographically exposed to first entry, such as Spain, France, Italy, Greece and, more recently, Cyprus.
After failing to reform the EU asylum system in the 2014-2019 legislature, EU lawmakers succeeded in the next one, delivering a new asylum and border management system — the EU Migration and Asylum Pact — which entered into force in June 2026.
The pact reaffirms the return principle, requiring asylum seekers who move onward to be transferred back to their EU country of first entry, which makes secondary movements from Italy to another EU country far more complicated.
In particular, the new Pact modified the Dublin rules by replacing the previous ‘take-back request’ procedure for secondary movements with a simpler notification mechanism. This removes the need for the responsible member state to formally accept a take-back request, which Italy virtually never did.
At the same time, the pact foresees a mandatory solidarity system among the EU countries, but the annual number of relocations remains too low to deliver any meaningful redistribution.
In 2026, only 8,878 migrant people will be relocated from countries considered "under migratory pressure", Italy, Spain, Greece, Cyprus and Malta, to other EU member states. Last year, over 66,000 irregular migrants arrived in Italy by sea and Frontex recorded almost 178,000 irregular crossings into the EU.
Despite the low numbers of intra-EU relocations, the Italian government has supported the new rules on migration. "The new agreement marks a positive turning point for Italy in the management of so-called 'Dublin' migrants," Meloni wrote in a Facebook post, replying to domestic critics.
"The new rules provide much greater protection for countries of first entry with regard to asylum claims and, with the strengthening of the 'safe third country' principle advocated by Italy, it will be easier to carry out accelerated returns," she added.
Returns, but where?
A key part of the EU migration package is the Return Regulation, finalised last June.
The mechanism aims to increase the number of rejected asylum seekers, as too few people whose applications are refused are actually sent back to their countries of origin.
EU governments have also pursued other ways to speed up returns, notably the creation of “return hubs” in non-EU countries. These would allow member states to send migrants to a country with which they have no direct or indirect connection.
But returning a migrant to their country of origin — or to a third country — requires a bilateral agreement. Italy has spearheaded this approach with a return hub in Albania, although Italian judges have repeatedly ruled against the scheme.
Germany, Austria, Greece, the Netherlands and Denmark are jointly working to establish return hubs outside the EU. The Greek daily Kathimerini reported earlier this month that negotiations for a facility in Uganda were at an advanced stage, with the aim of making it operational in 2027.
Still, the legal and practical hurdles involved in setting up return hubs in third countries mean they are unlikely to provide an immediate response to irregular arrivals. For now, that makes it easier for EU countries to return migrants within the bloc to their country of first arrival under the Dublin principle.
Ironically, the only two countries that have explicitly ruled out Dublin-based returns to Italy are Spain and France — the same two member states that have dismissed Meloni's return hubs as "ineffective" and opposed funding them with EU money.
"Meloni has fully endorsed the New Migration Pact, opting for political instrumentalisation that boasted Italy as leading the way in EU migration policy," Sara Prestianni, advocacy director at the NGO Euromed Rights, told Euronews.
"The Italian government did not properly fight Dublin's first-arrival principle, which makes little sense since it leaves migrants who want to reach a different destination country in a legal limbo for months or even years," Prestianni said.
Old fault lines resurface
Returns are now dominating Europe's migration debate, as most EU countries, regardless of political colour, push for a harder line, a shift sharpened further by the crisis in the Spanish exclave of Ceuta.
The Ceuta crisis triggered a major diplomatic rift between Rome and Madrid, after Meloni broke with the usual solidarity between frontline member states to suspend Schengen free-movement rules and reinstate border checks with Spain.
Now, the heating up of Dublin-based returns is reigniting a more traditional cleavage between frontier member states and countries of destination, a friction that has become particularly visible between Italy and Germany.
"If Italy maintains this stance, it will destroy the new European asylum system, which has only been in effect for a few weeks," Alexander Throm, the CDU/CSU parliamentary group's spokesperson on interior policy, told the German news agency DPA.
Meanwhile, Italian Interior Minister Matteo Piantedosi has announced he will host a meeting with his counterparts from the MED5 countries — Cyprus, Greece, Italy, Malta and Spain — to address the situation.
The Italian government considers the issue to be strictly intertwined with the activity of German-based non-governmental organisations rescuing people at sea, which it claims are a "pull factor" to attract irregular migrants.
Nicola Procaccini, a senior MEP from the ruling party Brothers of Italy, told Euronews Italy will take back the "Dublin" migrants when the new EU rules are fully in place, but doubled down on the request to Germany to crack down on the NGOs.
"In the past, these organisations, financed by previous German governments, brought large numbers of migrants to Italy. So a certain degree of irritation is legitimate, as Germany has not picked up the bill for this," Procaccini said.
Migration has become a central campaign issue as several EU countries head to the polls next year, including Italy, France and Spain, with radical-right parties continuing their projected growth and eroding the political centre.
In Italy, Meloni faces competition from a new hard-right party led by MEP Roberto Vannacci, while in Germany the coalition government is under pressure as the far-right Alternative for Germany, projected as the country's leading party, could win an outright majority to govern Saxony-Anhalt alone next month.

Israel may be about to destroy its greatest diplomatic victory
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:01:23 UTC
22:01:23 KST

Israel may be about to destroy its greatest diplomatic victory
The joint statement issued by the foreign ministers of eight Arab and Muslim countries was one of the clearest diplomatic signals of recent weeks. Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, Pakistan, Qatar, Egypt, Jordan, Indonesia, and the United Arab Emirates did more than condemn Israel’s E1 settlement project. They demanded that the plan be halted, the decisions approving it reversed, and sanctions considered against individuals and entities involved in settlement expansion. The signatories also reaffirmed that an independent Palestinian state based on the 1967 borders, with East Jerusalem as its capital, remains the only viable path toward a lasting settlement, according to an official statement released by the UAE Foreign Ministry.
This was not just another communiqué intended to register concern over unfolding events. The reference to possible sanctions suggests that even the region’s more cautious governments are beginning to adopt a tougher stance. Israeli leaders apparently assume that normalization with certain Arab countries has become irreversible and that their objections can therefore be safely ignored. The E1 project, however, may reveal just how badly mistaken that calculation is.
The plan calls for the construction of more than 3,400 homes in the strategically important corridor between East Jerusalem and the Israeli settlement of Ma’ale Adumim. If implemented, it would effectively split the West Bank into northern and southern sections while cutting East Jerusalem off from the main territory of any future Palestinian state. In other words, E1 would reshape not only the demographic but also the political geography of the conflict. This is not a routine expansion of an existing settlement. It is a step that could deprive the “two states for two peoples” formula of its territorial foundation.
Israel’s far-right finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, has made no attempt to conceal the project’s political purpose, openly presenting it as a way to finally “bury” the idea of Palestinian statehood. E1 received final approval in 2025, and the publication of construction tenders in 2026 transformed it from a political threat into a plan moving toward practical implementation.
Against this backdrop, the UAE’s participation in the joint condemnation is especially significant. It was Abu Dhabi, after all, that was the leading Arab participant in the Abraham Accords in 2020 and the most persuasive example of normalization with Israel. The two countries opened embassies, lifted visa requirements, signed a free trade agreement, and began expanding cooperation in technology, energy, investment, and security. At first glance, then, the UAE’s decision to join other major Arab and Muslim powers in denouncing E1 may look like a sharp foreign-policy reversal.
It is still too early to suggest that Abu Dhabi is abandoning the Abraham Accords. Rather, the UAE is changing the terms on which it is prepared to support normalization and reminding Israel that establishing diplomatic relations did not amount to endorsing every subsequent action taken by the Israeli government. For the Emirates, normalization has always been an instrument of statecraft – not a commitment to follow Israel unconditionally.
The annexation of Palestinian territory is a matter of principle for the UAE leadership. In 2020, Abu Dhabi justified its decision to normalize relations by arguing that its agreement with Israel had halted the annexation of Palestinian land and preserved the possibility of a two-state solution. This was intended to reassure Arab audiences that the Emirates had not abandoned the Palestinian cause but had instead chosen a different way of influencing Israel: direct dialogue rather than a boycott. The latest demarche should therefore be seen not as a repudiation of that earlier policy, but as an attempt to restore the Abraham Accords to their originally stated purpose.
The Israeli government’s actions, however, are steadily making that argument harder to sustain. If normalization does not restrain annexation, halt settlement expansion, or preserve the prospect of Palestinian statehood, it becomes increasingly difficult for Abu Dhabi to explain what political purpose its special relationship with Israel actually serves.
As early as September 2025, UAE representative Lana Nusseibeh described the annexation of the West Bank as a “red line” that could destroy the spirit of the Abraham Accords. At the time, the Emirates reportedly considered downgrading diplomatic relations, although a complete break was not under discussion. The E1 project has now brought Israel dangerously close to that line.
There is also a broader strategic calculation at work. Israel is becoming politically toxic even for Arab governments that embraced normalization only a few years ago. The problem is not Israel’s existence or the need to maintain working relations with it. What has become toxic is the course pursued by the current Israeli government, which openly rejects Palestinian statehood, continues to expand settlements, and expects its Arab partners to quietly accept the new reality.
Put bluntly, the Israeli leadership has lost its sense of proportion. It behaves as though the economic and defense interests of Arab countries allow it to disregard their position on Palestine indefinitely. But there are limits to that approach. Israel cannot expect to deepen its relations with the Arab world while systematically destroying the possibility of a Palestinian state.
For the UAE, association with this policy carries growing reputational costs. Abu Dhabi has no intention of sacrificing its standing in the Arab and Muslim world to pay for the radicalism of members of the Israeli cabinet. The Emirates understand that, as the regional order is reshaped, they must maintain stable relations first and foremost with their neighbors and the leading powers of the Islamic world.
In the long run, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Egypt, and Jordan matter more to the UAE than unconditional solidarity with every policy adopted by Israel. Turkey, Pakistan, and Indonesia must also be considered, as their influence over the emerging Islamic political consensus continues to grow. Iran’s geopolitical clout is likewise visibly increasing following the end of the hot phase of the joint US-Israeli war against Tehran.
The presence of Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan in this group is particularly important. Shortly before the statement was issued, the three countries formed the Mecca Defense Pact, which has already been described as a prototype for a “Muslim NATO.” The UAE did not join the alliance, and it would be wrong to portray it as a member. Yet the joint demarche over E1 shows that Abu Dhabi does not want to find itself outside the emerging Arab-Islamic political alignment. The Emirates are signaling that they can coordinate their position with the core members of the Mecca alliance while continuing to cooperate with Israel and the United States.
At the same time, the criticism of Israel was carefully calibrated. The eight countries cited not only international law and UN resolutions, but also Donald Trump’s peace plan and its rejection of West Bank annexation. This framed the Israeli government’s actions as a challenge not only to the demands of Arab countries but also to Washington’s own stated position. It allows the UAE to increase pressure on Israel without turning its demarche into an anti-American gesture.
For now, it is difficult to imagine Abu Dhabi opting for a complete break with Israel, although that possibility cannot be ruled out entirely. The cooperation built since the signing of the Abraham Accords has proved too valuable to the Emirates, particularly in the economic, technological, and security spheres.
A gradual cooling of relations is more likely. Official contacts may become less frequent, some joint projects could slow down, and statements from the Emirati leadership may grow increasingly blunt. If Israel continues pursuing the de facto annexation of Palestinian territory, however, Abu Dhabi may once again consider downgrading diplomatic ties.
At its core, the latest demarche is a warning, not a rupture. The UAE is making clear that normalization is not a blank check and does not give Israel the right to ignore the interests of the Arab world. The Israeli leadership has become far too confident that economic cooperation has permanently separated the Palestinian issue from its relations with Arab governments.
The E1 project proves otherwise. Normalization has political limits, and the Israeli government is moving dangerously close to crossing them.

Naro in Sicily becomes the latest Italian destination to offer homes for just €1

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:00:42 UTC
22:00:42 KST

For those with €1 burning a hole in their pockets, Sicily’s medieval town of Naro is offering homes for next to nothing. But, before you pack your bags, there are a few things to consider…
What can €1 buy you? If you’re willing to swap your hometown for Sicily, it could get you onto the property ladder.
That’s because Naro, a medieval town on the southwest of the Mediterranean island, is offering would-be homeowners the chance to snap up a property for the price of an espresso.
Joining a growing list of Italian destinations with home listings at low prices, Naro, which is within the Agrigento province, is looking to breathe new life into the historic town while giving buyers the chance to restore abandoned buildings, tackle depopulation and bolster local tourism.
This initiative has been given the green light by the Comune di Naro local government authority and is open to both Italian and foreign nationals, provided they meet local requirements for purchasing and maintaining a property.
Applications can be submitted via the online Case 1 Euro Naro platform, which is available in multiple languages and walks interested buyers through the process of potentially landing a property.
According to the platform, buyers should consider investing because Naro offers a “historic centre with a strong identity, Baroque architecture, the Chiaramontano Castle, inland landscapes of Agrigento, and connections to Agrigento and the southern coast”.
And now for the €1 questions: Is there a catch? Well, yes – several, actually.
Typically, you get what you pay for, and for the cost of a cup of coffee, it’s no surprise that you won’t find a plush villa waiting for you in their catalogue.
When Euronews Travel browsed the listings, all the properties were listed as “needing to be renovated”, with one three-bed home overlooking the historic urban area, requiring inspection.
Beyond the €1 price tag, buyers are responsible for covering all associated notary fees, registration and cadastral taxes.
There’s also the matter of fixing the place up. Buyers must also cover the costs for project design of the property and ensuring it is safety compliant, adheres to landscape regulations and has undergone urban planning. And, there’s likely to be a deadline for getting all the work done.
Things to do in Naro, Sicily
Whether you’ve a spare €1 to invest in a property or are looking to travel off Italy’s beaten path, Naro is a striking inland town steeped in history, architecture and Sicilian charm.
Following a 2005 landslide, young artists worked on the façades of some of the neighbourhood’s ruined buildings, creating the MAN open air museum which you can wander through.
Naro has also preserved its Golden Gate, known locally as Porta d’Oro, which has a history that goes as far back as the 13th century. The ancient structure, featuring a pointed arch and stone battlements, was once part of a network of seven access gates that surrounded the city during medieval times.
As with other parts of Sicily, in Naro you can naturally snack on delicacies, including the native cassata – a Sicilian dessert of fluffy sponge cake, ricotta cream, chocolate chips – and pasta reale, which is a local sweet paste of finely ground almonds flavoured with vanilla, all adorned with candied fruits. The sweet treat traces its history to Arab-Palermo, with its name deriving from an Arabic term for large bowl where cream cheese filling was mixed with sugar.
Street food favourites, such as arancina, a morsel filled with fried rice, and cannoli can also easily be found in Naro, however, there are local varieties special to the town that can’t be found elsewhere.

Misjudging personal space drives the need for distance in socially anxious people
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:00:40 UTC
22:00:40 KST

People with higher social anxiety did not automatically walk more slowly toward others or keep more physical distance from them, according to a virtual-reality study published in the Journal of Psychiatric Research. Instead, the link with personal space emerged particularly among people who believed they were closer to others than they really were.
Social anxiety is characterised by fear of social scrutiny and negative evaluation. Avoiding social situations is one obvious response, but researchers are also interested in much subtler behaviors: hesitating while approaching someone, avoiding eye contact, or maintaining a slightly greater physical gap. Such behaviors can matter because they may shape how other people respond during an interaction.
Previous experiments have often found that greater social anxiety is associated with keeping more distance. But personal space is not determined purely by the actual number of centimeters between two people. Someone who is physically a metre away but feels as though they are much closer may react differently from somebody who estimates the same distance accurately. Earlier work led researchers to propose that this kind of misjudgment could help explain why social anxiety and personal space are sometimes linked.
Led by Stefania Bucur at Radboud University in the Netherlands, the study placed participants in an immersive virtual-reality environment resembling a social gathering in a café. After three people were excluded because of faulty or missing data, 106 adults remained (average age 23.5 years, 70% female).
Participants completed a series of six trials in the virtual environment. Researchers recorded how fast they approached the groups of virtual people and how close they came without explicitly telling them that personal distance was the target measure. Later, participants were deliberately asked to choose a distance they considered comfortable. They also estimated how far away they had been, both numerically and visually, allowing the researchers to measure whether they tended to overestimate or underestimate distance.
Contrary to the team’s initial expectations, higher social-anxiety scores were not directly associated with walking more slowly or maintaining a larger interpersonal distance, whether distance was measured automatically during the task or deliberately afterwards.
Distance perception, however, complicated that result. Participants who believed they were closer to the virtual group than they actually were tended, under certain measures, to leave more space. More importantly, numerical underestimation changed the relationship between anxiety and consciously preferred distance. Among people who underestimated how far away they were, higher social anxiety was associated with preferring more distance. No comparable social-anxiety effect appeared among participants who overestimated their distance.
The researchers summarized the pattern by writing that “individuals with high [social anxiety] do not keep greater interpersonal distance per se, but only do so when they tend to judge the distance to others as very close.”
Some limitations are to be noted. For instance, social scenarios in VR may not trigger the full range of complex social fears that occur in real life. Additionally, the fixed trial order and ambiguity in distance-estimation instructions may also have influenced responses. Participants were asked to estimate their distance from a table, but they may have used different reference points when making that judgement.
The study, “Social Anxiety and Preferred Interpersonal Distance: The Role of Estimation Bias,” was authored by Stefania Bucur, Deepshikha Prasad, and Wolf-Gero Lange.

Personalized brain stimulation can ease chronic pain
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Personalized brain stimulation can ease chronic pain
A new process for mapping and treating severe pain shows promise
By mapping a woman’s pain in her brain, scientists could dial it down. A small series of case studies, published July 30 in Brain Stimulation, suggests that even tenacious, complex pain signals can be interrupted by hitting the right spot with electricity.
Unlike the acute agony of a broken arm, some sorts of pain last well beyond the healing stage. Chronic pain, generated by changes in the brain and spinal cord, is especially hard to treat. “We have been limited in what we can do for these patients, and they have a great deal of suffering,” says neurosurgeon Michael Lim of Stanford University School of Medicine. The results open up a new way to treat this sort of pernicious pain, says Lim, who wasn’t involved in the study.
One approach to treating chronic pain involves targeting the brain directly with deep brain stimulation, or DBS. The method relies on electrodes on thin wires implanted in the brain and a battery pack that’s implanted in the chest. DBS is most commonly used to treat Parkinson’s disease, and it’s being studied for its effectiveness in other conditions, including depression.
So far, tests of DBS for chronic pain have yielded inconsistent outcomes, working for some people but not others. That spottiness might have to do with the complexities of pain that comes from changes to the brain itself. The experience of pain is built by collections of brain networks, including those that handle sensory input, chemical signals and even emotional components, says Vivek Buch, a neurosurgeon and neuroscientist at Stanford University. “And somehow they’re coming together as an integrated signal to give a person a perception of pain.”
To add more complexity, each person’s brain may handle things differently. Chronic pain, as well as psychiatric disorders such as depression and obsessive-compulsive disorder, “are just not one-size-fits-all,” Buch says.
The study’s premise was simple: First, map a person’s specific collection of pain signals. Then once this map is drawn, deliver small, precise electrical signals to scramble the pain signals and ideally, provide relief.
Buch and his colleagues recruited three people, all of whom suffered from severe and chronic face pain. These volunteers underwent surgeries in which clinicians inserted temporary electrodes through small holes in the skull into key brain regions. Over the next three days, researchers systematically sent small blips of electricity through these wires to different spots in the volunteers’ brains.
This mapping yielded specific information about each person’s pain, says Karl Deisseroth, a neuroscientist, psychiatrist and Howard Hughes Medical Institute investigator at Stanford. “Finding out, for a particular person, the location, the pattern of stimulation that helps that person is crucial for determining what definitive treatment might work.”
Results varied for the three people. One of the volunteers didn’t get much relief from any of the combinations of stimulation; two people’s pain improved.
One participant, a woman in her 40s, went on to have four permanent electrode wires implanted in the regions of her brain that responded positively during testing. Six and 12 months later, she’s still feeling better. “She’s doing really great,” Buch says. “She sends us text messages routinely.” The second woman, who had relief during testing, plans on getting a permanent implant soon, Buch says.
The person who didn’t experience much relief from the electrical stimulation still taught the researchers a lot. Successful outcomes are important, Deisseroth says, “but it’s just as important to identify if the definitive treatment is not going to work.”
“To have an objective measure guiding whether or not you take someone through a particular course of treatment, that’s a dream in psychiatry and psychiatry-adjacent fields and disorders,” Deisseroth says. “And so to see this work, and to be able to guide us [to] who should get a treatment, is just a very important step for the field.”
Looking ahead, the researchers hope to explore more conditions with this brain-mapping approach, both as a therapeutic effort and a way to learn more about how the brain works. “From my perspective in psychiatry,” Deisseroth says, “I don’t know that there’s a ceiling on where we can go.”

Israel just took another major step towards West Bank annexation
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:00:00 UTC
22:00:00 KST

Israel’s Defense Minister, Israel Katz, has moved to transfer security authority over Israeli settlements and settlers in the occupied West Bank from the Israeli army to the civil police, a decision Palestinians read as a decisive step toward the de facto annexation of the territory, and one that places the settler movement, in effect, in charge of policing itself.
Katz gave the Israeli army two weeks to draft a plan to transfer powers to the police, while the army’s role in the West Bank would be limited to “managing” Palestinians and controlling borders.
The announcement, made last Monday, came after ten days of settlers besieging three Palestinian families in the village of Qusra, south of Nablus. Since August 9, Israeli settlers have cordoned off the families — including three women, one of whom is elderly, and two children — inside three houses, cutting off water, electricity, and blocking access by Palestinians and Israeli anti-occupation activists who tried to deliver food to them.
The Israeli army deployed troops to the area and declared it a closed military zone, evacuating the settlers’ tent, only for the settlers to re-establish it the following day. Israeli soldiers were filmed praying and shaking hands with the settlers, sparking a public controversy over the collusion between the army and the settlers.
While the army’s failure to resolve the crisis is seen by some to have triggered Katz’s decision, the decision’s implications extend far beyond Qusra.
Another step to annexation
On the surface, transferring security powers from the army to the civil police looks like a measure to restore order and rein in settler violence that has spiked since 2022 — well before October 7 — and sparked global condemnation, even from Israel’s staunchest allies.
However, in his first public response to Katz’s announcement, Mustafa Barghouti, leader of the Palestinian National Initiative, called the move “the actual beginning of Israel’s de facto annexation of the West Bank.” Talking to Alaraby TV, Barghouthi also noted that the Israeli police is controlled by Israel’s National Security Minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, who is a hardline settler himself. “All security powers over settlers in the West Bank will pass into the hands of settlers themselves,” Barghouthi said.
Ben-Gvir, a key ally of Benjamin Netanyahu, has systematically expanded settlers’ influence within the Israeli police since taking power.
More broadly, the decision fits a pattern that has been accelerating since the current Israeli government took office. Finance Minister Bezalel Smotrich, who holds sweeping authority over the West Bank’s civilian administration, has systematically inserted Israeli settlers into the decision-making structures of the occupation. In 2024, Smotrich said that he had “changed the DNA of the system” by creating a civilian body — staffed by settlers — inside the Israeli army’s Civil Administration, the body responsible for running the occupation’s civilian affairs in the West Bank.
This effectively replaced the military with a settler-run civilian government in an occupied territory, treating the West Bank as sovereign Israeli territory rather than occupied land. After assigning civilian governance of the West Bank to settlers and transferring security authority to police, which is all in line with the path to annexation, what remains is the formal imposition of Israeli law on the territory.
Opportunism or election politics?
The timing of Katz’s announcement is not coincidental.
The ongoing siege of Palestinian families in Qusra attracted international attention over the past week, after U.S. Ambassador to Israel, Mike Huckabee, slammed the actions of Israeli settlers in Qusra, calling them “terrorists” — an unusually sharp reaction from an official in U.S. President Donald Trump’s administration. The apparent trigger for the stern criticism is that several of the Palestinians trapped inside the three homes in Qusra were U.S. citizens.
On Monday, Palestinian-American Luai Abu Ridah arrived in Qusra from Ohio to join his family in their besieged house in the village. Once inside, Abu Ridah raised a U.S. flag on the rooftop, asserting his U.S. citizenship and deepening the crisis.
Although the logical end to the crisis would be the removal of settlers from the area surrounding the three houses and ending the siege, the political price associated with removing them is one that the current Israeli government wants to avoid at all costs, particularly with decisive Israeli elections being months away. Given that the settler movement is a main part of the voter base that is keeping Netanyahu’s right-wing coalition in power, images of Israeli forces evacuating settlers — however violent or illegal their conduct is — a few months ahead of Israeli elections, would cost the contested prime minister crucial votes.
In that sense, transferring security powers to the Israeli police, as a move, gives the impression that the Israeli government is taking decisive action. In practice, it does nothing to end the siege in Qusra: the settlers remain, and the Palestinian families stay trapped, and the new framework hands authority to a force whose minister is ideologically aligned with the settler movement. Simultaneously, the move manages the international optics of the crisis while advancing the annexation agenda, without resolving either.
Larger plan
Despite the media emphasis on the siege of Palestinian families in Qusra, it is only a moment of a sustained settler offensive, targeting and reshaping the eastern part of the West Bank.
Following October 7, Israeli settler groups launched a systematic campaign against Palestinian Bedouin communities in the eastern slopes of the Nablus and Ramallah hills, displacing almost all Palestinians from the area, and cutting off the central West Bank from the Jordan Valley.
Since last year, settler attacks have begun to focus more on the villages east of Ramallah and Nablus, particularly in the southeast of the Nablus governorate.
In July, Israeli settlers seized a house in Jaloud, southeast of Nablus, located in Area B, the 22% of the West Bank which falls under Palestinian Authority (PA) civil jurisdiction and Israeli security control under the 1993 Oslo Accords. Such attacks on built-up houses in these villages, which have escalated dramatically over the past year, achieve the strategic logic of establishing a continuous settler presence east of Nablus. This isolates the city from both the east and the south, thereby achieving geographic contiguity for settlements across the northern West Bank. This, ultimately, further fragments any prospect of a coherent Palestinian territory.
As settler violence intensified and went unchecked, the displacement of families from their houses became the defining feature of this phase. The siege of the two families in Qusra is its most extreme expression and its most internationally visible.
But beyond the immediate crisis, the Israeli government and its settler support base are claiming every opportunity to entrench annexation measures that would be very difficult for any future government to undo or reverse.
Transferring security powers in settlements to the Israeli police is one such measure. It is not an emergency response to a local incident, but a continuation of a plan that has been in the making for years.

Saudi Arabia’s MBS visits Macron in France: What to expect

Unknown Publisher

Saudi Arabia’s MBS visits Macron in France: What to expect
Saudi crown prince and French president are set to sign several agreements on health, transport and energy.
Macron and MBS attend Esports World Cup closing ceremony
Saudi Arabia’s Crown Prince, Mohammed bin Salman, (MBS), is on the second day of his two-day state visit to France, where he’s meeting President Emmanuel Macron.
In this explainer, we outline what they are expected to discuss and examine how their latest meetings build on an already evolving relationship.
What is on the agenda?
MBS’s visit to Paris began on Sunday evening alongside President Macron at the closing ceremony of the Esports World Cup. It was the first time the Esports tournament, which includes competitions ranging from video games to chess, had been held outside Saudi Arabia.
On Monday, Macron and Bin Salman are expected to sign several agreements on health, transport and energy.
French media reported that a deal to build a Dragon Ball-themed amusement park, backed by a Saudi investment fund and inspired by the iconic Japanese manga series, could be signed.
Valerie Pecresse, President of the Regional Council of Île-de-France in Greater Paris, told French broadcaster TF1 that the regional government had been working on the project for 18 months.
“There is a very important meeting at the Elysee today that may result in the signing of this agreement. We are waiting for the signature,” she said, describing the project as “on the scale of Disneyland”.
Bin Salman and Macron are also holding bilateral discussions on regional security and their economic ties.
That is expected to include discussions about energy routes that bypass the Strait of Hormuz, such as new pipelines, capacity upgrades and alternative port networks.
France is a major buyer of Saudi oil and mineral products.
Since the start of the US-Israeli war on Iran on February 28, shipping has been severely disrupted in the Strait of Hormuz – the vital waterway on which oil exporters in the Gulf are heavily reliant and where 20 percent of the world’s oil and natural gas supplies are shipped from during peacetime. The disruption sent oil prices soaring.
Before the war, a barrel of Brent crude – the global benchmark – cost about $66. Over the course of the conflict, prices have climbed above $100 – hitting a high of $119 early on in the war.
On Monday, Brent was trading around $93 a barrel.
Bin Salman and Macron are also expected to discuss the war in Iran, the bloodshed in Palestine, as well as developments in Syria and Lebanon, where Israel occupies around one-fifth of its territory.
Other expected topics on Monday’s agenda include global events that Saudi Arabia is set to host in the coming years, including Expo 2030, focusing on sustainability and urban innovation, and the 2034 football World Cup.
How much trade does Saudi Arabia do with France?
The two countries have a fairly equal trading balance.
In 2024, France exported $4.5bn worth of goods to Saudi Arabia and imported $4.6bn worth, according to data from the Observatory of Economic Complexity (OEC), an online platform that compiles and visualises international trade statistics.
Refined petroleum accounted for 72 percent of Saudi Arabia’s exports to France in 2024. Besides refined petroleum, Saudi Arabia exported crude petroleum and other mineral products to France. It also exported small amounts of machinery, chemicals and cars.
France’s exports to Saudi Arabia in 2024 were more diverse, including airliners, helicopters, gas turbines, pharmaceutical products and perfume, among other products.
What have relations between Saudi Arabia and France been like?
Sunday’s visit marked the third time MBS has visited France after trips in 2022 and 2023.
In December 2024, Macron visited Riyadh, where the two countries founded the Saudi-French Strategic Partnership Council, which formalised and upgraded political and economic ties between Saudi Arabia and France.
The current visit is also MBS’s first international trip since the August 7 signing of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, known as the Mecca pact – the mutual defence agreement between Saudi Arabia, Turkiye and Pakistan.
Signed by the prince, Turkiye’s President, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, and Pakistan’s Prime Minister, Shehbaz Sharif, the agreement commits all three states to treat an armed attack on any one of them as an attack on all three.
Analysts say the pact shows that Saudi Arabia is taking steps to diversify its security partnerships beyond Washington.

On 24 August, we celebrate Ukraine’s Independence Day. This occasion embodies the bravery, resistance and resilience of the Ukrainian people in the face of Russia’s vicious war of aggression. To mark the occasion, the European Commission unfurled the Ukraine flag in front of the Berlaymont building in Brussels, which was also illuminated in Ukrainian colours.
As we celebrate this milestone, the EU reaffirms its unwavering commitment to Ukraine’s sovereignty and territorial integrity. Since the beginning of Russia’s full-scale invasion, we have provided Ukraine and its people with unprecedented humanitarian, financial and military assistance. So far, this support amounts to €220.2 billion.
Over the past months, the EU has stepped up its support for Ukraine’s economy and defence - because Ukraine’s prosperity is Europe’s prosperity, and Ukraine’s security is Europe’s security.
We made the first disbursements under the €90 billion Ukraine Support Loan to help sustain the country’s financial needs and boost its defence capabilities. And on Ukraine’s Independence Day, we approved €6.1 billion in support for air and missile defence systems, missiles, ammunitions, and radars.
Standing with Ukraine is also about holding Russia accountable. In July, we adopted a 21st package of sanctions, further restricting Russia's ability to fund its illegal war and to carry out attacks on Ukrainian civilians and civilian infrastructure.
The EU has stepped up efforts to secure the return of Ukrainian children forcibly transferred or deported by Russia, and is making sure Russia faces accountability for its crimes through the International Claims Commission and the Special Tribunal for the Crime of Aggression against Ukraine.
Ukraine belongs in the European family and in the European Union. We remain committed to supporting and assisting Ukraine on this process. This summer, Ukraine opened two accession negotiation clusters, illustrating its impressive capacity to implement reforms even during times of war.
We continue standing with Ukraine in pursuing a comprehensive, just and lasting peace, and supporting their European path.

Crash involving coach carrying German students injures 16
- Published
Sixteen people have been injured as a coach carrying German high-school students collided with a delivery van in the eastern Netherlands, Dutch police have said.
Eight people including the van driver were seriously hurt, while the remainder suffered minor injuries, the police department of the Gelderland region said. All were taken to hospital, it added.
The cause of the accident, near Wezep, to the east of Amsterdam, is under investigation. It is unclear how many of the wounded were students.
More than 50 students and four teachers were on the coach travelling to Paris from a school in the northern German town of Schönberg, according to a notice on its website.
The students belonged to two grade 12 classes - typically for those aged 17 to 18 years old - it added.
The school said there had been no reports of life-threatening injuries and that all of those involved were receiving comprehensive medical care.
Police said they received a report of a serious accident on the A28 near Wezep at around time 04:20 local time (02:20 GMT) on Monday.
The coach collided with a delivery van, crashed through the guardrail, and overturned onto its side, according to Dutch and German media, citing local police.
The A28 highway remains closed in both directions following the accident.

Belgium issues 1-year government bond yielding 1.93% after tax
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:54:17 UTC
21:54:17 KST

Belgium’s new 1-year government bond has a net yield of 1.93 per cent, according to the announcement by the Federal Debt Agency. The 10-year government bond yields 2.59 per cent.
The gross interest rate on the 1-year government bond is 2.75 per cent, and 3.70 per cent on the 10-year bond. After deduction of the 30 per cent withholding tax, the net yields are 1.93 per cent and 2.59 per cent respectively.
What is a government bond?
A government bond is a bond issued by the Belgian government targeted at the public at large. A government bond means you are lending a sum of money to the government for a predetermined period. You receive interest on the amount each year. At the end of the term, you get your money back.
The 1-year government bond is currently offering a higher return than in recent years. For example, in the most recent issue, in June, the net yield was 1.75 per cent.
What does that return mean in euros?
How much that 1.93 per cent actually yields depends on your investment. If you decide to buy 5,000 euros’ worth of government bonds, you will receive 5,096.5 euros back from the Belgian government next year. That is your 5,000-euro investment plus 96.5 euros in interest.

Ukraine reveals scale of Behemoth kamikaze drone production line
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:53:21 UTC
21:53:21 KST

- Footage released around Ukraine's Independence Day shows dozens of Behemoth strike drones staged at a production facility, the clearest public look yet at manufacturing scale.
- Developed by GLEFA and Culver Aerospace, the 300 km-range drone carries a 75 kg tandem warhead and has already struck targets including the Chonhar and Henichesk bridges.
Rows of black, Shahed-shaped airframes stretch across a production floor in newly released footage marking Ukraine’s Independence Day, offering the clearest public look yet at how many Behemoth “mid-range” one-way attack drones the country is now building at once. The video shows dozens of the drones mounted on wooden and metal stands, wingtip to wingtip, inside what appears to be a converted industrial hall.
The Behemoth is a middle-strike kamikaze drone developed by the Ukrainian companies GLEFA and Culver Aerospace. It was first shown publicly in May 2026 at the Wild Drones event, where company representatives described it to the Ukrainian outlet Militarnyi as a system built for hitting targets at close and medium range.
The drone has a wingspan of 2.28 meters (7.5 feet), a length of 2.2 meters (7.2 feet) and a height of 0.5 meters (1.6 feet). Its stated range is up to 300 km (186 miles). The airframe carries two warheads in sequence: a 40 kg (88-pound) high-explosive fragmentation charge in the nose, followed by a 35 kg (77-pound) thermobaric charge, for a combined payload of roughly 75 kg (165 pounds).
Militarnyi and Ukrainska Pravda both reported in May that the drone had entered serial production and was already in use by Ukraine’s Defense Forces. The newly circulated Independence Day footage is consistent with those earlier reports of mass output, though it does not by itself establish a production rate or total unit count.
Behemoth supports fully autonomous, semi-automatic and first-person-view control modes. Developers say it is designed to fly at low altitude, which complicates detection and interception by air defense systems. Communications run through Starlink, according to reporting from suasnews.com and other outlets that covered the May unveiling.
The drone has since been used in combat. Ukrainian units struck the Chonhar Bridge, which links occupied Kherson Oblast to Crimea, on the nights of June 7 and June 9, using Behemoth drones alongside other systems, according to reporting by NV.ua. Ukrainian accounts also describe Behemoth strikes on the Henichesk road bridge connecting mainland Ukraine to the Arabat Spit, and on targets in Donetsk Oblast, including an ammunition depot in Staromykhailivka and a command post in Selydove.
Cost estimates for the system, drawn from open-source reporting, put each unit at roughly $35,000 to $50,000. That places Behemoth well below the price of guided missiles used for comparable strike missions, though the outlet did not attribute the figure to an official government source.
Culver Aerospace’s broader portfolio includes the Skif reconnaissance drone and other undisclosed projects. In April 2026 the company signed a cooperation agreement with the German defense technology firm Helsing to jointly develop and produce drones at a facility in Germany, with production financed by the German government, according to reporting from suasnews.com. Culver Aerospace separately reached a five-year agreement with Denmark’s Copenhagen Global A/S in February.
The Behemoth’s resemblance to Iran’s Shahed-136, and to the Russian Geran variant built from that design, has drawn frequent comparison in Ukrainian and Russian coverage of the program. Ukrainian developers have described the drone as a domestic answer to the Shahed and Geran drones Russia has used against Ukrainian cities and infrastructure since 2022.

Former commissioner Tim Finchem donates $13 million as PGA Tour reshapes its charity strategy
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24

Former commissioner Tim Finchem donates $13 million as PGA Tour reshapes its charity strategy
ATLANTA (AP) — Ten years after he retired as commissioner, Tim Finchem and his wife are donating $13 million to help launch a new charity strategy at a time when so much emphasis in golf is on profit in the new commercial enterprise of the PGA Tour.
The tour on Monday revealed plans for PGA Tour Charities ahead of the season-ending Tour Championship, which has a $40 million purse that awards $10 million to the winner.
Along with building its charity strategy around national campaigns with a more local impact, the PGA Tour is prepared to make up any difference, if needed, to maintain charity levels from tournaments that move down to the Challenger Series in the 2028 schedule.
“This next chapter is about generating even more focus, coordination, resources and visibility,” said Laura Neal, executive vice president of PGA Tour Strategic Philanthropy. “Launching an evolved PGA Tour Charities — with a legacy-defining, transformative gift from the Finchems — is an exciting next step in golf’s enduring commitment to giving back.”
The PGA Tour long has been the charitable leader in sports with a mechanism that has enabled its tournaments to generate more than $4.4 billion, all starting with a $10,000 donation at the 1938 Palm Beach Invitational. Each tournament operates independently and that doesn’t change.
PGA Tour Charities will launch and fund national priority campaigns around such themes as health, youth, access and service. The idea is to connect with tournaments on a broader scale when their missions align, which the tour hopes can attract new resources and raise visibility.
Lucas Glover, the Player Advisory Council chairman who joins the PGA Tour board next year, is leading a committee of players to help shape the initiatives.
“How I grew up on the tour ... what we hung our hat on as an organization was giving back,” Glover said. “With COVID and then LIV coming in, it became more about money in our pocket instead of money in the pocket of people who need it more than we do. It never went away. It just got put on the back burner, and it’s time we put it back on the forefront of our minds.
“When we talk about the PGA Tour, it shouldn’t be how much we’re making, how much we’re playing for,” he said. “It should be about what we’re doing in the communities where we play.”
PGA Tour Enterprises was launched as a for-profit commercial venture in January 2024 with an investment of up to $3 billion from Strategic Sports Group, which led to players receiving equity for the first time. The nonprofit PGA Tour still operates tournament and regulations. PGA Tour Enterprises is geared toward global business, commercial sponsorship and media rights.
The charitable engine doesn’t stop for groups like the Thunderbirds (WM Phoenix Open), Copperheads (Valspar Championship) or the Salesmanship Club of Dallas (The CJ Cup Byron Nelson). Tournaments typically donate all net proceeds — operation costs offset by national and local sponsorship — to local charities.
It has been key for attracting thousands of volunteers — the backbone of golf tournaments — who feel like they are contributing to their communities because of the charitable function.
What the tour wants to emphasize with PGA Tour Charities is a dedicated platform for direct community investment that gives players, corporate partners, tournaments and fans a clear way to get involved. The Finchems’ donation was seen as a catalyst.
“The PGA Tour family, its players, fans and communities have meant so much to us for so long, and we feel a connection to the golf world that endures to this day,” Holly Finchem said. “This donation to PGA Tour Charities, as it is reimagined for future generations of impact, is more than a capstone on Tim’s unwavering commitment to charity. It is a celebration of our belief in this great game and the PGA Tour. We can’t wait to see all the good this gift will inspire.”
Finchem, the tour’s third commissioner, oversaw massive growth during his tenure from 1994 until retiring in 2016, much of that seizing on the arrival of Tiger Woods. Along with a sharp increase in TV contracts and prize money, he helped to create The First Tee in 1997.
Finchem was commissioner when charitable donations of PGA Tour events topped $1 billion in 2005 and $2 billion in 2014.
Meanwhile, the PGA Tour disclosed Monday the remaining $2.5 million charity donation from Brooks Koepka — he was required to donate $5 million as part of his return from LIV Golf — is being equally allocated to charities designated by nearly 100 players.
