AP Decision Notes: What to expect in Georgia’s special congressional runoff
WASHINGTON (AP) — Residents of Georgia’s 13th Congressional District outside of Atlanta will get a new representative to Congress after a special election runoff Tuesday to replace the late Democratic U.S. Rep. David Scott, who died April 22.
The contest between two Democrats will further reduce an already thin Republican majority in the U.S. House.
The finalists for the seat are former Gwinnett County School Board Chair Everton Blair and Marcye Scott, daughter of the late congressman. They were the top two vote-getters among five contenders in the July 28 all-party special election. Scott received about 46% of the vote, compared to about 38% for Blair.
The winner will serve out the remaining few months of David Scott’s final term. Neither candidate is running in for the next full term in this seat, which begins on Jan. 3, 2027.
Blair was the only candidate in the special election who also ran for the full-term seat. He placed third in the May 19 Democratic primary with about 12% of the vote. State Rep. Jasmine Clark won the primary with 56% of the vote and will face Republican Jonathan Chavez in November. Chavez, who ran unopposed for the GOP nomination, challenged David Scott in the 2024 general election and received about 28% of the vote.
Clark did not file to compete in the special election. Doing so would have required her to resign from her seat in the state Legislature just as Republican Gov. Brian Kemp was calling for a special session to redraw the state’s congressional boundaries in time for the 2028 elections. The state constitution bars state officeholders from seeking a different office with a start date more than 30 days before the end of the officeholder’s current term. The special session did convene, but Republican leaders opted not to take up redistricting.
In recent years, Congressman Scott had faced questions over his age and health. At the time of his death at age 80, he was facing a tough primary challenge from Clark and others as he sought a 13th term.
Georgia’s 13th Congressional District is east and southeast of Atlanta and includes parts of six heavily Democratic counties: Clayton, DeKalb, Gwinnett, Henry, Newton and Rockdale. Of the six, the district’s portion of Gwinnett County has the lion’s share of voters, with about 46% of the district electorate in the 2024 general election.
Blair’s best performance in the July 28 special election was in his home base of Gwinnett County, where he received 56% of the vote. Marcye Scott, who lives outside the district in Fulton County as her father did, carried the other five counties in the district, scoring her highest totals in DeKalb, Clayton and Henry.
David Scott won his 2024 reelection bid with about 72% of the vote. In the presidential election that night, Democratic then-Vice President Kamala Harris received about 71% of the vote in the district, compared with about 28% for Republican Donald Trump. Trump had his best performance in the district in Gwinnett County, although that still only amounted to about 35% of the vote.
Here are some of the key facts about the election and data points the AP Decision Team will monitor as the votes are tallied:
When do polls close?
Polls close at 7 p.m. ET.
What’s on the ballot?
The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare a winner in the special runoff in the 13th Congressional District.
Who gets to vote?
Any voter registered in the 13th Congressional District may participate in the special runoff.
How many voters are there?
As of Friday, there were about 585,000 registered voters in the 13th Congressional District. Georgia voters do not register by party.
How many people actually vote?
A total of 20,510 votes were cast in the July 28 special election. Turnout in a runoff election tends to be lower than in the election that preceded it.
How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot?
About 47% of the total vote in the July 28 special election was cast early in-person or by mail.
As of Friday, about 5,200 ballots had already been cast in Tuesday’s election, with by far the largest share coming from Gwinnett County, followed by Clayton and Rockdale counties.
When are early and absentee votes released?
All six counties in the 13th Congressional District tend to release most or all of their results from early in-person and mail voting in the first vote update of the night, usually before any in-person Election Day results are released.
How long does vote-counting usually take?
In the July 28 special election, the AP first reported results at 7:05 p.m. ET, or five minutes after polls closed. The last vote update of the night was at 10:05 p.m. ET with about 99.9% of total votes counted.
When will the AP declare a winner?
The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why.
How do recounts work?
There is no automatic recount provision in Georgia, but a losing candidate may request a recount if the margin is less than or equal to 0.5% of the total vote. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.
Are we there yet?
As of Tuesday, there will be 70 days until the 2026 midterm elections.

YEREVAN, August 24. /TASS/. Armenian Prime Minister Nikol Pashinyan said he supports Yerevan’s expulsion from the Collective Security Treaty Organization (CSTO) and would welcome the move.
He also said in the parliament that Armenia would soon begin the process of applying for EU membership.
TASS has compiled the key points from the Armenian prime minister’s statements.
Preparing EU membership bid
- Armenia will soon begin the process of applying for EU membership, Pashinyan said, adding that Yerevan would at least heed calls from its Eurasian Economic Union (EAEU) partners.
- He said Armenia could hold a referendum on EU membership or remaining in the Eurasian Economic Union once discussions reach a turning point and it can prepare a roadmap.
- Yerevan must first formally apply for EU membership before holding such a referendum, he said.
- Pashinyan described the process as requiring extensive work.
Armenia’s CSTO membership
- Pashinyan said he would be very pleased if the CSTO decided to expel Armenia, noting that the organization’s charter provides for such a measure.
- This would free Yerevan from the dilemma of whether to leave the organization, he said.
- Pashinyan said Armenia’s 2026-2031 government program does not envisage stepping up its CSTO activities over the next five years, adding that Yerevan’s interest in the organization has run out.
Reaction
- Armenia may leave the CSTO if Yerevan no longer needs its membership, Russian Presidential Spokesman Dmitry Peskov told reporters.
- Peskov urged to remember the experience of Turkey and other countries whose EU membership bids have remained unresolved for years.
Armenia’s EAEU and CSTO membership
- On March 26, 2025, the Armenian parliament passed a law launching the process of joining the EU.
- Russian President Vladimir Putin has said EU integration would automatically end Armenia’s cooperation with the EAEU and cause it to lose all related benefits.
- At the May 29 EAEU summit in Astana, the leaders of Russia, Belarus, Kazakhstan and Kyrgyzstan adopted a joint statement supporting a nationwide referendum in Armenia on joining the EU or remaining in the EAEU.
- On August 11, Russian Deputy Foreign Minister Mikhail Galuzin told TASS that Armenia should decide whether to hold a nationwide referendum on joining the EU or retaining EAEU membership by December, when EAEU leaders are due to discuss possible further steps toward Yerevan.
- In September 2024, Pashinyan said Yerevan had frozen its participation in CSTO activities.
- He declared that the organization had created threats to Armenia’s sovereignty.
- In October 2024, Armenian Foreign Minister Ararat Mirzoyan said at an international security forum in Warsaw that Yerevan was assessing all risks associated with a possible decision to leave the CSTO.
- In December 2024, the Armenian prime minister said relations between Armenia and the CSTO had reached a point of no return.
- On June 10, 2026, Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov said CSTO members agreed to consider applying a charter provision to Armenia over two years of unpaid membership fees.
- On August 11, Galuzin told TASS that the CSTO summit on November 11 could consider stripping Armenia of its voting rights in the organization.

EU unlocks new tranche of €90 billion loan to Ukraine for weapons
The European Commission has approved €6.1 billion ($7.1 billion) in new weapons purchases for Ukraine, the commission said on Monday. The tranche is part of a €90 billion loan allocated by Brussels for budgetary and military aid to Kiev earlier this year.
Facing mounting battlefield pressure, Kiev is increasingly pushing for faster aid disbursements as it relies heavily on foreign funding to plug a widening budget gap and sustain its war effort against Russia. Moscow has argued that Western military aid to Ukraine, which comes at the expense of ordinary taxpayers, only serves to prolong the conflict.
In April, the EU approved a €90 billion ($105 billion) emergency loan for Ukraine that allocates €30 billion for budget support and €60 billion for military aid in 2026-2027. The loan, backed by joint EU borrowing and repayable only if Kiev receives war reparations from Russia, was pushed through after plans to seize Russian sovereign assets frozen in the West failed. Hungary, the Czech Republic, and Slovakia have secured exemptions from the scheme.
The latest tranche came on top of €16 billion of previously approved procurement plans, of which €8.35 billion has already been transferred to Kiev. The €6.1 billion disbursement is expected to finance air and missile defense systems, missiles, ammunition, and radars, according to European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen.
In February, the European Council set “strict conditions” for Ukraine to secure the funds, specifying that Kiev is obliged to purchase weapons and military equipment only from companies based in the EU, Ukraine, the European Economic Area, and the European Free Trade Association. Purchases from third countries are allowed in cases of urgent need, including when a defense product is not available in the EU.
The EU’s financial and military aid to Ukraine has drawn criticism from current and former officials in and outside the bloc. Earlier this month, former Ukrainian Prime Minister Nikolay Azarov said the West will never recover its loans to Kiev.
German MEP Fabio De Masi warned that the funds will enrich “corrupt oligarchs.” Former Austrian Foreign Minister Karin Kneissl told RT earlier this year that the EU is shifting from its traditional focus on trade toward an increasingly geopolitical and defense-oriented agenda.
In July, Russian President Vladimir Putin accused Kiev and the “so-called European pseudo-peacekeepers” of seeking to prolong the conflict. He said their goal is “not peace, but the continuation of the war with Russia to the last Ukrainian.”

NEW DELHI: The Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) has announced a youth march on September 5 in Delhi, accusing the government of failing to honour commitments that led to the withdrawal of the students’ protest at Jantar Mantar on July 25. The CJP said the government had failed to act on its assurance to withdraw FIRs against students and protesting students.The march will begin at India Gate and proceed towards the New Delhi Police Headquarters, according to a statement issued by the CJP National Working Committee, posted on X. The organisation said the protest would be led by families of deceased NEET victims and victims of alleged police brutality, with students and youth organisations expected to join.In the post, the CJP said, “The Cockroach Janta Party strongly condemns the Union Government’s failure to honour the commitments made to India’s youth on July 25, particularly those concerning the withdrawal of FIRs against students and protesters.”
“With the Government continuing to delay and avoid fulfilling its assurances, the CJP National Working Committee has decided to resume peaceful mobilisation,” it said.
The CJP said the decision followed a review of the commitments it alleges were made by the government on July 25, after which nationwide youth protests were withdrawn.The statement said the committee had expressed “serious doubts over whether the Government intends to honour its word at all”, alleging that the government had delayed action and avoided providing clear commitments.It also referred to proceedings before the Supreme Court, saying that on August 18, the court had sought a list of FIRs registered across the country so that it could consider dealing with them together. The CJP alleged that the government had not given a clear commitment on the issue.
The organisation also added, “This cannot continue. Our patience cannot be mistaken for weakness. Our good faith cannot become an opportunity for the Government to betray us.”Announcing the September 5 mobilisation, the CJP said, “We announce a peaceful protest march from India Gate to the new Delhi Police Headquarters on 5 September, led by the families of the deceased NEET victims and victims of police brutality, and joined by students and young citizens from across the country.”The group said it had returned to the streets because the government “appears determined to commit a ‘vishwasghaat’ with Gen-Z, the young generation of this country, and the families who have already lost their children.”It further said, “We withdrew a nationwide movement in good faith. A government cannot take the trust of an entire generation, use it to send them home, and then quietly retreat from its own word. We will not accept this attempted betrayal.”The CJP has urged students, youth organisations and young citizens to gather at India Gate on September 5. “The families who lost their children will walk at the front. Victims of police brutality will walk with them,” the statement said.Earlier, the CJP, that describes itself as a youth-focused movement, had led a 37-day protest at Jantar Mantar over the NEET-UG 2026 paper leak, alongside activist Sonam Wangchuk’s 26-day hunger strike.
On July 25, following talks with Union ministers J P Nadda and Jitendra Singh, the CJP said the government had accepted its demands, including suitable compensation for families of NEET aspirants who died by suicide and withdrawal of FIRs against protesters. “All our demands have been accepted, so we request the protesters to withdraw immediately and return home peacefully,” it said.The Supreme Court later directed states to release eligible students detained during the protests and barred coercive action against students for the time being.

A ghostly ribbon of stars reveals hidden dark matter
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:19:34 UTC
21:19:34 KST

A ghostly ribbon of stars reveals hidden dark matter
A ghostly stream of stars beyond the Milky Way is giving astronomers a new way to map the universe’s invisible dark matter.
- Date:
- August 24, 2026
- Source:
- Northwestern University
- Summary:
- A faint ribbon of stars around a distant galaxy has become the first globular cluster stellar stream ever identified beyond the Milky Way. Because the stars trace the galaxy’s gravity, researchers used the stream to estimate how much invisible dark matter surrounds it and how that matter is distributed. The breakthrough offers astronomers a promising new way to investigate one of the universe’s greatest mysteries.
- Share:
For billions of years, an ancient cluster of stars has been gradually coming apart, shedding stars that now form a faint, narrow ribbon across space. That delicate structure is offering astronomers a new way to investigate one of the universe's biggest mysteries.
An international research team, including an astrophysicist from Northwestern University, has identified the first stellar stream of this type ever observed outside the Milky Way. Astronomers have long predicted that such streams should exist around other galaxies, but their extreme faintness has made them difficult to detect.
The newly discovered stream also offers scientists an unusual tool for studying dark matter, which remains one of the major unanswered questions in astrophysics. By analyzing the stream's shape, researchers reconstructed the gravitational field of its host galaxy and used that information to determine how unseen dark matter influenced the stars' paths.
The findings could eventually help scientists investigate how dark matter is distributed across many different galaxies and throughout the universe.
The study was published Aug. 12 in the journal Nature.
"The stars in a stellar stream all travel along nearly the same orbit, and that orbit is shaped by the galaxy's gravity," said Northwestern's Tjitske Starkenburg, who coauthored the study. "By modeling that gravity, we can estimate the galaxy's total mass. We already know roughly how much of that mass comes from visible matter like stars, so the rest must be dark matter."
Starkenburg, an expert in extragalactic astronomy, is a research assistant professor at Northwestern's Center for Interdisciplinary Exploration and Research in Astrophysics. The study was co-led by Julie Kiel Holm of the University of Copenhagen and Sarah Pearson of the Technical University of Denmark.
First Stellar Stream Found Beyond the Milky Way
Globular clusters are densely packed groups of stars held together by gravity. As one of these clusters travels around its host galaxy, the galaxy's gravitational pull can slowly strip stars away from it.
Those stars do not simply scatter in every direction. Instead, they tend to continue along nearly the same orbital path, creating long, thin stellar streams that retain information about the gravitational forces they have experienced.
Astronomers have identified dozens of streams produced by globular clusters inside the Milky Way. Until now, however, no comparable stream had been detected in another galaxy. Such structures are generally so faint that they disappear against the light of their host galaxies.
The breakthrough came through archival observations from NASA's Hubble Space Telescope presented by study coauthors David Sand and Catherine Fielder, both astronomers at the University of Arizona. While study coauthor David Hendel was examining images of the ultra-diffuse galaxy UGC 9050-Dw1 for their publication, he noticed a faint, narrow arc that looked like a stellar stream.
UGC 9050-Dw1 lies roughly 115 million light-years from Earth. Because the galaxy contains relatively few stars, it provided an unusually dark background that made the dim stream easier to distinguish.
A New Way to Measure Dark Matter
The importance of the discovery extends beyond finding the stream itself. Researchers have now shown for the first time that a globular cluster stellar stream can be used to investigate dark matter in a galaxy beyond the Milky Way.
Dark matter accounts for roughly 85% of all matter in the universe. Because it does not emit or reflect light, astronomers cannot see it directly. Instead, they detect its effects through the gravitational influence it exerts on stars, galaxies, and other visible objects.
Once the stream was identified, the team ran thousands of computer simulations. The researchers tested different combinations of globular cluster characteristics and possible dark matter distributions to determine which scenarios could reproduce the stream's observed appearance.
The models that most closely matched the observations provided new estimates of UGC 9050-Dw1's total mass and showed how that mass is distributed throughout the galaxy. The results indicated that UGC 9050-Dw1 contains a large amount of dark matter, as astronomers had expected for an ultra-diffuse galaxy.
"Our results are consistent with previous studies and what they have shown about dark matter in this ultra-diffuse galaxy," Kiel Holm said. "We are measuring it with a completely new tool for this type of galaxy, demonstrating that this method also works beyond our own galaxy."
Stellar Streams Could Expose Dark Matter Structure
Although the current analysis centers on just one galaxy, the finding could lead to searches for similar stellar streams around many different types of galaxies. With a larger sample, astronomers may be able to learn much more about how dark matter behaves and how it is distributed.
Thin stellar streams may be especially valuable because small concentrations of dark matter can potentially disturb them, producing visible gaps or clumps.
"Thin stellar streams can develop gaps or clumps when small concentrations of dark matter pass through them," Starkenburg said. "Astronomers have long debated whether we've seen this happen in streams within the Milky Way. If we can confirm that's what's causing these features, that will give us an entirely new way to test how dark matter is distributed -- and ultimately learn more about its fundamental nature."
New Telescopes Could Find Many More Streams
Future observatories could make these elusive structures much easier to find. The European Space Agency's Euclid mission and NASA's Nancy Grace Roman Space Telescope are designed to survey far larger regions of the sky than Hubble, increasing the likelihood that astronomers will detect stellar streams around additional galaxies.
"It's exciting that we discovered a thin stellar stream around a galaxy other than our own with already-existing Hubble Space Telescope data and confirmed it with ground-based telescope data," Starkenburg said. "That makes it very promising for the new telescopes becoming available, including the Roman Space Telescope, which can see an area 100-times larger than that of the Hubble."
The study, "Evidence for the First Globular Cluster Stellar Stream beyond the Milky Way," was supported by VILLUM FONDEN (award number VIL53081) and the European Union (BeyondSTREAMS award number 101115754). Starkenburg also gratefully acknowledges support from the NSF (grant number AST-2510183) and NASA (grant numbers 22-ROMAN22-0055 and 22-ROMAN22-0013).

A 22-year-old man living in Bristol has been convicted of preparing acts of terrorism after travelling to Somalia with the intention of joining Daesh, following an investigation by Counter Terrorism Policing South East.
A 22-year-old man living in Bristol has been convicted of preparing acts of terrorism after travelling to Somalia with the intention of joining the proscribed terrorist organisation Daesh, the UK Defence Journal understands.
Mohamed Mohamoud, of Francombe Grove in Horfield, Bristol, was found guilty by a unanimous jury following a three-week trial at Winchester Crown Court. According to a Counter Terrorism Policing news update, Mohamoud was convicted of preparation of acts of terrorism contrary to Section 5 of the Terrorism Act 2006. The verdict was returned on 18 August, with details of the investigation published on 24 August.
Investigators said Mohamoud, a security guard who was born in Somalia, travelled there intending to join Daesh, which is proscribed in the United Kingdom. He purchased a ticket on 13 January 2025 for a journey from Heathrow to Somalia via Ethiopia, leaving the UK on 30 January and returning on 3 March. Counter Terrorism Policing South East later used evidence from his electronic devices, travel history and communications to establish the purpose of the journey.
Officers attended Mohamoud’s home on 20 January 2026 and arrested him, seizing a number of digital devices including a Samsung Galaxy mobile phone. Examination of location data from the handset showed that it had been present at various locations in Somalia between January and March 2025. Investigators also recovered a Telegram conversation in which Mohamoud asked for assistance travelling to Somalia so that he could join the “Mujahedeen”. In another message, police said, he expressed an ambition to become a “martyr”.
Further examination of the phone uncovered Daesh propaganda including battlefield footage, executions and beheadings, as well as material produced in a news-style format by the terrorist organisation. Counter Terrorism Policing said the material demonstrated that Mohamoud had adopted an extremist Islamist ideology. Messages recovered following his return to Britain also recorded what investigators described as his continuing intention to commit himself to jihad.
Detective Chief Superintendent Oliver Wright, Head of Counter Terrorism Policing South East, said, as quoted in the news update: “Mahmoud had become radicalised to adopt an extremist Islamist ideology and travelled to Somalia with the intention of joining Daesh.”
Wright added: “It is important to note that Mahmoud communicated to others about his intentions to travel to commit jihad and become a ‘martyr’.” The spelling of the surname in the quoted police remarks differs from the spelling used elsewhere in the Counter Terrorism Policing account, which identifies the defendant as Mohamed Mohamoud.
The conviction centres on preparation for terrorism rather than an allegation that Mohamoud carried out an attack in the UK. The prosecution case concerned his journey to Somalia, his stated intentions and the digital evidence recovered during the subsequent investigation. Daesh maintains an affiliate in Somalia, while the organisation itself remains proscribed under British terrorism legislation.
Mohamoud was charged in connection with the offence on 26 January 2026, six days after his arrest. He was subsequently tried at Winchester Crown Court, where the jury returned a unanimous guilty verdict after hearing evidence concerning his travel, communications and extremist material.
Wright also urged members of the public to report concerns where individuals appear to be moving towards extremist violence. He said: “If you become aware of anyone whose behaviour may have changed, who has adopted extreme views and is expressing similar intentions, please ensure you report this to police. Reporting can save lives.”

Facebook, TikTok promoted Colombian armed groups’ content to recruit children: NGO
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:15:00 UTC

Facebook, TikTok promoted Colombian armed groups’ content to recruit children: NGO
BOGOTA – Facebook and TikTok failed to prevent the spread of content produced by Colombian armed groups to recruit children, and in some cases even “appeared to promote these posts”, Human Rights Watch (HRW) reported on Aug 24.
HRW said the circulation of social media content by armed groups “glorifies life in armed group ranks” and promotes “deceptive job offers”.
Since 2021, around 1,500 children have been recruited by armed groups, according to HRW.
Armed groups use children for combat, handling weapons, drones and explosives, and intelligence gathering, the HRW report said.
In some cases, it said, children without combat training are used as “cannon fodder”.
According to the report, almost half of child recruits are indigenous children, despite indigenous people representing only around four per cent of the population.
Girls account for around 40 per cent of child recruits, and are “particularly exposed to sexual violence”.
In the report, HRW described social media posts showing members of armed groups flaunting wads of cash and jewellery.
In other posts, they appear in training camps or listening to “narcocorridos” – a Mexican music genre that celebrates the exploits of infamous drug traffickers.
In the comments sections, some users asked how they could join.
HRW said dissident groups that emerged from the now-defunct Revolutionary Armed Forces of Colombia (FARC) have been responsible for 74 per cent of child recruitment cases documented between 2021 and 2025.
HRW said it had informed Meta, Facebook’s parent company, and TikTok’s owner ByteDance of the problem. Both said they had removed the specific content mentioned.
Meta said it “constantly strives to refine (its) approach to combating it across (its) platforms”.
TikTok said it “proactively (prevents) illegal armed groups and organised criminal groups from using TikTok, including to target, exploit or recruit minors”.
The historic 2016 peace agreement ended a half-century of war between the government and the FARC guerrilla group, but remaining armed groups continue to control large swathes of territory in remote parts of the north-east and south.
Newly inaugurated President Abelardo de la Espriella has vowed to crack down on armed groups and plans to forge a military alliance with the US and Israel. AFP

====================================================================================================

China Focus: IPO, athletic feats and mass deployment show China's robot momentum
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
20:12:50 CST
21:12:50 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- The past week has been busy and fruitful for China's humanoild robot industry, which is qucikly racing from lab demos toward real-world deployment.
On Wednesday, as the 2026 World Robot Conference (WRC) opened in Beijing, drawing more than 300 exhibitors from 26 countries with over 3,000 products, Unitree Robotics became the first humanoid robot maker to list on China's A-share market.
On Saturday, the second World Humanoid Robot Games kicked off at the "Ice Ribbon," the 2022 Winter Olympics venue, with 666 teams and 2,056 robots from 16 countries.
ROAD TO PROFITABILITY
Unitree debuted on the Shanghai Stock Exchange's STAR Market on Aug. 19, opening at 1,100 yuan (about 162 U.S. dollars) per share -- a 629-percent premium. As of Monday's opening, although it had pulled back significantly, it still remained at a high level.
The sell-off from the opening high was a sobering signal. Financial observers noted that the sector will enter a digestion period that may last for months, predicting investors will shift their focus from rewarding "the only listed robot stock" to its actual business performance.
Still, Unitree's listing marks a watershed moment for China's humanoid robot industry.
The listing will transition the industry from "technological validation" and "narrative-driven hype" into an era of "commercial value verification," where profitability is the ultimate test, said Tian Lihui, a finance professor at Nankai University.
Unitree has already delivered a compelling answer. Established in 2016, the company shipped over 5,500 humanoid units in 2025 to secure the top spot worldwide. Its revenue surged to nearly 1.7 billion yuan in 2025, and the momentum continued into the first half of 2026, with revenue reaching approximately 1.15 billion yuan, up 48.54 percent year on year.
Unitree's success is underpinned by its strong emphasis on independent R&D and technological innovation. The company has achieved vertical integration by developing proprietary core components -- including motors, reducers, controllers, and LiDAR -- alongside high-performance perception and motion control algorithms. This in-house approach is backed by a portfolio of over 200 patent applications.
The company's founder Wang Xingxing attributed its growth to independent innovation, pragmatic execution and long-termism. He emphasized that, because the humanoid robotics industry remains in its dawn phase, navigating its significant challenges requires collective effort and sustained investment from the entire sector.
TECH LEAP IN PITCH
While the IPO measured progress in valuation, the robot games measured it in velocity, endurance and raw athleticism -- taking the technology off the lab bench and onto the pitch.
In the 100-meter heats, the Beijing-based humanoid robot Tien Kung Ultra crossed in 9.39 seconds, faster than Usain Bolt's 9.58-second human world record. Tien Kung Ultra also posted a standing high jump of 2.88 meters, well above the human mark.
The games also featured a dazzling array of human-machine showdowns: robots traded shots with Olympic table tennis champion Ding Ning and tennis Grand Slam winner Zheng Jie, and went toe-to-toe with former national football player Yang Chen.
Robot football offered a special glimpse of how far the technology has come. Beijing-based Booster Robotics' newly developed bipedal robot, Booster T2, is the star player in the large size group of the football tournament at this year's games. Beyond its taller stature and greater strength, the robot can kick balls at over 100 km/h, and its end-side computing power is 10 times that of the previous generation, with the system latency dropping from 10 milliseconds to 4 milliseconds.
Many events at the games were run fully autonomously, with no remote controls, testing robots' ability to perceive and decide independently. "Every centimeter higher, every kilogram heavier, reflects engineers' optimization of joint motors and reducers," said Jiang Guangzhi of Beijing's Bureau of Economy and Information Technology.
REAL-WORLD APPLICATIONS
As China's robots demonstrate formidable technological prowess, the industry is now focusing on expanding robots' real-world applications -- a widely recognized challenge within the industry.
The World Robot Conference serves as a resounding testament to China's pragmatic shift and its global resonance. At the event, Beijing Galbot Co., Ltd. drew crowds with robots folding clothes, fetching goods, and making breakfast. The company says its pharmacy sorting robots are already deployed in nearly 100 stores across more than 10 cities, including Beijing, Shanghai and Shenzhen.
At the Galaxea AI display area, visitors could scan a QR code to place an order and then watch a wheeled robot pick, pack and label items they ordered in real time. The company's robots will be rolled out to unmanned warehouses and supermarkets this year, and has already partnered with JD.com for warehouse sorting and shelving.
Practical robots took center stage, just as the Spanish news agency Agencia EFE reported on the conference, Chinese companies are transitioning robots from mere "attention-grabbers" to genuine "workers and practical consumer goods."
Xiong Youjun, CEO of the Beijing Humanoid Robot Innovation Center, said this year's conference showed an industry clearly transitioning from mere technological showmanship to industrial implementation. He added that the sector is currently on the "eve of the ChatGPT moment" regarding embodied intelligence, with companies across the board accelerating the deployment and validation of their technologies.
A recent Morgan Stanley report draws a striking parallel between the current trajectory of China's humanoid robotics industry and the electric vehicle sector a decade ago. The investment bank predicts that over the next five to ten years, humanoid robots are poised to become the next major driver of China's machinery exports.
BOOMING INDUSTRIAL LANDSCAPE
The rapid ascent of the robot industry perfectly aligns with China's national strategic blueprint for future development.
"Embodied intelligence" was first written into China's government work report in 2025. Furthermore, China's 15th Five-Year Plan (2026-2030) calls for a forward-looking layout of future industries, including embodied artificial intelligence, alongside mechanisms to boost funding and share risks in these emerging sectors.
Data underscores this momentum. Among companies currently queuing for an IPO on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange alone, 46 are robotics-related, highlighting China's systematic industrial advantage in embodied AI. As Bloomberg noted, the surge in robot IPOs "reflects the rapid rise of China's AI ecosystem."
This wave of listings comes amid China's robotics sector securing unprecedented global prominence. China is now home to over 140 humanoid robot manufacturers. With an annual shipment volume of 14,400 units, the country now accounts for eight out of every ten humanoid robots produced globally.
Global shipments of humanoid robots reached approximately 19,100 units in the first half of this year, with China accounting for over 97 percent of the global total, industry data shows.
According to Xi Yue, co-founder of Beijing-based leading robot maker Robotera, the nation's robotics industry now stands firmly in the first tier globally, boasting the world's largest application market, the most comprehensive supply chain, and a leading edge in embodied AI algorithms. ■

====================================================================================================

Feature: In Hong Kong, global ecologists restore biodiversity by putting together healthy forest
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
20:12:16 CST
21:12:16 KST

by Xinhua writer Liu Yinglun
HONG KONG, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Restoration ecologist Fernanda Cardoso grew up hearing grim stories about forest degradation in her home country Brazil and other places worldwide, which got her interested in studying plant ecology and forest restoration. Now she is trying to piece together a fully functional and diverse subtropical forest on the hillsides of Hong Kong's highest mountain Tai Mo Shan.
The forest restoration site Cardoso works on is a part of Kadoorie Farm and Botanic Garden (KFBG), a 70-year-old local non-profit organization dedicated to natural conservation. In 2013, it launched a project to turn its degraded grassy slopes into a diverse native forest that can support a wide variety of wildlife.
So far, over 50,000 seedlings representing hundreds of native species have been planted. Mammals, birds and insects are returning, including rare species like the butterfly Burmese Bush Blue.
MAXIMUM DIVERSITY
"A good forest is one that's alive at every level," said Cardoso. It is not just a canopy of trees, but the constant exchange of energy between hundreds of species -- different plant life forms, animals, fungi, pollinators and seed dispersers.
Unfortunately for the restoration site, hundreds of years of agricultural history as well as frequent wildfires had eroded the soil and deprived it of enough seed dispersers to restore biodiversity naturally, said Zhang Jinlong, senior ecologist at KFBG's Flora Conservation Department.
The missing links have to be reconstructed artificially, and ecologists at KFBG are doing it by mimicking the end result of natural succession. Based on extensive flora surveys on local natural forests and some others in south China, they drew up plans to plant diverse life forms including trees, shrubs, epiphytes, herbs, and climbers to recreate the structure of the best south China-Vietnam subtropical evergreen forest.
A big part of the restoration plan is nurturing seedlings of native plant species in KFBG's nursery, for which the Flora Conservation Department's fieldwork teams scour wild areas of Hong Kong to collect seeds under local government permission. To preserve genetic diversity, they make a special effort to source seeds from diverse mother trees from as many populations as possible.
"Hong Kong is incredibly rich in species, many of which have rarely if ever been cultivated," said Craig Williams, horticultural manager who used to work at botanic gardens in Britain and Singapore. The metropolis is home to over 2,200 documented plant species.
Williams and his team make it their mission to propagate and conserve rare and threatened species. Sometimes the job entails huddling with co-workers on a small pink boat, or "Barbie's boat," as Williams called it, on a field trip to a tiny island to take cuttings of the only known wild Lofty Strangling Fig (Ficus altissima) mother trees in Hong Kong. Now the fig tree is growing in the KFBG nursery.
When the seedlings become strong enough, they are taken from the nursery and planted in the restoration site, where arborists have developed practical tools to overcome the substandard conditions of degraded land.
The team strengthens the soil with a mixture of biochar, dead branches and fallen leaves and uses tree guards made from plastic mesh and steel poles to protect seedlings from over-foraging by animals, said Cyrus Cheung, senior arborist at KFBG's Flora Conservation Department.
BACK WITH LIFE
Over a decade of efforts has helped bring wildlife back to the slopes. KFBG's Fauna Conservation Department has detected activities of almost all native mammal species, as well as the chirping of over 50 kinds of birds.
Zhang expects the canopy on the restoration site to keep expanding over the next five to ten years while self-regeneration begins for some species. To completely restore the function and structure of natural forests, however, is a matter of at least a century.
The Forest Declaration Assessment 2025 found that 8.1 million hectares of forest were lost in 2024, a level of destruction 63 percent higher than the trajectory needed to halt deforestation by 2030. Ecologists worldwide are calling for more restoration efforts.
"Conservation directly benefits everyday living. Just look at how much Hong Kong residents enjoy hiking and spending time outdoors," said Cardoso. She appreciates that local residents make full use of their country parks, which cover about 40 percent of the city's expanse, to maintain a healthy lifestyle.
Williams called his job a "privilege" because it is a rare opportunity to focus on growing native plants as well as participating in ecological restoration.
"The seedlings we plant will grow into massive trees that, long after I pass away, I wouldn't even get my arms around. It feels great to imagine that," said Williams. ■

Feature: Afghan gemstones seek new luster through global trade
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
20:12:09 CST
21:12:09 KST

KABUL, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Behind the glass counters of Kabul's antique sellers' street, blue lapis lazuli, green emeralds, red rubies and multicolored tourmaline reflect the light of a market that has long connected Afghanistan's mineral-rich mountain regions with buyers across the globe.
For traders and jewelry designers in the capital, the stones represent more than valuable commodities. They are part of Afghanistan's cultural heritage and, potentially, a source of employment, export income and international recognition.
"Most customers, especially those who come from outside Afghanistan, are interested in emerald, ruby and tourmaline," said Khalid Haidari, who has worked in the city's antique market for 18 years.
"For many buyers, however, the appeal of Afghan jewelry extends beyond the stones themselves. Traditional designs remain especially popular."
Local merchants said that Afghan gemstone jewelry has gained rising popularity in overseas markets, with China serving as a key export destination. Online platforms have provided local sellers and designers with new ways to present their products to customers abroad and arrange exports without relying entirely on physical stores or international exhibitions.
Yet Afghanistan's natural gemstone wealth has not automatically translated into a mature domestic industry.
"The stones from Afghanistan are of very high quality," Haidari said. "The main problem is that the equipment and standards needed for extraction and shaping are not sufficiently available."
This presents a major bottleneck for the industry, as a gemstone's commercial value is largely created after extraction. Cutting, polishing, design, certification, packaging and marketing can transform a raw mineral into a high-value finished product.
Nader Khan, who has worked in the gemstone trade for 30 years and has operated on antique sellers' street for 15 years, said Afghan stones remain highly competitive in foreign markets.
"Afghan lapis lazuli, emeralds and rubies are of a quality that is difficult to find elsewhere," Khan said.
He said customers also attach great importance to handmade work and domestic designs. In his view, processing more stones inside Afghanistan would help preserve their original character while creating employment opportunities for local workers.
"We process the stones here with the machinery available to us and turn them into different designs," Khan said.
Khan also cautioned that sending stones abroad for additional modern processing could raise costs and risk affecting the stones' original quality. Developing local processing capacity, he said, would allow Afghan producers to retain more value while preserving the distinct cultural identity of their products.
The future of Afghanistan's gemstone trade is closely linked to access to international customers.
"International exhibitions had previously provided important opportunities for sellers to display their products and expand sales. The decline in such events has reduced direct contact," Khan said.
"Chinese customers remain among the most active buyers in Kabul's gemstone market, particularly for lapis lazuli and nephrite," Khan added.
At the same time, online sales are creating a new route to consumers. Afghan sellers and designers are using digital platforms to display jewelry, communicate with buyers and send products overseas.
The shift has opened opportunities for small businesses, but it also requires reliable product photography, accurate information about gemstones, secure delivery and consistent quality.
"I am very satisfied with my work, and most of my customers are particularly interested in lapis lazuli, emeralds and rubies," Ahmad, an online seller, said.
The charm of Afghan gemstones goes beyond their market value. For buyers, these precious stones carry unique emotional and cultural significance.
A piece of jewelry may serve as a souvenir, a gift, a symbol of cultural identity, or a reminder of a particular journey. Such associations add meaning to a product whose value begins in the earth but is completed through human workmanship.
"Customers use gemstones with a good design at home to improve their mood and to overcome some health problems because seeing the stone gives them a feeling of calmness and happiness," Ahmad told Xinhua.
Sula, a customer visiting the market to buy a gift for a friend, chose tourmaline bracelets, describing them as attractive, memorable and valuable.
The gemstone trade also unlocks profound cultural development potential. Distinctive traditional Afghan designs stand out in the competitive global jewelry market. Combined with high-quality local gemstones, these handcrafted pieces are both commercially competitive and closely connected to the country's profound history. ■

- Ground, aerial, and naval unmanned systems, including interceptor, reconnaissance, strike, and kamikaze drones, took part across three domains.
Ukraine held what organizers described as the world’s first military parade composed entirely of unmanned systems on August 24, 2026, marking the country’s Independence Day with a display of ground, naval, and aerial drones instead of traditional manned formations.
Dozens of ground robotic systems moved down Kyiv’s main street, built for logistics, reconnaissance, and combat missions. Ukrainian officials have said the country was the first in the world to stand up a dedicated military branch built specifically around drone warfare.
Independence Day fell on Ukraine’s 35th anniversary of statehood this year, the fifth marked since Russia’s full-scale invasion began.
Kyiv had not held a conventional military parade since 2022, instead using Khreshchatyk Street in recent years to display destroyed Russian military equipment as a symbol of resistance.

Russia launches new military spacecraft (VIDEO)
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24

Russia launches new military spacecraft (VIDEO)
Russia has successfully placed a new military spacecraft into orbit aboard a Soyuz-2.1b rocket launched from the Plesetsk Cosmodrome in Arkhangelsk Region, the Defense Ministry has said. The type and specific mission of the spacecraft have not been disclosed.
A combat crew of the Russian Space Forces launched the medium-class rocket at 5:40 AM Moscow time on Monday. The spacecraft was sent up “in the interests of the Russian Defense Ministry,” according to an official statement.
The spacecraft reached its designated orbit and was taken under the control of ground-based Space Forces systems.
“Stable telemetry communication has been established and maintained with the spacecraft, its onboard systems are functioning normally,” the ministry said. The flight and deployment proceeded as planned.
After the launch, the Soyuz-2.1b and its payload were tracked by the ground-based automated control complex of the German Titov Main Test Space Center, which is responsible for controlling and monitoring Russian military spacecraft.
The Soyuz-2.1b is a disposable three-stage medium-lift launch vehicle that has frequently been used to deploy both military and civilian satellites.
The mission comes after several military launches from Plesetsk earlier this year. On April 17, a Soyuz-2.1b carried several spacecraft into orbit for the Defense Ministry. Six days later, an Angara-1.2 light rocket was launched from the cosmodrome with military satellites.
Plesetsk is Russia’s northernmost major launch facility. Its high latitude makes it suited to place spacecraft into polar orbits, which are widely used for Earth observation and military missions. The facility began as a Soviet intercontinental ballistic missile base before being converted for space launches in the 1960s.
The cosmodrome’s first satellite launch took place in March 1966, when a Vostok-2 rocket carried the Kosmos-112 reconnaissance spacecraft into orbit. Plesetsk subsequently became a major launch site for Soviet and Russian military spacecraft and has hosted numerous versions of the R-7 family from which the modern Soyuz launch vehicle was developed.

Addressing an open letter to the education ministers across states, he said citizens have a right to know what steps are being taken to improve public education.He posed six questions to the ministers regarding the condition and facilities inside the government schools. He also asked them to publicly disclose details on infrastructure, teacher vacancies, funding, digital facilities and the workload of teaching staff.
Dipke posted a letter on his X account with the caption, "Letter to the Education Ministers of all states. The country needs to know what steps are being taken to improve government schools."

Teacher vacancies: How many teaching positions are currently sanctioned, how many are filled, and how many remain vacant?
School funding: How much money has been allocated for government schools in the last five years, and how much of it has actually been spent?
Need for more schools: How many additional government schools are required to ensure that every child has reasonable access to quality education?
Non-teaching duties: Apart from teaching, what non-teaching duties and responsibilities are assigned to government school teachers?
Basic and digital facilities: How many government schools currently have adequate access to computers and digital learning facilities, clean and functional toilets, and proper sports facilities and equipment for children?

This is about the future of our children," he said, adding that every child deserves "a safe classroom, clean drinking water, a functional washroom, a bench to sit on, and a teacher to teach them."He urged the ministry to make the requested information public and take urgent measures to ensure that inadequate infrastructure does not deny children access to dignified education.

Iran denies receiving invitation to join Mecca defense pact

Iran denies receiving invitation to join Mecca defense pact
Iran has denied reports that it has been invited to join the Mecca defense pact comprising Saudi Arabia, Türkiye, and Pakistan, while confirming that proposals have been made for talks with the three countries on regional security.
The clarification comes after Mehdi Rahimi, the head of the Iranian parliament’s Khaneh Mellat news agency, told Al Mayadeen on Saturday that Tehran had received an invitation to become a member of the Mecca pact and was considering it.
On Monday, however, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei rejected the claim, stating that no formal invitation had been received in Tehran. At the same time, he said that discussions with the pact members concerning broader regional security have been proposed and are under consideration.
The three founding members of the pact had previously repeatedly said the alliance could eventually expand to include other regional states, with Egypt being publicly mentioned as a possible candidate. Pakistan has also said it would have no objection to Iran joining.
The Mecca Joint Defense Agreement, which was signed on August 7, brings together Türkiye, which possesses one of NATO’s largest militaries and a rapidly growing defense industry, Saudi Arabia, which features enormous financial resources and ambitions to shape the Arab political order, and Pakistan, a nuclear-armed state with one of the largest militaries in the Muslim world.
The pact stipulates that an armed attack on one member would be regarded as an attack on all three, and also calls for closer military coordination, joint exercises and defense-industry cooperation.
Tehran initially said it had “no reason for concern” over the agreement, with spokesman Baghaei noting that its creation reflected a growing desire among regional states to develop their own security mechanisms.
Some observers have dubbed the new grouping an “Islamic NATO,” although experts have cautioned against treating it as a fully-fledged military bloc. Gulf Research Center chairman Abdulaziz Sager has said the pact could strengthen the members’ combined diplomatic and defense weight and contribute to a more regionally driven security system.
Israel, meanwhile, has responded to the pact with alarm, raising concerns that a bloc built around Saudi Arabia, Türkiye and nuclear-armed Pakistan could emerge as a counterweight to its own military dominance in the region.
The Mecca pact members, however, insist that the agreement is defensive, is open to other countries in the region, and is not directed against any other states.

The physiological reasons the human brain struggles to process information in extreme heat
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:00:42 UTC
21:00:42 KST

Ever feel that the arrival of summer sun makes you feel a bit dopey? You wouldn’t be the only one. Soaring temperatures are known for their ability to slow our thought processes, making even everyday tasks seem like a baffling ordeal.
But what is actually happening inside our heads when the heat is on? The explanation appears to lie in the extra work our brain and body have to do to keep us cool.
The brain and body are in constant conversation. When outdoor temperatures change, thermoreceptors which sit near the surface of the skin send signals to the hypothalamus – the brain’s temperature regulation centre.
When things become too hot or cold, the hypothalamus co-ordinates a series of responses to bring body temperature back towards normal (around 37°C). Keeping the core temperature at this level is critical for metabolism, activity of enzymes and many other essential body functions.
Being commander-in-chief of temperature regulation means that the brain becomes rather occupied when having to consistently regulate your temperature.
In hot weather, this means cooling the body down by switching on mechanisms that allow heat to radiate from the surface. This includes diverting blood to the skin, flattening skin hairs and sweating.
These responses are governed by nervous pathways that link the brain to blood vessels and sweat glands. This allows it to fine-tune the amount of heat the body sheds.
But the additional demand that keeping cool places on the brain may therefore leave less capacity for it to perform cognitive tasks which require sustained thought and attention.
This becomes particularly noticeable if you’re also exercising or exerting yourself at the same time. This is because working muscles and metabolism generate heat, which places additional strain on the body and brain’s cooling mechanisms.
Our neurons (nerve cells) may also start to function differently with rising heat. Neurons rely on the flow of electrical currents and the release of chemical neurotransmitters to function. These processes depend upon enzymes, proteins and the movement of charged ions in and out of the neuron – all of which are sensitive to temperature.
Although the brain is normally able to compensate and keep up with these demands, past a certain point the finely controlled balance becomes disrupted. This alters the way neurons fire and communicate with each other, which can affect processes such as memory, decision-making and concentration.
Another potential complication to consider is dehydration, which commonly occurs in hot weather as we lose more fluid in sweat. Failing to replace fluid losses adequately means additional strain is placed on the cardiovascular system as it tries to supply the skin and organs – including the brain – with blood.
Like many other organs, the brain is over 70% water. Even modest dehydration can result in impairment to attention, reaction times and short-term memory.
This is because dehydration can affect the brain in several ways. It can reduce cerebral blood flow, alter the way that neurons function and even affect the delicate balance of electrolytes needed for normal activity – all of which impact how well our brain works.
Another important consideration is not just how brain and body respond to heat in the moment, but also in the aftermath when they rest and recuperate – namely, through sleep. In hotter weather, it can become increasingly difficult to sleep. And, if you do manage to doze off, the time spent in deeper, restorative sleep may also be short-lived.
In disrupting sleep, hot weather adds another contribution to brain fog: inadequate sleep impairs attention, memory and thinking – furthering the effects of heat on cognitive performance.
Keeping cool
The degree to which the heat affects our thinking will probably vary between people. Some may cope well, whereas others may find difficulty in doing complex cognitive tasks or simple, everyday activities. This will be due in part to individual differences in physiology and heat tolerance.
Perception matters, too. Even a relatively small dip in attention or processing speed can feel much more dramatic when we notice ourselves struggling with something that would usually come easily.
Try not to be hard on yourself if this happens. Take a moment to chill, rehydrate and reclaim your thoughts.
You can fend off some of this summer brain fog by keeping yourself cool as best as you can. Simple measures such as cool clothing, bedding and taking regular breaks from heat exposure do work wonders. Good fluid intake is also paramount to making sure both body and brain stay hydrated.
While it’s frustrating when our brains just don’t feel like they’re firing on all cylinders on hot days, just remember that it’s only a temporary blip. And one that should start to ease off as we cool down.
This article is republished from The Conversation under a Creative Commons license. Read the original article.

China’s advanced chip supply to surge by 2035 despite equipment bottlenecks, Goldman says
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
12:00:13 UTC
21:00:13 KST

China’s advanced chip supply to surge by 2035 despite equipment bottlenecks, Goldman says
The increase will be driven by aggressive capacity expansion at SMIC, China’s largest contract chipmaker, as well as improving yields
China is on track to dramatically slash its deficit in advanced chips over the next decade as domestic foundries rapidly scale up production, though the weak link of lithography threatens to keep full semiconductor independence out of reach, according to US investment bank Goldman Sachs.
The supply of wafers made using 7-nanometre and below advanced processes is projected to grow at a compound annual rate of 46 per cent between 2025 and 2035, far outpacing the 17 per cent growth expected in domestic demand, Goldman analysts said in a report on Monday.
That would narrow the gap between domestic supply and demand to 34 per cent by 2035, from 92 per cent in 2025, according to the investment bank. China’s advanced-node wafer supply is expected to reach 410,000 wafers per month by then, compared with demand of 619,000 wafers.
Goldman’s model assumes SMIC adds monthly capacity of between 30,000 and 50,000 advanced-node wafers each year from 2026 to 2031, before adding another 20,000 wafers per month annually through 2035. It also assumes yields rise from 23 per cent in 2026 to 50 per cent in 2030 and 75 per cent by 2035.
The world’s No 1 foundry, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company (TSMC), which started mass-producing 7nm chips in 2018, achieves yields that can exceed 90 per cent, depending on chip design and die size.

Marcin Bosacki was asked about the issue on TVP Info on Sunday evening. In his response, the Polish deputy foreign minister stressed that "it is clear that every nation and its government have the right to choose the heroes they consider appropriate."
However, if figures "such as (Stepan) Bandera or (Roman) Shukhevych do indeed appear in Ukraine’s National Pantheon, this will significantly worsen Ukraine’s relations not only with Poland, but also with Europe as a whole," the Polish deputy foreign minister said.

Experts emphasise that inflating the threat of paper kites serves a darker strategic goal of reshaping demographic realities on the ground.
“Netanyahu does not need to invent a major issue out of the paper kites; rather, the primary goal is pushing the Palestinians towards displacement and dodging any political commitment,” Shaheen told Al Jazeera.
Suleiman Bisharat, a political researcher, explained that the government deliberately uses these weak excuses to instil a psychological state of fear within Israeli society, rallying domestic support for disproportionate force.
“It is true that we might consider these excuses superficial and weak, but ultimately … Israel ties them to the security equation,” Bisharat told Al Jazeera.

Taiwan unveils Strong Bow anti-ballistic missile specs in push for US$1.13 billion funding
Developers disclose details of Chiang Kung hypersonic interceptor with active radar to convince lawmakers to approve funding
The disclosure comes as the government prepares another attempt to secure funding after the system was excluded from a pared-back special defence spending package approved by the opposition-controlled legislature in May.
The defence ministry plans to resubmit Strong Bow and other programmes through a supplementary budget, which the cabinet could consider as early as Thursday before sending it to lawmakers.
The ministry has proposed spending NT$36.1 billion (US$1.13 billion) to produce two Strong Bow systems and 128 interceptor missiles.
Strong Bow, also referred to as Tien Kung (Sky Bow) IV, is a land-based mid-tier anti-tactical ballistic missile system designed to intercept incoming missiles at altitudes of at least 70km (43 miles) – higher than Taiwan’s existing Patriot and Tien Kung III systems.
According to the institute, the vertically launched missile can reach hypersonic speeds and uses a two-stage solid-fuel rocket motor. It relies on inertial guidance and radar uplink corrections during midcourse flight before switching to an active seeker in the terminal phase.

Trade between India and Russia growing – Moscow
Bilateral trade turnover between India and Russia grew 8% in the first half of the year, Russian First Deputy Prime Minister Denis Manturov said in Moscow on Monday, adding that both exports and imports showed expansion.
“Our goal is not only to increase the volume of trade turnover, but also to diversify its structure,” Manturov said at the 27th Session of the India-Russia Inter-Governmental Commission on Trade, Economic, Scientific, Technological and Cultural Cooperation, which he is co-hosting with visiting Indian Foreign Minister S. Jaishankar.
India and Russia are pursuing a bilateral trade target of $100 billion to be reached by 2030, which was set by President Vladimir Putin in December when he visited New Delhi.
Jaishankar said bilateral trade has increased more than fourfold in the last four years, from around $13 billion in 2021-22 to over $60 billion in 2025-26. He also noted, however, that the rapid expansion has increased the trade imbalance. The Indian foreign minister said progress on market access, removal of tariff and non-tariff barriers, and strengthening payment mechanisms will be critical in addressing the imbalance.
Manturov said the free trade agreement (FTA) that the Russia-led Eurasian Economic Union has been negotiating with India since August last year will be a new driver for sustainable trade growth. “Its preparation is in an active stage and it is important to maintain a high pace of negotiations,” he added.

Agriculture ministry reports NT$10.29 million in losses from torrential rain

20:56:09 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Agriculture said Monday that heavy rain in late August caused NT$10.29 million (US$323,000) in agricultural losses in southern Taiwan as of 5 p.m.
CNA had earlier reported that losses totaled NT$6.15 million as of 11 a.m., with Tainan accounting for 95% of the total.
The updated figures showed that Tainan suffered NT$7.19 million in losses, accounting for 70% of the total. Yunlin recorded NT$1.18 million, Pingtung NT$1 million, and Kaohsiung NT$920,000 in losses, according to an updated Ministry of Agriculture report.
The rain damaged 203 hectares of crops, with an average damage rate of 20%. The ministry said this was equivalent to the complete loss of 42 hectares of crops.
Watermelons suffered the largest financial loss at NT$3.69 million. Other affected crops included asparagus, non-heading Chinese cabbage, green onions, and water spinach.
The ministry reported no losses to livestock, fisheries, forestry products, or private agricultural facilities.
The figures were based on reports from local governments as of 5 p.m. Monday. The ministry said it would continue updating the agricultural damage report as more information became available.

Dutch broadcaster to boycott Eurovision for a second year, calling it a ‘platform for division’
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:53:02 UTC
20:53:02 KST

Dutch broadcaster to boycott Eurovision for a second year, calling it a ‘platform for division’
THE HAGUE, Netherlands (AP) — A Dutch broadcaster announced Monday it is boycotting the Eurovision Song Contest for a second year, calling it a “platform for division” because of tensions over Israel’s involvement.
The decision by AVROTROS comes after broadcasters in the Netherlands, Iceland, Ireland, Slovenia and Spain refused to take part in this year’s contest because of Israel’s participation.
“AVROTROS will not participate in the Eurovision Song Contest in 2027 because the event can no longer be considered neutral, with a participating country still involved in a large-scale military conflict,” it said.
The Dutch broadcaster, which has a long history of involvement with the competition, said it was leaving it up to the public network NPO to decide on any Dutch involvement.
“The Eurovision Song Contest was originally created to bring people and countries together. It is undeniable that international conflicts are increasingly affecting the contest, undermining its neutral character,” AVROTROS director-general Taco Zimmerman said in a statement. “The Eurovision Song Contest has therefore become a platform for division.”
Eurovision Song Contest Director Martin Green said in a statement that the organization regretted the move, but respects the views of member broadcasters. The contest is run by the Geneva-based European Broadcasting Union (EBU) — a group of public broadcasters from 56 countries.
“The Eurovision Song Contest has always been a place to bring people together, celebrate diverse communities, and show that a better world is possible even in the most difficult times,” Green said in a statement sent to The Associated Press.
“We will now continue our dialogue with NPO, the umbrella organization for Dutch public service media, regarding the opportunities for another broadcaster to participate. We very much hope that audiences and artists in the Netherlands can continue to be represented in the Eurovision Song Contest,” he added.
In a statement, the NPO said it recognized that “geopolitical tensions are having a divisive effect. That’s why this hasn’t been an easy decision for our colleagues. We will reflect on the upcoming edition and will come back to this at the right moment.”
NPO said it was “too early to comment on the next steps at this point; we’re currently deliberating on that.”
AVROTROS said it has called on the EBU to establish transparent rules for the participation of countries involved in military conflicts. “However, the recently announced changes by the EBU do not provide sufficient confidence that the independent and neutral character of the Eurovision Song Contest has been restored,” it said.
While AVROTROS did not mention Israel by name, it said the network will boycott Eurovision in 2027 “because the event can no longer be considered neutral, with a participating country still involved in a large-scale military conflict.”
It added: “The severe humanitarian suffering in Gaza and the ongoing restrictions on press freedom have contributed to increasing divisions surrounding the Eurovision Song Contest in recent years.”
The contest was founded in 1956, in part to help unite a shattered continent after World War II. It pits acts from dozens of countries against one another for the continent’s musical crown. Bulgarian singer Dara won the event this year with her infectious party anthem “Bangaranga.”
A number of performers and countries have called for the exclusion of Israel, which has taken part in Eurovision since 1973, one of a few non-European countries to compete.
___
Associated Press journalist Jamey Keaten in Geneva contributed.

AP Decision Notes: What to expect in South Carolina’s special U.S. Senate primary runoff
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:53:02 UTC
20:53:02 KST

AP Decision Notes: What to expect in South Carolina’s special U.S. Senate primary runoff
WASHINGTON (AP) — South Carolina Republicans will return to the polls Tuesday for the fourth time since June to replace the late U.S. Sen. Lindsey Graham on the fall general election ballot.
Graham won the June 9 Republican primary for renomination to the seat he first won in 2002, but his unexpected death on July 11 from an aortic tear created a vacancy not only for his current U.S. Senate seat but also as the party’s pick to compete for another six-year term.
The finalists for the Republican nomination are Graham’s sister, U.S. Sen. Darline Graham, who was appointed to serve out the remainder of her brother’s current term, and U.S. Rep. Ralph Norman, a five-term congressman who ran for governor earlier in the year and placed third in the primary.
Darline Graham placed first in the Aug. 11 special primary but fell shy of the vote majority needed to avoid Tuesday’s runoff. She received about 33% of the vote, compared to about 25% for Norman. U.S. Rep. Russell Fry placed third with about 20% of the vote.
Graham swept the counties across central South Carolina, including the Columbia area, as well as the state’s Lowcountry region, which includes Charleston. She scored her highest percentages in counties along the Georgia border.
Norman performed best in the state’s Piedmont and Upstate regions, including the Greenville area. Fry did best in the eight counties in the Pee Dee and Waccamaw regions that he represents in Congress.
Fry endorsed Graham after he lost the primary. She also has key backing from Republican U.S. Sen. Tim Scott and President Donald Trump, who was an early proponent of Graham and held a campaign rally with her Friday in Myrtle Beach.
Greenville County is the most populous in the state and typically contributes the most votes in statewide Republican primaries. It also has bucked against the front-runners in recent Republican primaries. Norman also carried Greenville County in the gubernatorial primary, and it was one of the only counties Lindsey Graham lost in his final election.
Democratic-leaning Richland and Charleston counties have the next-largest populations and contribute a sizable number of votes in Republican primaries, but they tend to be more influential in Democratic contests.
Horry, Lexington and Spartanburg counties are also large counties that have big impacts on Republican primaries. Spartanburg was the only other county Lindsey Graham lost in the June primary.
The winner will face Democratic nominee Annie Andrews, a Charleston pediatrician who challenged Republican U.S. Rep. Nancy Mace in the 1st Congressional District in 2022.
Lindsey Graham last won reelection in 2020 with 54% of the vote. Trump carried the state in 2024 with 58% of the vote.
Here are some of the key facts about the election and data points the AP Decision Team will monitor as the votes are tallied:
When do polls close?
Polls close at 7 p.m. ET.
What’s on the ballot?
The Associated Press will provide vote results and declare a winner in the special Republican primary runoff for U.S. Senate.
Who gets to vote?
Voters who participated in the Democratic primary on June 9 may not participate in the special Republican primary runoff on August 25. Only Republican primary voters or registered voters who did not participate in any party’s primary on June 9 may cast ballots in Tuesday’s election.
How many voters are there?
As of Friday, there were about 3.4 million registered voters in South Carolina. Voters in South Carolina do not register by party.
How many people actually vote?
About 465,000 voters cast ballots in the June 9 Republican U.S. Senate primary when Lindsey Graham was renominated. About 336,000 voters participated in the Aug. 11 special Republican U.S. Senate primary.
How much of the vote is cast early or by absentee ballot?
About 19% of the vote in Aug. 11 Republican special primary was cast early in-person or by mail.
As of Friday, about 45,000 ballots had already been cast in Tuesday’s election.
When are early and absentee votes released?
Nearly all of South Carolina’s 46 counties release all or almost all of their early in-person and mail voting results in the first vote update of the night, usually before releasing any results from in-person Election Day voting.
How long does vote-counting usually take?
In the Aug. 11 special primary, the AP first reported results at 7:13 p.m. ET, or 13 minutes after polls closed. The last vote update of the night was at 11:25 p.m. ET with more than 99% of total votes counted.
When will the AP declare a winner?
The AP does not make projections and will declare a winner only when it’s determined there is no scenario that would allow a trailing candidate to close the gap. If a race has not been called, the AP will continue to cover any newsworthy developments, such as candidate concessions or declarations of victory. In doing so, the AP will make clear that it has not yet declared a winner and explain why.
How do recounts work?
In South Carolina, recounts are automatic if the margin between the winning and losing candidates is 1% of the total vote or less. The AP may declare a winner in a race that is subject to a recount if it can determine the lead is too large for a recount or legal challenge to change the outcome.
Are we there yet?
As of Tuesday, there will be 70 days until the 2026 midterm elections.
___
Follow the AP’s coverage of the 2026 election at https://apnews.com/projects/elections-2026/.

Ceasefire monitors deploy in eastern Congo under Qatari peace deal
DAKAR, Aug 24 - A mission to observe implementation of a ceasefire between Congolese forces and Rwandan-backed rebels began on Monday in eastern Congo, the first field deployment under a monitoring mechanism established by a Qatari-mediated peace deal signed last year.
• The deployment of the mission is the latest sign of incremental progress under the Qatar-mediated talks, which began last year after AFC/M23 staged a lightning offensive in eastern Congo, seizing the region's two largest cities.
• The two sides signed a peace deal in November 2025 that established a framework for a comprehensive peace agreement and the implementation of ceasefire monitoring arrangements.
• The mission is taking place in the town of Minembwe, South Kivu province, which has seen a surge in fighting in recent weeks between AFC/M23 rebels and government forces, with each side accusing the other of ceasefire violations.
• AFC/M23 accused government forces on Monday of shelling a village near Minembwe, causing civilian casualties and displacing residents. A spokesperson for Congo's armed forces did not immediately respond to a request for comment.
• Congolese government and AFC/M23 representatives met in Switzerland last week and agreed on a new roadmap for negotiations, pointing to renewed momentum in the Doha peace process after months of stalled talks.
• The Doha process is running parallel to U.S.-mediated talks between Congo and Rwanda that Washington hopes will fuel Western investments in eastern Congo's minerals sector.
• Earlier this month, Congolese authorities released 15 prisoners and handed them over to AFC/M23 rebels, in the first known transfer of prisoners under the deal.
• The rebels control large swathes of eastern Congo after staging their offensive last year. REUTERS

Eastern Libya executes 10 convicted on 'terrorism' charges
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
