Israel freaks out over children's kites in Gaza
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:07:56 UTC
20:07:56 KST

Breadcrumb
Israel puts its military on 'high alert' over children's kites in Gaza
Nine-year-old Arkan Radi sat inside his family's tent in a displacement camp in Al-Zawayda in the central Gaza Strip, carefully making a small kite.
He cut the paper, attached thin wooden sticks, tied the string and chose colours resembling those of the Palestinian flag. He imagined it rising above the rows of tents as he and his friends ran after it.
For Arkan, it was supposed to be nothing more than a summer game and a brief escape from the tents, rubble and fear that have defined much of his childhood.
But when he finally stepped outside carrying the kite, his parents stopped him. At first, Arkan could not understand why.
"I made it to play with my friends," he told The New Arab. "I spent days working on it. I wanted to fly it and chase it after it, but my parents told me not to go out with it. I don't understand why they're afraid of it. It's just paper and string."
Wiping away his tears, he added, "I don't want to hurt anyone. I just want to play like children everywhere. We're even afraid of playing now."
Radi, his father, told TNA that "I would never have stopped Arkan from flying a kite if it were not for recent Israeli threats to target people launching kites from Gaza."
For days, Israel's concern over kites and balloons launched from Gaza has intensified, turning children's toys into a "security issue".
Israeli media claimed that several kites from Gaza had landed near areas surrounding the besieged coastal enclave.
In statements concerning some of the incidents, the Israeli military acknowledged that no suspicious materials or explosives were found and that the kites posed no danger to the public.
Israeli Defence Minister Yisrael Katz ordered the military to act "very forcefully and immediately" against kites and balloons launched from Gaza, treating them like drones.
"A balloon is like a kite, and a kite is like a drone, whether it carries explosives or not," Katz boasted.
Netanyahu and Katz warned that ongoing launches could lead to wider war, including targeted killings and evacuations.
They claimed they had warned Hamas that "if the launches toward Israel do not stop immediately, the army will increase targeted killings of those responsible", while also threatening to "evacuate residents from areas from which kites, drones, and balloons are launched."
Thus, the kites made of paper, string and wooden sticks have become entangled in a security narrative involving targeted killings, military raids and evacuation threats.
In Gaza, however, the question is far simpler: how did a children's toy become a source of fear?
"My son doesn't know anything about politics or what Israel is saying," Radi said. "He sees a kite and wants to play with it. But we adults know what it means when Israel threatens to target those who launch these kites, so we stopped him."
"We're afraid for him of anything that might attract attention. In Gaza, a child can't know where the danger is coming from. He might go out to play, and suddenly the whole area becomes a target," he added.
What hurts him most, however, is that kites were never a form of resistance for Gaza's children. They were simply a familiar summer pastime.
"Children here used to make and fly kites during the summer. It's perfectly normal for us. What's wrong with a child flying a kite? Why should a child be afraid of the sky too?" he asked.
A summer game turns into a source of fear
In another displacement camp in central Gaza, 13-year-old Mohammed made a kite with the help of his older brother. He chose several colours and attached a long tail, hoping it would rise high above the camp.
"Every year when summer comes, we make kites and go to an open space to fly them," Mohammed told TNA. "This isn't the first time I've done this, but this year my mother was very scared."
"She told me the Israelis could see us and shoot us. I don't want to die because of a kite. So, I kept it with me and didn't fly it," he said.
His mother, Ruba, said her fear was not of the kite itself, but of what could happen if Israeli forces saw her son carrying one.
"My son doesn't understand what's going on around him. He sees other children playing and wants to join in. But we've lived through war, and we know that anything can become a reason for bombing," she added.
"We want our children to laugh, even for just one hour. We don't want them to grow up afraid to play, but at the same time, we can't risk their lives," she explained.
Meanwhile, Hamas has rejected the Israeli narrative, describing the focus on kites as an attempt to create new justifications for escalation against Gaza.
Hamas spokesperson Hazem Qassem said the kites being discussed by Israel were essentially "children's toys in displacement camps", warning of the consequences of Israeli threats to target those who launch them.
"These threats, based on fabricated pretexts, are an attempt to justify the continuation of aggression and violations against our people, even going so far as to threaten children in the Gaza Strip," Qassem said.
He called on the US administration and mediating and guarantor states to pressure Israel to halt what he described as its "unbridled aggression" and not use the issue to undermine the ceasefire process.
Turning a toy into a pretext
For Gaza-based Palestinian political analyst Mustafa Ibrahim, the controversy over kites cannot be understood solely by whether they pose a physical threat.
"Rather," he told TNA, "it reflects the broader political and military context surrounding Gaza."
"When an unexploded kite becomes a security issue that warrants threats of assassination and evacuation, it means the issue transcends the actual danger posed by this tool," Ibrahim said.
"Israel is trying to portray everything coming from Gaza as a potential security threat, even when it involves children's toys. The danger here is not in the kite itself, but in its use as a pretext to broaden the scope of targeting," he added.
Ibrahim also linked the rhetoric to Israel's domestic political environment and the pressures facing Netanyahu.
"Israel's security rhetoric serves Netanyahu at a sensitive political moment because it allows him to appear as a leader who confronts any threat, no matter how small, and diverts attention from larger political and security issues," he explained.
He warned that turning incidents involving kites into grounds for military action could have serious consequences for civilians in Gaza, particularly amid the fragility of the ceasefire and the territory's continuing humanitarian crisis.
"The problem is that this rhetoric could quickly escalate from political threats to military action," he said. "Then the price won't be a kite that landed somewhere, but entire neighbourhoods are facing evacuation orders or airstrikes."
For children like Arkan and Mohammed, politics seems distant and incomprehensible. They see only a paper kite, summer wind, and fleeting childhood they try to reclaim. But in Gaza, even the sky is fearful.

Lebanon abolished the death penalty. Can it now deliver justice?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:06:18 UTC
20:06:18 KST

Breadcrumb
Lebanon abolished the death penalty. Can it now deliver justice?
Beirut, Lebanon - Lebanon became the first state in the Middle East to abolish the death penalty following a parliamentary vote on 11 August, formalising a two-decade moratorium on capital punishment in the country.
The achievement caps a nearly 30-year national campaign for nonviolence and has implications for Lebanon’s pursuit of justice in connection with other countries.
“It is a clear and firm commitment to strip the law and political authority of the power to kill,” Ogarit Younan, co-founder of the national abolition campaign, told The New Arab. “The death penalty kills, and I cannot accept being a citizen of a state of gallows.”
Lebanon last executed three men in 2004 at Roumieh Prison. Since then, death sentences have still been handed down but not carried out.
The abolition reverses a regional trend that has seen other states resume executions, pronounce death sentences or pass new death penalty laws.
In June, Jordan hanged six men in its first executions since 2017, and Syria sentenced nine men, including former dictator Bashar Al-Assad in absentia, to death earlier this month.
In March, Israel adopted a discriminatory death penalty law mandating executions for “terrorism-related” offences and applied exclusively to Palestinians.
“The Lebanese authorities, the judiciary, will not be resorting to this cruel and irreversible punishment,” Ramzi Kaiss, Lebanon researcher at Human Rights Watch, told The New Arab, hailing the new law as a step in the right direction.
According to Minister of Justice Adel Nassar, abolition in Lebanon can set an example for other states.
“Historically, Lebanon was known to be a country that has modern laws, that is keen to protect fundamental rights, to be a pioneer in the region,” Nassar told The New Arab.
“Because of what we lived through here, I think we can give the proper message to the world. We are providing a counterexample.”’
Removing a barrier to justice?
Abolishing the death penalty in Lebanon opens a path toward resolving one of the most sensitive justice issues in the country: accountability for the 2020 Beirut port blast.
Lebanese authorities have previously sought extradition of Russian-Cypriot Igor Grechushkin, former owner of the Rhosus container ship allegedly carrying the ammonium nitrate that detonated at the port, in connection with the investigation into the explosion.
In September, Bulgarian authorities detained Grechushkin on an Interpol notice, but a Bulgarian court rejected Lebanon’s extradition request. Grechuskin’s lawyer had argued Lebanon’s laws on capital punishment put her client’s life at risk.
“Under international human rights law, individuals should not be extradited to areas where the death penalty is used,” Kaiss said. “In Lebanon, there have been several obstacles to justice as a result of the death penalty being in effect.”
With this obstacle removed, Lebanese authorities may be able to move forward with the investigation and potential prosecutions of those deemed responsible for the port blast.
The same principle, however, could complicate efforts to hold accountable Syrian members of the Assad regime accused of committing atrocities.
In February, Lebanon and Syria signed a judicial cooperation agreement providing for the transfer of convicted Syrians held in Lebanon to serve out their sentences in Syria.
Lebanon has also arrested former regime officials and received an extradition request from Syria; the transfer of Syrian officials who fled the country after Assad’s fall has previously been a subject of discussion between the neighbouring countries’ authorities.
“Lebanon will not pursue extradition without assurances that an individual will not be subject to the death penalty,” Nassar said, once the law enters into force upon its publication in the official gazette.
If Syrian authorities carry out the death sentence against former security chief Atef Najib and the death penalty remains on the books in Syria, Lebanon could be forced to deny extradition of other regime officials in accordance with international law.
Last Tuesday, Lebanon’s public prosecutor, an office with a degree of independence from the government, approved the extradition of former Syrian general Adel Issa under the terms of a 1951 bilateral judicial agreement.
An anonymous official told AFP that legal and judicial requirements for extradition had been met. The transfer, carried out the following day, raises questions about Lebanon’s obligations under the International Convention on Civil and Political Rights, to which it is a party and which imposes a duty on countries to refrain from extraditing individuals to countries where their right to life is at risk.
Controversial amnesty on the heels of abolition
A day after the vote on abolishing the death penalty, Lebanon’s parliament also approved a general amnesty law aimed at reducing rampant prison overcrowding.
The controversial measure could see around one-third of the country’s approximately 8,500 incarcerated people released. The majority of the prison population is comprised of those awaiting trial, and rights groups have previously criticised dangerous conditions for inmates.
The government has publicly disavowed associations between the death penalty abolition law and the general amnesty, though critics attribute the latter’s passage to sectarian demands that could allow former members of extremist groups to walk free.
The exact scope of the amnesty remains unclear, and the law does not provide for broader structural reform to the prison and justice system.
The text of the abolition bill, in addition to removing all death penalty provisions from Lebanese laws, distinguishes between new penalties for prior sentences and future ones.
For previous death sentences, such as those handed down to the estimated 85 individuals still on death row, it substitutes life imprisonment with hard labour; for future prosecutions of crimes previously punishable by death, the highest penalty will be life imprisonment with aggravated hard labour.
Activists and rights groups see the abolition victory as a stepping-stone to greater change, including rehabilitation for those accused of crimes.
“This campaign was for the culture of nonviolence, not just to change the law,” Younan told The New Arab. “We want a civilised state that protects life.”
Paul Hefel-James is an independent journalist based in Beirut, covering migration and refugee issues, the humanitarian sector, and conflict
Follow him on X: @paul_hj_

EU approves $7.1B in new defense aid for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:04:46 UTC
20:04:46 KST

Seyma Erkul Dayanc
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
The European Commission on Monday approved €6.1 billion ($7.1 billion) in new defense aid for Ukraine, including air and missile defense systems, missiles, ammunition and radars.
“On Ukraine's Independence Day, Europe shows our support is unfaltering and concrete,” European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said.
“Today, we have approved €6.1 billion ($7.1 billion) for the air and missile defense systems, missiles, ammunition and radars that Ukraine urgently needs,” she added.
“As Russia intensifies its attacks, we are stepping up to help Ukraine protect its people and defend its skies. Europe stands with Ukraine and we will deliver what it needs, when it needs it,” von der Leyen said.
The funding is part of the €90 billion ($105.1 billion) Ukraine Support Loan, which provides €60 billion ($70.1 billion) for defense and €30 billion ($35 billion) in budgetary support for 2026-2027.
The commission said Russia's increased use of ballistic missiles and jet-powered drones has made it increasingly urgent to strengthen Ukraine's air defenses and accelerate deliveries of critical defense equipment.
The latest approval adds to €16 billion ($18.7 billion) in defense procurement plans already approved under the loan, of which €8.35 billion ($9.7 billion) has been disbursed, according to the commission.
Most of the procurements will be sourced from European defense companies.
The commission said deliveries should be increased through drawing on existing stocks, reprioritizing orders and increasing production.
It added Ukraine can request payments by submitting contracts signed with defense companies.
It will review the contracts before releasing funds to ensure they cover procurements agreed with EU member states and the commission.
The €90 billion ($105.1 billion) Ukraine Support Loan was established by the European Parliament and the EU Council in February 2026.
The EU and its member states have provided €220.2 billion ($256.9 billion) in overall support to Ukraine since 2022, including €3.8 billion ($4.4 billion) from proceeds generated by immobilized Russian assets, according to the commission.

Breaking the law makes people seem less moral, even when the act is unchanged
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:00:40 UTC
20:00:40 KST

Being told that an action was illegal made people judge the very same behavior as more morally wrong, and the person doing it as less moral, according to our new research published in the Journal of Experimental Social Psychology.
Laws can be understood as reflecting society’s moral values. Behaviors that people consider especially harmful or unacceptable are more likely to be prohibited. Research supports this direction of influence, showing that public opinion and prevailing moral attitudes can shape legal decisions and even affect the perceived legitimacy of the law.
But the relationship may also work in reverse. If the law tells us what society, or an authoritative institution, has deemed acceptable or unacceptable, could knowing whether something is illegal actually change how morally wrong we think it is?
Previous studies investigating this possibility have produced mixed findings. High-profile legal decisions have sometimes shifted public attitudes in the direction of the law, sometimes had little effect, and sometimes produced more complicated responses. One explanation is that real-world legal rulings are accompanied by political debate, media coverage, and strong pre-existing beliefs, making it difficult to isolate the influence of legality itself.
Mane Kara-Yakoubian (myself: @ManeYakoubian) and colleagues therefore examined whether an action’s legal status could serve as a simple cue that people use when making moral judgments. Across four experiments, we tested whether this influence would persist when people broke laws unintentionally, when laws came from a totalitarian rather than democratic government, and when legal rules agreed or conflicted with prevailing social norms.
Across the four studies, the final analytic samples included 1,053 participants. Experiments 1-3 recruited participants from a Canadian university psychology research participant pool, resulting in final samples of 228, 250, and 254 participants, respectively. Experiment 4 recruited Canadian residents through Prolific and retained 321 participants after exclusions.
Participants read ten scenarios describing morally relevant behaviors carried out in fictitious countries, such as burning a national flag, using a racial slur, hunting deer, or abandoning a shopping cart, among others. Depending on the experiment and condition, the same behaviors were described as illegal or “not illegal.”
Participants rated how morally wrong each action was on a seven-point scale from 1, “not at all wrong,” to 7, “very wrong,” and rated the actor’s moral character on a seven-point scale from “extremely immoral” to “extremely moral.” They also completed the 30-item Moral Foundations Questionnaire, which measures concerns related to harm, fairness, loyalty, authority, and purity; our analyses focused particularly on its six-item Authority component.
Experiment 1 manipulated legality within participants, whereas Experiment 2 used a between-subjects design that also varied whether an illegal act was committed intentionally or unintentionally. Experiments 3 and 4 used mixed designs, varying legality within participants while manipulating government type or social norms between participants. Specifically, Experiment 3 varied whether laws came from a democratic or totalitarian government, while Experiment 4 varied whether local residents considered the behavior socially acceptable, socially unacceptable, or provided no social-norm information.
Across all four experiments, legality consistently influenced moral judgment. Participants rated identical actions as more morally wrong when they were described as illegal rather than not illegal, and they also evaluated the people performing those actions as less moral. Importantly, this was not simply because intentionally breaking a rule was viewed negatively.
In Experiment 2, illegal actions were judged more harshly even when participants were explicitly told that the person had broken the law unintentionally, although intentional law-breaking produced the harshest judgments.
In Experiment 3, the effect also persisted regardless of how the law had been created. Illegal actions and their actors were judged more negatively whether the laws came from a democratically elected government or a totalitarian government in which citizens had no say.
Social norms mattered too, but they did not simply replace the influence of the law. In Experiment 4, participants judged behaviors more harshly when local residents considered them socially unacceptable and more favourably when residents considered them acceptable, yet legality continued to affect moral evaluations across the social-norm conditions.
Legality had its greatest influence when the law and prevailing social norms pointed in the same direction—for example, when an illegal action was also socially disapproved of. When legality and social norms conflicted, however, the effect of legality was no longer significant.
Individual differences mattered as well: in three of the four experiments, participants who more strongly viewed respect for authority as a moral virtue showed a larger effect of legality on their judgments.
One limitation is that although we also used fictitious countries to minimize pre-existing beliefs about particular nations and their laws, participants may still have projected their own associations onto those countries.
Taken together, our findings suggest that laws may do more than regulate behavior or reflect existing moral values: legal status itself can become part of the information people use to decide what is morally right or wrong and how they evaluate the people involved.
The research, “Between law and conscience: Act legality shapes moral evaluation,” was authored by Mane Kara-Yakoubian, Jonathan A. Fugelsang, and Alexander C. Walker.

The Best Home Theater Projectors in 2026: XGIMI, Hisense, Leica, and More
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:00:00 UTC
20:00:00 KST

I've seen some of the best movies and tested some of the best home projectors this year. Massively entertaining films like The Odyssey, Project Hail Mary, and Toy Story 5 have made 2026 a standout year for movies, and new home theater projectors like the Xgimi Titan Noir Max and the AWOL Vision Aetherion Max have upped the game in terms of beautiful, cinematic, color-accurate images at home.
I've been reviewing the best TVs and projectors for years. That's why I put these latest home theater projectors to the test, running benchmarks to check for vividness, brightness, skin tone variations, and whether dark scenes look too washed out. I watched countless Netflix movies and 4K Blu-ray films—all for the cause. My main takeaway? These top models are giving the local cinema something to worry about. Bring some popcorn and a comfortable recliner, and you're basically there.
For more TV recommendations based on our expert testing, check out our related guides, including the Best RGB TVs, Best TVs, Best Large TVs, Best OLED TVs, and Best Cheap TVs. If you’re really undecided, read our guide on How to Buy the Right TV in 2026.
Love WIRED? Add us as a preferred source on Google to see more of us.
Best Overall
Picking the best projector was not easy, especially since there's so much competition. The Xgimi Titan Noir Max won me over because of the dynamic, self-adjusting iris. As you watch a movie or show, the projector adjusts to allow more light in (for bright scenes) or closes to reduce light (for dark scenes). For example, during a nighttime sequence in the movie Hoppers on Disney+, the iris will close to make the blacks and grays look dark and richly detailed. That feature alone sets the Titan Noir Max apart.
But it’s also highly capable in many other ways. It has an outstanding 10,000:1 native contrast ratio and a 7,000-lumen brightness rating, which helped it blast through all of my benchmarks and test scenarios. An early morning scene in the movie The Creator looked exactly like I would expect it to in real life, showing texture on the seaside cliffs. Even in a sun-drenched room, battle scenes in the movie War Machine looked bright and clear—outperforming the Hisense XR10 model.
More functionally, it has four adjustable feet that allow you to adjust the height or even set the projector on a side table and angle it toward a wall.
One downside is that, like many projectors, it doesn't natively run a streaming OS like Google TV, but I prefer to connect a Blu-ray player or Google TV Streamer anyway.
Best for Gaming
I’ll never forget the first time I played the game 007 First Light projected on a wall in my house using the Hisense XR10. An ocean scene looked bright blue and realistic, thanks to the excellent color processing on this projector. I felt very little lag using the low-latency mode, and the built-in speakers (the best I've tested on a projector) never felt lacking.
The big and boxy XR10 is exactly what I would expect a high-end cinema projector to look like. It’s heavy at 23.4 pounds, but that’s because of its massive speaker and lens. Although I prefer the long adjustable legs on the Xgimi Titan Noir Max, the XR10 is stable and has a nicely subdued dark metallic look.
The iris is adjustable (in seven different ways) to allow more light in or to make darker scenes even more vivid. Games in particular looked rich and colorful, including one of my all-time favorites, Senua's Saga: Hellblade II. A beach scene had a texture and moodiness that was truly jaw-dropping.
I loved watching the movie Awake on Netflix, which is dark in almost every scene. (It was the first time I noticed a guy in the background of one scene wearing a blue shirt.) Most projectors render these dark scenes without enough contrast, but the XR10 makes them look stunning.
The XR10 is a monster of a home cinema projector, with only the Titan Noir Max performing just a bit better on color and brightness. And you do need to adjust the iris manually in the settings, though (unlike the automatic adjustments of the Titan Noir Max).
Best for Movies
Leica has a rich history making cameras, and this Leica Cine Play 1 projector is a showcase of that superior craftsmanship. The Leica Summicron lens renders ultra-realistic video with extreme clarity and exceptional color accuracy. I watched Hoppers in a windowless testing room, and the furry creatures all looked stunningly realistic—you could even see individual strands of fur cleanly.
That’s why I think it's the best projector for movies and shows. Colors pop on the screen like you are watching in a theater. This model exceeds the BT.2020 color gamut spec by 107 percent, and you can tell in movies like Spider-Man: Across the Spider-Verse. In one segment, the reds and blues looked even more vivid than I remembered at the theater.
The compact size (about the same as a large lunch box) and good portability (weighing about 15 pounds) were two highlights for me. I also like the metallic design with the iconic red Leica logo on top. The projector can easily sit on a table, or you can add the Cine Play 1 Floor Stand for $495. The power cord connects to the base of the stand, which makes for a very clean setup.
It's impressive, but not as impressive in a bright room, unfortunately—this projector is best utilized at night. And it lacks the dynamic iris of the Titan Noir Max (which is, admittedly, much pricier).
Best Budget
I had to double check the price of the BenQ W4100i because it's so much cheaper than my other top picks. Yet, of all the home cinema projectors I've tested in the last few months, the quick and easy setup on this model, plus a few unusual perks, made it a top pick.
It's easy to configure, even though it uses the older Android TV operating system. I asked the onboard Google Assistant bot to start the install process and it only took a few minutes to do the whole thing. While the dark gray enclosure is understated, I liked how easy it was to adjust the focus and throw distance using analog levers on the top of the projector.
At this price, the W4100i is not meant to compete with the titans of home cinema like the Hisense XR10, and it matches an older color gamut spec (Rec.709). The lumens rating is only 3,200, far below the Titan Noir Max's 7,000.
Still, there are a few interesting perks with the BenQ W4100i. It has a mode that can match the 24p frame rate of movies for a more fluid look. With the refresh rate cranked to 240 Hz, playing the game NTE on my gaming laptop, I came to realize just how much I like using this projector for low-latency gaming. My controller flicks were rendered immediately during chaotic battle scenes.
I’m not sure why BenQ insists on still using a dongle attachment for the operating system. You can skip it altogether if you use one of the HDMI ports for a Blu-ray player or another device. In the end, the lower-than-expected price, low latency, and easy setup are what sold me on this BenQ.
Honorable Mentions
Epson Lifestudio Grand Plus for $3,800: A powerhouse for movies and shows, this short-throw projector can be set right next to your projector screen or blank wall and display a huge image. It also, surprisingly, has Google Gemini built in, which can do some surprising tasks like create slideshows, fit with animations, original images, voice-overs, and more.
AWOL Aetherion Max RGB Laser UST Projector for $4,449: I’m currently in the middle of testing this short-throw model, and it is an engineering marvel. The incredible 6000:1 contrast ratio and triple-laser light source are just the beginning. I’ve been impressed by the color accuracy, brightness, deep blacks, and extreme clarity across the entire image.
Frequently Asked Questions
Why Use a Home Theater Projector?
It’s an eternal debate—should you pull the shades, fire up a home theater projector, and watch a movie like you’re at the local cineplex? Or is it better to use a massive OLED or RGB television that will show a clearer image during a sunny day? Here’s my take after testing tons of the latest projectors and TVs: I prefer projectors for movies because I can max out the screen size to 120 inches or more. There’s just nothing like watching a 12-foot projected image of a movie with Dolby Atmos surround sound at home.
What Do You Need to Use a Home Theater Projector?
The short answer is quite simple: You just need a white wall. Purists will say a true home cinema experience requires a projector screen and a windowless room, and I have a testing room just for that purpose. However, all of the models I’m recommending are so bright and colorful that they perform quite well on a large wall without needing a projector screen. I do recommend room-darkening shades, though, because a darker room does create a better image.
Why Are Home Theater Projectors So Expensive?
Consumer-grade home theater projectors cost around $3,000 or more. In my experience, the latest large OLED and RGB televisions can easily cost just as much. I strongly recommend sticking to the $3,000 price point for a home cinema projector, though, because many midrange models (e.g., under $2,000) don’t look that colorful or bright. They also suffer from some serious contrast problems. For serious movie and TV fans, I’d avoid projectors that cost less than $1,000.

Guidance: The Defence Ordnance, Munitions and Explosives Safety Regulator (DOSR) – Regulatory Notices
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:55:07 BST
19:55:07 KST

The Defence Ordnance, Munitions and Explosives Safety Regulator (DOSR) – Regulatory Notices
DOSR Regulatory Notices may detail new or revised safety criteria or parameters for scenarios under the remit of the DOSR.
Documents
Details
The Defence Safety Authority’s (DSA’s) regulators provide regulatory advice, normally through issuing Regulatory Notices or Regulatory Instructions. These are published by the individual DSA regulator as stand-alone documents. All regulatory advice is strongly recommended practice. The burden of proof that the regulation is satisfied rests entirely with the regulated community. Care is taken to ensure that regulatory advice details what is required and to what standard but is not prescriptive as to how it is to be achieved.
These scenarios include: Defence Ordnance, Munitions and Explosives (OME) Acquisition, Defence In-service and Operational Safety Management, Defence Ranges, Major Accident Control, and Laser Safety, covered by the DOSR Publication suite DSA 02.OME and DSA 03.OME.
Regulatory Notices are usually issued to facilitate a change in procedure or require an action to be undertaken to improve the level of protection or instruction in a potentially dangerous situation. DOSR Regulatory Notices remain extant until either cancelled or incorporated into DSA 02.OME regulations or DSA 03.OME guidance material and should be acted upon within a reasonable time if a time period is not stated.

India used pellets, grenades on Gen Z protests: What Amnesty report reveals
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:53:21 UTC
19:53:21 KST

India used pellets, grenades on Gen Z protests: What Amnesty report reveals
Security forces used tear gas, pellet guns and electric shock devices against student protesters, Amnesty found in its investigation.
New Delhi, India – An investigation by human rights group Amnesty International has confirmed that Indian government forces used lethal weapons, including pellet-firing shotguns, grenades, batons and electric shock devices against demonstrators in Gen Z protests that rocked the national capital last month.
On July 20, thousands of protesters had all but shut down New Delhi, blocking off Parliament Street, demanding the resignation of then-Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan following a string of examination scandals involving the leaking of national exam papers and other irregularities.
More than 100 students were injured in the crackdown by police and paramilitary forces that day. Indian newspapers obtained hospital records that showed that doctors had treated pellet wounds in several cases.
India’s opposition, led by Congress party leader Rahul Gandhi, has since called on Home Minister Amit Shah, seen as Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s confidant, to answer questions about the alleged police brutality and has joined protesters in calling for his resignation.
But despite mounting evidence and growing political criticism, the Modi government repeatedly insisted that security forces had been measured in their response to the protests and denied using excessive force.
Now, an Amnesty investigation has found the use of tactics that Indian law enforcement rulebooks themselves warn against using in all but exceptional circumstances.
What happened on July 20 in New Delhi?
In July, the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), a satirical, youth-led movement which gathered momentum in response to the national examinations scandal, called on its supporters to march on the Indian Parliament after a monthlong sit-in failed to oust the education minister.
Two days before the march, the police forcibly removed renowned activist Sonam Wangchuk, who had been taking part in a hunger strike. That move galvanised public anger, bringing out more protesters in New Delhi.
On the morning of the march day, the police used tear gas as protesters swelled, then attacked them with electric shock batons, as well as shooting at them with pellet guns, Amnesty International’s Evidence Lab has verified from video and photographic evidence alongside witness testimony.
Amnesty also found that government forces had put up barricades and enforced a communications blackout.
“The weapons were deployed in a manner that breached international law and standards and domestic policing guidelines,” Amnesty said in a statement on Monday.
The rights group’s report also noted that the Delhi Police had publicly denied any disproportionate use of force, specifically pellet guns. The police also repeated this before India’s top court during a hearing about the alleged use of excessive force.
Amnesty says the evidence it has gathered “directly contradicts [the police’s] account”.
Four days after the July 20 march, as protests spread across the country, police in Bihar state’s Siwan town opened fire on protesters, injuring at least three youths.
Did government forces fire pellets at protesters?
Following the July 20 protest, several videos and photos emerged of protesters with injuries consistent with pellet wounds, which were reflected in their medical records as well.
The Evidence Lab verified two videos showing a paramilitary Rapid Action Force officer firing a shotgun into the crowd at the intersection of Connaught Place and Parliament Street in New Delhi, where protesters had gathered.
At least two protesters had wounds consistent with those caused by birdshot, a hunting round that fires a large number of small metal pellets, the group noted.
“The doctors confirmed that they were pellet injuries. Thankfully, my bones have been saved, but my body has been scarred badly,” one protester told Amnesty.
Amnesty said birdshot ammunition has not been developed for law enforcement purposes due to the widespread dispersion of the metal pellets, which “is inherently inaccurate and presents a high risk of serious injuries to the targeted person and even bystanders”.
Amnesty also said the police did not issue a public warning before firing pellet guns, as recommended by the Indian government’s Bureau for Police Research and Development.
Police and security forces have used metal pellets for more than a decade in Indian-administered Kashmir, leading to the first mass blinding during a 2016 civilian uprising.
Posting on X, Delhi Police called the reports of pellet injuries during the latest protests “fake news”, “completely false and misleading” and warned that “appropriate legal action” would be taken against anyone “spreading rumours”.
A subsequent internal inquiry by India’s paramilitary forces, however, reportedly found that personnel had fired at least seven rounds of ammunition containing metal pellets.
“Instead of facilitating the right to protest, Indian authorities suppressed it first with a communication blackout, barricades and transport disruption. They then attempted to crush it with unnecessary or excessive use of force against peaceful protesters, including children,” said Aakar Patel, chair of the board, Amnesty International India.
“This heavy-handed response was state-sanctioned violence masked as crowd control. The continued impunity after a month is a testament to that,” Patel said.
Did police use tear gas grenades and batons?
Government forces did use tear gas grenades to disperse the crowd at several places in New Delhi, as seen by Al Jazeera and verified by Amnesty, not just on July 20 to prevent CHP supporters’ march to Parliament.
“Tear gas grenades releasing an excessive amount of explosive energy are extremely dangerous and should be prohibited for use in public assemblies,” Amnesty said, referring to videos of tear gas shells exploding near students.
The group also noted that witnesses observed that “tear gas grenades were launched directly at protesters instead of at an angled trajectory above the head of protesters, at odds with UN Guidance on the use of Less-Lethal Weapons in Law Enforcement”.
Amnesty has also verified claims that the police used lathis, the Indian version of batons, to beat protesters.
The UN special rapporteur on torture considers lathis to be inherently cruel, inhuman or degrading as “they deliver a greater level [of] kinetic force than conventional batons, causing excessive pain and increasing the risk of serious injury” and has called for them to be prohibited, a position that Amnesty supports.
The group also found men in civilian clothing beating protesters “while uniformed officers, who escorted them toward the crowd, stand beside them and make no attempt to intervene”, as visible in videos seen by Al Jazeera. Several officials were not wearing their name tags or badge numbers, as required.
What has been the reaction to the use of excessive force?
A day after the crackdown in New Delhi, CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke told the crowd, “Every police person who attacked you would be identified and dragged to the courts”.
The group also launched a platform for protesters to upload videos and photos from the crackdown.
The opposition, led by the Congress’s Gandhi, pushed the home minister for a discussion on the issue in Parliament, an issue that plagued the monsoon session with Shah missing.
Gandhi argued that either Shah ordered the usage of lethal weapons, in which case “he is guilty”, or he was unaware of the situation, which makes him “incompetent” for the job.
Sahil Lochab, a 19-year-old who lost vision in one eye due to pellet injuries, said the police had been refusing to register his complaint. In response, Gandhi staged a seven-hour sit-in outside the office of the Delhi Police chief, insisting that a case be registered over the use of pellet guns on protesters, alongside Lochab.
After Gandhi’s pressure, the police relented. A student at the University of Delhi, Lochab received multiple pellet injuries on his chest, back, arms and face. Several pellets could not be taken out, he said in his complaint.
“My medical documents show that there are over 200 pellets in my body. Doctors have told me that the possibility of my eyesight coming back is less than 1 percent,” Lochab wrote in his complaint.

Eastern Libya executes 10 convicted on terrorism charges, sparking rights outcry

Eastern Libya executes 10 convicted on terrorism charges, sparking rights outcry
CAIRO (AP) — Authorities in eastern Libya said they executed 10 people after their conviction by military courts on terrorism-related charges.
The executions, announced Sunday, triggered condemnations by rights groups in the North African country that is divided between rival administrations, each backed by a set of militias and foreign governments.
The office of the military prosecutor in eastern Libya said the 10 people were executed by firing squad after yearslong trials. The office is overseen by the self-styled Libyan National Army, which is commanded by powerful Gen. Khalifa Hifter and controls the eastern and southern parts of Libya.
The people were convicted of charges ranging from joint terrorist groups to assassinations of military personnel and civilians, the office said in a statement.
The statement didn’t provide further details about the charges, and when or where the executions took place, but said they were executed after “all legal procedures” were concluded.
Local media reported that the executions took place in the notorious Qarnada military prison in the northeastern town of Shahat, and that their families were notified to receive their bodies from a hospital in the city of Benghazi.
Rights groups condemned the executions and questioned the trials. The National Institution for Human Rights in Libya said military trial of civilians “raises fundamental questions concerning jurisdiction, judicial independence, and guarantees of a fair trial.”
The group called for Libya’s chief prosecutor and judicial authorities to investigate the executions and all procedures taken through their trials.
It cited a Constitutional Court ruling that said the trial of civilians before military courts for terrorism-related offenses and crimes against the state was unconstitutional.
International rights groups have repeatedly criticized the detention and sometimes execution of people after unfair trials. Amnesty International has said that Libya has retained the death penalty for a wide range of offenses, with courts in both eastern and western Libya continuing to impose death sentences for murder following “grossly unfair trials.”
Libya was plunged into chaos and division after a NATO-backed uprising that toppled and killed its longtime autocrat Moammar Gadhafi in 2011.
The county has been divided for years between rival administrations in the east and west, each backed by armed groups and foreign governments.

Wheelchair basketball coach Soltani pleased with Turkey camp
TEHRAN - Iran national wheelchair basketball team head coach Behrouz Soltani expressed satisfaction with his team’s preparations in Turkey, saying the squad followed their plans and are now ready to begin their campaign at the Ottawa 2026 IWBF World Championships.
The Iranian national wheelchair basketball team, preparing for the upcoming World Championship, held a training camp in Turkey and played six friendly matches against Turkey and Poland. Iran recorded four wins and two defeats during the camp.
Soltani said the camp and the friendly matches had significantly contributed to the team’s preparations and helped the coaching staff gain a deeper understanding of the players and the team’s overall condition ahead of the 2026 IWBF World Championships.
“Turkey, as the hosts, and Poland were our opponents in the tournament. We played three matches against each team. We defeated Poland in all three games, while we beat Turkey once,” Soltani said.
“However, the main objective of the camp and these matches was not the results. We wanted to improve our preparations for the World Championship, and we achieved that very well.”
The head coach added that his players’ performances in Turkey had increased his confidence ahead of the tournament.
“Based on what I saw from the players in Turkey, I am more hopeful that we can reach an ideal level for the World Championship,” he said.
The World Championship will also determine the continental qualification berths for the Paralympics qualifying tournament. Soltani stressed that Iran will be targeting positive results while also using the competition as an important step toward the Asian Para Games.
Iran’s next training camp will begin in Tehran on Sept. 6 and continue without interruption until the team’s departure for Canada.
Regarding Iran’s opponents, Soltani said his team have been drawn into Group D alongside Morocco, Germany and Canada.
“Our opponents are currently playing preparation tournaments. We monitor their situation on a daily basis because, if we want to achieve our desired result at the World Championship, we must get positive results from the group stage,” he said.
Soltani also confirmed that Iran’s 12-player squad for the World Championship has already been finalized and expressed hope that preparations would continue according to plan until the team travel to Canada and the tournament officially begins.
The Ottawa 2026 IWBF World Championships will be held from Sept. 9 to 19.

Will Iran's ambassador to Lebanon leave when his visa expires?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:47:38 UTC
19:47:38 KST

Breadcrumb
Will Iran's ambassador-designate to Lebanon leave when his visa expires?
Uncertainty surrounds the case of Mohammad Reza Sheibani, the Iranian ambassador-designate to Beirut, who Lebanon has not accredited, and whether he will leave Lebanese territory when his visa expires on Monday, 24 August.
This follows confirmation from the Lebanese Foreign Ministry that "his continued presence is contrary to a final sovereign decision that must be enforced and is not subject to any regularisation of status".
The development comes as political tensions rise in Lebanese-Iranian relations over Iran's position on Lebanese state decisions concerning the exclusive possession of arms, which Lebanon considers interference in its internal affairs.
With no statement issued by the Iranian Embassy in Beirut, The New Arab has learnt that Sheibani may apply to extend his stay in Lebanon in his capacity as a civilian rather than a diplomat, although this would not allow him to perform any official diplomatic duties.
In a statement to a local media outlet last Thursday, 20 August, Lebanese Foreign Minister Youssef Raggi said that "this matter leaves no room for interpretation or discretion. Once any diplomat is declared persona non grata, they are required to leave the territory of the host state, and no visa, entry permit or residence permit previously granted to them has any legal effect that would allow their continued presence. Therefore, talking about renewing any of these constitutes a legal absurdity and contradicts the most basic rules of international law and established diplomatic norms".
Raggi stressed that "any talk of Sheibani's visa remaining valid or of the possibility of renewing it has no legal standing and cannot constitute a basis for his continued presence in Lebanon".
"Sheibani's continued presence on Lebanese territory after a decision declaring him persona non grata was issued is contrary to a clear sovereign decision by the Lebanese state. This decision is final and must be enforced and cannot be subject to exceptions, interpretation or circumvention. Nor can it be subject to any regularisation of status under any name," he noted.
In this context, lawyer and constitutional expert Said Malik told TNA that "with the expiry of Sheibani's residence in Lebanon, he may apply for a six-month extension of his residence as a civilian rather than a diplomat, as is the case with other Iranian nationals".
"The relevant authorities must, in accordance with the decision of the Lebanese Foreign Ministry, reject the extension, because the decision to declare the aforementioned ambassador persona non grata in Lebanon is unequivocally a sovereign decision that all authorities are required to abide by. Any decision to the contrary by the competent authorities would be considered a violation of the sovereignty of the state, its laws and its decisions and would require accountability in accordance with due process," he added.
On 24 March, Lebanon decided to withdraw Sheibani's accreditation and gave him until 29 March to leave, citing what the Lebanese state described as "Tehran's violation of the established norms and rules governing diplomatic relations between the two countries".
The move sparked a major internal dispute, particularly between Hezbollah and the Amal Movement, headed by Parliament Speaker Nabih Berri, and their opponents.
It also strained relations between the two sides, with Hezbollah and Amal rejecting the decision on one hand and the presidencies of the republic and the government on the other.
The Lebanese Foreign Ministry said at the time that "the decision to withdraw approval for the accreditation of the Iranian ambassador, based on Article 9 of the Vienna Convention on Diplomatic Relations, does not constitute a severing of diplomatic relations with Iran. Rather, it is a measure against the ambassador for violating the rules and obligations of diplomatic conduct, given that he is an ambassador-designate to Lebanon. Article 41 of the aforementioned convention prohibits diplomats from interfering in the internal affairs of the states to which they are accredited."
Since the latest developments in Lebanon and the region, the Lebanese government has adopted tough positions towards Iran over its attacks on Arab and Gulf states, in addition to imposing stricter measures on Iranians.
This followed Israeli airstrikes on two hotels in the capital and its outskirts during the March offensive, which Israel said were targeted because they housed members of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, as well as Israeli threats to target Revolutionary Guard members in Lebanon.
During a Cabinet session held on 5 March, Prime Minister Nawaf Salam asked the relevant ministries and departments, as well as security and military agencies, to issue appropriate directives and instructions to verify the presence of members of Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps in Lebanon.
He also called for them to "take firm and immediate action to prevent any security or military activity or operation they may carry out from Lebanese territory, regardless of their status or the cover under which they operate, and to arrest them under the supervision of the competent judiciary in preparation for their deportation".
The Cabinet also decided to reinstate the requirement for Iranian nationals to obtain entry visas to Lebanon, "for the purpose of controlling the borders and preventing any activity or operation that could undermine security or the use of Lebanese territory to carry out specific objectives".

See states’ kindergarten vaccination rates—from highest to lowest
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:46:18 UTC
19:46:18 KST

It’s back-to-school season. For most parents of the U.S.’s school-aged kids, that means filling out medical forms and making sure the children are up to date with their vaccinations. But this ritual is shifting: The 2025–2026 school year saw a record low number of kindergartners vaccinated for measles, polio, tetanus, and more. At the same time, more kids in this age group had exemptions from at least one vaccine that school year than at any other point in the past decade.
Meanwhile the diseases these vaccines protect against are making a comeback. Take measles, for example: The U.S. officially eliminated the disease in 2000 with the combined measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. But in the past few years, that progress stalled, and measles is on the rise. So far this year, officials have recorded more than 2,500 measles cases in the U.S.—the most since the virus was wiped out in the U.S. 25 years ago.
We analyzed the latest vaccine data to better understand what states in the country are most at risk of an outbreak and how vaccination rates are changing among the U.S.’s schoolkids.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
How Vaccine Rates Are Changing among Kindergartners
More than 90 percent of U.S. kindergarteners still get the MMR vaccine. But according to the latest data from the U.S. Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, MMR vaccination rates among kindergarteners have fallen from about 95 percent to 92.4 percent in the past 10 years. The country saw similar declines for vaccines that protect against polio, hepatitis B, and diphtheria, tetanus and acellular pertussis.
For the most contagious diseases, even a small dip in vaccination can trigger population-wide problems. “Measles is the single most contagious disease that we know of,” says Adam Ratner, a professor of pediatrics and microbiology at New York University. “It is more contagious than flu or COVID or polio or Ebola or anything else you can think of.” Around 90 percent of unvaccinated people exposed to the virus will become infected.
In most states, specific childhood vaccinations, including MMR, are required to attend public school. Depending on state policy, parents may be able to opt out of certain or all vaccines by claiming an exemption for medical, religious or philosophical reasons. Nationwide, the proportion of kindergartners with nonmedical exemptions has doubled in recent years—from about 1.9 percent 10 years ago to 4 percent today.
How States Break Down
Not all states are equal. Many have seen sharp declines in vaccination rates—kindergarten MMR vaccinations in Idaho, for instance, has seen a drop of 15 percentage points in the past decade. Others have remained mostly stable or even increased, however. In the past 10 years in Connecticut, for instance, kindergarten MMR rates have increased from 96.7 percent to 98.6 percent in the 2025–2026 school year. In Maine, rates have risen from 94.9 percent to 98 percent over the same period. And in New York State, rates have stayed relatively flat over the past decade, with a slight rate uptick from 97.3 percent to 97.7 percent.
In general, states that don't allow personal exemptions have higher vaccination rates, says Lori Handy, an associate director at the Vaccine Education Center at the Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia. (About two thirds of states don’t allow personal exemptions, although only four states prohibit both personal and religious exemptions.)
That doesn’t mean outbreaks of diseases such as measles don’t or won’t happen in these states. Even in places with the highest vaccination rates, pockets of unvaccinated people can enable viruses to spread. Virginia, for instance, has an overall MMR vaccination rate above the national average. But it’s also seen 177 measles cases this year.
Why Vaccines Rates Are Still in Decline
A county’s or state’s total vaccination rates may reflect a combination of state and local laws, community customs, individual beliefs—and the influence of antivaccine rhetoric. Vaccination rates began to dip after the COVID pandemic. The emergence of this trend was in part because of the challenges of getting to a doctor’s office during that time but was also likely driven by a wave of vaccine skepticism.
“We’ve seen, really, just a shift in the American public in terms of individuals who have lower trust in the health care system, more skepticism around vaccines [and] a lot more misinformation around vaccines,” Handy says.
That misinformation is hard to ignore when it is coming from the highest echelons of power. The new CDC data were released just days after President Donald Trump signed an executive order seeking to break up the MMR vaccine into separate shots for the three diseases it protects against, a change that health experts say would only confuse and discourage parents from getting their children vaccinated. The overwhelming evidence shows that the MMR vaccine is safe and effective as a single shot.
“All parents—regardless of their feelings about vaccines—nobody wants harm to come to their kids. It makes the job of a parent very difficult if you have people on the news, people in the newspaper, people high up in government who are stoking doubt about vaccines,” Ratner says.
Now, as millions of families get back to school—and back to germs—Ratner and Handy both recommend that parents speak with their children’s doctors about any vaccines they may need.
For children who can’t be vaccinated for medical reasons or pregnant teachers and family members, a lack of herd immunity can be life-threatening, Handy explains. And for unvaccinated families, it poses a health risk, as well as the possibility that children will need to isolate at home for several weeks. Vaccinated families generally don’t need to worry about those risks, she adds.
“The lower the vaccination rates are, the more we anticipate outbreaks,” Handy says.

Melting Arctic ice, threatened forests and the growing toll of extreme weather
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:45:38 UTC
19:45:38 KST

Rachel Feltman: Happy Monday, listeners! For Scientific American’s Science Quickly, I’m Rachel Feltman. You’re listening to our weekly science news roundup.
We spotted lots of important climate-related stories last week, so we’re going to hunker down and focus on the environment today—with the exception of a couple of very fun stories we’ll save for the end of the show, as a treat.
First up, we’ve got some troubling news about forests. Last Tuesday the U.S. Department of Agriculture proposed a plan to kill something called the 2001 Roadless Area Conservation Rule. This Clinton-era rule pretty much does what it says on the tin: it took tens of millions of acres of national forests and grasslands that did not yet have roads on them and deemed that they would remain roadless. In the decades leading up to the Roadless Rule’s introduction, the logging industry had been encroaching on these wooded areas with access roads. Roadless areas ensure that swaths of these national forests are preserved, protecting animal habitats and allowing for recreational activities like hiking.
On supporting science journalism
If you're enjoying this article, consider supporting our award-winning journalism by subscribing. By purchasing a subscription you are helping to ensure the future of impactful stories about the discoveries and ideas shaping our world today.
The USDA described the policy in last week’s press release as a “one-size-fits-all restriction” that has “frustrated land managers and served as a barrier to wildfire risk reduction work.” It’s worth noting, however, that the Roadless Rule has always allowed roadbuilding and tree cutting when needed to reduce wildfire risk or otherwise support human health and safety. And experts have pointed out that, with most wildfires stemming from human activity, road construction and industrial incursions will likely make wildfires worse, not better.
The proposed rule will go through a 30-day public comment period before it can be finalized. You can submit a comment by going to Regulations.gov.
Speaking of humans traveling through places that used to be none of our business, last week China launched a summer cargo shipping route that will skirt the northern coast of Russia—a route that would be impossible without climate change. Here to tell us more is Scientific American’s chief newsletter editor Andrea Gawrylewski.
Thanks so much for coming on to talk to us about this.
Andrea Gawrylewski: Thank you so much for having me
Feltman: So this shipping route couldn’t exist, now it does. Let’s start with who’s actually doing the shipping?
Gawrylewski: Yeah. Earlier this month, a Chinese shipping company launched a new shipping route over the Arctic Ocean as kind of an expressway to get to Europe. This route will run along the northern coast of Russia to Europe, so through the North Sea. And experts expect that this shipping route will become a lot more traveled in the summer months because of the lack of ice at the Arctic.
Feltman: Yeah, so this was like actually not a passable route. How much melt had to happen to make this possible?
Gawrylewski: A tremendous amount of melt, and I will just back up with a fun historical fact since I just read a great book about this. But Captain James Cook was one of the explorers from Britain 250 years ago who was trying to find the Northwest Passage. This was a real desired route by the Admiralty of Britain and other European superpowers who wanted to find a faster way to get goods from the Pacific to Europe. And at the time of Cook’s final voyage, he was met with a wall of ice when he tried to find the Northwest Passage.
So much ice has melted, in fact, that NASA data is showing that the Arctic sea-ice extent is shrinking by 12% at least every decade. So it’s a tremendous amount of Arctic ice melt.
Feltman: And can you quantify a little bit, sort of, how valuable this is to shipping companies? You know, how much time is this gonna save?
Gawrylewski: So this subpolar route is way shorter than the standard one. So this trip that this Chinese cargo vessel will go on should take about 20 days compared to 40. So you’re looking at 50% faster movement of these goods around the Earth, which is pretty incredible.
Another major advantage of taking this route is that it stays entirely out of the way of some more heavily trafficked shipping routes like the Strait of Hormuz. Some experts are starting to refer to this new route as a new Silk Road, the “Ice Silk Road,” right? That would avoid a lot of these traditional routes and become a major artery in getting goods around the globe.
Feltman: Well, obviously this is, kind of, inherently a little disturbing because it couldn’t exist without climate change. Are there any other reasons to be concerned about this?
Gawrylewski: Yeah, for sure. I mean, just the fact that you will have tankers and cargo ships up in the Arctic Ocean, you might at the very least have more black carbon emissions from the shipping fuel, which would contribute to this positive feedback loop and cause the sea ice to melt even more quickly. Heavy fuel oil, which is like this cheap, high-energy and, and very tar-like material, which is left over from refining crude oil, has been banned in the Arctic since 2024, but people still get around it all the time.
These cargo ships that travel around the world have not been built to travel in the Arctic Ocean, right, where you have giant ice on the water. So you’re potentially, by exposing these cargo ships to these polar conditions, increasing the risk of oil spills and accidents, which as you know, is very damaging to local ecosystems.
Feltman: Well, thank you so much as always for, uh, coming on to share this with us.
Gawrylewski: Thrilled to be here.
Feltman: Listeners don’t forget to subscribe to Today in Science to get stories like this one in your inbox everyday.
Now for our last climate story of the day. A new poll conducted by the Walton Family Foundation and Gallup found that 38 percent of Americans lived through an extreme weather event in the past year. People within that group were more likely to say they feel pushed by circumstances beyond their control, and less likely to say that they “mostly feel able to shape [their own] path[s], even when things are difficult.” In other words, the report, which surveyed almost 7,000 adults from across the U.S., suggests that enduring an extreme weather event such as a flood, hurricane, tornado or hailstorm can make you more anxious and pessimistic about the future.
But it isn’t all gloom and doom. The report authors conclude that nearly three-quarters of U.S. adults “believe their community is worth investing in, even when they acknowledge it has room for improvement”—and this outlook doesn’t seem to disappear in the wake of extreme weather. But as the report points out, caring about your community can only do so much if you’re not given the tools to actually protect and improve it.
Now that we’ve swallowed our medicine for the week, here are those treats I promised. You know that feeling you get during cold and flu season, when it seems like your head is so full of snot that it’s hard to picture any room for your poor brain? Is that just me? I don’t think it's just me. Anyway, that’s basically what every winter is like for the long-clawed shrew. They’re not full of snot, per se—at least as far as I’m aware—but they are quite literally all nose. In a study published last Wednesday in Proceedings of the Royal Society B, scientists report that Sorex unguiculatus, aka the long-clawed shrew, has a wider snout in the winter than it does the rest of the year.
Having a seasonal schnoz surplus would be weird enough, but this story gets even weirder. See, scientists already knew that many shrews—along with some weasels, voles and moles—experienced changes in their skulls during the winter. But this seasonal flux, known as Dehnel’s phenomenon, involves winter shrinkage, not growth. Many animals reduce the overall mass of their bodies and internal organs to conserve energy in cold months. In shrews and those other scurrying mammals I referenced earlier, that includes a marked reduction in skull size and even brain mass. In the case of the long-clawed shrews featured in this new study, the average height of the braincase in specimens collected during winter was 12 percent smaller than those seen in young shrews collected in August and September. Meanwhile, the average snout was 6 percent wider in the winter shrews. As is the case with the skull and brain, this change seems to reverse when it gets warm again. One possible evolutionary benefit for a seasonal nose shift could be to warm up chilly winter air, or perhaps to better sniff out scant sources of food.
While we’re on the topic of wild noses, let’s talk about narwhals. So, not actually their nose but their unicornesque tusks are the only ones in the animal kingdom known to grow in a straight line. While the overall structure struts out straight from their faces, the tusk itself is actually a tight spiral—and those spirals always seem to go counterclockwise. Such uniformity is rare, which of course made scientists very curious. A study published last week in Nature Communications aims to explain the origin of this leftward spiral. Using advanced x-ray scanners, the researchers took a closer look at the microscopic threads of collagen that come together to form narwhal tusks. It turns out that they grow in a sort of double helix, with the internal collagen structures spinning right while the external structure spins left. These two opposing layers balance each other out and help the tusk grow in a straight line.
That’s all for this week’s news roundup. We’ll be back on Wednesday to talk about how damaged sperm could contribute to the risk of recurring miscarriages—and what would-be dads can do about it.

Our theme music was composed by Dominic Smith. Subscribe to Scientific American for more up-to-date and in-depth science news.
For Scientific American, this is Rachel Feltman. Have a great week!

Ukraine hosts European leaders as war with Russia intensifies
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:40:00 UTC
19:40:00 KST

Ukraine hosted key European allies Monday to press for more air defense support and increased pressure on Moscow, as Russian attacks kill civilians at the highest rate since the war’s opening months.
A meeting of the Coalition of the Willing will be jointly chaired by leaders of France and Germany, who will participate remotely, and U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who has arrived in Kyiv for his first trip abroad since taking office.
The leaders of Luxembourg, Moldova, Estonia and EU Council President Antonio Costa are also in Kyiv for the talks hosted on Ukraine's Independence Day and which come amid the war's latest escalation.
"Right now, things are really very difficult for all of us. But there is a force holding us firmly by the hand," Volodymyr Zelenskyy said in his address, adding: "It is the strength of our mutual circle."
He called on allies to give Ukraine "everything it needs to stop this war," after Russia has recently pounded Kyiv with ballistic missiles, ripping open apartment blocks and killing dozens in the capital.
The escalating Russian strikes have pushed civilian deaths to their highest levels since the first months of Moscow's 2022 invasion.
After almost every attack – which sees thousands hunker in shelters across Kyiv – Zelenskyy has issued public pleas for more air-defense support.
The European Union said Monday that it had released another 6.1 billion euros ($7.1 billion) in military aid for Ukraine to boost its air defenses.
The finance is part of a 90 billion-euro loan, including 60 billion euros in military aid, that the EU has said will go to Ukraine.
The meeting also comes amid political tensions for Zelenskyy, who rejected this weekend the call for wartime elections made by his former Defense Minister Mykhailo Fedorov.
Ahead of the talks, Ukraine has forged ahead with its campaign against Russia's logistics sites, hitting multiple warehouses belonging to e-commerce giant Ozon.
Ozon reported fires early Monday at its warehouses in Krasnodar and Makhachkala, both in southern Russia, adding that sites in Adygeysk and Nevinnomyssk were evacuated due to threats of drone attack.
Russian authorities also said debris from a Ukrainian drone attack killed two children and wounded nine others.
Russian leader Vladimir Putin said Saturday Kyiv had "opened Pandora's box" by targeting Russia's economy and promised further escalation, including against Ukrainian agriculture.
Russia is demanding hardline territorial and political concessions that Kyiv has rejected as a capitulation that would only enable another Russian attack.
"Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve," Burnham said in a statement before his arrival in Kyiv.
"We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace."
Burnham is set to announce that the British government is authorizing defense firm MBDA to release classified information needed to help Ukraine and France set up local production of the long-range SCALP missile.
Earlier Saturday, French President Emmanuel Macron pledged Paris would deliver new interceptor missiles.
The ballistic missiles Russia has been firing in their dozens are incredibly fast and travel with a high-arching trajectory, making them difficult to stop.
Kyiv's homegrown weapons cannot shoot them down, meaning Ukraine is reliant on advanced systems – chiefly, U.S. Patriot interceptors – to protect its skies.
But due to shortfalls globally since the U.S. launched its war on Iran, Ukraine has been left exposed.
Ahead of the meeting, Zelenskyy revealed the extent of the deficit, releasing usually closely guarded numbers.
He said deliveries of crucial Patriot interceptors had halved since 2023.
"Over the entire of 2023, Ukraine received 675 missiles, and over all of 2025 – 364, even though Russian missile strikes have increased," Zelenskyy said.
"For 2026, as currently projected, it is 264," he added, saying Ukraine was seeking a package of at least 300 for the upcoming winter.
The United States faces its own shortfall of the missiles during its war on Iran and has resisted releasing large numbers to Ukraine.
Zelenskyy said Russia could produce around 100 ballistic missiles a month.
Ukraine, meanwhile, has accelerated its own campaign of long-range strikes on Russian energy and logistics sites – including oil refineries and retail warehouses.
The Coalition of the Willing is a Franco-British initiative to deliver support to Ukraine and ramp up pressure on Russia.
Originally designed as a group of countries that would be willing to deploy peacekeeping troops to Ukraine in the event a ceasefire was reached, it has become a parallel forum for marshaling support to Kyiv as uncertainty persists over U.S. commitments under Donald Trump.

BANGKOK, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Thailand's labor market continued to grow in the second quarter of 2026 due to increases in both agricultural and non-farm employment, led by the construction sector, official data showed on Monday.
The number of employed persons in the Southeast Asian country rose 5.1 percent year-on-year to 41.5 million in the April-June period, accelerating from a 4.6 percent gain in the previous quarter, according to the National Economic and Social Development Council (NESDC).
Agricultural employment increased 6.5 percent from a year earlier, supported by higher farm output and agricultural prices, even as delayed rainfall pushed up the seasonally inactive labor force, the state planning agency said in a statement.
Meanwhile, the non-farm sector expanded 4.5 percent, benefiting from an 8.3 percent pickup in construction jobs in line with stronger private investment and a 5.8 percent increase in hotel and restaurant employment fueled by growing domestic tourism, particularly during long-holiday periods.
However, the nation's overall unemployment rate stood at 0.95 percent in the second quarter, representing around 400,000 unemployed individuals, edging up from 0.91 percent in the same period last year, said NESDC secretary-general Danucha Pichayanan.
The number of quasi-unemployed individuals working fewer than 24 hours per week climbed 8 percent year-on-year, driven by elevated underemployment, especially in the non-agricultural sector, Danucha told a news conference.
Looking ahead, he identified employment risks in the farm sector owing to the El Nino weather pattern, which is expected to intensify toward the year's end as lower rainfall and longer dry spells have already caused drought conditions in several areas, putting more pressure on agricultural production and rural labor. ■
