The Art of Mess in the AI Era
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
10:00:04 UTC
19:00:04 KST

Look closely at a painting, and you might be able to see where an artist changed their mind. Beneath the finished surface, there may be an abandoned line, a figure moved several inches to the left, a color that looked splendid in the morning and became unbearable by night. There may be a smudgy fingerprint at the edge of the canvas. The back may hold a date, a repair, uneven staples, a signature, or the name of a previous owner. These messy marks were once incidental to the artwork. Today they are considered evidence.
AI can produce an image in nano-seconds, then create hundreds of variations before a painter has mixed a color or cleaned a brush. Some of the results are technically bewildering and others inspire disbelief: How is this possible? Yet their abundance is changing our relationship to novelty. When nearly any visual idea can be summoned on demand, newness becomes easier to manufacture but harder to believe in. In an age of effortless images, the mess left behind by making something may become part of what makes it valuable.
So much recent visual culture can appear at once new and strangely familiar. Generative systems learn from immense archives of existing images, then assemble patterns according to statistical relationships. Their output can startle us, though the surprise often arrives cloaked in a recognizable visual fluency: the cinematic light, the dreamlike architecture, the glossy portrait or the eerily composed impossibility. After enough exposure, even the surreal can begin to feel conventional.
A study presented at the 2024 CHI Conference proffers one perspective about how this happens. Participants who used an AI image generator during a visual ideation exercise became more fixed on an initial example and produced fewer ideas, with less variety and originality, than those in the control group. The study involved only 60 people, so its findings should be treated cautiously, though they articulate something many artists and designers have begun to notice: a tool built to accelerate imagination can also narrow it by presenting a polished answer before a more difficult, original idea has had time to form.
Against this flood of frictionless imagery, fine art acquires another kind of presence. A physical artwork occupies time and holds emotion. An artist stood before it, considered it, changed it, ruined it, waited for it, and eventually decided to either finish or abandon it. All artwork contains a sequence of often messy choices that could have gone in any number of directions. The object becomes a record of attention, and attention is becoming one of the scarcest materials we have.
Researchers have already observed a version of this shift. Across six experiments involving 2,965 people, participants consistently valued art labeled “AI-made” less than work labeled “human-made,” even when the images themselves were identical. Awareness of the machine changed the perceived value of the human hand.
This preference extends beyond art. A 2015 study in the Journal of Marketing found that people considered handmade objects more attractive in part because they believed those objects symbolically contained the maker’s love. The participants were projecting on and responding to an imagined human presence embedded in the object, expressed through the perceived time and care required to make it.
Nostalgia is part of the current attraction to the handmade. We remember darkrooms, paste-up boards, paint-stained clothes, and the physical tools that digital technology has made unnecessary or irrelevant, and often forget the expense and tedium the processes demanded. Still, the renewed power of visible erasure or the pleasure of encountering an unrestrained line reaches beyond nostalgia. These marks allow us to envision the intent and the decisions behind them.
AI can attempt to imitate these marks. It can add a false thumbprint, invent pentimenti, reproduce a stray brush bristle, and generate an image that appears to have survived a century in an attic. But mess itself will soon prove very little. Provenance and an intelligible creative process will become more important as appearance ceases to represent authenticity.
In educated hands, AI can still become a profound artistic medium. Photography and digital tools have disrupted ideas about skill and authorship before becoming vehicles for extraordinary art. AI will be shaped by artists whose choices are specific enough to resist its defaults, and those artists may create work we cannot yet imagine. The presence of a tool has never settled the question of artistic value; the depth and consequence of the decisions made with it still matter.
We are entering a period in which polished images and endless variations are available on command. The works we retain or collect may be those that let us encounter another person’s limits: the place where control faltered or the artist had to surrender to something unresolved.
I think our nostalgia for mess is growing from a hunger for evidence that making something still requires time, effort, commitment, and—dare I say it—love.

Scientists just imaged the hidden quantum shape of a molecule
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
09:55:19 UTC
18:55:19 KST

Scientists just imaged the hidden quantum shape of a molecule
A new imaging breakthrough could let scientists watch a molecule’s quantum wavefunction change in 3D on femtosecond timescales.
- Date:
- August 24, 2026
- Source:
- University of Göttingen
- Summary:
- Researchers have found a way to create a complete 3D image of a molecule’s wavefunction, one of quantum mechanics’ most fundamental yet elusive features. By combining advanced photoelectron measurements with newly designed algorithms, the University of Göttingen team reconstructed the molecular orbital of a nanometer-sized organic molecule in remarkable detail, even resolving features smaller than the spacing between its carbon atoms.
- Share:
Quantum mechanics has long challenged the familiar idea that an object must occupy one precise place at a given moment. Fundamental particles such as electrons are instead described by a "wavefunction," a mathematical representation that researchers can use to calculate the probabilities of properties such as position and momentum.
Inside molecules, electron wavefunctions are known as "molecular orbitals." These orbitals contain valuable information about how a molecule behaves and interacts with its environment, including how it absorbs light and how chemical reactions may unfold. Obtaining a complete three-dimensional picture of a wavefunction would therefore give scientists a powerful view of molecular behavior, but producing such an image has been extremely difficult.
Now, an interdisciplinary team at the University of Göttingen has successfully imaged the three-dimensional wavefunction of an organic molecule only nanometers in size. The researchers accomplished this by combining advanced photoelectron spectroscopy with sophisticated mathematical algorithms. Their findings were published in Nature Communications.
Reconstructing an Elusive Quantum Wavefunction
"The wavefunction is a fundamental quantity in quantum mechanics, yet it cannot be directly observed or measured," explains Professor Stefan Mathias at the University of Göttingen.
Because the wavefunction itself cannot simply be measured, the researchers used an indirect technique called photoelectron spectroscopy. The method measures the momentum of electrons emitted from the molecule, giving scientists access to one half of the wavefunction without physically changing its state.
Advanced computer algorithms were then used to reconstruct the missing half. This allowed the team to produce an image of the complete molecular orbital and distinguish features that are even smaller than the distance separating the carbon atoms within the molecule.
Until now, extending this approach into three dimensions required lengthy measurements at major synchrotron research facilities. That requirement made the technique difficult to use widely and created an especially large obstacle for efforts to image "dynamical" wavefunctions as three-dimensional videos at atomic scales.
Toward Ultrafast 3D Movies of Molecules
Dr. Matthijs Jansen, University of Göttingen, and co-leader of the study, highlights the originality of the team's approach: "We introduce two powerful new concepts. First, by redesigning the computer algorithm from the ground up, reliable 3D images can now be obtained using much less experimental data. Second, the experiment is based upon a powerful, lab-based soft-X-ray light source that provides ultrashort light pulses. It is the combination of these two techniques that has this remarkable impact."
The redesigned algorithm dramatically reduces the amount of experimental data required to generate dependable three-dimensional images. At the same time, the researchers can perform the measurements using a powerful soft X-ray source in the laboratory that produces extremely short pulses of light. Together, these advances could make three-dimensional wavefunction imaging much more practical.
Dr. Wiebke Bennecke, first author of the study, adds: "This technique might mean that stroboscopic videography becomes a reality, allowing us to observe not just the shape of wavefunctions, but also to see how it changes with ultrafast, even femtosecond or one quadrillionth of a second, resolution. This will mean we can learn how a molecule adapts to optical, electronic, or chemical changes and find new ways to control these interactions at the level of a few atoms."
If the technique can be extended in this way, researchers could move beyond static images and watch molecular wavefunctions evolve over time. Such observations could reveal how molecules respond to light, electronic effects, and chemical changes on femtosecond timescales, potentially giving scientists new ways to understand and control interactions involving only a few atoms.
Story Source:
Materials provided by University of Göttingen. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Wiebke Bennecke, Thi Lan Dinh, Jan Philipp Bange, David Schmitt, Marco Merboldt, Lennart Weinhagen, Bent van Wingerden, Fabio Frassetto, Luca Poletto, Marcel Reutzel, Daniel Steil, D. Russell Luke, Stefan Mathias, G. S. Matthijs Jansen. Table-top three-dimensional photoemission orbital tomography with a femtosecond extreme ultraviolet light source. Nature Communications, 2026; 17 (1) DOI: 10.1038/s41467-026-74308-1

Ajit Doval in Beijing: India-China border talks set for August 25; what's on agenda?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
09:54:00 UTC
18:54:00 KST

NSA Ajit Doval arrives in Beijing for India-China border talks. Representative image: ANI
NEW DELHI: India's national security adviser Ajit Doval arrived in Beijing on Monday for a two-day visit. He is set to hold the 25th round of Special Representatives' Talks on the India-China boundary question with Chinese foreign minister Wang Yi on Tuesday. The visit comes as New Delhi and Beijing seek to build on recent signs of a thaw in ties.The ministry of external affairs (MEA) said Doval arrived in Beijing "at the invitation of Wang Yi".The talks come amid efforts by the two sides to gradually normalise relations following years of tensions along their disputed Himalayan border.
"The NSA will also call on China's vice president Han Zheng during his visit," the MEA said.
Boundary question and border stability on the agenda
The central focus of the talks will be the unresolved India-China boundary issues, with both sides expected to discuss the management of differences and the preservation of peace and tranquillity along the Line of Actual Control.Chinese foreign ministry spokesperson Lin Jian said the two sides would continue discussions in accordance with agreements reached by their leaders.India and China share a roughly 3,500-kilometre disputed border.
Relations came under severe strain after the deadly military clash in eastern Ladakh in 2020, following which the two sides held repeated military and diplomatic talks to address the situation.The latest Special Representatives’ meeting comes against the backdrop of a broader effort to stabilise the relationship.
Recent thaw in ties
Doval's Beijing visit follows his meeting with Wang in New Delhi in June on the sidelines of the BRICS National Security Advisers' meeting.The MEA described those discussions as part of the process of rebuilding bilateral ties.According to MEA spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal, the two sides "reviewed recent developments in bilateral relations and noted progress towards gradual normalisation".Jaiswal said Doval had stressed the importance of maintaining a stable relationship."NSA underlined that stable, predictable and constructive bilateral relations contribute to building trust and better understanding between the two sides," he said, adding: "The discussions were constructive and forward-looking."The latest visit also comes after subsequent meetings between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and Chinese president Xi Jinping on the sidelines of major international summits.At the SCO Summit in Tianjin last year, PM Modi and Xi welcomed what the two sides described as positive momentum and steady progress in bilateral relations following their previous meeting in Kazan in October 2024.
The two leaders had also reaffirmed that India and China were development partners rather than rivals, and that differences between them should not be allowed to become disputes."A stable relationship and cooperation between India and China and their 2.8 billion peoples on the basis of mutual respect, mutual interest and mutual sensitivity are necessary for the growth and development of the two countries, as well as for a multipolar world and a multi-polar Asia befitting the trends of the 21st century," the MEA had said in a statement after the leaders' meeting.The Special Representatives’ mechanism has been one of the key diplomatic channels for addressing the boundary dispute between India and China. The 25th round comes at a time when both governments are seeking to consolidate the recent improvement in relations without setting aside their differences over the border.
For New Delhi, maintaining a stable and predictable relationship with Beijing is also significant as India prepares for the BRICS summit next month, where it hopes Xi will attend.
Subhadra Srivastava is a journalist with The Times of India, covering geopolitics, international and national affairs. With over three years of experience, she focuses on national and global developments, conflict, diplomacy and their impact on India. Her work combines breaking news with in-depth analysis, offering readers context and clarity on the stories shaping the world.

DAMASCUS, Syria (AP) — A former Islamic religious leader was sentenced to life in prison on Monday in the latest Syrian court trial of officials affiliated with the rule of ex-President Bashar Assad.
Former grand mufti Ahmad Badreddine Hassoun, an Assad loyalist who was vocally in support of the government’s policies, was convicted of inciting violence and justifying murder. He held the position of mufti from 2005 to 2021, when the position was abolished.
Judge Fakhreddine al-Aryan, head of the Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus, said the official religious establishment under Assad’s rule had “justified the use of barrel bombs that targeted civilian areas and caused widespread destruction, which constitutes a violation of the rules of international humanitarian law.”
Several other senior Assad-era officials -- including Assad himself and his brother, Maher -- have been sentenced to death in recent weeks, many of them in absentia. Hassoun was in custody and present in the court.
Some human rights groups have expressed concerns that the trials are being rushed and are potentially unfair, but the sentences have been welcomed by many Syrians who had previously expressed frustration that the new government was not moving with enough speed or strength against Assad-era figures.
Mass anti-government protests erupted in Syria in 2011 and were met by a brutal government crackdown, spiraling into a nearly 14-year civil war that left about half a million people dead and displaced more than half of Syria’s prewar population of 23 million.

BREST, 24 August (BelTA) - The 11th meeting of the working group on cooperation between Belarus and Russia's Irkutsk Oblast will take place on 25 August, BelTA has learned from the Brest Oblast Executive Committee.
A Belarusian delegation has already arrived in the Russian region. It is led by Chairman of the Brest Oblast Executive Committee Piotr Parkhomchik, who is the point man in the Belarusian government for cooperation between Belarus and Irkutsk Oblast of Russia. The parties will discuss the outcomes of cooperation in the first half of 2026 and outline projects for the near future. A plan of action on cooperation in trade, economy, science, technology, culture and humanitarian matters for 2026–2028 is expected to be signed.
The working group meet alternately on Belarusian and Russian soil.
A representative Belarusian delegation comprises both officials and business representatives. They are set to tour local enterprises and participate in the Baikal International Partners Forum, a business matchmaking event for exporters and importers, and a trade and procurement session with retail chains.
 
The Belarusian delegation’s visit will run through 27 August.

China issues multiple alerts for rainstorms, typhoons
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
17:46:43 CST
18:46:43 KST

BEIJING, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- China's National Meteorological Center (NMC) on Monday issued blue alerts for typhoons and severe convective weather and a yellow alert for rainstorms, with multiple typhoons forecast to bring heavy rainfall and strong winds to parts of the country.
The China Meteorological Administration also raised its emergency response for major meteorological disasters from Level IV to Level III around Monday noon.
Heavy rainfall is expected in parts of Fujian, Guangdong, Guangxi and Hainan from Monday to Wednesday, according to the NMC. Strong winds are also forecast over the Beibu Gulf, the Taiwan Strait and the East China Sea, as well as their coastal areas.
Some areas of Liaoning and Jilin will see heavy rainfall on Monday, while a significant rain spell is expected to sweep eastward through the eastern part of northwest China, north China and northeast China from Tuesday, accompanied by severe convective weather, the NMC said.
Typhoon Narra, the 19th typhoon of the year, was located at 4 p.m. Monday in waters about 260 kilometers southwest of Beihai City in south China's Guangxi Zhuang Autonomous Region, with maximum winds of 23 meters per second near its center.
It is expected to track eastward from Monday night and then travel northward at a speed of 5 to 10 kilometers per hour, gradually approaching the coastal areas from Guangxi to the western Leizhou Peninsula in Guangdong Province, according to the NMC.
China's National Development and Reform Commission has allocated 50 million yuan (about 7.37 million U.S. dollars) in the central budget to support emergency recovery in Guangxi, where Typhoon Narra has already brought severe rainfall and floods.
The fund will focus on restoring damaged roads, water infrastructure, schools and hospitals to help resume normal production and daily life as soon as possible, according to the commission.
Typhoon Gaenari, the 20th typhoon of the year, made landfall along the coast of Quanzhou in east China's Fujian Province at around 12:30 p.m. on Monday, the local meteorological observatory said.
Meanwhile, the NMC said Typhoon Saudel, this year's 18th typhoon, is expected to enter the East China Sea on Wednesday and gradually approach the coastal areas of east China.
The NMC has advised local governments to take precautionary measures.
China has a four-tier color-coded weather warning system, with red representing the most severe, followed by orange, yellow and blue. ■

Japan's militarism challenges global peace: KCNA
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
17:46:42 CST
18:46:42 KST

PYONGYANG, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- The Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK) on Monday lambasted Japanese politicians for visiting the notorious Yasukuni Shrine on the anniversary of Japan's surrender in World War II, warning the country "will perish in the flames of neo-militarism."
In a commentary issued by the official Korean Central News Agency (KCNA), the DPRK condemned Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi for sending a ritual offering and paying a "surprise tribute" to the shrine, calling her move "a blatant challenge to the desire of humankind for global peace and security."
Since Takaichi took office, the Japanese government has pursued an extremely dangerous military policy, it said, stressing the remote tribute highlights her militaristic ambitions.
In her address to the so-called national ceremony for mourning the war dead after her "tribute" to the shrine, Takaichi neither spoke any words of reflection on Japan's history of aggression nor made no-war pledge, it said.
On the contrary, she employed a crafty trick in her speech to evade responsibility for the Japanese wars of aggression that inflicted untold misfortune and pain upon the Asian people, according to the article.
Moreover, the Japanese defense minister, who is reportedly in charge of "national security," also visited the shrine this time, a clear demonstration of the dangerous nature of the Yasukuni visit.
"Japan is bound to repeat its past as it never draws a lesson but wantonly denies its past as a war criminal country and a defeated nation," said the commentary. ■

Analysis: Four things we learned in Spain's matchday 2
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
17:46:17 CST
18:46:17 KST

MADRID, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- FC Barcelona, Atletico Madrid and Real Madrid, whose players featured in the last four of the FIFA World Cup, began their La Liga campaigns in the second round. Here are four things we learned this weekend in Spain.
1. Barcelona lays down gauntlet
FC Barcelona kicked off its title defense with a 5-0 win away to Elche, an even more impressive result considering some players had less than two weeks of training following the World Cup and new signing Rodri did not play.
Coach Hansi Flick can be pleased with the contributions of new signings Anthony Gordon and Karim Adeyemi, while Fermin Lopez and Raphinha provided plenty of movement in attack.
2. Espi saves the day for Real Madrid
Young striker Carlos Espi, who joined Real Madrid from Levante, showed his potential with a 90th-minute goal to give Jose Mourinho's side a winning start to the season away to Espanyol.
Espanyol looked set to hold on for a draw after Alex Calatrava had canceled out Jude Bellingham's opening header, but Espi was in the right place to finish after Kylian Mbappe caused confusion in the penalty area.
After helping Levante avoid relegation with his goals in the closing weeks of last season, Espi could prove a useful option as Real Madrid vies for the title this season.
3. No forgiveness for Alvarez
Julian Alvarez was named on the substitutes' bench for Atletico Madrid's 2-2 draw with Villarreal after saying he wanted to leave the club over the summer.
The Argentine has trained with the club for the past fortnight, but it was clear that fans at the Metropolitano Stadium had not forgiven him, as his name was greeted by a loud chorus of boos and whistles when it was announced, with further jeers when he came on as a late substitute.
4. Individual errors sabotage Terzic's Athletic debut
Edin Terzic's debut as Athletic Club coach ended in a 3-1 home defeat to Sevilla, with individual errors undermining his team's efforts.
Athletic was already down to 10 men after Yuri Berchiche was shown a red card in the 11th minute before Spain international goalkeeper Unai Simon gifted Sevilla the opening goal four minutes later when he dwelled on a clearance.
A misplaced pass from Benat Gerenabarrena allowed Sevilla to launch the counterattack that made it 2-0, before a backheel from Jesus Areso gifted possession to Sevilla in the build-up to the third goal. ■

Sashakt Behna Utsav Yojana in Dehradun
Uttarakhand chief minister Pushkar Singh Dhami inaugurated stalls set up by self-help groups under the Mukhyamantri Sashakt Behna Utsav Yojana in Dehradun on Monday.After visiting the stalls, the Chief Minister encouraged the women associated with the groups.CM Dhami also purchased rakhis made by the women of local self-help groups and appreciated their skills and hard work. The Chief Minister encouraged their efforts and said that the Sashakt Behna Utsav Yojana has provided livelihood opportunities to a large number of women, with many also benefiting from the initiative last year.On Sunday, CM Dhami participated in two Raksha Bandhan programmes held in Dehradun and celebrated the festival with the women.According to the Chief Minister's office, he first attended a Raksha Bandhan ceremony at Chaudhary Farms, followed by another programme at Survey Stadium in Hathibarkala. At both events, a large number of women tied Rakhi to the Chief Minister and wished him a healthy and long life.The Chief Minister extended Raksha Bandhan greetings to all the women and expressed gratitude for their affection and blessings.The Chief Minister extended Raksha Bandhan greetings in advance to all mothers and sisters of Uttarakhand and prayed that the sacred festival would bring happiness, prosperity and new joy into everyone's lives.
He said that being among the women made him feel as though a brother had returned to his own home and family. The love and trust he receives from the women of the state, he said, are his greatest strength and continue to inspire him to work tirelessly in the service of every citizen of Uttarakhand.
He said Raksha Bandhan is not merely a festival celebrating the love between brothers and sisters, but also a sacred occasion symbolising unbreakable affection, trust, dedication and the lifelong commitment of a brother to protect his sister. The festival also teaches that relationships are strengthened not merely by rights, but by the fulfilment of duties and responsibilities. A brother's affection and commitment to his sister's safety, along with a sister's unwavering trust in her brother, are sacred bonds further strengthened by Raksha Bandhan, the release said.The Chief Minister said Raksha Bandhan also reminds us of the importance of respecting women. "Respect for women is not only our duty but also the foundation of our culture and values. Women are the foundation of families and a fundamental force behind society and culture. A society that respects women is truly prosperous and cultured," he said.

Syria sentences Assad-era mufti Hassoun to life imprisonment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
09:41:40 UTC
18:41:40 KST

Breadcrumb
Syria sentences Assad-era mufti Ahmed Hassoun to life imprisonment
A Syrian court on Monday handed a life sentence to Ahmed Hassoun, the country's former grand mufti under ousted leader Bashar al-Assad, convicting him of crimes including inciting sectarian strife and exploiting his position.
Hassoun, the 10th Assad-era figure to be sentenced under the new authorities, was Syria's top Muslim cleric for 16 years.
He was known for his close ties to the former president and frequent appearances alongside him on religious occasions.
Judge Fakhr al-Din al-Aryan said Hassoun, 77, was guilty of a raft of charges including "inciting civil war and sectarian strife", for which he was jailed for life.
The cleric was also convicted of "incitement to intentional homicide", "principal complicity in intentional homicide", and "inciting sectarian and racial strife", for which he was handed additional terms ranging from three to 20 years.
The court also decided to confiscate Hassoun's assets and hand them to the public treasury.
His sentencing is the first against a religious figure since Syrian authorities began trying Assad-era officials in April.
On 11 August, Syria sentenced Bashar al-Assad, his brother Maher and five other security officials to death in absentia for atrocities committed during Syria's civil war, the first such ruling under the new authorities.
The former president fled Syria as his government fell in December 2024 and is believed to be in Russia.
Authorities have also handed death sentences to Atif Najib and Wassim al-Assad, cousins of the former ruler who were tried in person.
Hassoun, a native of Aleppo whose late father was also an important religious figure, was arrested at Damascus airport in March last year as he tried to flee the country.
Though he held the post of grand mufti for more than a decade, Hassoun lost the title in 2021 when Syria abolished the position.
The United Nations and human rights organisations have voiced opposition to the death sentences handed to Assad-era officials.
Human Rights Watch on Sunday said the sentences "raise important legal issues the government should urgently address".
"Advancing justice for the litany of serious crimes committed in Syria requires more than just convictions, but building a system that can deliver competent, impartial, and independent justice," said Balkees Jarrah, the group's Middle East and North Africa director.
Syria began legal proceedings in April against Bashar al-Assad and other officials accused of atrocities during the civil war, which erupted in 2011 with brutal repression of pro-democracy protesters.
More than half a million people were killed and millions displaced during the conflict, while tens of thousands disappeared.

Israel launches new S. Syria incursion day after de-escalation talks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
09:40:00 UTC
18:40:00 KST

The Israeli military carried out a new raid in the countryside of southern Syria's Daraa Monday, local media reported, a day after Damascus and Tel Aviv held a de-escalation meeting.
"Israeli occupation forces advanced with several military vehicles into the village of Maariya in the western Daraa countryside," Syrian Alikhbariah TV reported.
According to local sources, Israeli troops launched an incursion into the village of Maariya with six vehicles and infantry personnel, who deployed near a neighborhood adjacent to the main road amid intensive drone activity over the area.
The forces then carried out a raid and search operation in the area before withdrawing toward the Al Jazeera military post.
Earlier Sunday, Israeli forces raided the town of al-Rafid in Quneitra province and arrested a shepherd, according to the channel.
Areas in southern Syria have witnessed near-daily Israeli incursions and attacks, particularly in Quneitra and Daraa provinces, including raids, searches, arrests and the establishment of military checkpoints.
The latest attacks come despite Syrian and Israeli officials met in Jordan for high-level U.S.-mediated talks in Jordan Sunday.
The meeting was aimed at easing tensions following recent Israeli strikes on Syrian territory, Syria's state news agency SANA reported, citing a diplomatic source at the Foreign Ministry.
The talks focused on practical mechanisms to halt Israeli strikes, arrests and targeted operations and on reviving negotiations toward a security agreement that could lay the groundwork for a broader future accord, SANA said.
"The meeting came as part of efforts aimed at reducing escalation following the latest Israeli shelling of Syrian territory and rising tensions in southern Syria," one diplomatic source said.
The two sides also discussed efforts to ease tensions between Israel and Türkiye.
Syria's Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani told Reuters Saturday that Damascus expected security negotiations with Israel to resume soon, although he added that there was a lack of trust between them.
Talks had been suspended since the start of the Iran war, while Syria cut off contact entirely after Israeli strikes on Syria’s Abu al-Duhur air base last week, according to al-Shaibani.
Washington has for more than a year sought to broker a security agreement between Israel and the government of Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa.
Al-Shaibani said the two sides had agreed on paper to "almost everything” around the beginning of the year, including arrangements for security zones in southern Syria and a buffer zone where only United Nations forces would be present, but Damascus doubted Israel's willingness to implement the agreement.
The Israeli prime minister's office did not reply to a request for comment on al-Shaibani's remarks.
At Sunday’s meeting, SANA said, Syria indicated that its immediate priorities remained an Israeli withdrawal to positions held before Bashar Assad's overthrow on Dec. 8, 2024 and the full restoration of a 1974 disengagement agreement.
Damascus also told the Israeli delegation it would not accept arrangements restricting its right to rebuild and develop its armed forces or determine its alliances and partnerships, SANA said.
Syria reiterated that the Israeli-occupied Golan Heights were Syrian territory but said discussions over the region's final status were premature, according to the SANA report.
Israel has carried out repeated strikes on Syrian military sites since Assad's fall, claiming its actions were necessary to protect its security. Syria has denied posing a threat to Israel and has demanded an end to Israeli strikes and incursions.
Syria and Israel have technically been at war since 1948. Israel captured the Golan Heights from Syria in the 1967 Six-Day War and later annexed it, a move recognized by the United States but not by most of the international community.

ann veronica janssens fills Hermès ginza with light, fog and shifting perception
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
09:35:32 UTC
18:35:32 KST

For her first solo exhibition in Japan, Ann Veronica Janssens is taking over Le Forum at Ginza Maison Hermès in Tokyo with things that are notoriously difficult to hang on a wall: light, air, time and perception itself. Titled 5 Chome 4-1 Ginza, Tokyo after the building’s own address, the exhibition opens on September 11, 2026, and brings together more than ten works conceived around the physical conditions of the space, alongside pieces from the artist’s ongoing practice since the 1990s.
Born in Folkestone in 1956 and based in Brussels, Janssens has spent decades testing how little an artwork might need in order to completely reorganize a room. After initially working with materials including plywood, glass and concrete, she increasingly turned toward light, sound and artificial fog around the beginning of the 1990s. Rather than filling architecture with objects, her installations tend to loosen its edges, using reflection, transparency and shifting atmospheric conditions to make space feel considerably less dependable than it did five minutes earlier.
Donut, 2003 | image: Florian Hölzherr, courtesy of CCA Wattis Institute for Contemporary Arts, San Francisco
LIGHT, GLITTER AND A SWING THAT REMEMBERS YOUR TOUCH
Among the works presented in Tokyo is Rose (2007), an installation in which seven spotlights cut through suspended particles, turning dispersed light into something that appears almost solid. Janssens repeatedly works in this uneasy zone between matter and immateriality, where a beam can behave like sculpture and an apparently empty room suddenly acquires thickness. In Untitled (blue glitter), open sculpture #1 (2015–2026), blue micro-glitter spreads across the floor, catching changing light and registering the fleeting effects of movement, viewpoint and time.
The body gets an even more direct role in Swings (2000–2023). Made from rope and wood, the suspended seats are covered with heat-sensitive film that changes through contact, allowing a visitor’s touch to briefly alter the work. Janssens has long resisted the idea of the viewer as a politely stationary observer: movement, interaction and the presence of other bodies become part of what is being exhibited. Here, looking is not quite enough — perception has to get up and move around.
Swings, 2002-2023 | image: Andrea Rossetti, courtesy of Pirelli Hangar Bicocca
AN INVISIBLE ARCHITECTURE TAKES OVER LE FORUM
Elsewhere, works including Donut extend the exhibition into projected light, duration and the less tangible materials that have defined Janssens’ practice. Taken together, the installations manipulate light, air and circulation to produce what the Fondation d’entreprise Hermès describes as a kind of invisible architecture: spaces generated not through walls and ceilings, but through changes in atmosphere and sensation. The title’s insistence on a precise street address makes that strategy particularly pointed, anchoring an exhibition dedicated to unstable perception to one very fixed point on the map.
Janssens’ experiments have often intersected with research into the relationship between space, time, the body and the brain, including through the Brain Space Laboratory, which she co-founded with Nathalie Ergino in 2009. At Ginza Maison Hermès, however, the experiment does not require much explanation. Glitter shifts, light gains volume, surfaces react and architecture becomes unexpectedly porous. 5 Chome 4-1 Ginza, Tokyo runs at Le Forum on the eighth and ninth floors of Ginza Maison Hermès through January 11, 2027, with free admission.
IPE 650, 2009-2017 | image: Peter Cox, courtesy of De Pont Museum Tilburg
Untitled, Blue Glitter, 2015-2026 | image: Julie Joubert, courtesy of Kamel Mennour
Rose, 2007 | image: Andrea Rossetti, courtesy of IAC Villeurbanne
Green, Yellow and Pink, 2017 | image: Andrea Rossetti, courtesy of Esther Schipper
Blue Papegaai, 2010-2017 | image: Andrea Rossetti, courtesy of Esther Schipper
Blue Glass Roll (405), 2017 | image: Andrea Rossetti, courtesy of Esther Schipper
from zucchini ballet flats to shoes covered in flowers and dandelion seed heads, the artist turns fleeting plant materials into playful studies of footwear.
lions, tigers, acrobats and balloons, costumed and created to fit in a suitcase, make up one of alexander calder's foundational works in play and wire.

They Dedicated Their Lives to Teaching. Then the Deepfakes Started
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
09:30:00 UTC
18:30:00 KST

For Luis DeSantiago, a substitute teacher in Los Banos, California, it started with a few text messages. On March 12, as he was working his other part-time job at a coffee shop, his phone lit up. A fellow barista said there was an AI photo circulating on social media. Her cousin wanted to know if it was DeSantiago.
At first, DeSantiago wasn’t worried—he figured that inappropriate photos violated TikTok’s community guidelines and were usually quickly removed.
“When I finally saw the image, that’s when it felt like a punch to the gut,” DeSantiago tells WIRED. Parts of it resembled a mirror selfie that he remembered taking at a job in college. But instead of his work uniform, he was wearing lingerie. And instead of standing normally, as he had been in the original photo, he was posing suggestively.
The texts kicked off a monthslong saga that crossed two schools and involved students and administrators. And DeSantiago is far from the only educator who’s been victimized this way.
WIRED spoke with three other teachers who allege that their students made sexualized photos and videos of them, likely using AI. They say the incidents have been profoundly distressing and disappointing—and in some cases, it’s led them to reassess how they view their work and their relationships with their students.
“This Could Include Other Students”
After he received the texts, DeSantiago began to piece together who might have been behind the image. One account that shared it used their real name in their TikTok profile—it was a student DeSantiago knew from the local middle school, where he regularly filled in. DeSantiago suspected the involvement of two other students based on people who followed and interacted with that account, and his knowledge of student friend groups. He was scheduled to work at that very middle school the next day.
DeSantiago reported the incident to the assistant principal, who assured him that the school would "take care of it.” Later that evening, he decided to look for the image by searching his name on TikTok. He discovered that a different student had created an account impersonating him—it used his name, slightly mispelled, and had the same photo as their profile picture.
Over the next few weeks, DeSantiago says, he went back and forth with school administrators, the parents of the students, and even the police.
“If these students aren't afraid of generating and posting these images of me, I am concerned of what they may be circulating privately through text messages and group chats,” DeSantiago wrote to the principal. “Keep in mind this could include other students as well.”
One student, who admitted to creating the image, was disciplined with in-school suspension. DeSantiago was later told that the image was also shared on Snapchat. But DeSantiago says the image continued to proliferate, and other students began posting it. He says he also received several crude, sexual comments on his TikTok account.
DeSantiago told administrators he didn’t want to take assignments at the middle school “until this matter is fully addressed.” The district did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
He took a substitute assignment at the local high school, but the problems followed him. During one class, he received an AirDropped photo of the same AI-generated image before it was quickly revoked. He could tell it was circulating among the class.
The principal told him the school was launching an “immediate investigation” and offered to meet with DeSantiago or make the school counselor available, but DeSantiago says he probably won’t return to the district this year.
He tells WIRED that, at least right now, he doesn’t feel safe doing so.
“It Makes You Question Everything”
When fake nude images of nonconsenting adults are disseminated, it could constitute cyberstalking and violate the federal Take It Down Act, which makes it a crime to publish nonconsensual “intimate visual depictions of individuals, both authentic and computer-generated,” on the internet.
In most of the accounts shared with WIRED, the teachers didn't directly report the content to the platforms on which it appeared. Snap spokesperson Monique Bellamy shared the company's policies on harassment and sexual content, which prohibit sharing AI-generated or manipulated content to humiliate or sexually harass others. She told WIRED that the company has "established processes" for reporting such content, and that it continues to "develop features and tools designed to support the safety, privacy, and well-being of our community." TikTok did not provide comment before publication.
Donna Ballman, a retired employment advocacy lawyer, tells WIRED that if a student creates and shares sexual images of a teacher, it constitutes a “clear case” of sexual harassment in the workplace.
Ballman says that under federal antidiscrimination laws, employers have an obligation to create a workplace free of sexual harassment. In a school, this could mean disciplining the student or moving them to a different classroom. She adds, however, that there's “no blueprint” for how schools need to respond to these incidents. Administrators don’t even have to tell a victimized teacher how a student may have been disciplined.
“They just have to make [and] create a safe environment for the victim,” Ballman says.
One middle school teacher in her mid-twenties tells WIRED that she’s seen so much AI-generated content used to harass teachers that she’s bracing for the next wave. (She requested anonymity because she did not have permission from her school district to speak about her experience.)
Last year, she says, students found public photos of a teacher in her sixties, manipulated them to make it appear that she was committing sex acts, and shared them with each other in a Snapchat group chat.
A few months ago, the teacher says, she learned from a student about a TikTok account impersonating her. It looked AI-generated—her face had the characteristic smoothness of AI-generated content, her mouth was moving unnaturally while speaking, and the sound of her voice didn’t match her own. Some of the videos showed her doing things like skydiving or backflips. But others depicted her talking about sexual acts she performed and enjoyed.
She says she told her principal about the account and that they assured her that they would “see what we can do.” Throughout the day, students continued to warn her about the account. She says that some told her that they knew who made the account—one of their classmates. She says the student was known to have behavioral problems.
“I know a lot of the kids that reported it to me genuinely believed that was my account, and that I was saying those things,” she tells WIRED. “I was like, ‘Oh my god, you guys—that is not me.’” She asked them to report it to TikTok, and she says the account was quickly taken down.
Still unnerved by the incident, she mentioned the TikTok account during the next monthly teacher meeting. A colleague said he had seen a seemingly AI-generated fake video of himself getting arrested, which he believed was generated by the same student.
As days and weeks passed, she says, she became the target of escalating, in-person harassment from this same student, who began “cursing me out, calling me names, telling me to fuck off, calling me a bitch.” She raised it at the next faculty meeting, and the assistant principal said that the same student was calling and texting them in the middle of the night and posting apparent AI-generated photos of them to TikTok.
She says the principal removed the student from her class and tried to limit his access to her. But she says that the harassment continued until the student ultimately left the district, and TikTok removed the account.
She says that these behavioral issues aren’t exclusive to this particular student. “It's kind of unsurprising that we are dealing with that, because these kids just have a hard time,” she says. "I'm just worried about this happening again.”
Other teachers say their experiences have fundamentally changed the way they relate to students.
Alice, who asked to be identified by her first name, works for a UK college that trains students aged 16 to 19 in trades like construction. Her job combines administrative responsibilities, like taking attendance, with the role of a college counselor. She says she individually meets with about 150 students throughout the year and takes pride in being able to be a sounding board, give them advice, and serve as a mentor.
This winter, she says, school administrators told her that a student filed a report claiming two videos were circulating among his classmates. One appeared to be real, and it showed her having a conversation with a student. The other one, they said, appeared to be a manipulated version of the first. But instead of talking to the student, it showed her taking her clothes off and dancing around in what was either underwear or a bikini.
Alice tells WIRED that as a qualified youth worker, part of her job often involves talking about things that students may feel “too embarrassed to tell their parents about,” like drugs, parties, or having safe sex. She says she had several of those conversations with the student she suspected had created the video. The student denied it when questioned by administrators and soon dropped out of the school. (The college did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.)
“It makes me reflect as well on those conversations, thinking, did he think that he could overstep a line because we were having these discussions?” she says. “It makes you question everything,” she says.
Afterward, the college gave her permission to step away from the class for a few weeks and took steps to educate students about the danger of creating or distributing deepfakes. But when she returned, she says, the atmosphere had chilled.
“I did have a really good rapport with my students—I do have a good rapport with my students,” she says. And she still loves her work. “But it's definitely made me a bit more cautious, a bit more vigilant when it comes to folks.”
“It Crosses the Line”
Like DeSantiago, Arizona-based sixth-grade teacher Luke Red says his students circulated an AI-generated photo of him in the comments of his public TikTok account. The image depicted him and another male teacher kissing each other.
Red says he reported the accounts to TikTok—not for content violations but for being under the minimum age of 13—but says TikTok didn’t remove the accounts. He says that the school immediately launched an investigation and quickly identified the student, who admitted to creating and sharing the image. The student received a three-day suspension—the most severe punishment kids their age can receive for a first-time sexual harassment offense, according to the school district handbook. The district did not respond to WIRED’s request for comment.
Red tells WIRED that reflecting on the experience “has kind of sent me into a spiral.” His concerns, he says, are not necessarily about what happened to him. They’re more focused on the enthusiastic, permissive culture surrounding AI use among his students.
“It just got to the point where students felt comfortable enough creating inappropriate images,” Red says. “Obviously when you're making your teachers do sexual things with these images, that's where it crosses the line.”
Ultimately, he feels more sorry for the students than for himself.
“It's just clear [that] so many kids nowadays just don't understand not only how what they're doing can affect others, but just what happens on the internet and how dangerous it can be,” Red says.

Belarus hosts around 160,000 visa-waiver travelers from Europe since 1 Jan 2026
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

09:26:00 UTC

Berezinsky Biosphere Reserve
                    
                    MINSK, 24 August (BelTA) – Since 1 January 2026, Belarus has welcomed 159,906 travelers from 38 countries included in the visa-waiver program. The majority of travelers came from Lithuania, Latvia and Poland, BelTA learned from the State Border Committee of Belarus.  
A total of 1,418,075 European residents have visited Belarus since 15 April 2022 when the visa waiver program was launched for Lithuanian and Latvian citizens, alongside Latvian non-citizen status holders, and expanded to Polish citizens on 1 July 2022. Belarus has welcomed 718,721 visitors from Lithuania, 451,909 people from Latvia and 158,580 visitors from Poland. On 19 July 2024 the visa-waiver program was extended to include 35 more countries. A total of 88,865 citizens of these countries have visited Belarus.
The visa-waiver program for citizens of 38 European countries has been extended until 31 December 2026. Detailed information about the visa waiver is available in the special section on the website of the State Border Committee and the Border of Belarus app.

Taiwan seeks stronger regional cooperation on climate, disaster response
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
09:21:12 UTC
18:21:12 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan Deputy Representative to the Philippines Lee Ting-sheng (李廷盛) said Taiwan wants stronger regional cooperation on climate change and disaster response, CNA reported Monday.
Speaking at the conference “Towards a Peaceful and Sustainable Future: Addressing Climate and Conflict in ASEAN,” hosted by the Stratbase Institute and the German Embassy in the Philippines, Lee said extreme weather had become an urgent regional threat.
Lee said the Philippines, Taiwan, and Japan are on the front line of climate change. He called for closer cooperation to improve disaster preparedness and emergency response.
He said cooperation could focus on three areas: sharing weather warnings in real time, exchanging smart-governance technology, and strengthening regional resilience. He said these measures could help governments respond more quickly to extreme weather.
Lee also proposed a cross-border humanitarian assistance system involving Taiwan, the Philippines, Japan, and other partners along the first island chain. He said such a system could reduce disaster damage and strengthen security and prosperity in the western Pacific.
Taiwan and the Philippines have cooperated on weather monitoring and disaster prevention since the 2000s. Taiwan has helped the Philippines establish an upper-air observation station, more than 10 automated weather stations, and an information display center to improve typhoon tracking and forecasting.
The two sides also launched the VOTE research program in 2016. The program focuses on volcanoes, oceans, typhoons, and earthquakes.

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Kaohsiung City Government’s Water Resources Bureau defended its progress on flood mitigation after the National Audit Office criticized the city for slowly implementing measures proposed following Typhoon Gaemi.
The National Audit Office said the city had completed fewer than 20% of the 59 flood mitigation measures proposed after the typhoon, per UDN. It reported that the city government had failed to purchase mobile water pumps on schedule and that maintenance records for existing equipment contained errors.
The office also noted that 19 of the 59 measures still lacked funding as of the end of 2025. It highlighted several flood mitigation facilities that had remained in disrepair for years.
The Water Resources Bureau said emergency repairs and other measures implemented after Gaemi had helped reduce the impact of recent heavy rainfall, per Newtalk. It explained that flood mitigation projects are designed to provide medium- to long-term improvements and therefore require more time to complete.
Regarding funding shortages, damaged facilities, and the delayed purchase of mobile water pumps, the bureau said its budget was limited but that it would continue monitoring the situation and making improvements.
The bureau also faced criticism from opposition politicians. Kaohsiung City Councilor Chen Mei-ya (陳美雅) urged the city government to determine why flooding remained a problem despite roughly NT$580 million (US$18.21 million) having been invested in flood-mitigation projects, per UDN.
KMT Legislator Ko Chih-en (柯志恩) visited Dianbao Village in Kaohsiung’s Ziguan District and called on the government to reassess flood mitigation measures in the area, per Liberty Times. She urged a comprehensive review of the village’s infrastructure, saying it had experienced repeated flooding.
In response to Chen’s criticism, the bureau said mitigation measures had reduced the areas affected by flooding but warned that engineering solutions have limitations when faced with extreme rainfall.
In a related development, department stores across Kaohsiung remained open despite the city’s suspension of work and classes, drawing criticism from workers, per CNA. Employees said that even E-DA Theme Park, located in a mountainous area of Kaohsiung, did not allow workers to take the day off.
The theme park said employees could request breaks if flooding or other safety concerns prevented them from working. Two minor landslides occurred Sunday on a road leading to the theme park, per SETN.

The market’s most heavily weighted stocks dragged down the index, with TSMC falling 1.45% to close at NT$2,375. MediaTek declined 0.66% to NT$3,765.
Delta Electronics dropped 0.86% to NT$1,735, and Foxconn fell 0.81% to NT$243.5. ASE gained 0.85% to NT$592, according to Anue.
UMC rose 6.01% to NT$123.5 on the second-highest trading volume among individual stocks. The chipmaker reported first-half consolidated revenue of NT$129.8 billion, up 11.28% from a year earlier and the second-highest level for the same period.
UMC has also invested in silicon photonics foundry services for more than 10 years, according to recent reports. Market research firm Yole estimates that the global silicon photonics market will grow from NT$8.85 billion in 2024 to NT$85.96 billion by 2030. The estimated annual growth rate of 46% is higher than the roughly 30% expected for AI high-performance computing chips, per CTEE.
High-priced stocks were also in focus. King Slide Works rose 7.66% to NT$14,410, narrowing the gap with Aspeed Technology, the TAIEX’s highest-priced stock at NT$15,115.
Myson Century hit its daily limit for a seventh consecutive session, closing at NT$28.6. The company benefited from strong demand in the health and wellness market and improving results from its biotechnology and health products business, according to Sinotrade.

Silicon wafer stocks stood out after reports that prices for 6-inch, 8-inch, and 12-inch wafers were being raised. Formosa Sumco Technology and Avid Electronics both hit their daily limits, while GlobalWafers gained 7.33% to NT$1,010. Sino-American Silicon Products and Wafer Works also moved higher.
Petrochemical stocks came under pressure. Formosa Petrochemical fell 7.78%, while Formosa Plastics, Nan Ya Plastics, and Formosa Chemicals & Fibre all declined more than 4%.
Other recently popular sectors, including printed circuit boards, shipping, passive components, and optical communications, also saw profit-taking. Among PCB stocks, APCB hit its daily limit down, while Glotech Industrial fell nearly 9%. In optical communications, LandMark Optoelectronics, Visual Photonics Epitaxy, and LuxNet all declined more than 5%.
Analyst Yang Huei-yu (楊惠宇) said the market had recently been weighed down by profit-taking and selling by investors seeking to cut losses on shares purchased at higher prices. With trading volume falling, the TAIEX is likely to remain in consolidation as investors assess their next moves.
She said the recent consolidation could help clear out weaker positions and lay the groundwork for a recovery. Yang expects individual stocks to remain the focus until the broader market shows clearer signs of recovery and trading activity picks up, per CTEE.

In Ramallah, Israeli forces closed the western entrance to the town of Al-Mughayyir, in the northeast of the city, preventing vehicles from entering or leaving, local sources told Anadolu.
They also raided the Al-Jalazone refugee camp and escorted occupiers during a raid on Khirbet al-Zaytoun in Kafr Malik village, where occupiers released their livestock onto Palestinian land, the sources added.
In Qalqilya, in the northern West Bank, Israeli forces set up a military checkpoint at the city’s southern entrance, known as the Habla tunnel, stopping Palestinian vehicles and checking IDs and obstructing movement, according to Wafa.
Israeli forces also stormed the town of Azzun, east of Qalqilya, patrolled its streets and carried out raids and searches, eyewitnesses told Anadolu.
In a separate development, Israeli forces arrested three Palestinians from the town of Azzun in Qalqilya province, local sources told Anadolu.
Israeli forces stormed the town from its main northern entrance and entered the Al-Mansour and Al-Shamiya neighborhoods, raiding, searching and damaging property in several homes, before carrying out arrests, sources said.
In Hebron province, in the southern West Bank, Israeli forces arrested four Palestinians, including three from the town of Sa’ir and one from Hebron city, according to Wafa.
Israeli forces raided and searched the detainees’ homes, Wafa reported.
Separately, Wafa quoted rights activist Aref Daraghmeh as saying Israeli forces forced a Palestinian from the village of Ein al-Beida, in the northern Jordan Valley, to demolish several agricultural structures he owned, claiming they were built without a permit.
The occupied West Bank has seen a steady escalation in Israeli army raids and occupier attacks against Palestinians since the start of Israel’s war on Gaza in October 2023.

Storm leaves thousands without power in Lithuania
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
09:12:22 UTC
18:12:22 KST

Ilayda Cakirtekin
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
More than 111,000 consumers remained without power in Lithuania on Monday, three days after a powerful storm battered the country, broadcaster LRT reported.
 
Grid operator Energijos Skirstymo Operatorius (ESO) said more than 111,000 consumers were still without electricity on Monday, down from a peak of around 268,000 during the storm.
 
“We really did have an exceptional storm – when we compare it with previous ones, we see it was almost 35% more intense than the last major one, in 2024. And we’re not basing that assessment on damage to our own grid, but on call-outs to the Fire and Rescue Department,” Renaldas Radvila, head of ESO, told LRT.
 
ESO further warned that some connections might not be restored until Aug. 27-29.
 
While the storm left thousands without water, power, mobile signal, or heating, several towns were reportedly close to declaring a local state of emergency.
 
Rail services were also disrupted after fallen trees and branches blocked tracks and damaged overhead lines, affecting around 3,500 passengers, according to the report.
 
Although the obstructions have since been cleared, power disruptions remained in parts of the railway network, potentially causing delays of up to 30 minutes on Monday.
 
Meanwhile, storm-related insurance claims in Lithuania could reach €3 million ($3.4 million), according to Mantas Norkus, head of the customer service center at Lietuvos Draudimas.
 
While the storm has already caused more than €1 million in insured losses, the company expects the total to rise further, potentially reaching €3 million.
 
“This was undoubtedly the largest storm of the year,” Norkus said.
 
Most of the damage was reported to buildings and other property, caused by strong winds, falling trees and branches, and heavy rainfall.
 
According to Lithuania’s Hydrometeorological Service, some areas saw nearly a month’s worth of rainfall within just 12 hours.
 
Near the Baltic coast, the town of Silute experienced rainfall equivalent to 93% of its typical total for the entire month of August.

Europe hesitates to name Russia in defense plant attacks
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
09:10:24 UTC
18:10:24 KST

- Five 2026 episodes affected seven European defense-industry-related locations, including three confirmed arson or sabotage cases.
- Russian involvement remains under investigation in Czechia and Estonia; authorities in France, Bulgaria and Italy have not linked their cases to Moscow.
Europe’s defense industry has faced a growing series of fires, explosions and deliberate attacks in 2026, many of them affecting companies that manufacture weapons, ammunition, drones or other equipment for Ukraine. Western intelligence sources increasingly view the incidents as part of a Russian campaign intended to disrupt military supply chains, intimidate manufacturers and test how far Moscow can act inside NATO territory without provoking a collective response.
The suspected operations are designed to preserve plausible deniability. Russian intelligence services can recruit local criminals through intermediaries, while individual attacks may resemble industrial accidents or be claimed in the name of antimilitary, environmental or pro-Palestinian activism. This method complicates attribution and allows each incident to be treated as an isolated criminal case, technical failure or act of domestic extremism rather than part of a coordinated foreign campaign.
That ambiguity has also shaped Europe’s public response. Authorities must meet a high evidentiary threshold before accusing another state, but the resulting caution can fragment or minimize the wider pattern. Western intelligence sources cited by The Telegraph said some governments in Western Europe were reluctant to connect attacks to Moscow because of concerns about escalation. Italian and Bulgarian officials have rejected or played down a possible Russian role in incidents that remain under investigation, while authorities in Czechia and Estonia have publicly acknowledged that Russian involvement is one of the theories being examined.
Moscow has also issued a public warning against European defense production supporting Ukraine. In April, the Russian Defense Ministry published the names and addresses of European companies it accused of manufacturing drones or components for Kyiv. Dmitry Medvedev, deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, called the facilities potential targets for the Russian armed forces and wrote: “When strikes become a reality depends on what comes next. Sleep well, European partners!” Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov later declined to say whether Russia was considering attacks on the listed facilities. Reuters documented the warning and publication of factory addresses.
The events form part of a much larger security problem. The Munich Security Report 2026, using ACLED data, plotted roughly 150 suspected Russian hybrid incidents in EU and NATO countries between January 2022 and December 2025. Its categories included arson, sabotage, spying, vandalism, drone overflights and incendiary parcels. The report said many operations were constructed to remain deniable or ambiguous, allowing Russia to exert pressure while making direct attribution difficult.
The first 2026 attack examined here occurred before dawn on March 20 at LPP Holding’s facility in Pardubice, Czechia. The company develops optics, autonomous systems and drones, including equipment supplied to Ukraine. The fire damaged production buildings and stored products but caused no injuries. LPP said the damage did not interrupt a planned delivery of 40 attack drones to Ukraine.
Czech police treated the fire as a deliberate attack and investigated it as possible terrorism. A previously unknown pro-Palestinian group claimed responsibility, alleging that LPP was producing weapons for Israel. LPP said it had no cooperation with Elbit Systems and did not manufacture equipment for Israel after a proposed partnership announced in 2023 failed to proceed.
The company said the anti-Israel claim could have been intended to conceal a Russian-directed operation against its work for Ukraine. Police publicly said they were considering several motives but did not confirm Russian direction. Reuters reported that a Russian connection remained one of the lines under examination. Authorities in Czechia and Slovakia later detained four suspects on terrorism-related allegations. The arrests identified suspected participants but did not establish who may have directed them.
The next episode targeted electrical infrastructure serving defense manufacturers rather than the factories themselves. During the night of April 6 to 7, fires damaged installations at La Chapelle-Saint-Ursin, Bourges and Saint-Florent-sur-Cher in central France. The sites included transformers, a high-voltage substation and a power pylon connected to networks serving KNDS and MBDA facilities.
The Cher prefecture described the incidents as coordinated and particularly serious. About 3,000 homes lost power, while repairs were expected to take months and cost several million euros. Investigators found graffiti at one site reading “Actions against the war.” The Bourges prosecutor opened an investigation, but French authorities had not publicly attributed the operation to Russia by Aug. 24.
The attack illustrates how an operation against the defense industry can be presented as domestic activism. The available evidence supports a coordinated antimilitary sabotage case, but it does not establish whether the slogan reflected the perpetrators’ actual motive or was intended to divert attention from another sponsor. The Cher prefecture published the initial official account, while TF1 reported the defense-industry connections, outages and damage.
A fire and explosions destroyed an ammunition storage building at EMCO’s plant near Belitsa, Bulgaria, on Aug. 10. Workers were evacuated and no casualties were reported. Investigators considered accidental ignition, a deliberately introduced fire source, altered components and safety violations among the possible causes.
EMCO manager Slavcho Dimiev said the fire appeared to have begun inside the building and that there were no grounds at that stage to claim outside interference. He identified spontaneous ignition of a propellant charge as one possible explanation. Prosecutors kept deliberate action among the lines of inquiry, but had not identified a leading cause while the site was still being secured. The Bulgarian News Agency reported that the investigation remained open to all possible causes.
Suspicion surrounding EMCO is rooted in the company’s earlier history. Its owner, Emilian Gebrev, survived a poisoning in 2015. Bulgarian prosecutors later investigated six Russian citizens in connection with the poisoning and four explosions at Bulgarian arms depots between 2011 and 2020. Prosecutors said the evidence indicated an effort to stop ammunition supplies to Georgia and Ukraine. That history provides grounds for close examination of the 2026 fire, but it is not evidence that Russian intelligence caused it. Reuters reported the findings of the earlier Bulgarian inquiry.
Three days after the EMCO fire, a blaze in the powder-pressing area of the KNDS Ammo Italy plant at Colleferro was followed by a powerful explosion. All 24 workers at the site were accounted for and no injuries were reported. The facility produces medium- and large-caliber ammunition for land and naval systems, along with solid propellants for aerospace applications.
The timing prompted comparisons with the Bulgarian incident, but Italian Defense Minister Guido Crosetto said the government had seen nothing suggesting Russian involvement. He said the available information pointed to an internal problem. Prosecutors and KNDS continued separate investigations into the cause. As of Aug. 24, the Colleferro case remained an unexplained fire and explosion at an ammunition plant, not a confirmed act of sabotage. Reuters reported the government’s assessment and continuing inquiry.
In Tallinn, a building used by Milrem Robotics caught fire overnight into Aug. 15 after a resident reported suspicious activity nearby. Estonian prosecutors said the fire was deliberate and premeditated. Three suspects were detained in Latvia, and Estonian authorities began efforts to bring them to Estonia.
Milrem produces THeMIS unmanned ground vehicles and other robotic systems used in Ukraine. Chief Executive Kuldar Väärsi said the fire did not disrupt production, supply chains or deliveries to Ukraine. Prime Minister Kristen Michal said investigators were examining whether Russia was behind the arson, but neither prosecutors nor the government had announced a final attribution. ERR reported the arrests and the prosecutor’s finding that the fire was premeditated. Reuters reported that deliveries continued and that Russian involvement remained under investigation.
These unresolved cases sit beside operations for which European investigations have produced firmer findings. In March 2026, European police agencies said they had identified 22 people connected to incendiary parcels that ignited at logistics facilities in Germany, Poland and Britain in 2024. Five suspects were charged, and investigators said Russia’s GRU military intelligence service was believed to be behind a plan to place incendiary devices aboard US-bound cargo aircraft.
Lithuanian authorities separately accused the GRU in January 2026 of organizing attempted arson at a plant that supplied radio-frequency scanners to Ukraine’s military. Six people were arrested, while investigators said the network had also prepared attacks in Poland, Romania and Czechia. The suspects came from several countries and were allegedly offered between 5,000 and 10,000 euros.
A German court added another documented case on Aug. 18. It convicted a Ukrainian man of assisting an operation ordered through an intermediary linked to Russian intelligence. The group sent GPS-equipped parcels to examine transport routes that could later be used for incendiary attacks. Two co-defendants were acquitted because the court found insufficient evidence that they understood the operation’s purpose.
The European Union has formally described sabotage, attacks on critical infrastructure, cyber operations and physical violence as elements of Russia’s continuing hybrid campaign against member states and partners. National authorities are therefore examining new fires and explosions against the background of an already documented Russian program that relies on recruited proxies and deniable assignments.
Not every incident at a European arms plant can be attributed to Russia without evidence from the individual investigation. At the same time, treating each case exclusively as an unrelated accident or act of local activism risks overlooking the defining feature of the campaign described by European investigators: operations structured so that Russian direction remains difficult to prove even when the target, recruitment method and political purpose fit an established pattern.

US threat of ‘economic D-Day’ for Iran tests Trump’s China detente
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
