Several local religious figures objected to the food arrangements, saying the programme was taking place during the holy month of Sawan.What BJP claimsReacting to the controversy, Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath accused Ajay Rai of “duplicity” over the alleged fish feast.“You saw the behaviour of the Congress state president: he goes to offer prayers at Hanumangarhi, but later outside he enjoys a feast of fish. He could have eaten whatever he wanted outside—anywhere other than Ayodhya. Yet, this is the duplicity they display. Even a chameleon would be put to shame by these people; it would wonder what kind of human species this is—chanting 'Ram-Ram' inside the temple and feasting on fish the moment they step out.
This is their history—the history of this Congress state president," Yogi said.BJP MLA Ved Prakash Gupta criticised the Congress over the alleged fish feast, saying, “scores of Hindus are immersed in the worship of Lord Shiva during Sawan. Organising a fish feast at such a time is an open display of Congress’ anti-Hindu mindset.”He alleged that visiting temples in Ayodhya and then attending an event where fish was served exposed the Congress party’s “dual standards”.UP BJP president Pankaj Chaudhary described the event as “highly condemnable and unforgivable” and demanded that the Congress publicly apologise to saints and devotees.What Congress saidResponding to the controversy Ajay Rai denied any involvement in the food arrangements and challenged Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath to provide evidence."The CM is criticising; does the CM have any photos? If he can produce any pictures, I will be ready to resign immediately. Nishad Samaj invited me to a program in Ayodhya yesterday. If they were getting fish prepared there, it would be their concern. I attended the program and returned," Rai said.Congress MP Pawan Khera criticised the Bharatiya Janata Party, saying that such controversies were being raised to divert attention from more pressing issues, including paper leaks."Such issues are raised so that important issues like paper leaks are not raised. Today, when people think of Ayodhya, they are reminded of the theft of donations. Can 'Maach-Bhaat' make people forget about the theft of donations in Ayodhya? People in Nagpur think fish should not be consumed. Ajay Rai is a vegetarian, even if he were not, what is wrong with it?" Khera said.
Ajay Rai had earlier defended the event, saying it was organised by members of the Nishad community, for whom fish forms an important part of their food culture.“Yeh Nishad samaj ka karyakram tha. Nishad samaj machhli ka vyapar karta hai. Unke liye machhli sabse achha bhojan hai jo woh kisi ko de sakte hain… and how can one check a host from cooking what they want,” Rai said.He also questioned the allegation that his presence at the event amounted to a violation of Sanatan traditions. “Where is the proof that I violated Sanatan tradition?” he asked.
Rai also hit back at the criticism by drawing a comparison with BJP leaders. Referring to BJP national president Nitin Nabin and an earlier controversy involving non-vegetarian food, he said, “Nitin Nabin consumed non-vegetarian food in Andhra Pradesh and claimed that he had eaten jackfruit. They are treating me with the same lens.”

3 children killed in Ukrainian drone attack on Ozon warehouse in southern Russia
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Elena Teslova
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
At least three children were killed and seven others injured after debris from a Ukrainian drone, targeting the warehouse of an e-commerce company Ozon, fell on a private children’s center in Russia's southern city of Krasnodar, Russian authorities said on Monday.
Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said on Russian social media platform Max that initially the drone was shot down by air defenses during a large-scale attack overnight.
Russian Commissioner for Children's Rights Maria Lvova-Belova confirmed the death toll.
"A terrible tragedy in Krasnodar Krai. Last night, as a result of a massive Ukrainian attack, according to preliminary information, three teenagers — aged 13, 15, and 16 — were killed," she said in a statement on Max.
The overnight attacks also targeted several Ozon logistics facilities across southern Russia.
Ozon said its facilities in Adygeysk in the Adygea region, Makhachkala in Dagestan and Nevinnomyssk in the Stavropol region came under drone attack.
Employees were evacuated from the Adygeysk and Nevinnomyssk facilities because of the threat of further attacks.
Ozon also confirmed that its logistics center in Krasnodar was attacked. The company had earlier said a fire broke out at the facility.
A separate Ozon logistics center in the Takhtamukaysky district of Adygea also caught fire following a drone attack, according to Russian authorities.
Meanwhile, the Russian Defense Ministry said it carried out overnight strikes on Ukrainian port infrastructure and vessels used to deliver supplies to the Ukrainian military.
The Russian Defense Ministry said strikes hit the port of Pivdennyi in Ukraine’s Odesa region, including a tanker carrying fuel intended for Ukrainian forces, five fuel storage tanks, 10 storage facilities containing military-related equipment and port infrastructure used to unload and store military cargo.
Russia also said it had struck the Adzhalyk-330 substation, about 28 kilometers (17.3 miles) northwest of Odesa, which it said sends supplies to Pivdennyi Port.
The claims regarding the targets and damage at the Ukrainian port could not be independently verified.

‘Barrel bomb mufti’ Ahmad Hassoun handed life sentence in Syria trial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24

17:18:12 KST

‘Barrel bomb mufti’ Ahmad Hassoun handed life sentence in Syria trial
Judge Fakhr al-Din al-Aryan sentenced Hassoun to life in prison for crimes including incitement to hatred and violence.
Ahmad Badreddin Hassoun, a top Muslim religious official under ousted Syrian President Bashar al-Assad, has been sentenced to life in prison for crimes committed during the country’s nearly 14-year civil war.
The Fourth Criminal Court in Damascus issued the ruling on Monday, finding Hassoun guilty of a range of crimes, including inciting violence, justifying killings and the abuse of his office.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Syria’s foreign minister says door open for diplomacy with Israel
- list 2 of 4Envoy says Israel did not give the US notice before strikes on Syrian base
- list 3 of 4Israel bombs Syria as US envoy says base attack aimed at ‘baiting’ Turkiye
- list 4 of 4Syria, Israel hold US-mediated talks in Jordan to de-escalate tensions
Hassoun, who was Syria’s grand mufti between 2005 and 2021, was arrested at Damascus airport in March 2025, after he emerged from hiding a month earlier. His trial began on June 25.
The court handed Hassoun several prison sentences for various charges, including 20 years after being found guilty of inciting killings.
The judge also sentenced him to 10 years in prison after being found guilty of prolonging the killings.
The court ordered the Muslim leader to pay compensation to make restitution to a number of his victims.
Judge Fakhr al-Din al-Aryan said that Hassoun and the official religious institution he headed were used to provide religious cover for military and security operations during al-Assad’s rule.
His teachings also justified the use of barrel bombs that targeted civilian areas and caused widespread destruction, which constitutes a violation of the rules of international humanitarian law, the judge said.
The court found that Hassoun also urged Syrian military officers and soldiers in his religious lectures to confront the country’s opposition, and made public calls through Syrian media for civilians in eastern Aleppo to evacuate their homes.
He also called on the army to “annihilate and destroy” the areas from which shells were launched, threatening the people of Idlib with killing and displacement.
The court confirmed that Hassoun is barred from any general or special amnesty, given the gravity of the crimes he was found guilty of committing.
His money and properties will also be confiscated by the state for the benefit of the public treasury, the court said.
Foreign minister Asaad al-Shaibani welcomed the verict, writing on X that “defending the rights of our people” is a “sacred duty that began with the first cry for freedom and whose echo has not yet faded”.
The verdict comes weeks after Bashar al-Assad, his brother Maher and five other security officials were sentenced to death in absentia for war crimes and crimes against humanity.
Authorities have also handed death sentences to Atif Najib and Wassim al-Assad, cousins of the former ruler who were tried in person.
Reporting from Damascus, Al Jazeera’s Heidi Pett said Hassoun is an “unusual” example of the transitional justice cases that Syria has held since al-Assad’s ouster in 2024.
“All of the other ones were senior members of the regime itself, many of them were members of the Assad family,” said Pett.
“We’ve seen death sentences handed down to Bashar al-Assad, the former president, two of his cousins as well. But Sheikh Ahmad Hassoun, he is the first Sunni to have been tried, and he does still enjoy some level of popular support here in Syria.”
His supporters, who have largely mobilised online, say his statements have been taken out of context, Pett reported.
Many of his critics, however, had called for a death sentence, she added.

Ukraine seeks interceptor missiles from Japan: Report
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:17:09 UTC
17:17:09 KST

Riyaz ul Khaliq
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
Ukraine is seeking interceptor missiles from Japan, the war-torn nation’s prime minister has said.
“I would like to kindly ask one and only thing ... anti-ballistic missiles,” Ukrainian Prime Minister Sergii Koretskyi told Kyodo News in an interview released on Monday.
Koretskyi “expressed hope that Japan will provide Kyiv with air defense systems.”
The Russia-Ukraine war has been ongoing since February 2022.
“It's the most important thing we need to protect our people, infrastructure ... through this (winter) heating season," Koretskyi said about the interceptor missiles.
“I very much hope (for) and count on your country," he told the Japanese news agency.
Ukraine is supplied with Patriot interceptor missiles by a coalition of Western nations, but its stockpile has been depleting.
Japan, a defense ally of the US, is one of the manufacturers of the Patriot surface-to-air missile interceptors under a US license, the report added.
However, Japanese arms exports, under the country’s three principles on the transfer of defense equipment and technology, “to countries in which conflicts are taking place is, (are) in principle, prohibited.”
In April, Tokyo revised limits on defense equipment exports.
The revised terms “on the transfer of defense equipment and technology require countries to sign agreements with Japan on protecting related classified information to be eligible for the transfer of lethal weapons,” it said.
“Even if an agreement for the transfer of defense equipment and technology is signed, the provision of interceptor missiles would need to be green-lighted by (Prime Minister Sanae) Takaichi,” according to Kyodo News.
Koretskyi said: "I do believe in our bright future and cooperation and partnership regarding the reconstruction and development of our country. Even now, we do not want to wait before the war (is) over.”

Through such occasions, we aim to inspire our students to carry the spirit of patriotism, unity and service into every sphere of their lives.”
Bhushan Ramkrishna Gavai, Former Chief Justice of India

Ukraine’s Mi-8 gets drone interceptor launchers to hunt Shaheds
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:09:54 UTC
17:09:54 KST

- Ukraine has mounted interceptor drone launchers on a Mi-8 helicopter, with footage shown in Zelensky's Independence Day address, Militarnyi reported.
- The helicopter carries at least three launch rails per side for up to six interceptors, similar to a configuration already used on a converted An-28 aircraft.
Ukraine has mounted interceptor drone launchers on a Mi-8 helicopter, with footage of the system shown in President Volodymyr Zelensky’s Independence Day address, Militarnyi reported.
The footage shows an interceptor launching from beneath one of the helicopter’s hardpoints, using simple metal launch rails mounted under the airframe. The drone is likely controlled either from inside the Mi-8’s cabin or remotely through Starlink, according to the outlet.
The helicopter carries at least three launch rails on each side, room for six interceptors in total. Militarnyi also reported the aircraft is likely fitted with an optical system for spotting aerial targets visually. The outlet did not disclose the unit flying the helicopter, the interceptor’s manufacturer, or when the modification entered service.
Ukraine has already fielded a similar concept on a fixed-wing aircraft. The Defence Blog reported in April 2026 that Ukrainian pilot Tymur Fatkullin had converted an Antonov An-28 light turboprop into an airborne interceptor platform, arming it with wing-mounted P1-Sun and Merops AS-3 Surveyor interceptor drones. Fatkullin said at the time that the aircraft-launched interceptor method had already proven effective against Shaheds in combat, not just in testing.
“Aircraft-launched P1-Sun interceptor against hostile Shaheds. This method has already proven effective in real combat conditions. We have also tested several other interceptor drones during training flights. You could call it a cheap air-to-air missile. For us, it is also a step toward technology that will allow drones to operate in zero visibility,” Fatkullin said.
The An-28, a Soviet-era transport aircraft never designed for intercept work, also carries a six-barrel M134 Minigun alongside its interceptor pylons. As of May 2026, the converted aircraft had destroyed 213 enemy drones using a combination of its onboard weapons and interceptor drones, part of a mix of tactics rather than interceptors alone.
The new Mi-8 configuration follows the same underlying logic as the An-28 conversion: use an aircraft already in the air to carry interceptors aloft, giving crews altitude, loiter time, and the ability to vector toward a target using onboard sensors before release, rather than relying only on ground-launched interceptors or gun-armed helicopters.
Ukrainian Mi-8 crews have engaged Shahed-type drones since at least 2024, but earlier missions relied on door-mounted or nose-mounted machine guns rather than dedicated interceptor drones. Footage from those operations showed gunners firing 7.62 mm PKT machine guns, and in some cases U.S.-supplied M134 miniguns, sometimes with a second helicopter carrying an optical tracking system to guide the engagement.
Ground-launched interceptor drones have separately become a larger part of Ukraine’s air defense mix through 2026. Zelensky has said interceptors have downed dozens of Shaheds in single overnight Russian attacks, and Ukrainian groups such as Wild Hornets have scaled production of systems like STING in response.

OTTAWA, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- A vast majority of Canadians support the federal government's decision to walk away from trade negotiations with the United States, according to a recent poll.
The survey conducted on Aug. 22-23 by the Angus Reid Institute shows that 76 percent of respondents endorse the federal government's stance, with majority support spanning every province. Even among supporters of the main opposition Conservative Party, 53 percent agreed that walking away was "right" rather than accepting a bad deal.
Canadians also demonstrated strong backing for the government's plan to impose dollar-for-dollar retaliatory tariffs on Sept. 8, with 62 percent calling the counter-tariff scheme "about right under the circumstances."
Data show that 64 percent of Canadians believe the country will ultimately emerge stronger as Canada reduces its economic dependence on the United States, while 26 percent express concern about long-term damage to ties with its most important trading partner.
However, the survey also reveals anxiety over employment risks stemming from the trade dispute. About 13 percent of Canadian workers reported being "very concerned" about losing their own job, with an additional 25 percent expressing varying levels of anxiety.
Industry experts previously predicted that a no-deal situation would shave 0.4 percent off Canada's GDP and as many as 90,000 jobs. ■

Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge
NEW DELHI: Congress president Mallikarjun Kharge on Monday slammed the PM Modi led BJP government over unemployment and alleged that its policies had weakened the path from education to employment for young Indians.In a post on X, Kharge cited Niti Aayog and PLFS figures to claim that 8.7 crore Indians aged 15 to 29 are neither in education, employment nor training, while youth unemployment stands at 15.6%.Kharge said the unemployment rate among young women was 19.5%, and questioned the government over job creation, the employment situation among graduates and its earlier promise of creating 2 crore jobs every year.
Kharge claimed that graduates account for 67% of unemployed Indians aged 20 to 29, while unemployment among graduates aged 15 to 25 is nearly 40%.He said families were spending their savings and students were taking education loans to obtain degrees, only to find that sufficient employment opportunities were unavailable.“Where are the jobs after graduation?” Kharge asked, questioning PM Modi over the employment prospects of young Indians.He also questioned the government over its earlier promise of creating 2 crore jobs every year.“What happened to the promise of 2 crore jobs every year?” Kharge said, adding that the promise would have translated into 24 crore jobs over 12 years.
Kharge alleged that lakhs of government posts remained vacant while secure employment was increasingly being replaced by contractual and part-time work.He also blamed expensive and inadequate education, examination paper leaks, delays in recruitment, a widening skills gap and a shortage of quality jobs for putting young people's future at risk.
“Who is turning India's demographic dividend into a demographic disaster?” Kharge asked.He further accused the government of failing to deliver on its promises despite PM Modi's claim that his government would achieve what previous governments could not accomplish in 70 years.“You, Modi ji, promised to achieve what previous governments could not do in 70 years!”
Kharge concluded by attacking the government's education policies, examination system and employment outcomes.“You have certainly delivered on that boast: an Education system that costs more, infested with RSS, examinations young Indians cannot trust, and degrees that increasingly come without jobs.”

Russia claims it shot down Flamingo missile with gunfire
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:03:37 UTC
17:03:37 KST

- Russian officials claim a volunteer air defense unit in Kursk Region shot down a Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile with machine-gun fire overnight August 22 to 23, 2026.
- The claim, unverified by independent sources, has not been confirmed by Ukraine, and the missile's reported speed was below the Flamingo's stated cruise speed.
Russian officials say a volunteer air defense unit in Kursk Region shot down a Ukrainian FP-5 Flamingo cruise missile using machine-gun fire during an overnight attack this weekend, an unusual claim for a weapon Russia has typically engaged with surface-to-air missile systems.
Kursk Region Governor Aleksandr Khinshtein said the intercept happened overnight Saturday into Sunday, August 22 to 23, 2026. According to Khinshtein, a mobile air defense team from the BARS-Kursk brigade, a unit made up largely of local residents from the border region, received an alert about an incoming strike and detected a “huge” missile flying at roughly 500 km/h (310 mph) at an altitude below 50 m (164 feet). The team engaged the missile with gunfire, causing it to lose altitude and crash into a wooded area, Khinshtein said.
As evidence, Russian sources published footage recorded on a thermal camera, showing the missile passing overhead and then falling. Separate footage showed what was described as wreckage from the missile itself.
The exact date of the strike has not been independently confirmed, and no outside party has verified that small-arms fire, rather than a surface-to-air missile system or an aircraft, brought the missile down. Some pieces of the recovered wreckage reportedly showed damage patterns consistent with hits from a large-caliber machine gun, though this detail also comes from the Russian side and has not been independently examined. At least one Russian commentator described the released footage as “ambiguous.”
The Flamingo, built by Ukrainian defense firm Fire Point and first unveiled in August 2025, is a large ground-launched cruise missile. It weighs about 6,000 kg (13,200 pounds) at launch, carries a warhead of roughly 1,150 kg (2,540 pounds), and has a stated range of 3,000 km (1,860 miles). Its listed cruise speed is 850 to 900 km/h (530 to 560 mph), well above the roughly 500 km/h Khinshtein described for the intercepted missile, and its flight ceiling reaches 5,000 m (16,400 feet). Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky has called it the country’s “most successful missile.”
Russia has claimed multiple Flamingo intercepts since the missile entered use, generally citing dedicated air defense systems. In October 2025, Russian media said a Buk surface-to-air missile system downed a Flamingo at an altitude of about 100 m (330 feet). In February 2026, Russian officials reported additional intercepts during a large-scale missile alert spanning 13 regions.

Kazakhstan’s ruling party secures landslide victory in parliamentary election
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:02:07 UTC
17:02:07 KST

Elena Teslova
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
Kazakhstan’s Adilet party won 71.17% of the vote in the country’s first election to its new one-chamber parliament, according to preliminary results announced by the Central Election Commission on Monday.
Adilet, the political successor to the former ruling Amanat party, secured a wide lead over the six other parties contesting the Aug. 23 election, held under Kazakhstan’s new constitutional system.
The Aul party received 6.26% of the vote, followed by Respublica with 5.56% and Ak Zhol with 5.21%.
The Nationwide Social Democratic Party received 5.11%, while the People’s Party of Kazakhstan and the Green Party Baytak received 3.11% and 1.07%, respectively.
A total of 2.51% of voters selected the “against all” option.
The Central Election Commission said 9,351,539 citizens took part in the election, putting preliminary turnout at 74.08%.
The election was the first for Kazakhstan’s new 145-member Kurultai, which replaced the former bicameral parliament following the adoption of a new constitution earlier this year.
All seats were contested through party lists, with parties required to secure more than 5% of the vote to enter the legislature.
During the election campaign, Adilet outlined state reform, economic development, digitalization, education, regional development and social protection as its priorities.

Speaking at his weekly press briefing on Monday, he emphasized that Iran will not let the end of war be decided based on the terms and conditions of aggressor.
“We certainly didn't initiate the war, but we won't allow the end of the war to be decided based on the terms of the aggressor,” Baghaei underlined.
"We will not show any appeasement towards the aggressors ... the Islamic Republic of Iran did not start the war and has defended its own rights, territorial integrity and national sovereignty. Naturally, the aggressor must be held accountable. We certainly did not start the war, but we will not allow the end of the war to be based on the aggressor's terms," he emphasized.
Referring to Pakistan's Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir’s visit to Tehran and its relation with the visit of the Omani foreign minister to Tehran, he emphasized, "This visit is scheduled to take place today within the framework of very good and distinguished relations between Iran and Pakistan.”
The bilateral relations between Iran and Pakistan are going through one of their best stages, and both sides are determined to expand these relations in all areas, he said, adding that the visit of the Omani foreign minister to Tehran has nothing to do with this issue, it is only almost simultaneous in terms of time and is scheduled to take place tomorrow and both bilateral relations and issues related to the security of the Strait of Hormuz and traffic routes will be discussed.
In response to the question of whether there is a plan to end the war, the spokesperson stated that all the relevant issues are considered by policymakers in the country expertly. Did we initiate the war? In these two years, Iran's goodwill has been answered with malice for several times. Iran’s nuclear deal, aka known as JCPOA, was a clear example. In this one and a half years, Iran did everything it could to prevent war and secure national interests. After the Islamabad understanding, they [United States] violated all its commitments.
Baghaei also dismissed US claims regarding normal shipping traffic through the Strait of Hormuz, labeling such assertions as media warfare.
On regional diplomatic engagements, he confirmed that Pakistani Army Chief Field Marshal Asim Munir is scheduled to arrive in Tehran today, while Omani Foreign Minister Sayyid Badr Albusaidi will arrive tomorrow for scheduled discussions on bilateral ties and maritime security.
He additionally denied receiving any invitation regarding a reported tripartite pact between Iran, Turkey, and Saudi Arabia.
Regarding relations with Afghanistan, Baghaei highlighted recent high-level talks between President Masoud Pezeshkian and Mullah Baradar aimed at resolving legal and border obstacles to expand trade, noting that the Foreign Ministry has successfully maintained its operations and administrative reforms despite enduring wartime conditions.
In response to questions regarding diplomatic attempts and the origin of recent conflicts, Baghaei emphasized that Iranian policymakers have consistently accounted for all political factors.
He stated that Tehran’s goodwill has repeatedly been met with hostility and broken promises, pointing to the 2015 JCPOA, the June 18 ceasefire agreement, and the Islamabad understanding as primary examples of violated commitments.
Baghaei stressed that over the past eighteen months, Iran did everything within its power to prevent war and protect its national interests. While acknowledging the severe economic hardships, business disruptions, and damage inflicted on oil reserves and refineries as part of decades-long US pressure tactics, he affirmed that government efforts remain focused on minimizing the impact on citizens.
He stated that Iran neither started nor welcomed the war, reiterating that the responsibility lies entirely with the opposing side for repeatedly breaking commitments.
Elsewhere in his remarks, he pointed to the naval blockade imposed by the US government on Iran, stating that the ongoing blockade constitutes an explicit act of aggression.
He warned that any escalation of this situation would carry serious consequences, emphasizing that Iran will not stand by idly with tied hands in the face of such aggressive measures.
Regarding France's actions in expelling the Iranian cultural advisor, he said, "We had already taken action. Two employees of the French Embassy took actions that were outside their legal duties. We gave them the necessary warnings. The French ambassador was summoned and Iran's written and verbal protests were conveyed. Unfortunately, they distorted the reality. France's action is an illegal act that was in response to Iran's legal action.
Regarding the closure of the Chilean Embassy in Iran, Baghaei said, "They decided to close their embassy to save money. Countries often make adjustments, but this does not mean severing diplomatic relations."
Regarding the latest situation of citizens detained in Kuwait, the Foreign Ministry spokesman said, "The Kuwaiti side must be held accountable in this regard. After much effort, our ambassador was able to meet with four imprisoned Iranian citizens. We hope that these dear ones will be released as soon as possible."
Regarding the situation of Iranian pilots in Qatar, Baghaei added: "As for Qatar, as long as the situation is not clarified, our demand remains in place."
With regard to the ways to neutralize the sanctions imposed against Iran, he maintained, "It is a mistake to test Iranians because of their civilizational richness. They know very well that the effect of these sanctions is on the citizens. Iran will definitely use all multilateral capacities to confront the sanctions. We had previously made the necessary predictions."
Regarding the recent Iranian Parliament Speaker Mohammad Bagher Ghalibaf’s visit to neighboring Iraq and the repetition of fake titles for the Persian Gulf, the foreign ministry’s spokesman stated, "First of all, you all know that the Persian Gulf is bigger and more generous than to be affected by political issues. What one group of Afghan women and their supporters make of international engagement with the Taliban
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:01:09 UTC
17:01:09 KST

You’ve heard it before. Women and girls pay a heavy price during humanitarian crises. She Said is an ongoing collection of reporting in which women offer glimpses of their lives, speaking with The New Humanitarian from situations of conflict and displacement, and other global emergencies.
AMSTERDAM, The Netherlands
Five years after the Taliban returned to power in Afghanistan, Afghan women and their supporters gathered last week on Amsterdam’s Dam Square to protest the continued erosion of women’s rights.
Rows of empty school desks and chairs stood across the square, with notebooks and yellow pens laid out on them: a visual reminder of the many girls whose educations have been cut short.
Sahar Shirzad, a Dutch-Afghan human rights activist and organiser with the Azadi Collective, led the crowd in a chant: “Azadi Afghanistan!” She asked: “What do we demand?” The crowd answered: “Let her learn!”
Since the Taliban returned to power in August 2021, international sanctions, frozen assets, and aid cuts have been intended to pressure the government over its treatment of women and girls. Yet the measures have also deepened economic hardship, weakened public services, and made it harder for businesses to access finance. Taliban restrictions have also compounded the economic damage.
Afghanistan has strengthened ties with Russia, China, India, Iran, and Türkiye, despite lacking widespread formal recognition. But closer diplomatic relations have done little to resolve practical problems for Afghans seeking visas, education, banking access, or work abroad. The situation has renewed calls for pragmatic engagement alongside continued pressure on human rights, even as some criticise this approach as only likely to embolden the Taliban while bringing limited to no easing of restrictions.
Mozhda Poyan/TNH
Empty school desks and chairs, along with notebooks and pens, symbolised the many Afghan girls whose educations have been cut short.
Mozhda Poyan/TNH
Sahar Shirzad, a Dutch-Afghan human rights activist and organiser with the Azadi Collective.
The demonstration in Amsterdam came as the European Union has been holding talks with the Taliban about the return of Afghan nationals. The EU does not recognise the Taliban government and says the talks are technical. But for Afghan women, the distinction between practical contact and normalisation matters.
Those at the demonstration offered different answers. Some argued that refusing to talk achieves little and can make it harder to address problems affecting ordinary Afghans. Others said engagement risks weakening pressure on a regime that has restricted women’s education, work, and public life. Deportations have sharpened the debate, with several interviewees warning about the risks facing Afghans returned to the country.
Here is what they said:
Melika Azimi, 20, Dolle Mina member and demonstration organiser
Azimi, a member of the Dutch feminist organisation Dolle Mina, initially questioned whether organising a demonstration would make a difference. But after seeing young Afghan girls post emotional videos asking people to stand behind them, she changed her mind.
“I realised that it would make a difference, because we are breaking that atmosphere. We are shouting that we see them and that we are fighting for them,” said Azima, who is Afghan by heritage but has never lived in Afghanistan.
After seeing footage of Afghan women protesting their arrests in Herat, she said she was struck by their courage. The ensuing crackdown left at least one person dead and several injured: “They were killed, yet they kept going. I felt so inspired by them; I could not do otherwise.”
Azimi said she believes there should be communication with the Taliban, but worries that engagement could become a compromise that encourages further human rights abuses.
“I understand that every country acts in its own interests, but I wonder where the line lies between tactical communication and compromising our values,” she said. “I think there should certainly be more discussions about the Taliban regime. Let’s address the elephant in the room: Do we really have so little backbone? Do we no longer stand for basic human rights?”
Sadia Tayeb Sadat, 19, student living in Kabul
Sadat was in eighth grade when the Taliban returned to power and girls’ schools were closed. She said she had hoped to become a dentist: “My dreams were put on hold, and I felt that my future had been taken away from me.”
Interviewed via text and voice messages from Kabul, Sadat said international discussions about Afghanistan have increasingly focused on migration, deportation, security, humanitarian aid, and diplomatic engagement, while the situation of Afghan women has become less central.
“I think many Afghan women now feel forgotten. When the world’s attention faded, our struggles continued, but fewer people were listening,” she said.
“Practical engagement may sometimes be necessary to help ordinary Afghans, but if that engagement gradually turns into acceptance of the Taliban as a normal and legitimate government, the international pressure for women’s rights could become weaker,” Sadat added.
For her, engagement should come with clear principles, with women’s rights and girls’ education remaining part of every serious conversation about Afghanistan.
“You can speak to the Taliban without forgetting the people who live under their rule,” she said. “Engagement should not mean silence about women’s rights.”
Jalwa Rahimi, 22, Afghan woman living in the Netherlands
Rahimi spent 20 years in Afghanistan before moving to the Netherlands eight months ago. She came to the demonstration because she wants girls’ schools to reopen beyond the sixth grade.
“It is education that creates a country,” she said. “The right of a woman is to study. If she wants to work, she can work.”
Rahimi supports European cooperation with the Taliban, arguing that talking to them does not necessarily mean recognising them.
“By talking, you can solve difficulties,” she said. “They don’t have to recognise them, but they can talk about the problems of Afghans.”
She also opposes deportations and warned that if Europe and the United States continue sending Afghans back, other countries could follow.
“If Afghanistan is good, no one would want to come here,” she said. “If the world forgets Afghanistan, there will be nothing left.”
Hamasa, 42, former teacher and women’s rights activist
For Hamasa, who prefers this adopted activist name for security reasons, the consequences of the Taliban’s rule are not abstract.
She lived in Afghanistan until January 2025 and now lives in an asylum centre in the Netherlands. She turned her home into a classroom, teaching girls and women for free; she said she initially taught 63 students.
After the Taliban takeover, she joined protests demanding education for girls and the right for women to work. She said Taliban fighters beat and kicked protesters during a September 2021 demonstration, causing her to lose her unborn child. She later said she was arrested and tortured after the Taliban discovered a gathering she had organised, and that threats against her family prompted her to leave Afghanistan.
She is strongly opposed to deportations. Questioning why European governments would demand rights for women at home while accepting their denial in Afghanistan, she said: “I want to ask the European government how they want democracy for their people, that women go to school; they should have the same wish for Afghanistan.”
On deportations, she asked: “And the European countries that unfortunately deport Afghans from their countries, and when those Afghans come to Afghanistan they die, don’t they regret doing this?”
Laura Iqbal, 35, Party for the Animals representative and Dolle Mina co-founder
Iqbal, who is Dutch and whose father was born in Pakistan, is a prominent Dolle Mina activist and was a candidate for the Party for the Animals in Amsterdam. “There is no ‘pragmatic’ middle ground with a regime that erases half of the population from society. The Taliban are waging a systematic, institutional war against women. We call that: gender apartheid,” she said.
Iqbal was particularly critical of European cooperation over deportations, arguing that it risks legitimising the Taliban while undermining the women protesting against them.
“European governments claim to stand up for women’s rights, but make those principles subordinate to a cruel migration agenda. You cannot say you are protecting human rights while making deals with the oppressors.”
Iqbal said European governments should instead stop deportations and put greater pressure on the Taliban. She also argued that European governments should involve Afghan women and women’s rights defenders in decisions about Afghanistan.
Meena Maryam Ahmad, 16, Afghan girl living in France
Ahmad, who was not at the protest, left Afghanistan in 2023, citing the closure of girls’ schools, a lack of job opportunities, and uncertainty about the future. She had been in eighth grade when the Taliban returned to power.
Interviewed via text and voice messages from France, she recalled watching her brothers continue their education while she was unable to do so: “I often felt sad and hopeless when I saw my brothers going to school while I was unable to continue my education.”
She said global attention on the plight of Afghan women has decreased even though the situation for women and girls has not improved.
“Sometimes I feel that the world has become used to the suffering of Afghan women,” Ahmad added.
She had a direct message for Europe’s politicians and lawmakers: “I want to tell European policymakers that Afghan women are not just a political issue; we are people with dreams and futures. If they negotiate with the Taliban, they should not forget the rights and voices of Afghan women.”
Despite the hardships of the past five years, she said she has not lost hope.
“I truly believe that no one can destroy a girl’s dreams forever. We are not only victims; we are women who continue to stand despite all the pain. We still have dreams, and we will continue to fight for a better future.”
Petra Hoogerwerf, Dutch strategic adviser to charities and non-profits
Hoogerwerf, a Dutch supporter of Afghan women who was at the demonstration, drew a distinction between necessary practical contact with the Taliban and normalisation of the regime.
She said contact can sometimes be necessary to facilitate humanitarian aid and support the Afghan population, but worries when returns and deportations become a major driver of engagement.
“Afghan women must not pay the price for European migration policy,” she said. “Necessary practical contact can only take place if the rights and position of women and girls remain firmly on the table. Diplomatic contact may be necessary for humanitarian and practical matters; normalisation is something else.”
She also called for continued political and financial support for organisations working with Afghan women and girls, and urged policymakers to listen directly to Afghan women.
“Not only talk about them, but with them,” she said.

Cofnas Suspended by Ghent University
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
08:00:22 UTC
17:00:22 KST

Cofnas Suspended by Ghent University
Nathan Cofnas has been suspended from his postdoctoral philosophy position at Ghent University.
In a July 21st post on his newsletter, Cofnas accused Jason Arday, professor of sociology of education at the University of Cambridge, of plagiarism and fraudulent scholarship, and accused the university of covering this up.
Am international media blitz followed, with hundreds of articles reporting on Cofnas’s accusations and investigating Arday’s work and his autobiographical claims. Eventually, on August 5th, Cambridge announced it had decided to investigate Arday. Arday resigned shortly thereafter. The worldwide pile-on continued. On August 14th, Arday was found dead, presumably by suicide.
This past Thursday, Cofnas stated on X.com that he had been suspended from Ghent University and is being investigated.
Many had objected to his being hired there in the first place.
Most of the text of the suspension letter can be found here. Among the main reasons for the suspension, according to the letter, are the following:
- Cofnas’s continued work on “race realism” and the “hereditarian revolution” at Ghent “are fundamentally inconsistent with the contractual scope of your employment and constitute a manifest violation of your professional obligations towards this University”. Apparently, when he applied for the position, Cofnas had described the research he’d be engaging in as being about “the future of liberalism” and “liberalism as a political doctrine emphasizing individual liberty and equality,” not about “race realism” and “hereditarianism”.
- Cofnas’s ideas conflict with the Ghent University Code of Ethics, which “prohibits spreading ideas of racial superiority or inciting racial segregation.”
- “The current situation poses a risk to the proper functioning of the university and to the psychosocial wellbeing of members of its community”
Meanwhile, a Trump administration official has called for Cofnas to be reinstated, and others are defending him as a “whistleblower.”
Since Arday’s tragic death, Cofnas has defended himself in assorted public writings and appearances (for example).
Cofnas’s current suspension is until August 28th.

Cricket captains from around the world renew appeal for medical treatment of Imran Khan
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24

Cricket captains from around the world renew appeal for medical treatment of Imran Khan
ISLAMABAD (AP) — Famous cricketers from around the world have renewed their appeal for the medical treatment of former star player turned politician Imran Khan in a letter to Pakistan Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif.
A group of 22 former international cricket captains, including Sunil Gavaskar and Kapil Dev of India and Australian greats Greg Chappell and Ian Chappell, signed a second such letter to the Pakistan prime minister within six months.
The latest appeal comes days after Khan was taken to a government hospital in the capital for a medical examination. The examination was conducted in the presence of one of his sisters, and Khan was then returned to Adiala prison in the garrison city of Rawalpindi. Doctors declared him 100% medically fit.
However, the group of cricket greats questioned the procedure of Khan’s medical checkup.
“ Pakistan’s Supreme Court ordered that Imran Khan be transferred to hospital for examination by a medical board that was to include his own personal physicians and his sister, Dr. Uzma Khan,” the cricketers said in a letter.
“Concerningly, Mr. Khan’s hospital stay lasted only a few hours. He was examined by a state-appointed team rather than the board the court had directed, declared ‘medically fit,’ and returned to Adiala jail before that board could complete its work.”
Khan, 73, led Pakistan to the 1992 Cricket World Cup title and later served as prime minister from 2018 until his ouster in 2022.
The 22 former national team captains said they don’t seek to adjudicate on Pakistan’s domestic legal process and had written to the prime minister “not as politicians, but as former colleagues and rivals (of Khan) who share a bond forged on the cricket field.”
In February, 14 former international cricketers expressed their concern over Khan’s health after his family said he had lost about 85% of the vision in his right eye, a claim disputed by the government. Authorities later said his condition was improving following treatment.
Khan’s lawyers and family have also accused the government of defying a court order that required him to be examined at the private Shifa International Hospital in Islamabad. Pakistan’s government rejected the allegations over the weekend, saying Khan was examined by doctors from the private hospital and that he could not be taken to Shifa International for security reasons.
The government said Khan’s supporters had begun gathering outside the private hospital in violation of the court order, which required them to stay away from the medical facility to avoid inconveniencing other patients.
The government has also rejected allegations from Khan’s family that he was being subjected to “cruelty, mental torture, punitive solitary confinement and medical neglect.”
Khan is not being held under a government order but as a “convicted prisoner” serving sentences imposed by courts following judicial proceedings, the Ministry of Information said in a written response to The Associated Press last Friday.
The ministry also rejected allegations that Khan was being held in solitary confinement or denied meaningful contact with his family. It said Khan had received more than 900 visits from family members, lawyers, doctors, political representatives, and other approved visitors since his imprisonment in 2023. He has also been allowed weekly meetings with his wife, as well as telephone and WhatsApp contact with relatives in Pakistan and abroad, the ministry said.
It said his sisters had met with him as recently as Aug. 18 and 19.

The Taphou Kuki Village Authority, in a statement, strongly condemned the loss of property and demanded that the culprits be identified within 24 hours.More than 260 people have been killed and thousands rendered homeless in ethnic clashes between the Meitei and Kuki-Zo communities since May 2023.

Australia marks keel-laying for new anti-sub frigate
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
07:49:19 UTC
16:49:19 KST

- BAE Systems Australia laid the keel of NUSHIP Hunter, the lead ship of Australia's Hunter class frigate program, on August 24, 2026, at Osborne Naval Shipyard.
- The ceremony followed a first steel cut in June 2024, with more than 60 percent of the ship in fabrication or construction as of June 2026.
Shipbuilders at BAE Systems Australia laid the keel of NUSHIP Hunter on August 24, 2026, marking the formal start of hull assembly on the first ship in Australia’s Hunter class frigate program.
The ceremony took place at the Osborne Naval Shipyard in South Australia. Minister for Defence Industry Pat Conroy and Chief of Navy Vice Admiral Matthew Buckley joined shipyard workers to place a coin beneath two ship blocks, a naval custom meant to bring good luck to the vessel and its future crew. The two blocks are among the first structural sections that will form the base of the frigate as additional blocks are added.
NUSHIP Hunter is the lead ship of a class Australia plans to build to replace its aging Anzac class frigates. The Royal Australian Navy’s current program covers six Hunter class ships, with contracts signed for the first three. Construction on Hunter began with a first steel cut in June 2024, and by June 2026, more than 60 percent of the ship was in fabrication or construction, according to BAE Systems. Work on the second ship in the class, NUSHIP Flinders, is preparing to move into fabrication.
The Hunter class design is a heavily modified version of BAE Systems’ Type 26 Global Combat Ship, the same base design being built in Glasgow for the United Kingdom’s Royal Navy. Australia’s version integrates the U.S. Navy’s Aegis combat system with a local interface built by Saab Australia, along with the Australian-designed CEAFAR2 phased-array radar. The ships will displace roughly 8,800 tons at full load, run about 150 m (492 ft) long, and carry a crew of 180, with berths for up to 208. Each frigate will also be built to operate the MH-60R Seahawk maritime helicopter.
David Shepherd, Managing Director of BAE Systems Australia’s Surface Ships business, spoke at the ceremony.
“Today’s ceremony is the culmination of years of hard work by our people and partners in the pursuit of delivering a world-leading warship to the Royal Australian Navy.”
“The Hunter class will form the backbone of the Royal Australian Navy’s fleet for decades to come, with its unique capabilities, weapons, sensors and modular mission bay enabling it to undertake a wide range of missions in addition to hunting submarines.”
“While today we have physically laid the keel of the first Hunter class frigate, the Hunter program itself has laid the foundations of a Continuous Naval Shipbuilding and Sustainment capability in Australia.”
“This milestone is a proud moment for our workforce, our partners and the thousands of Australians contributing to a sovereign naval shipbuilding enterprise that will support Australia’s security and prosperity for generations.”
The frigate is designed primarily for anti-submarine warfare, built around a hull configuration meant to minimize the acoustic signature that submarines can detect. Its weapons fit includes a 32-cell Mark 41 vertical launch system, capable of firing Standard 2 and ESSM missiles, along with torpedo tubes and a modular mission bay that can carry small boats, unmanned systems, or additional mission equipment depending on the task assigned.
The Hunter class program is being carried out under Project SEA 5000 Phase 1, which Australia’s Department of Defence signed with BAE Systems Maritime Australia, now operating as BAE Systems Australia, in December 2018. The head contract was amended in June 2024 to cover construction of the first three ships.
Ahead of cutting steel on Hunter, BAE Systems ran a prototyping program at Osborne beginning in December 2020, building five prototype hull blocks based on the Type 26 reference design to test construction methods, tooling, and workforce training before full production began. A separate mast prototyping effort ran between 2023 and 2026 at the company’s Henderson shipyard in Western Australia, where crews are now building the mast for NUSHIP Hunter.

3D printed standalone alarm clock lets you smash a giant arcade button to wake up
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
07:45:16 UTC
16:45:16 KST

cinderclock treats the alarm clock as a standalone computer
Endothermal Systems’ CinderClock is a 3D printed standalone desktop alarm clock designed to keep the phone away from sleep and morning routines. Measuring 140 × 160 × 170 mm, the device combines a 3.12-inch monochrome OLED display with a joystick, tactile buttons, a 100 mm arcade button, removable battery cells, local audio storage, and environmental sensors, and performs without connecting to an app or subscription service.
The project grew from the designers’ frustration with using smartphones as alarm clocks. Their response is to reconsider what an alarm clock needs to be. The team established three principles at the outset: the device should be standalone, its interface should be mechanical, and its significant components should be modular and replaceable.
CinderClock uses an ESP32-S3 processor and a DS3231 real-time clock, while a removable microSD card stores WAV alarm sounds. A BME280 sensor adds temperature, humidity, and pressure readings, and a light sensor adjusts the screen brightness to the surrounding room. The electronics are mounted as modules on a through-hole main board, with expansion headers exposing the device’s buses for future modifications.
all images courtesy of Endothermal Systems
programmable alarms without a phone
The main point of difference of the clock is its alarm system, which supports schedules based on specific weekdays, intervals, on/off duty cycles, sunrise, and sunset. A weekly cycle can express patterns such as weekdays or every other Tuesday, while a daily cycle can create schedules such as every three days or two days on followed by two days off. Sunrise and sunset times are calculated locally from coordinates entered by the user, so these functions do not require an internet connection.
CinderClock’s interface is designed to make these rules understandable. Alarm lists translate settings into plain language, while each alarm editor shows a calculated next-ring time. A calendar can then display scheduled alarms across a month, giving users another way to check whether a recurrence behaves as intended. The joystick handles navigation and changing values, four buttons provide action, back, confirm, and menu functions, and the large arcade button duplicates the action control. Its size is intentional: dismissing an alarm should not require finding a small button or looking closely at a screen.
Snoozing can work differently. Depending on the selected mode, users may need to press a button multiple times or complete a randomly generated sequence of joystick movements. Endothermal Systems‘ idea is to make snoozing a conscious action rather than something performed automatically while half asleep.
a 3D printed standalone desktop alarm clock designed to keep the phone away from sleep and morning routines
a small computer rather than a connected appliance
Beyond alarms, CinderClock includes timers, a stopwatch, Pomodoro sessions, ambient sound and animation modes, an hourly chime, and eight simple games. Audio files remain on the removable card, while the clock can temporarily create its own WiFi hotspot for transferring sounds or installing firmware. The WiFi connection is deliberately limited. It is switched off at startup and activated manually by the user. Firmware can also be installed from a file through the local portal, without an account or external server. The device can connect to home WiFi for an optional update process, but it does not check for updates automatically.
One of the more unusual aspects of CinderClock is how openly Endothermal Systems documents its development. The design study records not only successful decisions but also the problems encountered during prototyping.
Audio, for example, went through several approaches before the team settled on direct WAV playback through a dedicated FreeRTOS task. An initial software buffer actually made audio stutter worse, while a larger DMA allocation later caused memory fragmentation. The eventual solution was to simplify the system and rely more heavily on hardware already providing sufficient buffering. The first single-piece 3D printed shell took 26 hours to produce and proved unusable. The designers subsequently split the enclosure into two parts along the same 70-degree plane that defines the viewing angle. The halves connect with a sliding dovetail, making the case easier to print and iterate.
This willingness to document failure is significant because the project presents repairability as more than a marketing claim. The designers describe the reasoning behind component choices, expose the board architecture, and plan to publish the PCB files, enclosure models, and bill of materials alongside the firmware and documentation.

Local governments will continue collecting information on damage and recovery needs. Lee said Cho has instructed officials to work within the reduced budget, visit affected areas when conditions allow, and help local governments with recovery and reconstruction under existing rules.

Taiwan’s economics ministry explains changes to energy law
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
07:41:24 UTC
16:41:24 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The Ministry of Economic Affairs said Monday that enterprises should strengthen energy self-reliance, according to a ministry press release.
The legislature approved amendments to the Energy Administration Act on Friday. The ministry welcomed their passage and said the aim is to lighten the burden on the power grid, give local governments the means to enforce energy-conservation rules, and impose harsher fines as deterrents.
On electricity use, the ministry said large energy users adding or expanding capacity beyond a specified threshold must install self-use generation or energy-storage equipment to improve self-sufficiency and reduce reliance on the power grid. The requirement could apply to artificial intelligence data centers and electronics companies.
Taiwan Power Company Chair Tseng Wen-sheng (曾文生) said the utility does not mandate full energy self-reliance but provides recommendations for reference, per CNA.
On enforcement, the ministry said the central and local governments are to impose measures and incentives to ensure energy-conservation goals are met. It added that besides subsidizing equipment-efficiency upgrades, local governments may hire agencies or specialists to conduct on-site inspections to ensure enterprises meet requirements.
On deterrence, the ministry said penalty provisions and fines have been adjusted to reflect current circumstances. It added that in cases involving consumer rights, authorities may disclose the names of offending businesses and the reasons for the violations to encourage reform.

Taiwan’s life expectancy rises to 81.27 years in 2025
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
07:41:10 UTC
16:41:10 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s average life expectancy rose to 81.27 years in 2025, nearing its 2020 peak as deaths declined for a third consecutive year, the Ministry of the Interior said Monday.
The figure increased by 0.5 years from 80.77 in 2024, with life expectancy reaching 84.75 years for women and 77.93 years for men, according to a ministry press release. Taiwan recorded 199,639 deaths in 2025, down 1,674 from the previous year.
The ministry said the rebound in average life expectancy was driven by the decline in deaths and a 3.7% drop in the standardized mortality rate, which is adjusted for age differences. The 2025 figure remained 0.05 years below the 2020 level, while women’s life expectancy was roughly unchanged and men’s remained 0.18 years lower.
Among Taiwan’s six special municipalities, Taipei had the highest average life expectancy at 83.98 years, followed by New Taipei at 81.54 and Kaohsiung at 79.80. Hsinchu had the highest life expectancy among other cities and counties at 82.13, while Taitung County had the lowest at 76.49.
Life expectancy was highest in northern Taiwan, followed by central, southern, and eastern regions, according to the report. Taitung had the largest gap between women and men, at 9.24 years, with life expectancy of 81.54 years for women and 72.30 years for men.
Average remaining life expectancy increased across age groups as the pandemic’s impact eased. A 60-year-old could expect to live another 24.89 years, while the corresponding figures were 17.03 years for a 70-year-old and 10.16 years for an 80-year-old.
Taiwan’s life expectancy remained above the global average in 2025, according to UN data. Global life expectancy was 76.2 years for women and 70.9 years for men, putting Taiwan 8.6 years higher for women and 7 years higher for men.
Among Asian countries, Taiwan’s life expectancy was lower than Japan, Singapore, and South Korea, but higher than China, Malaysia, and Indonesia. Life expectancy in major countries generally declined during the pandemic before beginning to recover, with many returning to pre-pandemic levels by 2025.
Taiwan became a super-aged society last year, with 4.67 million people aged 65 or older accounting for 20.06% of the population. The government said it would continue developing policies to improve housing, public spaces, health, and other services for the aging population.

On Independence Day, EU adds $7B for Ukraine
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
07:40:04 UTC
16:40:04 KST

- The European Commission approved $7 billion in new defense procurement for Ukraine on August 24, 2026, covering air and missile defense systems, missiles, ammunition and radars.
- The funding is part of a $105 billion Ukraine Support Loan, and adds to $18.68 billion in previously approved procurement, of which $9.75 billion has been disbursed.
The European Commission approved €6.1 billion ($7.12 billion) in new defense procurement funding for Ukraine on August 24, 2026, the same day Ukraine marked its Independence Day.
The money covers air and missile defense systems, missiles, ammunition and radars. Commission President Ursula von der Leyen tied the timing directly to the war.
“On Ukraine’s Independence Day, Europe shows our support is unfaltering and concrete. Today, we have approved €6.1 billion for the air and missile defence systems, missiles, ammunition and radars that Ukraine urgently needs. As Russia intensifies its attacks, we are stepping up to help Ukraine protect its people and defend its skies. Europe stands with Ukraine and we will deliver what it needs, when it needs it.”
The Commission cited 376 missile strikes recorded against Ukraine in July alone as the backdrop for the approval. Most of the procurement will go to companies within the EU defense industrial base.
The €6.1 billion ($7.12 billion) comes out of the Ukraine Support Loan, a €90 billion ($105.08 billion) package the European Parliament and Council established under Regulation (EU) 2026/467 in February 2026. The loan splits into two tracks: one for Ukraine’s defense capabilities and defense industrial capacity, the other for keeping the Ukrainian state functioning, covering public services and broader economic resilience. Under the loan, €30 billion ($35.03 billion) is earmarked for budgetary aid and €60 billion ($70.05 billion) for defense spending across 2026 and 2027, with €28.3 billion ($33.04 billion) of that defense allocation set for this year.
Ukraine submitted its financing strategy for the loan in March 2026. The Council followed with an implementing decision on April 23, 2026, allocating up to €45 billion ($52.54 billion) for the year. That figure breaks down into €16.7 billion ($19.50 billion) in budget support, split evenly between the Ukraine Facility and Macro Financial Assistance at roughly €8.35 billion ($9.75 billion) each, and €28.3 billion ($33.04 billion) for defense industrial capacity.
Today’s €6.1 billion ($7.12 billion) adds to €16 billion ($18.68 billion) in procurement plans the Commission had already approved before this announcement. Of that earlier total, €8.35 billion ($9.75 billion) has already been disbursed to Ukraine.
To draw down the new funds, Ukraine has to submit signed contracts with defense companies to the Commission. Commission staff review each contract before releasing money, a step meant to confirm the funds go toward the procurements Ukraine agreed on with member states and the Commission.
The Commission has flagged Russia’s growing use of ballistic missiles and jet-engined drones as a reason EU suppliers need to move faster. It is pressing companies to draw down existing stockpiles, reorder production priorities, and expand output to keep pace with Ukraine’s needs.
The defense funding track under the loan is also meant to do more than supply weapons for the current fight. The Commission describes it as reconstructing and modernizing Ukraine’s defense technology and industrial base, with an eye toward folding that base into the European Defence Technological and Industrial Base over time.
Since Russia’s full-scale invasion began in 2022, the EU and its member states have provided €220.2 billion ($257.19 billion) in total support to Ukraine. That figure includes €3.8 billion ($4.44 billion) drawn from the proceeds of immobilized Russian state assets.

How much more are you spending on petrol since the war in Iran began?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
07:26:15 UTC
16:26:15 KST

How much more are you spending on petrol since the war on Iran began?
At least 145 countries have reported increases in petrol prices since the attacks on Iran by the US and Israel began on February 28.
Since the United States and Israel launched their war on Iran six months ago, petrol prices have risen in at least 145 countries, adding to the burden on consumers worldwide.
The figures are based on data from GlobalPetrolPrices, which tracks fuel prices in 170 countries and territories. Petrol prices in Myanmar rose the most, increasing by 56 percent from $0.77 per litre of 95-octane fuel on February 23 to $1.20 on August 17. Bhutan recorded the next-largest increase at 55 percent, followed by Cuba at 51 percent, the UAE at 50 percent and 48 percent in Nigeria.
In 25 other countries, most of them oil producers with heavily subsidised fuel, prices have either remained unchanged or fallen by single digits.
The table below lists the 145 countries where petrol prices at the pump increased over the past six months.
How higher fuel costs shrink your driving range
Before the war, the US national average for a gallon [3.78 litres] of regular petrol was $2.94. It now costs $4.09, an increase of 39 percent, according to AAA Fuel Prices, which tracks retail fuel prices for the American Automobile Association (AAA).
The extra cost directly affects how far people can travel. Before the war, $50 worth of fuel in the US could take a family sedan roughly 718 km (446 miles). Today, the same amount takes you about 536 km (333 miles) – 183 km less, a 25 percent reduction in driving distance.
That gap varies depending on where you live.
Set your country, car and budget below to see how far your money takes you. If you’re filling up in the US, you can also select a state and fuel grade.
How high oil costs drive up the price of food
Oil prices and food prices move in lockstep, with energy prices affecting every stage of the food supply chain, from the fertilisers used in the fields to the trucks that carry food from field to supermarket shelf.
Rising oil prices also directly impact shipping and the cost of transport.
“The lifeblood of the global economy is transport,” economist David McWilliams told Al Jazeera. “It’s getting stuff from A to B – it’s a logistics problem, a supply chain problem and ultimately transportation is the energy of the global economy.”
In lower-income countries, where populations spend a far greater share of their earnings on food and import large quantities of grain and fertiliser, rising oil prices could rapidly translate into food shortages.
What products are made from oil and gas?
Oil and gas are used for far more than just fuel. They are raw materials for thousands of everyday products.
Plastics, including water bottles, food packaging, phone casings and medical syringes, are all derived from crude oil.
Crude oil is also the hidden ingredient in synthetic fabrics, such as polyester, nylon and acrylic, which are used to make everything from sportswear to carpets. It also underpins the cosmetics industry, as it is used to make products such as petroleum jelly (Vaseline), lipsticks and concealers.
Household items also rely on oil-based ingredients, with laundry detergents, dishwashing liquids and paints all derived from petroleum products.
The global food supply is essentially built on natural gas in the form of fertilisers, used to enhance crop yields and ensure that food production can meet demand.

Las Vegas Raiders’ Ashton Jeanty suffers apparent injury during practice
HENDERSON, Nev. (AP) — Las Vegas Raiders running back Ashton Jeanty had to be helped off the field after apparently being injured late in Sunday’s practice and was unable to put pressure on his right leg.
The Raiders did not provide a statement on Jeanty’s status and there was no indication of when an update would come. Coach Klint Kubiak is not scheduled to speak with reporters until Tuesday.
Jeanty went down after trying to catch a pass, and his teammates at the club’s indoor practice facility quickly went quiet. The entire team then knelt and prayed.
Drafted sixth overall out of Boise State last year, Jeanty had hoped to build on a rookie season in which rushed for 975 yards despite playing behind what was statistically the NFL’s worst offensive line. His 1.6 yards per attempt before contact, according to Pro Football Reference, was third worst among backs with more than 100 carries.
Similar to other starters, the Raiders had tried to preserve Jeanty in preseason games, playing him briefly in the opener against Arizona. He rushed just three times for 16 yards against the Cardinals and didn’t play Thursday at Houston.
Should Jeanty be out for any notable length of time, rookie Mike Washington Jr. likely would move to the top of the depth chart. He was drafted in the fourth round out of Arkansas and has had a promising training camp. Washington even at times has received practice snaps with the starting offense.
He has 15 carries for 119 yards this preseason.
The Raiders conclude their preseason schedule by hosting San Francisco on Thursday night.

The health of Norway’s King Harald deteriorated over the weekend but he is stable now
OSLO, Norway (AP) — Crown Prince Haakon visited his father King Harald of Norway on Monday at the hospital, after the king’s health deteriorated over the weekend, public broadcaster NRK reported.
The 89-year-old monarch, who has been on sick leave for several weeks, was admitted to the National Hospital a week ago. He is now receiving antibiotics for a bacterial blood infection and has responded to treatment, the royal palace said late Sunday, adding that his condition is stable.
Haakon, has been serving as regent during that time, the palace said.
The king has hemolytic anemia and was being treated with cortisone, leading to fluid accumulation in the body that required hospital treatment, the palace said last week.
Norway’s prime minister sent his wishes for the king and said that “all of Norway is following and thinking about the king,” NRK reported.
“My strong wish is that he continues to receive good treatment from the good healthcare system we have,” Prime Minister Jonas Gahr Støre said.
Harald, who has been monarch since 1991, has been in and out of the hospital several times in recent years.
In February, he was admitted to a hospital in Spain’s Canary Islands during a winter vacation for treatment for a skin infection.
Two years ago, the king fell ill during a private vacation with the queen in Malaysia and received a temporary pacemaker there. Harald returned aboard a medical airplane to Norway, where he was fitted with a permanent pacemaker.

Burnham and European leaders arrive in Kyiv as Ukraine marks Independence Day
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
07:23:02 UTC
16:23:02 KST

European leaders mark Ukraine’s 35th Independence Day as Russian invasion pushes on
KYIV, Ukraine (AP) — European leaders joined President Volodymyr Zelenskyy in Kyiv on Monday for celebrations marking the 35th anniversary of Ukraine’s Independence Day as Russia pressed on with its 4-year-old invasion of the country.
One of President Vladimir Putin’s key goals in starting a war with Russia’s neighbor in February 2022 was to place Kyiv in Moscow’s orbit. Ukrainian lawmakers voted on Aug. 24, 1991, to proclaim the country’s independence from Moscow, and a nationwide referendum later that year overwhelmingly approved it.
With no significant changes on the front line for months and no apparent progress after more than a year of U.S.-led peace efforts, both countries are locked in a spiral of escalating aerial attacks that are killing civilians and smashing infrastructure.
EU leaders rally around Ukraine
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham, on his first overseas trip since taking office last month, joined almost a dozen other European leaders, as well as other dignitaries including European Council President Antonio Costa, in Kyiv on Monday.
“For Ukraine, independence is not an abstract idea. We defended it against all odds,” Ukrainian Foreign Minister Andrii Sybiha said on social media. “In times like these, nations learn how important it is to have allies by your side.”
Burnham was to co-chair a meeting of what has been dubbed the Coalition of the Willing — a group of countries helping Ukraine resist Russia’s onslaught, with the leaders of France and Germany expected to join online.
Zelenskyy said in a speech at Kyiv’s St. Sophia Square that the presence of European leaders reflected continental fears about Russia’s wider ambitions.
“We all understand that in this Russian war against us — against Ukraine — far more is being decided than the future of Ukraine and Eastern Europe,” Zelenskyy said, adding that foreign help was vital.
“No nation in a war like this could rely solely on its own weapons,” he said. “No nation could withstand attacks of such intensity without the world’s help.”
Ukraine eyes local production of French and British missile
The visiting leaders brought pledges of further military and financial support. Burnham is expected to announce that his government has agreed to allow defense company MBDA to release classified information relating to British components used in the SCALP long-range missile, according to his office. That would pave the way for France and Ukraine to advance plans for production of the weapon in Ukraine.
SCALP is the French version of the UK’s Storm Shadow missile, with both systems incorporating shared French and British technology.
“Ukraine has been Europe’s protector, not a drain on our security, but the front line of keeping Europe safe,” Burnham said in a speech, adding that Kyiv and its partners “must keep up the pressure on Moscow.”
Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov said the Kremlin views the plan “extremely negatively.” He accused the U.K. of “taking part in this war” on Kyiv’s side.
Ukraine has leaned heavily on NATO countries for help fighting Russia’s bigger army, although relations with the United States have been cooler under President Donald Trump.
Russia, meanwhile, is getting help from North Korea and China.
Ukraine shows off its drones in a Kyiv parade
Ukraine’s swift development of innovative drone technology has enabled it to blunt Russia’s battlefield progress as well as hit targets deep inside Russia, as far as 2,000 kilometers (1,200 miles) from their border. The St. Sophia Square speeches were accompanied by a street parade of domestically produced weapons.
Both Russia and Ukraine are trying through long-range strikes to inflict economic pain, disrupt military supplies and erode public morale.
Ukraine’s long-range drones have repeatedly hit facilities in Russia’s vital oil industry, causing fuel shortages, and have also engaged in a campaign against Russia’s largest online retailer, Wildberries.
But foreign suppliers also have to take into account their own needs, weapon production levels and the depth of stockpiles.
As the air war has intensified, Ukraine’s stocks of U.S.-made Patriot interceptors to counter Russia’s ballistic missiles have run desperately low. Kyiv urgently needs more interceptors before winter, when Russia routinely bombards its power grid, but the demands of the Iran war and slow output of the sophisticated interceptors have left Ukraine short and vulnerable.
Ukrainian strikes kill 3 teenagers
Three teenagers were killed and six children were wounded in the southern Russian city of Krasnodar, Russia’s children’s rights ombudswoman Maria Lvova-Belova said, as Ukraine attacked several warehouses of Ozon, another online retailer, for the third straight day, according to officials and the company.
The company said a large fire raged at an Ozon logistics facility in the suburbs of Krasnodar following the overnight attack.
A drone also hit the grounds of an Ozon logistics center in the southern Russian region of Adygeya, regional Gov. Murat Kumpilov said, although the company said its Adygeya warehouse wasn’t damaged.
In all, four Ozon premises appeared to have been targeted.
Meanwhile, Ukraine’s General Staff said its forces struck the Russian state-owned Kamenetsky Combine defense company in the Rostov region, overnight, starting a fire. The plant produces fuel for rockets and missiles, it said.
Russia’s Defense Ministry said its air defenses overnight intercepted and destroyed 351 Ukrainian drones over eight Russian regions, the Crimean Peninsula and the Azov and the Black seas. Moscow illegally annexed Crimea in 2014.
The ministry also said that its forces overnight continued to strike Ukrainian ports and vessels delivering cargo for the armed forces.
Russia has also turned its sights on Ukrainian shopping malls, supermarkets and gas stations in recent months. Russian drones struck a shopping center in central Ukraine in a daytime attack Friday, killing 16 people and wounding 130, Ukrainian officials said.
Ukraine’s southern Odesa region came under a large-scale Russian missile and drone attack Monday, with food storage facilities and energy infrastructure among the targets, regional authorities reported.
Eighteen people, including two children, were injured in a Russian drone strike on Chernihiv in northern Ukraine, according to Ukraine’s Emergency Service.
It was not possible to independently verify each side’s reports.

EU, Russian aircraft help Serbia battle wildfires
EU crews and a Russian aircraft help Serbia fight major wildfires as extreme heat and drought fuel fires across the Balkans.
Serbia requests international assistance to battle wildfires
Helicopters and firefighters from the European Union are working alongside Serbian teams to contain a large wildfire that has been burning for weeks in a protected nature reserve near the capital, Belgrade, according to state media.
The operation in Deliblatska Pescara continued into Monday as Serbia’s RTS reported that a separate fire in the southwestern Stolovi mountain range had been brought under control, with help from a Russian Ilyushin Il-76 water-bombing aircraft.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
