- list 3 of 3At least 12 people killed in Hungary bus crash
RTS said the Russian aircraft dropped 168 tonnes of water on the two fires on Sunday — 126 tonnes in Deliblatska Pescara and 42 in Stolovi.
Serbia’s Interior Minister, Ivica Dacic, described the situation as “extremely difficult,” according to Euro News, with more than 400 personnel deployed to the area each day.
President Aleksandar Vucic said Belgrade had turned to both the EU and Russia once it became clear Serbia’s own resources were not enough.
“The very second we realised that our own forces were no longer sufficient, we immediately requested urgent assistance from Russia and the European mechanism,” he said.
Serbia is not an EU member but can request aid under the bloc’s Civil Protection Mechanism, a system that allows EU countries to pool emergency resources for disasters. Belgrade formally asked for help on Friday.
The EU response includes four Black Hawk helicopters from Romania, Slovakia and the Czech Republic, along with teams of firefighters and vehicles from Germany and Romania.
The EU’s mutual aid system has worked both ways during the summer there.
Serbia sent a firefighting helicopter and response team to Spain earlier in the wildfire season, when various blazes stretched the bloc’s own resources thin.
Fires are also burning across the border in North Macedonia, where a blaze near the town of Strumica reportedly damaged at least one home.
“It was devouring everything,” said Ljubce Ivanski, a farmer near one fire, describing how strong winds overwhelmed firefighting planes and helicopters.
The wildfire season now unfolding across the Balkans has been driven by an unusually hot, dry summer that has left much of the region primed to burn.
A large fire also broke out over the weekend between Bosnia and Croatia, forcing the closure of the main road linking Trebinje to the Croatian tourist city of Dubrovnik, stranding thousands of travellers and prompting the evacuation of nearby villages.

CM Yogi slams Rahul over Manusmriti remarks
NEW DELHI: Uttar Pradesh chief minister Yogi Adityanath on Monday stepped up his attack on Congress leader Rahul Gandhi over his remarks on the Manusmriti, while also targeting the party's state leadership over its alleged conduct in Ayodhya.Speaking in Raebareli, CM Yogi said Rahul Gandhi, as leader of opposition, had a responsibility to uphold the Constitution and respect India's traditions and heritage.
“Recently, I was reading a statement made by the Member of Parliament from Raebareli, Rahul Gandhi. He made a statement in Maharashtra urging women to break free from the shackles of the Manusmriti. Rahul ji, the country does not have high expectations of you merely as Rahul Gandhi; in fact, it has no expectations at all. However, your role as the Leader of the Opposition in Parliament entails accountability towards the country's democracy. You took an oath to uphold the Constitution of India, yet you seem to consider it your birthright to disparage India's traditions and heritage.”CM Yogi accused Gandhi of insulting Uttar Pradesh and India during visits outside the state and abroad. He also alleged that the Congress had questioned the existence of Lord Ram in Ayodhya and referred to the Emergency imposed in 1975.
The UP chief minister said Rahul Gandhi should study ancient Indian texts to understand Manu and India's heritage.“You make comments regarding Manu, Ram, or India's heritage. If you wish to understand Manu, read the Atharvaveda, the Shatapatha Brahmana and the Matsya Purana; you will find all the information there.”Yogi also criticised remarks directed at the Prime Minister, saying such statements amounted to an attack on an institution rather than an individual.“When you insult India's institutions, when you make derogatory remarks about the Prime Minister of India, you are not merely insulting an individual; you are insulting an institution of India. The Prime Minister is not just an individual; the Prime Minister is an institution of India.”He added that such criticism could undermine public confidence in constitutional institutions and urged Gandhi to refrain from what he called irresponsible behaviour.
CM Yogi targets Congress state
CM Yogi also attacked the Congress state president over an alleged incident involving a visit to Hanumangarhi in Ayodhya, accusing him of displaying duplicity.“You saw the behaviour of the Congress state president: he goes to offer prayers at Hanumangarhi, but later outside he enjoys a feast of fish. He could have eaten whatever he wanted outside—anywhere other than Ayodhya. Yet, this is the duplicity they display. Even a chameleon would be put to shame by these people; it would wonder what kind of human species this is—chanting 'Ram-Ram' inside the temple and feasting on fish the moment they step out. This is their history—the history of this Congress state president.”
CM Yogi further alleged that the Congress leader had bowed before a mafia figure who had allegedly killed his brother, claiming the situation changed only after the government acted against the accused.“When a mafia don murdered his brother, this man did not testify against the criminal; instead, he knelt and bowed in submission before him. He knelt before the very man who had brutally killed his brother. It was only when the government stepped in and crushed that mafia element that the situation changed; otherwise, these people had turned the state into a mafia-dominated territory, creating an identity crisis.”CM Yogi also said society could have no future if it forgot its ancestors and accused unnamed groups of attempting to weaken India's traditions, values and ideals.

Centre for Child Rights set up at Lohiya Law University
Ambika Pandit / TNN / Updated: Aug 24, 2026, 13:31 IST
Comments
Share
AA
Text Size
Small
Medium
Large
RMLNLU to build ecosystem where every child is heard
LUCKNOW: The multidisciplinary Centre inaugurated over the weekend will focus on research, capacity building and evidence-informed advocacy on matters concerning the rights of the child.The new Centre was inaugurated by former Supreme Court Judge Justice (Retd.) Madan B Lokur on Saturday during a two day consultation at RMLNLU titled - "From Policy to Practice: commemorating 10 years of Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act 2015.
Justice Lokur described the Centre for Child Rights at RMLNLU as a "big step forward". He highlighted that such Centres can play a critical role in steering change through research to create a stronger Juvenile Justice framework. He particularly expressed worry over denial of bail to juveniles and the concerns arising out of the existing pre-assessment process for transferring a juvenile to the adult criminal system. He highlighted the need to bring clarity and transparency in the existing provisions of the JJ Act.The two- day national consultation with special focus on Uttar Pradesh ended on Sunday evening.The meet saw stakeholders including child rights activists, civil society organisations, Juvenile Justice Board members, people working with or having experience of the juvenile justice system like observation homes, lawyers, academics, researchers and students came together to dwell on the learnings and challenges faced in the implementation of the 2015 Act that had replaced the JJ Act 2000.
Representatives from women and child department of Uttar Pradesh also participated.The consultation over various sessions looked at specific concerns starting from the first interaction of the child in conflict with law with the JJ system, challenges surrounding bail and pre-inquiry and the concerns arising out of the assessment process that is a critical aspect in cases involving the transfer of children to the adult criminal justice system. The consultation also drew attention to the challenges in rehabilitation and re-integration.Meanwhile, Dr Kumar Askand Pandey, Associate Professor, RMLNLU, shared that at the Centre for Child Rights one of the key institutional initiatives proposed include working on data evaluation and research.It is also proposed to bring out policy briefs, practical handbooks, standardised tools and annual reports on status of child rights and juvenile justice in Uttar Pradesh.The University also proposes to curate and rollout, after the requisite approvals, post graduate diploma programmes targeted at professionals working on child rights.As of now education of child rights and related laws in the form of a course is available to law students at RMLNLU by way of an elective subject from 8th to 10th semester for LLB students who are specialising in criminal law. The elective subject is also available for students specializing in criminal laws in the LLM programme.
With the new Centre in place, RMLNLU as per its vision document seeks to build a "child- sensitive, rights - based and evidence - driven ecosystem in which every child is heard, protected, respected and provided access to justice, care and opportunity".The focus areas include juvenile justice and restorative practice, child protection, POCSO and institutional care, right to education and inclusion, child labour, trafficking and migration, children in the digital environment and children with disabilities.

NEW DELHI: The government on Monday said discussions about arrangements for a leader’s public appearance are a “normal practice,” clarifying the context of US Ambassador to India Sergio Gor’s remarks regarding the bilateral meeting between Prime Minister Narendra Modi and US President Donald Trump in June.“Discussions regarding arrangements for public appearances of leaders are normal practice ahead of any VVIP visit, and in this regard, the Indian side had communicated its standard practice for such visits,” government sources told ANI.
The clarification followed statements by Gor at the Economic Times World Leaders Forum on Saturday, where he stated that India had “specifically requested” the US administration not to take questions from the media following the bilateral interaction between PM Modi and President Trump on the sidelines of the G7 summit in France.Also Read | 'As long as he's the leader, India is going to play a big role': Trump's massive praise for PM ModiAccording to Gor, although Trump initially agreed to the request, he subsequently opened the floor to reporters, turning the session into a 45-minute press conference with PM Modi sitting alongside him.Recalling the sequence of events, Gor described his “brief conversation” with Trump before the bilateral meeting with PM Modi.“We were behind the scenes, behind the stage, and at one point it was just the president and I, and he asked me, he goes, ‘What the Indians are going to raise?’ We went over some topics,” Gor recounted.
“And he (Trump) said, ‘Do they have any asks?’ And the MEA had one ask. He said, and it was, ‘Let’s bring in the media, but let’s not do a full press conference,’” the ambassador added.He noted that he directly conveyed the Indian side’s preference to Trump.“I told the president, I said, the Indians prefer no questions. He said, 'Sure, no problem',” Gor recalled.The interaction subsequently began with media personnel and technical crews present in the room. Gor noted that about 50 cameras were set up as PM Modi and Trump sat across from each other to deliver their opening statements.“So the meeting starts, the press comes in, there must have been 50 cameras, the president is sitting here, the prime minister is sitting there, they both speak for a few minutes,” he recalled.
However, immediately after the opening statements, Trump turned to the assembled reporters and asked, “Any questions?”“And that opened everything up,” the ambassador recalled, describing the interaction as turning into “a 45-minute press conference” where “everything was on the table."The bilateral meeting on June 17 came days after three Indian mariners were killed in an attack by the US Navy on a commercial vessel in the Strait of Hormuz.The safety and protection of Indian seafarers navigating the region were among the key issues raised by PM Modi during the exchange.The June visit proved significant as New Delhi and Washington worked towards finalising a bilateral trade agreement amid continuing tensions in West Asia that affected maritime shipping and global energy supplies.Trump also observed during the interaction that the two nations were “very close” to concluding the trade deal.

U.S. racks up 40 trillion dollars in debt, raising concerns over economic crisis
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
15:12:14 CST
16:12:14 KST

WASHINGTON, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- The U.S. government has racked up 40 trillion dollars in debt, raising concerns that the mounting burden could trigger a major economic crisis if left unaddressed.
U.S. government debt has surged from 19.4 trillion dollars a decade ago, nearly doubling after massive COVID-era spending and years of deficits.
In July, the most recent month for which figures are available, the U.S. Treasury Department reported a monthly budget deficit of 432.3 billion dollars, the highest level since March 2021.
Critics have voiced growing concern that, if left unchecked, the country's mounting debt could eventually trigger a major debt crisis.
U.S. federal debt currently stands at about 123 percent of GDP. However, the debt-to-GDP ratio that the U.S. economy can sustain is about 210 percent of GDP, according to a study released in June by the University of Pennsylvania's Wharton Business School.
"Above this level, there is no feasible future additional tax on broad-based labor income that can finance the interest payments at the returns demanded by financial markets," the study said.
A national debt crisis would be "an event somewhere between the Great Recession of 2008-09 and the Great Depression of the 1930s," according to Clay Ramsay, a researcher at the Center for International and Security Studies at the University of Maryland.
The economic collapse of nearly two decades ago led to the loss of millions of jobs and widespread financial hardship. Millions of Americans lost their homes, pensions and life savings, while the stock market took roughly six years to return to its pre-recession level. The downturn was surpassed in severity only by the Great Depression.
Experts said a debt crisis could trigger damage that would take years to repair.
"Even after the economy stopped contracting, it would take years for it to rebuild," Ramsay told Xinhua.
Such an event could also have far-reaching political repercussions.
"Politically, such a crisis would make the argument over income taxes and wealth taxes much more intense than the one we have today," Ramsay said.
"Currently the top 10 percent of households own 64 percent of the national wealth. If trends continue, this imbalance would be far greater at the time of a national debt crisis," he said.
One model from Wharton Business School suggests that, if current trends continue, U.S. debt could become unsustainable by 2048, Ramsay noted.
This model does not take into account a major shock, such as the bursting of an artificial intelligence bubble, that could accelerate the process, he added.
"In practice, debt always looks sustainable up to the point that bond investors collectively decide that the government cannot make needed adjustments. If bond investors believed the government can't reform, things would unravel quickly," Ramsay said.
Some have argued that the economy's resilience and future growth could help ease the debt burden.
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent recently downplayed concerns over the 40 trillion-dollar debt level in an interview with CNBC, saying that "there's nothing magic about the 40 trillion number" and that the country could "grow our way out of that."
Bessent added that President Donald Trump's administration plans to rely on global economic growth and future fiscal consolidation efforts to tackle the debt burden.
Meanwhile, some experts said the issue has received relatively little attention in the run-up to the November midterm elections.
"The heavy debt level has not been an issue in the campaign so far. It is such a large number it is hard for people to grasp or see it as having any effect on their lives," Darrell West, a senior fellow at the Brookings Institution, told Xinhua. ■

Singapore unveils measures to boost family support
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
15:12:07 CST
16:12:07 KST

SINGAPORE, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Singapore will strengthen support for families by increasing childcare leave, expanding financial assistance for children, reducing preschool fees, and increasing housing access, Prime Minister Lawrence Wong said on Sunday.
Under the new childcare leave arrangement, every working parent will receive eight days every year for one child aged 12 and below, 10 days for two children and 12 days for three or more children, he said while delivering his National Day Rally 2026 speech.
Each newborn will receive almost 70,000 Singapore dollars (about 55,141 U.S. dollars) in direct financial support over their childhood, including annual child credits and education-related top-ups.
The government also aims to reduce full-day childcare fees to 150 Singapore dollars a month and infant care fees to 300 Singapore dollars a month, regardless of household income, while providing additional subsidies to lower-income families.
The government will also raise household income ceilings for subsidized public housing and give first-time families with children greater priority in securing new flats, as part of broader measures to help Singaporeans raise families.
The government will raise income ceilings for subsidized Build-to-Order flats to 16,000 Singapore dollars from 14,000 Singapore dollars and for executive condominiums to 18,000 Singapore dollars from 16,000 Singapore dollars.
Wong said the measures were aimed at supporting parents throughout the journey of raising children, rather than concentrating assistance around the time of birth. ■

The team of the second special counsel, Kwon Chang-young, who led investigations into leftover martial law allegations and other corruption, indicted seven individuals under detention and 51 without detention.
Yoon was indicted on charges stemming from his directive to spread messages to allied countries justifying his short-lived martial law declaration.
The emergency martial law was declared by Yoon on the night of Dec. 3, 2024, but it was revoked hours later by the National Assembly.
Yoon was accused of ordering the dissemination of distorted messages to major allies, including the United States, between Dec. 3 and 4, 2024, to validate the legitimacy of the martial law.
Former National Security Adviser Shin Won-sik and former Principal Deputy National Security Adviser Kim Tae-hyo were indicted on charges of conspiring with Yoon to distribute the justification messages.
The special counsel team also indicted former Joint Chiefs of Staff Chairman Kim Myung-soo and former National Intelligence Service Director Cho Tae-yong for their key role in the insurrection from Yoon's martial law bid.
Yoon's wife, Kim Keon-hee, was indicted on charges of meddling in a presidential residence relocation in 2022.
Yoon was sentenced to life in prison in February for the insurrection stemming from his martial law declaration and 30 years in prison in June for the general treason relevant to the infiltration of drones into the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
He was indicted under detention in January 2025 as a suspected ringleader of the insurrection, becoming the first sitting president to be arrested and indicted. ■

The right to health in Gaza is now a privilege
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
07:08:07 UTC
16:08:07 KST

The right to health in Gaza is now a privilege
The devastated healthcare system cannot reach Gaza’s most vulnerable – those who live in displacement camps.
These days, Gaza’s healthcare system is not in the news. There are no violent raids on hospitals, as happened to Al Shifa Hospital, while I was working there in November 2023; there are no bombings of hospital wards or sniper killings in their yards; there are no new claims of secret tunnels under medical facilities.
And yet Gaza’s medical system continues to suffer from worsening collapse. Perhaps, this is the most apparent in displacement camps, where the most impoverished and vulnerable people are forced to live. There, the devastated healthcare system cannot reach those who need it the most, nor are the ill and injured able to come to its few functioning points. Lack of sanitation, safe potable water and constant exposure to unbearable heat or cold make the health crisis even worse.
Last month, I had the opportunity to visit an informal camp that has emerged on the grounds of what is left of Hassan Salama school in the Nasr neighbourhood of Gaza City. The school was devastated after it was bombed along with the neighbouring Nasr school in August 2024, which resulted in the deaths of at least 30 people.
Today, hundreds of people who have been rendered homeless and destitute by the war live in tents in the schoolyard and what is left of the school building. No organisation runs the camp, so there is no provision of any services, including medical ones.
I joined a team of several medics from a local private clinic who offered free check-ups at the camp for a day. Our arrival was warmly welcomed. We saw at least 150 patients.
Complaints ranged from high blood pressure to chronic diseases, such as diabetes and kidney problems, and infections, such as hepatitis and scabies. We also saw many children with chickenpox, gastroenteritis, diarrhoea and respiratory infections.
Although we provided just basic services, the gratitude we received was immense.
For many patients in displacement camps, reaching a doctor has become an almost impossible journey that requires effort, energy and resources that are not available to everyone. Transportation costs, long distances and exhaustion caused by displacement and extreme heat all contribute to some patients delaying medical care, despite their urgent needs.
One patient we had, 46 years old, had a bad foot injury caused by shrapnel and needed crutches to move. He had hypertension problems but could not go to the nearby Al Rantisi Hospital as the facility is partially functioning and offering services mostly to children and oncology patients.
Walking a long distance to another hospital was clearly not an option for him. To get to a doctor to assess his hypertension problem for free and receive a prescription for medication, he would have had to pay at least $8 for transportation to the nearest health facility.
That is a large sum of money for most people in displacement camps who struggle to secure even their daily meals.
Delayed medical care, combined with the lack of medication and difficult living conditions, can worsen diseases and can even be fatal.
All of this could be prevented if basic healthcare returns to Gaza, particularly under the umbrella of a large organisation such as UNRWA.
After the Nakba, UNRWA played an instrumental role in setting up basic healthcare provision for the Palestinian refugees who came to Gaza. It established clinics in each refugee camp, which helped secure a basic level of free healthcare provision.
Before the war, UNRWA ran 22 clinics across the Gaza Strip. According to a recent report, only six of them are operational today. Just 19 of Gaza’s 34 hospitals are partially functioning – and “partially functioning” is the key word here. Most wards in these hospitals are not working because of the destruction they have sustained.
Today, in the whole of the Gaza Strip, there are just 2,200 inpatient beds available to serve 2 million people. Before the war, just Al Shifa Hospital alone had 700 beds.
Various medical services, including lab tests, surgeries and treatments, are no longer available because there are no supplies for them or living medics to perform them.
The destruction of medical facilities and the dispossession of Gaza’s residents have transformed the right to healthcare into a privilege.
We urgently need a healthcare intervention that focuses, not only on rebuilding hospitals, but also on re-establishing basic care clinics and reaching the most vulnerable in displacement camps.
The views expressed in this article are the author’s own and do not necessarily reflect Al Jazeera’s editorial stance.

As AI agents act in unexpected ways, is ‘rogue AI’ really here?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
07:06:59 UTC
16:06:59 KST

The idea of machines independently handling tedious everyday tasks – from answering emails to booking flights and making dinner reservations – has long been part of the vision for artificial intelligence.
Now, that future is beginning to arrive, but with an unexpected catch: what happens when the machine does exactly what it was asked, just not in the way the user intended?
As AI moves beyond chatbots toward agents capable of taking actions in real-world systems, a string of recent incidents has intensified concerns over how much control humans will retain as the technology becomes increasingly autonomous.
For John Thickstun, an assistant professor of computer science at Cornell University who researches machine learning and generative models, the defining feature of these AI agents is that they keep working after the human steps away.
“You can have a shower, you can go, you can go to sleep,” he told Anadolu.
Increasingly, those agents have demonstrated that they can take unexpected routes to reach their goals.
In July, AI agents compromised Hugging Face, a platform widely used by AI developers to share models, datasets and tools, during an OpenAI cybersecurity test.
OpenAI said the models were “hyperfocused on finding a solution” and went to “extreme lengths” to achieve their testing goal. Those steps included breaking out of the sealed-off test environment by exploiting a security vulnerability to reach the open internet and gaining access to “secret information” that could be used to “cheat” the test.
After the incident became public, Anthropic reviewed its own cybersecurity testing and disclosed that its Claude models had also escaped testing environments on three occasions.
Then, on Aug. 4, the UK's AI Security Institute said that Anthropic's Mythos and OpenAI's Sol AI models had engaged in a level of "autonomy and deception" it had not seen before. In the most serious case, Mythos AI used fake accounts mimicking real people to gain access to a service for attempted cyberattacks – and then tried to hide its tracks.
“This is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world,” the institute said of the incident.
The following day, Meta disclosed that one of its models had also breached another company's systems during a cybersecurity evaluation conducted by testing firm Irregular.
Unexpected agent behavior, however, has not been confined to laboratories.
This year, an Australian man reportedly used an AI agent to secure a place in a heavily booked Pilates class. Instead of simply making the reservation, the agent hacked the gym's booking system, booked further in advance than permitted and canceled another customer's reservation to move its user up the waiting list.
For Thickstun, such incidents illustrate what researchers describe as an alignment problem: the AI successfully pursues the objective it has been given but does so in a way its operator did not intend.
But Thickstun cautioned against treating every such incident as evidence of “rogue AI.”
The technology, he argued, remains far removed from the science-fiction scenario in which AI rapidly becomes more intelligent and capable until humans can no longer control it.
“This does not seem to be a scenario that has come to pass,” he said.
Thickstun is also skeptical of how AI companies present incidents involving their own systems.
“This is the sales pitch, where companies like OpenAI have always had an interest in hyping up the capabilities of their systems,” he said. “All publicity is good publicity.”
He argued that such hype can drive investment while also influencing the emerging debate over regulation. OpenAI, he said, could benefit from regulations that put major AI companies at the center of oversight and control.
Bruce Schneier, a cybersecurity expert and lecturer at Harvard Kennedy School, takes a different view, saying the growing number of incidents makes them increasingly difficult to dismiss as publicity stunts.
There had initially been suggestions that the Hugging Face incident was a marketing gimmick, Schneier told Anadolu. But he pointed out that similar behavior has since emerged in other evaluations, including the testing by the UK AI Security Institute.
“It went from, oh, that's interesting, to it's happening everywhere. And I think that's what's important,” he said.
He compared the problem to the genie of folklore – a creature that grants exactly what someone asks for, even when the outcome is very different from what they intended.
“It approximately means when the AI does the thing you want in a way you didn't want,” Schneier said.
He called the Australian gym incident “a perfect example” and offered a more consequential hypothetical: “The flight's full and the AI hacks the database to get you in.”
Agents can “misconstrue context and then do the wrong thing,” he said, meaning greater autonomy can create greater consequences when their interpretation of an objective diverges from human expectations.
“They are not trying to be malicious. They are using the understanding they have,” he said.
The stakes become even higher when increasingly autonomous agents are deployed in cybersecurity.
Taiwan said last Thursday that government agencies had been targeted in an AI-assisted cyberattack originating overseas in July. Authorities said the attack was successfully mitigated.
Cybersecurity researchers separately described the operation as “near-autonomous,” saying multiple AI agents mapped and exploited vulnerabilities across Taiwanese government systems and changed tactics when they encountered obstacles.
For Schneier, such developments illustrate the risk of increasingly capable models operating outside controlled environments.
“This is all changing so fast. I worry about the power of the models in unauthorized hands,” he said, adding that the pace of development makes solutions difficult because democratic governments move slowly.
The latest developments have prompted companies and governments to respond.
OpenAI said Aug. 7 it was pausing internal activities involving its in-development Astra model that did not meet strengthened security requirements after evaluations showed advances in autonomous coding and cybersecurity. The company said it could not rule out Astra reaching its “critical” cyber capability threshold and announced tighter testing and monitoring.
Anadolu reached out to Anthropic for comment, but the company said its team was unavailable for an interview.
In July, 1,378 employees of frontier AI companies, including the chief scientists of OpenAI, Anthropic, Meta AI, and Thinking Machines signed an open letter urging the US government to support an international effort to regulate AI models.
“Each company – and country – is under intense competitive pressure not to unilaterally slow that acceleration. And today, the world lacks the technical and governance tools to deliberately pace frontier-wide progress,” the letter warns.
The International Telecommunication Union, a UN agency, said in July that AI was moving “beyond assistive tools” toward autonomous agents, warning of risks including “taking unauthorized actions across interconnected systems.” It has launched an initiative to develop international standards for safe and accountable AI agents.
Political pressure is growing in Washington as well.
US Sen. Bernie Sanders this month urged the leaders of OpenAI, Anthropic and Meta to “pause AI development,” warning that otherwise “my colleagues and I in the US Senate will.” A group of House Democrats has separately called for congressional hearings with the leaders of major AI companies.
For Thickstun, however, policymakers face major challenges.
“It's a hard question because we hardly even understand what the challenges are going to be with the rollout of AI,” he said.
Some level of international cooperation “seems necessary,” he said, suggesting discussions between the United States and China could be particularly important because relatively few countries and companies have the resources to develop frontier AI models.
US President Donald Trump has said that he will discuss issues involving artificial intelligence with Chinese President Xi Jinping during their planned meeting in Washington next month.
“It's not a big, broad collective action problem. There's a few people that, if you could get in the room, could potentially come to some agreement about how to proceed,” Thickstun said.

Iran War Updates: U.S. to unveil new sanctions Trump said would hit Iran with an "economic D-Day"
What to know about the Iran war today:
- President Trump said Monday that Iran was "collapsing" as the U.S. prepared to unveil new sanctions that Treasury chief Scott Bessent vowed would amount to "the single greatest financial offensive ever marshalled against an adversary." The move is part of a shift in U.S. strategy in the nearly six-month war to heap economic pressure on Iran's rulers in the hope of breaking the stalemate between the two countries.
- Talks between Iran and Oman on future management of the Strait of Hormuz are set to continue Tuesday. The two countries have negotiated for weeks over a new system to manage commercial shipping traffic through the vital waterway, with the notion of fees being imposed a recurring theme.
- Iran's president said Sunday that he believes the memorandum of understanding signed by the U.S. and his country in June remains the best path to end the war. The agreement set a 60-day period for a wider peace deal to be negotiated, but that deadline expired with no agreement, and both countries have declared the deal dead.
Trump says Iran is "completely collapsing"
Hours before the U.S. Treasury was set to unveil a raft of new sanctions aimed at squeezing Iran's economy to force the Islamic Republic to capitulate in the war launched by the U.S. and Israel almost six months ago, President Trump declared the theocracy to be "completely collapsing."
In a brief post on his Truth Social network Monday, Mr. Trump wrote simply that "IRAN IS COMPLETELY COLLAPSING!!!," without offering any further context.
He previously vowed that the new U.S. tactic in the war, which represents a shift from military strikes and threats to sanctions-based financial warfare, would impose an "economic D-Day" on Iran.
Iran has, thus far, dismissed the U.S. plans to ratchet up sanctions, noting that the Islamic Republic has already withstood decades of U.S. economic punishment.
Iran's central bank chief says U.S. has long wielded sanctions, and "they were unable to do anything"
Iran's Central Bank Governor Abdolnaser Hemmati said Monday that the country's leaders must speak honestly with the public about economic difficulties facing the country, but he argued that pressure from the U.S. will ultimately fail to force the nation to capitulate.
"I believe we must speak honestly with the people," Hemmati said at the Entrepreneurs' Assembly in Tehran. "We are meeting the people's basic needs. If our exports are cut off, we have made preparations for that as well."
Hemmati compared the current situation, as the Trump administration prepares to impose an "economic D-Day" on Iran, with the previous "maximum pressure" campaign adopted by Mr. Trump during his first term in office.
"I was also the head of the Central Bank from 2018 to 2020. Our circumstances were almost exactly like this. They imposed maximum pressure, imposed secondary sanctions, sanctioned all our banks, sanctioned all our agriculture, sanctioned all our oil purchases — they sanctioned everything," he said. "The country stood and got through that period. It is the same now. We stood through those conditions and, in practice, they were unable to do anything."
Hemmati questioned what additional measures Washington could even impose after having already subjected Iran to extensive sanctions for many years, and he argued that the U.S. has a greater interest than Iran in bringing the conflict to an end, and quickly.
"It won't take very long," Hemmati said. "The information I have tells me that it will not last long. They need this matter to be resolved sooner than we do."
Iran will respond to U.S. sanctions, foreign ministry says
Iran's foreign ministry spokesman warned Monday that Tehran would respond harshly to new U.S. sanctions, including with measures against countries it sees as cooperating with Washington.
"Any escalation of this situation will undoubtedly bring about consequences," Esmaeil Baghaei said. "Our hands are not tied."
Iran downplays potential impact of new sanctions
Iran's foreign ministry spokesman downplayed the potential impact of new economic sanctions the U.S. is set to unveil on Monday.
Asked by a reporter about their impact, spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei said previous similar attempts by the U.S. to pressure Iran had failed, and "the Iranian people will show that they are determined and steadfast in safeguarding their rights."
Baghaei said the new measures were being imposed because the Trump administration had "miscalculated" its attacks and believed "military aggression could bring the Iranians to their knees."
South Korea says U.S. canceled military exercise over Iran war
The South Korean military said Monday the U.S. canceled a large, joint military exercise that had been scheduled to take place next month due to force limitations amid the war with Iran.
The Ssang Yong (Twin Dragons) exercise is a joint amphibious landing drill conducted regularly since 2012 by the South Korean Navy and Marine Corps alongside U.S. Navy and Marine Corps. British and other allied forces have taken part in previous years.
A spokesperson for the South Korean Marines said its U.S. counterparts had notified the force in June that "due to the situation in the Middle East," the U.S.'s ability to deploy forces for the exercise was constrained this year.
The news of this year's Ssang Yong drills being called off came a week after the U.S. cut short another major joint military exercise with South Korea, on President Trump's orders, fueling concern in Seoul, and in Japan, that Washington is becoming a less dependable ally in the face of rising threats from North Korea and China.

Iranian currency hits new record low
Iran's currency hit a record low against the dollar on Monday as the U.S. government prepared to unveil new sanctions in a bid to further squeeze the country's economy to force Iran's theocratic rulers to capitulate in the nearly six-month war.
The rial dropped to 2.02 million to the U.S. dollar as trading opened on informal currency markets. Iran's official Central Bank rate stood at around 1.5 million rials to the dollar, but the informal rate is what most Iranians pay.
The currency had already been under pressure before the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran on Feb. 28, with double-digit inflation and negative growth, but it has been hitting new lows as the war takes an even greater toll.

The incident caused a fire on the main deck of the vessel, but the crew was safe, UKMTO said in a brief statement.
The incident took place 63 nautical miles west of the Saudi city of Yanbu, the agency reported.

Greek military reportedly moves Patriot interceptor systems in response to Iranian threats
The Greek military on Monday moved one of its Patriot missile interceptor systems to the island of Crete in response to Iranian threats to hit U.S. military bases in Europe, local media reports said.
The battery was moved from the eastern island of Karpathos to Crete, where there is a major U.S. base at Souda, the reports said. Media images showed the Patriot system on a truck waiting to be loaded on a barge.

The spokesperson said Oman's foreign minister will travel to Tehran to meet with Iranian officials.

Treasury Secretary warns Iran, allies of "economic D-Day"
Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent has warned Iran and its allies the U.S. will unleash an "economic D-Day" on Iran as part of a shift in strategy to pile economic pressure in the hope of breaking the stalemate in the conflict – a term first used by President Trump last week.

The secretary also urged Iran's allies to sever ties with Tehran, saying that doing so would "deepen their access to global capital, reinforce confidence in their markets and attain the standing they seek in the world economy."

After months of military pressure and a failed agreement to negotiate an end to the war, Mr. Trump signaled in recent weeks a shift in the strategy to exert economic pressure on Iran.

Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian defended the memorandum of understanding signed with the U.S. in June as the best way for the country to move beyond what he described as a situation of "neither war nor peace."

The deal known as the Memorandum of Understanding was signed by President Trump in June. It set an ambitious 60-day deadline for ending the war with Iran and reaching an accord on its nuclear program. That period ended last week, after weeks of stalled progress and flare-ups, with both sides declaring they had abandoned it. There appear to be no signs of compromise on the crucial issue of reopening the Strait of Hormuz, vital to global shipping.

Iran says any country joining U.S. sanctions is considered an "enemy"
Iran on Saturday warned countries against participating in the United States' "economic war" against the Islamic republic, saying they would be considered enemies.

If the countries concerned refuse to "distance themselves" from the United States, Iran would "harm" their interests, he added.
Rezai also insisted Iran had more cards to play in the war, claiming, "We have not yet attacked any American economic interests."

A ‘Tsunami’ for Ukraine: Zelensky Rejects Wartime Elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
07:00:04 UTC
16:00:04 KST

Volodymyr Zelensky may be under pressure to hold elections in Ukraine, including from his former defense minister Mykhailo Fedorov, but in remarks over the weekend, the Ukrainian President argued that doing so during the ongoing conflict with Russia would “destroy” the country.
“I believe that in a war like this, elections as such are a huge risk,” Zelensky said in remarks to journalists during a two-hour meeting Saturday—parts of which were made public on Sunday. “Elections right now are a tsunami for the country that will split Ukraine.”
The renewed push for wartime elections was bolstered by Fedorov, who, in a video posted to social media last week, argued that "democracy cannot be held hostage by Russia.” Zelensky fired Fedorov, once his longtime ally, in July over disagreements in how to run the war with Russia.
“I believe that if we want to destroy the country, then during such a war we can move towards elections,” Zelensky said.
Fedorov’s call for elections is the latest leadership test for Zelensky, whose five-year term expired in May 2024 but continues under wartime rules. Elections are suspended under martial law.
Zelensky recently fired a top aide amid a growing corruption scandal involving members of his office. Zelensky himself has not been implicated, but it has added to his political woes.
For the first time with journalists, Zelensky addressed the ongoing controversy involving Fedorov on Saturday, claiming that the former defense minister’s actions were misguided.
Zelensky added that “there can be no conflict at such a level between leaders,” referring to Fedorov's conflict with the former Armed Forces commander-in-chief Gen. Oleksandr Syrsky. Zelensky also replaced Syrsky last month after Fedorov’s removal spurred massive protests within the military and on the streets of Kyiv.
Syrsky was widely viewed as part of the old guard, while Fedorov had pushed for the adoption of modern warfare technology, including drones.
“I really had and still have a very positive attitude towards Mykhailo [Fedorov],” he said, according to local news outlet Interfax. “We’ve been through a lot together. But I think that he himself is going—or he's being pushed—into the wrong things.”
In a post on X, Zelensky also mentioned that the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense was under severe strain with a $27 billion shortfall.
“At the beginning of the year, decisions were made at the Ministry to use in the first half of the year funds that were intended to be disbursed in the second half, and that money went toward drone production and other needs,” Zelensky posted. “Now, in the second half of the year, those funds need to be compensated for and supplemented.”
Zelensky discussed the defense budget deficit during a summit with Nordic and Baltic leaders in Kyiv on Sunday, where the leaders of Denmark, Estonia, Finland, Iceland, Latvia, Lithuania, Norway, Sweden agreed to continue to provide military and financial support.
U.K. Prime Minister Andy Burnham is set to visit Ukraine Monday, in his first international visit.
“Russia should be in no doubt of our resolve. We will not back down until there is a just and lasting peace,” Burnham said in a statement Monday.
Successive polls have shown a lack of public interest in holding elections during the war. The latest, conducted by the Kyiv International Institute of Sociology from July 20 to Aug. 3, shows that 57% of Ukrainians believe elections should be held after fighting has ended, down from 69% in March. Experts have previously said that the invasion, which Russian President Vladimir Putin launched in 2022, nixed the possibility of holding safe and secure elections in Ukraine.
Zelensky has denied postponing the polls to cling to power, and told reporters on Saturday that holding elections “is impossible under the conditions we have now, when Putin does not want to accept any ceasefire options.”
In the same conversation, Zelensky said he believes Russia will draft an additional 300,000 troops to fight in Ukraine after Russian parliamentary elections, which are scheduled on Sept. 18-20.
Zelensky said Russia could also draft more troops in 2027. He expects most of the additional forces to be deployed in the Donetsk region in eastern Ukraine, where military clashes are ongoing.

Text description provided by the architects. The House of Memories is born from the desire to move ahead with the times and satisfy dynamic requirements, while enshrining familial memories and celebrating its roots. It is located on a 165' x 55' plot in Valsad, a city filled with beautiful farmland and lotus ponds that make a beautiful inclusion in this narrative too, celebrating the context. The home occupies the place of the family's earlier abode, a rambling 22-room structure, which also functioned as their office, standing next to a small well. The client had purchased it from a Parsi gentleman, complete with beautiful wooden furniture. While the rooms were numerous, they were tiny, and the spatial orchestration was not at all user-friendly. Plus, with ageing family members, particularly one who is physically challenged as well, the need to shift to a modern home with an inclusive, barrier-free design became crucial and pressing.

Ukraine’s allies convene in Kyiv as Zelenskyy seeks air defence boost
‘Coalition of the Willing’ leaders gather on Independence Day as Kyiv presses for air defence supplies.
Ukraine will host a meeting with its key European allies to discuss air defence and press for greater pressure on Moscow as Russia continues to escalate missile attacks.
The “Coalition of the Willing” meeting in Kyiv will be jointly chaired by the leaders of France and Germany, who will join remotely, and UK Prime Minister Andy Burnham, who arrived in the Ukrainian capital early on Monday.
Recommended Stories
list of 3 items
- list 1 of 3Photos: Ukraine celebrates National Flag Day
- list 2 of 3Russia, Ukraine trade attacks as Putin warns of ‘far more destructive’ hits
- list 3 of 3Putin warns Ukraine has opened ‘Pandora’s box’, rejects peace proposals
European Council President Antonio Costa is also attending in person.
Kyiv is expected to seek additional interceptor missiles from allies after weeks of Russian missile and drone attacks that have driven record numbers of the capital city’s residents to metro stations and basements to seek shelter.
President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has made frequent public appeals for more air defence supplies from allies.
The meeting takes place on Ukraine’s Independence Day and comes a day after the country marked National Flag Day, when a group of leaders from Nordic and Baltic countries met Zelenskyy in Kyiv and pledged to boost their support for Ukraine.
Norway said it would provide another 85 billion kroner ($9.1bn) in 2027, matching the support it gave Ukraine this year.
Escalating air attacks
Russia and Ukraine have escalated air attacks with drones and missiles in recent weeks, striking targets far beyond the front line.
Ukraine has increasingly targeted Russian logistics sites, carrying out attacks on locations linked to e-commerce companies Wildberries and Ozon.
Ozon reported fires early on Monday at its warehouses in four cities including Krasnodar and Makhachkala, both in southern Russia, adding that sites in Adygeysk and Nevinnomyssk were evacuated due to threats of drone attack.
Russian authorities said two children were killed and nine other people were wounded, including seven minors, when drone debris hit a private childcare centre in Krasnodar on Monday. Debris also fell on apartment buildings and set warehouses alight in the city, Governor Veniamin Kondratyev said.
In the Stavropol region, which hosts many chemical production facilities, Governor Vladimir Vladimirov said a drone attack on an industrial area had been repelled early on Monday.
In Ukraine, at least two women were killed and five people injured when a Russian drone hit an electric train in the Kharkiv region on Sunday, regional officials said. An attack on the outskirts of Kharkiv city killed three people and injured eight.
Ukraine’s allies have pledged to boost Ukraine’s depleted air defences in the face of Russia’s growing missile attacks.
Before the meeting, Zelenskyy said deliveries of crucial Patriot interceptors had halved since 2023.
“Over the entire of 2023, Ukraine received 675 missiles, and over all of 2025 – 364, even though Russian missile strikes have increased,” he said.
“For 2026, as currently projected, it is 264,” he added, saying Ukraine was seeking a package of at least 300 for the upcoming winter.

Pakistan’s army chief Munir returns to Iran: Can he break US war deadlock?
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
06:30:37 UTC
15:30:37 KST

Pakistan’s army chief back in Iran: Can he break peace talks deadlock?
Pakistan says it can offer a channel between Tehran and Washington, but analysts differ over how much influence it really has.
Islamabad, Pakistan — Pakistan’s Chief of Army Staff and Chief of Defence Forces, Field Marshal Asim Munir, is traveling to Tehran on Monday for talks with senior Iranian officials, Iran’s Foreign Ministry announced on Sunday.
It will be Munir’s third visit to Iran this year as Islamabad continues its push to mediate an end to the United States and Israel’s war on Iran.
Recommended Stories
list of 4 items
- list 1 of 4Iran holds firm on Hormuz conditions as Pakistan’s Naqvi visits Tehran
- list 2 of 4US-Iran MoU ends: What happens next?
- list 3 of 4Iran signals readiness for ‘US ground operations’ as strategy shifts gear
- list 4 of 4Iran prepares to keep economy alive as US threatens further sanctions
Pakistani officials, speaking on condition of anonymity, confirmed to Al Jazeera that the trip would take place but declined to elaborate on its agenda.
The Pakistani military’s media wing, the Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR), as well as the Foreign Ministry and Information Ministry, did not respond to Al Jazeera’s requests for comment on the visit, which was unusually announced by Tehran rather than Islamabad.
Foreign Ministry spokesperson Esmaeil Baghaei said the trip would build on Pakistan’s efforts to “help strengthen peace and security in the region”.
Munir will hold talks with senior Iranian officials during his stay, Baghaei told reporters in Tehran.
The visit follows two phone calls between Munir and Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi within four days, on Wednesday and Saturday.
The two officials discussed “regional developments” and ways to strengthen “peace, stability and security” in West Asia, according to Iranian state media.
A third trip this year
Munir’s first visit to Tehran this year came in April, days after the Islamabad Talks, the first direct US-Iran negotiations in more than four decades, ended without a breakthrough.
He returned in May, arriving hours after US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said there had been “slight progress” in talks between Washington and Tehran.
His latest visit comes as the diplomatic track underpinning the Islamabad MoU has all but stalled, while Washington prepares a new round of sanctions.
The discussions are also expected to touch on this month’s announcement of the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement between Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, which Munir attended in Mecca.
Yemen’s Houthi fighters, whose attacks on shipping lanes have repeatedly threatened to widen the conflict, are also likely to feature in his conversations with Iranian officials. The Houthis are widely believed to receive support from Tehran.
The issue carries particular weight for Islamabad.
Three Pakistani sailors were killed and several others wounded when Houthi forces struck a Tanzania-flagged commercial vessel in the Bab al-Mandeb Strait on August 11.
Deputy Prime Minister and Foreign Minister Ishaq Dar called the attack a violation of international law and “strongly condemned” it at the time.
Munir is expected to meet Iran’s newly appointed senior military leadership during the visit, including Islamic Revolutionary Guards Corps chief Major-General Ahmad Vahidi, Chief of General Staff of the Iranian Armed Forces Major-General Ali Abdollahi and the new Secretary of the Supreme National Security Council Mohsen Rezaei.
The officials were all appointed earlier this month.
A lapsed deal
The visit comes at a fraught moment for Pakistan’s mediation effort, which it has led after the war began six months ago.
The 60-day window set out in the Islamabad Memorandum of Understanding (MoU), signed by Pakistan, Iran and the US on June 17, lapsed in mid-August without either side agreeing to extend it.
Iran has kept the Strait of Hormuz shut, insisting that Washington first lift its naval blockade, end oil sanctions, unfreeze Iranian assets abroad and halt military threats. Tehran says the US has not met those conditions.
Munir’s trip also coincides with a fresh round of US economic pressure.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is due to detail on Monday what American officials have called the “toughest sanctions in history” against Iran, a package he has said is intended, alongside the continuing naval blockade, to “collapse” the government in Tehran.
Iran’s Foreign Ministry has called the plan “economic warfare”.
The trip also follows a month of regional realignment. Pakistan, Saudi Arabia and Turkiye signed the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement on August 7, a mutual defence pact under which an attack on one signatory would be treated as an attack on all three.
Pakistan’s Interior Minister Mohsin Naqvi travelled to Tehran earlier this month to revive the stalled mediation push but returned without any concrete results.
Tensions elsewhere in the region have sharpened too.
The United Arab Emirates suspended trade and financial transactions with Iran last week after saying it had come under fire from two ballistic missiles launched from Iranian territory, a claim Baghaei denied.
But Munir’s visit, analysts say, signals that key regional mediators have not given up on efforts to revive talks, either direct or indirect, between Iran and the US, even as they try to balance their own relations with Tehran and Washington.
Oman’s Foreign Minister Badr bin Hamad Albusaidi, who, like Munir, has held recent telephone conversations with Araghchi, is scheduled to visit Tehran on Tuesday, Iran’s state-owned IRNA news agency has reported.
What leverage does Islamabad have?
Analysts remain divided on what Munir’s visit can realistically achieve, given Pakistan’s limited ability to enforce any understanding it helps broker.
“Both sides see Pakistan as a country that has helped facilitate dialogue without any personal stake in the outcome, nothing to gain for itself,” said Qamar Cheema, a political analyst and head of the Islamabad-based Sanober Institute. “That gives it a certain clarity, and the ability to offer an off-ramp to everyone involved.”
Javad Heiran-Nia, director of the Persian Gulf Studies Group in Tehran, said Pakistan’s persistence was driven partly by self-interest.
“Pakistan is concerned about escalating tensions and the outbreak of another all-out war between Iran and the United States, which would further destabilise the region,” he told Al Jazeera, pointing to Islamabad’s reliance on energy imports from the Gulf and the risk of disruption to remittances from Pakistani workers there if instability spreads.
Zahid Mehmood, a retired two-star general and Pakistani defence strategist, went further, describing Munir as still carrying Washington’s own offer to Tehran.
“Pakistan is still carrying, in effect, Washington’s off-ramp to Tehran,” he told Al Jazeera. “The country remains the most trusted conduit available.”
Not every analyst sees Pakistan’s role as this central.
Andreas Krieg, an associate professor of defence studies at King’s College London, said Qatar, not Pakistan, remained the primary channel.
“Qatar is leading the political mediation and remains the essential communication bridge between Washington and Tehran,” he told Al Jazeera.
Munir’s contribution, he said, was narrower, a “military-to-military channel into an Iranian system in which the IRGC and wider security establishment have become increasingly important to decisions about war and peace”.
What Munir can deliver, and what he can’t
Some analysts believe Munir’s visit could set the stage for the finalisation of an Iran-Oman agreement on jointly managing the Strait of Hormuz.
Krieg was more cautious about what Munir’s visit could deliver. The most meaningful outcome, he said, would be “confirmation that Iran’s security establishment would abide by a specific Hormuz deconfliction arrangement and restrain escalation through Yemen or Iraq if Qatar can secure reciprocal American movement”.
Without that, according to Krieg, “the communication bridge remains open, but the two sides continue moving towards another coercive cycle”.
Mehmood, the retired Pakistani general, was less equivocal.
“Pakistan is really the only exit card available to either side for their off-ramp,” he told Al Jazeera.

Oslo Architecture Triennale 2026 Announces Programme for 9th Edition Under "What if Nature Comes First?"
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
06:30:00 UTC
15:30:00 KST

The 2026 Oslo Architecture Triennale will take place from September 17 to October 1 at Sofienberg Church in Oslo, bringing together more than 30 international architecture projects around the question "What if Nature Comes First?" For its ninth edition, the Triennale will adopt a two-week festival format, combining an exhibition with conferences, seminars, workshops, film screenings and guided walks. Curated by Line Ramstad, the programme will examine how placing nature at the starting point of architectural decision-making could influence what is built, preserved, transformed or left untouched.
The main exhibition will occupy both the interior and exterior of Sofienberg Church, a 19th-century building constructed in 1877 that is currently being transformed into a local cultural venue in Oslo's Grünerløkka neighborhood. Developed using reused materials, the exhibition brings together projects from Norway, Denmark, Sweden, Germany, France, Spain, Switzerland, Austria, the United Kingdom and the United States. Rather than treating sustainability as an additional consideration within architectural projects, the Triennale frames nature as a starting point for decisions concerning materials, buildings, land and broader systems.
The curatorial framework is organized across four scales: Materials, Structures, Territories and Systems. These categories consider questions ranging from the selection and reuse of construction materials to the lifespan of buildings, the relationship between architecture and land, and the economic and regulatory systems that shape development. Among the projects presented are Carmody Groarke's Gent Waste Brick, made with recycled municipal waste, Pihlmann Architects' transformation of the Thoravej 29 factory in Copenhagen, and Built Architects' Grønn liste, which maps buildings in Oslo with potential for reuse.
Related Article
The Tallinn Architecture Biennale 2026 Unveils Full Program, Venues, and Participants for 'How Much?'
The programme will extend beyond the exhibition throughout the two-week event, with activities taking place from early morning into the evening. The Triennale will open on September 17 with a conference introducing the theme and its four scales, featuring speakers including Chief Curator Line Ramstad, Jonathan Grinham of the Harvard Graduate School of Design, Zeynep Topçu of BC Materials, Tine Hegli of the Oslo School of Architecture and Design, and Sian Ricketts of Carmody Groarke. The following days will include a series of morning talks, seminars and workshops addressing natural materials, reuse, urban planning and ecological economics, alongside film screenings and walks through Oslo's landscape.
A recurring element of the programme will be "The Daily Sermon," presented from the pulpit of Sofienberg Church each morning from September 18 to October 1. The short talks will introduce a specific architectural or environmental challenge alongside a proposed response, while weekend sessions will allow for longer discussions. Other events include "The New Stone Age," a seminar exploring the use of stone and natural materials in architecture, and "Nature and Economy," which will examine the role of ecological economics in shaping urban development.
The Triennale will also address the relationship between cultural heritage, reuse and development through a September 22 seminar organized with Norway's Directorate for Cultural Heritage. "How Can We Make Reuse Pay Off?" will consider the financial, cultural and practical factors involved in transforming existing buildings, bringing together architects, heritage professionals and advisors for presentations and an open discussion. The event forms part of the broader programme's focus on existing resources and alternative approaches to construction.
The 2026 edition is curated by Line Ramstad, a landscape architect and Director and Chief Curator of the Oslo Architecture Triennale. Her approach to the programme focuses on existing materials, buildings and knowledge as resources for addressing the environmental impact of construction and land use. "Materials are heavy and should stay local; knowledge is light and can be spread globally," Ramstad states, summarizing one of the principles underpinning this year's programme.
The Oslo Architecture Triennale 2026 will conclude on October 1 with a closing conference reflecting on the festival's discussions and projects. The programme follows a series of major architecture biennales and triennales scheduled for late 2026, including the inaugural Pan-African Biennale in Nairobi from September 7 to 11, the Tallinn Architecture Biennale from September 9 to November 30 under the theme "How Much?", and the Sharjah Architecture Triennial, which opens November 14 under the title "Architecture Otherwise: Building Civic Infrastructure for Collective Futures."

Global markets start a busy week with a sell-off trend, driven by US growth and inflation data, the Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium and Nvidia's balance sheet.
Investors entered the week nervously as uncertainties regarding a cease-fire in the Middle East continued to complicate pricing, testing macroeconomics, monetary policy and the artificial intelligence theme simultaneously.
As negotiations between the US and Iran yielded no concrete results, the mutual defiance of the parties spreading to the economic field rather than remaining limited to the military front increased current uncertainties.
US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent is expected to announce new economic sanctions against Iran on Monday.
Oil prices maintained their high levels as geopolitical uncertainty persisted over the Strait of Hormuz, which plays an important role in energy supply, keeping concerns about inflationary pressures alive on a global scale.
Analysts said current pricing in money markets indicated the Fed could raise interest rates once by the end of the year, while these expectations could change depending on announced economic data and geopolitical developments in the Middle East.
The lack of clarity over the Fed's policy steps, in addition to ongoing uncertainties, turned attention to statements Fed Chair Kevin Warsh will make at the Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium on Friday.
US growth data and the personal consumption expenditures (PCE) price index, an inflation indicator, remained among the important topics in investors' focus.
The data is expected to guide expectations regarding the Fed's interest rate path through the strength of economic activity and the course of inflation.
Financial results to be announced by Nvidia also remained among the important items to follow this week to gauge whether the artificial intelligence theme will continue, in addition to these developments.
Analysts said Nvidia's profitability and growth expectations and its forecasts for the future of the semiconductor sector could increase volatility in the markets.
The tariff issue between the US and Canada was also among the developments occupying the agenda.
Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said the US proposed "economically unviable and unfair" conditions in ongoing trade negotiations, adding that Canada will respond in kind to Washington's new tariffs to protect workers, farmers, families and businesses.
 
Gold at 14-week high
 
Selling pressure eased in the bond market for a while after the US Treasury Department doubled its long-term bond buyback operations.
The 10-year US bond yield, which ended the week at 4.74% with a three-basis-point increase on Friday, started the new week at 4.71%.
The two-year US bond yield also dropped to 4.23%, a decrease of two basis points.
Expectations that the US Treasury Department could increase its interventions in the bond market continued to put pressure on the dollar.
The US dollar index started the new week flat at 98.8.
Finding support from the weakening dollar and the curbing of the rise in bond yields, an ounce of gold hit a nearly 14-week high, rising to $4,657 at the start of the new day.
The price of Brent crude oil for October delivery hovered at $93 per barrel, down 1.5%.
US index futures also started the week on a negative note.
 
European index futures follow mixed course
 
Index futures in European derivatives markets started the week on a mixed course amid uncertainties regarding geopolitical developments in the Middle East.
Markets considered it certain that the European Central Bank (ECB) will raise interest rates next month as concerns continued that high oil prices in the region will increase energy costs.
The Consumer Price Index (CPI) for July in the Eurozone came in line with expectations last week, increasing 0.2% monthly and 2.9% annually.
Inflation remaining above the ECB's 2% target was among the factors supporting expectations of monetary policy tightening by the bank.
Investors will follow growth and the economic confidence index in Germany, European Central Bank (ECB) meeting minutes on Thursday, the unemployment rate in Germany on Friday and the consumer confidence index in the Eurozone this week.
Markets will also closely monitor messages regarding monetary policy at the Jackson Hole Economic Policy Symposium in the US.
 
Asian stock markets follow negative course
 
Asian stock markets started the week on a negative note in light of current developments.
Developments in the Middle East and messages at the Jackson Hole meeting are expected to affect the direction of regional markets.
The rise in US-Canada trade tensions brought concerns that a new tariff agenda toward the region could emerge.
Shares of China's leading e-commerce and technology company Alibaba fell 9.8% on reports that the company planned to sell $10.2 billion in shares to finance its investments in artificial intelligence.
South Korea-based electronics company Samsung Electronics announced it would transfer 90 trillion to 110 trillion won, around $65 billion to $80 billion, to shareholders this year.
Samsung shares lost 8% in value because the record $80 billion shareholder return plan did not meet expectations.
With these developments, Japan's Nikkei 225 index dropped 0.5%, South Korea's Kospi index 2.9%, China's Shanghai Composite Index 0.9% and Hong Kong's Hang Seng Index 2% near the close.

The Central Bank of the Republic of Türkiye (CBRT) decided to restart one-week repo auctions, which were suspended on March 1, 2026.

Japanese lawmakers visit Beijing seeking to mend ties after fallout from Takaichi’s Taiwan remark
TOKYO (AP) — A cross-party group of Japanese lawmakers headed to Beijing on Monday seeking to mend strained ties following Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi’s comment on Taiwan that angered China and led to tensions that have spilled over into the economy.
The group, which includes Gaku Hashimoto, a lawmaker of Takaichi’s governing Liberal Democratic Party and a former health and welfare vice minister, and a lawmaker each from the Komeito and Centrist Reform Alliance opposition parties, will meet with Chinese Communist Party officials during a visit through Thursday.
“Communication has been severed in all areas and we are beginning to see their impact in many areas,” Shinichi Isa, a spokesperson for the CRA party, told reporters before leaving Tokyo’s Haneda airport. “I hope we can somehow find a clue to restart a dialogue.”
Soon after taking office, Takaichi said a Chinese attack on Taiwan could constitute “a survival-threatening situation” for Japan that would justify the use of force, enraging Beijing.
Isa, who has served as a diplomat at the Japanese Embassy in China, wrote on X earlier this month that bilateral ties have sunk to their worst since the 1972 normalization of relations. He wrote that officials had always remained in communication even during previous lows: “Now all channels between officials and ministries have been cut off.”
The situation is not in the national interest of either side, Isa said at the time, and the Chinese side accepted a request from Japanese lawmakers for a “window for dialogue.”
China’s Foreign Ministry last Friday noted “some people of insight from both Japan’s ruling and opposition parties” are concerned about the state of China-Japan relations and hoping to make efforts to push them back on track. “We urge those running the Japanese government to take these voices seriously ... and take concrete actions to create the necessary conditions for normal exchanges between the two countries.”
Takaichi’s remark crossed what China considers a red line in its relations with other countries about Taiwan, which is a self-governing island that Beijing claims as its territory.
Takaichi has not retracted her comment, but when marking Japan’s World War II surrender on Aug. 15, she prayed remotely instead of visiting the controversial Yasukuni Shrine, seen by China and South Korea as lacking remorse for Japan’s wartime militarism and atrocities.

Vietnam records nearly 100,000 HFMD cases in over 8 months

HANOI, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Vietnam has recorded nearly 100,000 cases of hand, foot and mouth disease (HFMD) in the first eight and a half months of the year, more than 2.5 times the number reported during the same period last year, local daily Ha Noi Moi reported Monday, citing the Ministry of Health.
Over 3,000 new cases have been reported nationwide each week over the past four weeks, with infections concentrated in southern Vietnam, according to the ministry's Vietnam Administration of Disease Prevention.
Vo Hai Son, the administration's deputy director, said the surge coincides with the start of the new school year, when children have more frequent contact and interaction in group settings.
He warned of a high risk of outbreaks and wider transmission if personal hygiene and environmental disinfection measures are not strictly followed and cases are not detected early.
The administration has urged parents, caregivers and educational institutions to strictly follow the "three clean" principle, which includes clean food and water, a clean living environment and clean hands, the report said. ■

Vietnam tightens regulation on overseas jobs for contract workers
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
14:18:41 CST
15:18:41 KST

HANOI, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Vietnam on Monday tightened its regulations on overseas jobs for contract workers as the National Assembly passed a revised law, local media Tuoi Tre reported.
The revised law prohibits Vietnamese workers from taking overseas jobs that violate national security, social order and safety, or social morality, or endanger the health of workers and the community, as well as jobs not permitted by the receiving country.
It bans organizing overseas employment or recruiting, preparing and sending Vietnamese workers to areas affected by armed conflict or areas that competent authorities have advised people not to visit or to limit travel to.
The law also bans Vietnamese workers under contract from taking massage jobs abroad and organizations from sending workers overseas for such work.
The revised law will take effect on March 1, 2027, the government portal reported. ■

WELLINGTON, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- New Zealand's government moved ahead with plans to ban children under 16 from using social media, with legislation set to be introduced to parliament on Monday.
The Online Safety Bill would require high-risk social media platforms, including Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat and Facebook, to take reasonable steps to verify that users are over the age of 16, using methods such as existing account information, facial age estimation, digital ID services and formal identification, said a government statement.
The legislation would also require platforms used by children to regularly assess the risks they pose and report on how those risks are being identified and reduced, it said.
Companies that fail to meet their obligations could face penalties of up to 10 percent of a platform's global revenue. The bill would also bring emerging technologies, including AI companion platforms, within the regulatory framework.
An online safety regulator would be established within the Department of Internal Affairs to independently monitor compliance, investigate platforms and enforce the law, the statement said.
"Social media is exposing them to harmful content, addictive technology and pressures they are not equipped to deal with and it's affecting their family life, mental health, sleep, and education," Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said while making the announcement.
Education Minister Erica Stanford said the bill would bring New Zealand into line with other countries, placing greater responsibility on technology companies to protect children online.
"The bill places legal obligations on platforms. No penalties are proposed for children, their parents or caregivers," Stanford said.
Winston Peters, leader of New Zealand First, a partner in the governing coalition, said his party shared concerns about children's online safety but would not support the ban, warning that enforcement could come at the expense of parental rights, individual freedoms and privacy.
Cassandra Mudgway, a senior law lecturer at New Zealand's University of Canterbury, welcomed the proposed online safety regulator and stronger platform accountability but questioned whether a ban on social media for under-16s would achieve the government's aims.
Mudgway warned that age verification could carry significant privacy costs, saying a ban would not necessarily make the online environment safer. ■
