Feature: Chicago concert bridges cultures through Chinese, American folk songs
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:21:13 CST
14:21:13 KST

CHICAGO, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- The familiar strains of "Shenandoah" brought tears to Marci Jarog's eyes during a downtown Chicago concert on Saturday. For a song she thought she knew by heart, something was different this time.
Performed in a newly arranged symphonic choral version featuring a Chinese community chorus, the American folk classic offered Jarog a fresh perspective on a melody deeply rooted in American musical tradition.
"I thought I had heard this song a million times already, and then today I heard it differently," Jarog told Xinhua after the performance. "I think that hearing an unexpected cultural representation of 'Shenandoah' was even more moving than anything I would have expected."
More than 500 musicians, singers, dancers and community artists took part in the concert titled "Bridges We Build, Memories We Keep" at Chicago Symphony Center, drawing an audience of more than 2,000. The event was organized by the Midwest Asian Health Association.
Among the highlights were the world premieres of newly arranged symphonic choral versions of the American folk song "Shenandoah" and the Chinese folk song "Jasmine Flower."
"Music has a unique power to connect us across cultures, generations, and memories," said Elizabeth Jia, artistic director of the concert.
"I wanted those traditions to listen to one another, speak to one another, and ultimately create something that none of them could create alone," she said.
The concert brought together Western classical repertoire, Chinese art songs and instrumental works, opera, choral music and dance, taking audiences on a journey across different musical traditions.
Internationally acclaimed violinist Liu Yang performed an excerpt from the Chinese violin concerto "The Butterfly Lovers." Chinese baritone Hu Sihao, a member of the Patrick G. and Shirley W. Ryan Opera Center at Lyric Opera of Chicago and a prizewinner of China's Golden Bell Awards, also took the stage alongside soprano Boya Wei and other featured artists.
"It was fantastic. It was very well put together, and everyone was very professional," Jackie Carreras, who attended the concert at the invitation of a friend, told Xinhua after the performance.
"It's just beautiful to learn about different cultures, such as the Chinese culture, so I really enjoyed it," she said.
For Shelly Carter, the concert left her wanting to learn more. "It was like the whole world was up there, that mixed a lot of culture," she said, adding that she hoped to learn more about Chinese music and culture in the future.
As two folk traditions met in newly created symphonic arrangements and artists from different cultural backgrounds shared the same stage, the concert became more than a performance -- it served as a musical bridge connecting cultures, generations and memories. ■

NEW DELHI: A three-inch difference in his leg lengths, persistent back pain and other physical problems have forced 29-year-old Kunal Arora to cut his table tennis training by more than half. Yet, the thalassemia major patient and international para table tennis player is set to leave for Finland on August 26 with the Indian team, even as doctors have advised him to get a prosthetic extension to improve his alignment and mobility.The Moradabad athlete has won 27 national and 10 international medals and recently clinched gold at the 1st UTT Para National Ranking Table Tennis Championship 2026-27 in Indore.Arora will also be felicitated on Sunday by the Thalassemia Patients Advocacy Group (TPAG), in collaboration with Thalassemics India, at an event in New Delhi honouring thalassemia patients for their achievements and resilience.Diagnosed with thalassemia major at birth, Arora said severe iron overload led to two major leg surgeries in 2010. He said it would also help during training, though it is unclear if he can wear it in competitions. The prosthesis is estimated to cost Rs 2,66,910 including GST, which his family cannot afford.“My father is a small businessman and my mother is a homemaker. I also help my father with his business whenever he needs me,” Kunal told TOI.The physical problems have cut his training from 7-8 hours in two sessions to about 2.5-3.5 hours in one session. “The difference in my leg length causes pain and affects my daily activities as well as my training. I am now hoping for support to get the prosthetic extension, which costs around Rs 2.7 lakh.
I want to continue playing for India and need this support to manage my mobility and training,” he said.Arora has represented India internationally since 2014 and is seeking sponsorship for international tournaments, which he says would help him compete more frequently and work towards the Commonwealth Games, Asian Games and Paralympic Games. For now, he is managing without the prosthesis and plans to give his measurements in the first or second week of September. The device is expected to take about a month to prepare.“Life gave me thalassemia major, but also a choice: to be defined by my diagnosis or my determination. I chose the paddle,” Arora said.

Senator Deborah O'Neill in March shared allegations in parliament from a whistleblower that KPMG partners had repeatedly used clients' confidential information to win lucrative audit contracts.
The firm in May said it had been aware of the allegations since 2024 and that its internal investigation was not rigorous enough.
O'Neill told a parliamentary inquiry into the allegations earlier in August that many more whistleblowers had come forward to raise concerns about misconduct at KPMG. ■

Trump to award Congressional Space Medal of Honor to Artemis II astronauts
- Date:
- August 24, 2026
- Source:
- NASA
- Summary:
- The Artemis II crew will receive the Congressional Space Medal of Honor after becoming the first humans in more than 50 years to travel beyond the Moon. Their 10-day Orion mission also carried them farther into space than anyone in history.
- Share:
President Donald J. Trump will present the Congressional Space Medal of Honor to each member of NASA's Artemis II crew during a ceremony at Johnson Space Center in Houston. The event is scheduled for 11 a.m. EDT on Friday, Aug. 28.
The medal is one of the highest honors associated with human spaceflight in the United States. It recognizes astronauts whose achievements have made an exceptional contribution to the nation's space program.
Artemis II Made Human Spaceflight History
NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover, and Christina Koch, along with CSA (Canadian Space Agency) astronaut Jeremy Hansen, completed a 10-day mission around the Moon on April 10.
The flight marked the first time astronauts had traveled aboard NASA's Orion spacecraft, which is designed to carry crews on missions beyond low Earth orbit. Artemis II served as a major test of the spacecraft and its systems with humans on board.
During the mission, the crew became the first people in more than 50 years to travel beyond the Moon. They also ventured farther into space than any humans had ever traveled before, setting a new distance record for human spaceflight.
A Major Honor for the Artemis II Crew
The Aug. 28 ceremony will recognize the crew's role in advancing NASA's Artemis program and returning astronauts to deep space.
NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman will join President Trump and the four astronauts for the awards ceremony at Johnson Space Center.

Gauff beats Pegula for 2nd Cincinnati Open title; France’s Fils beats American Tiafoe in men’s final
MASON, Ohio (AP) — Coco Gauff defeated fellow American Jessica Pegula, 6-2, 6-4, to capture her second women’s Cincinnati Open title on Sunday, and Arthur Fils of France defeated American Frances Tiafoe 6-3, 1-6, 6-0, in the men’s final for his first Masters 1000 title.
In Saturday’s semifinals, Pegula beat defending champion Iga Swiatek and Gauff defeated Sara Bejlek to set up the first all-American women’s final at the Cincinnati Open in 56 years.
The last time two American women played in the Cincinnati final was in 1970, when Rosie Casals beat Nancy Richey.
Pegula’s best finish in Cincinnati came in 2024, when she lost to Aryna Sabalenka in the final.
Gauff, who won the 2023 title beating Karolina Muchova, stormed out to a 5-0 lead in the first set on Sunday before winning 6-2. Pegula battled back to within 5-4 in the second before Gauff closed out the win. Gauff won five of six break points.
“I think it was a long journey, but I’m happy,” Gauff said. “I think it’s night and day, the player I was last year to now. I don’t think that this is an indicator that I’m going to do well in New York. Just knowing the quality ones that I had this week, hopefully I can use that experience.”
Gauff had five wins in straight sets in Cincinnati.
“I thought she just played at a really high level and didn’t really have many dips,” Pegula said. “I didn’t really think I played bad. The more you construct the point (against her), the worse it is because she almost likes to run. It was tough today. A dangerous, confident Coco is going to New York.”
The head-to-head series between Gauff and Pegula is now tied at five apiece. Sunday was their second meeting in a final, with Gauff winning at Wuhan last year.
The Fils-Tiafoe match was the first time two Black players have met in an ATP Masters 1000 final.
Fils is the third Black man to win a Masters 1000 title, joining Ben Shelton, who won twice in Canada, and Jo-Wilfried Tsonga, who won in Paris in 2008 and Canada in 2014.
At 22 years old, Fils is the youngest French champion in Masters 1000 history. He became the second French player to win a Cincinnati final, joining Guy Forget in 1991.
“Very happy with that,” Fils said. “It’s been a tough last year. I didn’t play the French Open (due to a hip injury). I lost early in Washington. People think that I’m done. But here we are. I got the title.”
It was the second time Tiafoe has appeared in the Cincinnati Open final, losing to Jannik Sinner in 2024. He was looking to become the first American male to win in Cincinnati since Andy Roddick in 2006.
“I’m going to have two Cincinnati finals trophies at the crib,” Tiafoe said. “I wish they were both champion ones. Losing on Sunday sucks. I’ve had a tough summer. I was able to play five great matches and beat quality players.”
Fils overpowered Tiafoe early in the first set on Sunday, winning 12 of 13 points to take a 3-0 lead. Tiafoe was dominant in the second, rolling to a 3-0 lead.
Tiafoe used the time break before the third set to stretch and receive massage treatment on his upper left leg and lower back.
“My hip bothered me a little bit, but that’s neither here nor there,” Tiafoe said. “It’s not about how I feel. I’ll be alright in a week (for the US Open).”
Tiafoe saved three championship points in the final game before Fils closed out the victory.
The Frenchman had 11 aces and won 71% of his points on first serve. He improved to 10-0 in deciding sets this year and 8-0 against American opponents.
Fils also won his only previous meeting with Tiafoe in Miami last year, also in three sets.
“It feels very good to have a trophy next to me, especially Masters 1000,” Fils said. “Never won one before. You just have to stay positive and find a way to make it work. Being positive is going to help me in the next weeks in the US Open.”

3-year college degrees grow more popular in the US, saving time and cash. But critics aren’t sold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:23:01 UTC
13:23:01 KST

3-year college degrees grow more popular in the US, saving time and cash. But critics aren’t sold
Giles Sims, 34, was sick of getting passed over for jobs because he didn’t have a college degree.
But with a wife and a widowed mother to help support, he needed a quick solution. So the laid-off web developer turned to one of a growing number of three-year degree programs.
“I can’t afford to be out of the workforce for four years. That just seems like forever, and the three-year made it seem less daunting,” said Sims, a student at Ensign College, a private Salt Lake City school that recently changed all its bachelor’s degrees to require fewer classes than a traditional four-year degree.
The condensed programs have exploded in popularity. As of this spring, 26 U.S. states have a college that offers at least one reduced-credit, three-year bachelor’s, according to the nonprofit research group RAND.
Advocates say these programs are a solution to the college affordability crisis and a godsend for non-traditional students like Sims.
Critics, however, worry that they’ll narrow too much what students learn, confuse employers, limit graduate school options and create headaches in fields that require state licenses.
The American Association of University Professors, for one, says the programs devalue the meaning of a college credential.
“This is not innovation. This is just cutting corners,” said Todd Wolfson, AAUP’s president.
A new option to graduate more quickly, but with reduced credit
For decades, colleges have offered accelerated programs that let students finish faster, often by forgoing long summer breaks, maximizing transfer credits and condensing semester-long courses into shorter, five- to 10-week terms.
But those programs maintained the same course load, measured as credits. The new programs let students finish faster by completing as few as 90 credit hours. That shaves a year off the typical 120-hour bachelor’s degree.
Three-year bachelor’s degrees are common in other countries including the United Kingdom, India, France and Italy. But they can create complications for graduates seeking admission to U.S. graduate schools, which sometimes require extra coursework.
Some of the earliest colleges in colonial America, modeled after English institutions like Oxford and Cambridge, initially had three-year degrees, said John Thelin, the author of “A History of American Higher Education.” By the 19th century, the four-year format had taken hold, partly because there wasn’t an established system of public high schools to prepare students, Thelin said.
“The colleges would have to kind of start from scratch,” he said.
A change in accreditation opened the door to shorter degrees
The idea of bringing three-year degrees to the U.S. got attention in 2009 when Robert Zemsky, the founding director of the Institute for Research on Higher Education at the University of Pennsylvania Graduate School of Education, argued in a Newsweek cover story that three-year degrees could shake up a broken system.
But there was a roadblock, he recalled recently. “Accreditors said, ‘College is 120 credits, not 90 credits,’” he said.
Years passed. And in 2022, amid mounting concerns about college affordability, Zemsky helped revive the idea. The College-in-3 Exchange was born, and dozens of higher education institutions joined the network to look for ways to help students get degrees faster.
The Northwest Commission on Colleges and Universities was the first accreditor to say yes in 2023, when it approved reduced-credit programs at Ensign and Brigham Young University-Idaho. Other accreditors quickly followed.
As of May, 119 reduced-credit programs had been publicly announced, according to the RAND analysis, which was conducted to help education officials in Ohio as they weigh the feasibility of reduced-credit degrees.
It comes at a time when tuition and fees averaged $11,950 for in-state students at public schools and $45,000 at private nonprofits last school year, although many students get discounts that reduce the price, according to a report from the College Board, the nonprofit that oversees the SAT.
Some degrees are easier to compress
Private nonprofit schools offer three-quarters of the reduced-credit programs, frequently online. Typically, they compress the majors by reducing electives. Business degrees in fields such as marketing and management are the most common, followed by computer and information sciences.
Other majors, such as engineering, with its extensive math requirements, have been harder to shrink. And RAND found just six reduced-credit degrees in teacher education, which involves real-world experience requirements and state licensure.
Jill Cohen, 42, lives on a ranch in rural Yoder, Colorado, and is completing her teaching degree through one such program at Indiana Wesleyan.
She quit her old job selling life insurance and turned to teaching after a farming accident nearly claimed her life. Already, she is in the classroom, teaching middle school English, as she works on the degree through a special “Grow Your Own” program designed to address staff shortages.
Because her home is busy — she has twin 12-year-olds, along with a menagerie that includes horses, goats and chickens — she appreciates the streamlined degree.
“Why do I need to take, you know, underwater basket weaving when I could just take the evolutionary structure of the English language — what I’m going to be teaching,” she said.
However, programs with state licensing requirements are one of the biggest worries for Jenna Kramer, a policy researcher at RAND.
Indiana Wesleyan, which has a growing slate of reduced-credit offerings, said its education programs are specifically designed to meet Indiana licensing requirements. Students from elsewhere will need to check if the programs meet their state requirements, said Pam Downing, the school’s director of communications, in an email.
The RAND report also found the programs are so new that there are no standard practices for admitting three-year degree recipients into graduate school.
Students acknowledge it’s a gamble
Gabriella Staten, a 20-year-old student in the reduced-credit digital marketing program at Mount Mary University, a Catholic women’s institution in Milwaukee, estimates it will save her at least $20,000. While she sometimes wonders whether employers will take her degree as seriously as a four-year degree, she decided she could prove herself.
“Even if they were to look a little bit down on the three-year pathway, I can show them otherwise with the work,” she said.
Wesley Hardy, who is three semesters into a bachelor of applied science in accounting at Ensign, also sees the pros and cons. He likes that the three-year format will get him into the workforce faster.
But he noted that the requirements to become a certified public accountant — something he has considered — vary by state. Many require 120 semester hours to sit for the exam and 150 to become licensed. Graduate school often is needed.
Bruce Kusch, president of Ensign, said he has talked to multiple college presidents and doesn’t anticipate that graduate school will be a problem. But Hardy, 22, has questions about how it would work.
“Would I have to take extra classes?” he asked. “It’s definitely something I’ve thought of.”

What to know about Iceland’s vote on whether to restart talks to join the EU
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:23:01 UTC
13:23:01 KST

What to know about Iceland’s vote on whether to restart talks to join the EU
REYKJAVIK, Iceland (AP) — When U.S. President Donald Trump said he wanted a “piece of ice, cold and poorly located,” the people of Iceland had every reason to worry even if he was referring to Greenland.
Their concern was not only that the object of Trump’s desire was their nearest big neighbor, but that he repeatedly called it Iceland — four times.
That gaffe, as Trump continued to press for control of Greenland earlier this year, could help push the fiercely independent Iceland and its 400,000 people closer to Europe as voters decide Saturday whether to restart talks to join the European Union.
“We can’t really trust the U.S. anymore,” said Hildur Knútsdóttir, a horror fiction writer who plans to vote in favor of EU membership. “Trump was not joking about Greenland. There was a lot of fear here in Iceland because if he takes Greenland with force, we’re probably going to be next.”
Iceland’s decision is whether to continue going it alone successfully and maintain control of precious natural resources like its lucrative and well-managed fisheries, or to strengthen ties with Europe to better insulate the country from geopolitical instability and gain economic benefits such as the more stable euro currency and lower interest rates and inflation.
Iceland, which is a member of NATO, already participates in the EU’s single market through the European Economic Area and is part of the Schengen free-travel zone.
Sovereignty is at the heart of the divide
For both sides of the debate, it’s really a matter of sovereignty, said Hulda Thorisdottir, a political science professor at the University of Iceland.
Opponents argue that the nation that won its independence from Denmark in 1944 enjoys all the benefits of European integration with no drawbacks. Why surrender that when they’re doing so well? she said.
“The independence of Iceland is the most precious resource that we have,” said Haraldur Olafsson, a physics professor who is chairman of Heimssýn, a Euroskeptic group that opposes EU membership. “The possibility of making your own law and deciding how things are done is essential.”
EU proponents, however, see it through the lens of a rapidly changing world in which shifting alliances pose a security risk. Being outside the EU makes Iceland vulnerable and that threatens its sovereignty, Thorisdottir said.
Foreign and Defense Minister Thorgerdur Katrín Gunnarsdóttir, who supports joining the EU, said when she asks people from smaller countries such as Ireland, Finland or Luxembourg, whether they feel they’ve lost their sovereignty, “they look at me like I’m a crazy woman” and say membership has made them stronger.
This is not the first time Iceland has considered joining the EU
Prime Minister Kristrun Frostadottir’s center-left coalition government was elected in 2024 on a platform that called for a vote on EU membership.
Icelanders did not vote on the decision to apply for EU membership in 2009, after the country’s debt-burdened banking sector collapsed during the 2008 global financial crisis. Accession talks were suspended in 2013 after a center-right government came to power, and they formally ended in 2015.
The referendum is a first step to potentially joining the 27-nation bloc. Voters will answer a simple yes-or-no question: Should Iceland resume accession negotiations with the European Union?
If voters reject the proposal, the issue would be put to rest. A yes vote would lead to a yearslong negotiating process with the European Commission assessing 35 sets of criteria from financial systems to fisheries, transport networks, agricultural regulations, and freedoms such as speech and religion.
Any agreement would need to be approved by all current EU member nations and then voters in Iceland would have the final say on whether to join.
The fish factor could be a deal breaker
The descendants of Vikings who settled Iceland have been living off the sea for centuries, and fishing remains part of the country’s cultural identity. They fought the so-called Cod Wars with Britain to win control of their fishing grounds in the 1970s.
Their rich North Atlantic fishing grounds have always been a key sticking point to joining the EU over concerns they would have to join the Common Fisheries Policy that would allow Spanish, Dutch and other trawlers into their waters.
Any deal with the EU that doesn’t protect Iceland’s fishing rights is seen as dead in the water, but Gunnarsdóttir and other officials are confident any deal will offer an exemption for Iceland’s fisheries.
“We are a superpower when it comes to fisheries,” she said. “We will not sign any agreement which will not underline our sovereignty and full control of our fisheries.”
Heiðrun Lind Marteinsdóttir, the CEO of Fisheries Iceland, said the seafood trade organization doesn’t oppose joining the EU if there is a permanent opt-out from the fisheries policy, but she said that would be unprecedented.
“I think we need to be very realistic on the negotiation process and what we can get out of the negotiations,” she said. “To be honest, I think, we’re aiming high.”
Others in the industry are more skeptical that any protection of Icelandic fisheries would be lasting — especially for open water species like herring, capelin and mackerel that migrate between different fishing zones.
“We are going to see European fishing vessels here in Iceland,” Einar Sigurdsson, chairman of Isfelag fishing company, predicted.
Trump’s Greenland obsession sped up election timetable
The government had planned to hold the vote by next year but moved it up after Trump’s repeated overtures about taking over Greenland, a self-governing territory of Denmark, a longtime U.S. ally.
The U.S. State Department reassured Iceland officials that Trump meant Greenland during his repeated slip of the tongue at the World Economic Forum in Davos, Switzerland, Gunnarsdóttir, the foreign minister, said.
It didn’t help that William Long, the newly arrived U.S. ambassador in Reykjavik, once joked that Iceland would become the 52nd U.S. state and he’d be its governor. He apologized, but the remark prompted thousands of Icelanders to sign a petition urging the prime minister to reject his appointment.
Gunnarsdóttir said Trump’s saber-rattling emphasized the importance of the EU’s collection of small and large nations standing as one with Greenland and Denmark.
“That is so important for us to see a group of like-minded nations stand together on principles and values,” she said. “That is also what I’m looking at when I see the European Union in this volatile world.”

Uganda and Burundi military officials visit Israel to discuss Gaza troop deployment
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24

Uganda and Burundi military officials visit Israel to discuss Gaza troop deployment
TEL AVIV, Israel (AP) — Military officials from Uganda and Burundi visited Israel last week to discuss deploying troops to Gaza as part of an international security force envisioned by U.S. President Donald Trump’s Board of Peace for the fragile ceasefire, according to officials.
A Board of Peace official told The Associated Press that Ugandan officials joined a Burundian military delegation, and that Uganda is finalizing details of its participation after its parliament approved the troop contribution this month.
Nothing has been finalized with Burundi, but the official said they look forward to starting the process.
“We shared significant knowledge with one another, and the Burundi representatives expressed interest in our mission,” the official said, speaking on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to discuss talks with potential troop-contributing countries ahead of any agreement.
A Burundian military official told the AP that three other senior military officers led the delegation to Israel and that Burundi appeared intent on joining. The official spoke on condition of anonymity because he was not authorized to speak to the media.
It was not clear what Uganda or Burundi might be offering or what they might receive in return. Spokespersons for their militaries did not respond to requests for comment.
Progress on the international force has been slow
If Burundi moves ahead, the African nations would be the latest to join the international force for Gaza after Morocco, Kosovo, Kazakhstan and Albania made commitments. Uganda has committed around 1,200 personnel, and Morocco has committed up to 500. Kosovo, Kazakhstan and Albania in total have committed around 80.
Indonesia earlier said it was preparing to send 8,000 troops — by far the largest commitment — but put that on hold after the U.S. and Israel attacked Iran.
The 20,000-strong force would be led by U.S. Maj. Gen. Jasper Jeffers. Troops committed remain far short of that goal.
Last month, Trump announced a deal for Hamas to disarm and for Israel to withdraw its forces from Gaza. According to the deal, the International Stabilization Force would be deployed to areas of the Palestinian territory administered by an incoming technocratic committee, and Israeli forces would withdraw.
The force would help monitor the ceasefire, train Palestinian police and secure the delivery of aid, among other tasks.
The ceasefire that took effect in Gaza last October has stalled due to disagreements regarding Israel’s withdrawal from the strip and Hamas’ disarmament. A U.S. delegation met for hours earlier this month with the Hamas leader and then with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to press them forward. Hamas has agreed to the new U.S. deal.
Netanyahu has rejected it, saying Israel will not withdraw from any of the roughly 60% of the territory it controls in Gaza until Hamas has been completely disarmed. Even after Netanyahu’s meeting with the U.S. team, which included negotiator Jared Kushner, officials offered no concrete commitment by Israel.
Uganda and Burundi have peacekeeping experience from Somalia
Paul D. Williams, director of the security policy studies program at The George Washington University, said Uganda and Burundi have gained considerable peacekeeping experience through long-term deployments in Somalia as part of an African Union force resisting the al-Qaida-linked al-Shabab extremist group.
Their countries’ leaderships have “shown they are willing to tolerate high numbers of casualties without withdrawing,” he said.
Williams added that, with the mission in Somalia winding down, both countries will be searching for ways to accrue financial and material support for their militaries: “Deploying to Gaza with U.S. support is one way to do that.”
A Ugandan military officer with knowledge of the upcoming deployment said troops were being selected to go to Gaza. The officer spoke on condition of anonymity because they weren’t authorized to speak to the press.

P Chidambaram; ex-diplomat Navdeep Suri
NEW DELHI: Former Union minister P Chidambaram on Monday said the Election Commission of India (ECI)’s ongoing Special Intensive Revision (SIR) of electoral rolls could leave 10% of India’s eligible population — or nearly 10 crore people — without the right to vote, after a former diplomat detailed difficulties he faced establishing his citizenship during the exercise in Punjab.Navdeep Suri, who served as India’s Ambassador to Egypt and the UAE and High Commissioner to Australia, questioned what the experience of a common citizen might be if he himself faced difficulties despite having represented the country in three nations.“Based on the outcomes so far, at the end of the S.I.R. process, 10% of India’s adult population will be ‘citizens’ but without the right to vote, thanks to the ECI. That is nearly 10 crore people. The ECI has created a new category of ‘non-voting citizens’,” the senior Congress leader wrote, referring to Suri’s post.
Earlier, Suri said his details did not match the 2003 electoral rolls used for verification because he was posted in London at the time and had not participated in that revision.“Sharing my experience with #SIR in Punjab. Went to BLO, submitted Voter ID and Aadhaar card, was assured that everything is in order.
Got a message today from a volunteer saying some details don't match with SIR in 2003!!” Suri posted on X.According to the former diplomat, officials later asked him to produce his passport as proof of citizenship.“Spoke with BLO, was told that I should come and collect the notice. And then come again with unspecified documents that show I am an Indian citizen... I happen to have documents other than voter ID and Aadhaar card.
But can’t help asking: If I have trouble establishing my citizenship after representing India in three countries, what’s the fate of the common citizen? Ease of Living, I presume!” he added.Meanwhile, the Punjab Chief Electoral Officer assured citizens that receiving a notice was not a cause for concern.“As part of the ongoing SIR process, notices are being delivered to voters where required. Received a notice? Don't worry! Simply check the details, submit the required documents, and complete the process,” the Punjab CEO stated on X earlier.The draft electoral roll for Punjab was published on August 13. The state is currently undergoing the second phase of the SIR, which involves reviewing the draft electoral rolls and filing claims and objections.

Taiwan machine tool orders see improvement
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
04:03:23 UTC
13:03:23 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — Taiwan’s machine tool industry is seeing a recovery in orders as market conditions improve, with several manufacturers expecting stronger operations in the third quarter, CTEE reported Sunday.
Machine tools are used to shape metal and other materials into precision parts for a wide range of products. They play a key role in manufacturing, as many industrial machines and products rely on components made using these tools, according to Gugu Fund.
Order visibility at many companies has extended to at least two to three months, while some manufacturers have bookings stretching into 2027. Component-related manufacturers, including Hiwin Technologies Corp., Chieftek Precision Co., and Tbi Motion Technology Co., have reported better order visibility and stronger revenue growth than other companies in the sector.
All three companies are benefiting from continued orders from the semiconductor and automation industries and are targeting double-digit revenue growth this year. Their backlogs extend into at least the fourth quarter.
Tongtai Machine & Tool Co. has benefited from strong orders for printed circuit board drilling machines. PCBs are the boards on which electronic components are mounted and interconnected, while drilling creates the holes needed to connect different circuit layers and install components, according to Stockfeel and Business Weekly.
The company has also made progress in semiconductor applications, including chip-on-wafer-on-substrate (CoWoS) advanced packaging. This has increased its total order backlog from NT$2.8 billion (US$88 million) at the start of the year to NT$3.2 billion.
Meanwhile, manufacturers of large-scale equipment are also seeing longer order visibility. Honor Seiki Co. and Shieh Yih Machinery Industry Co. have delivery schedules of at least six months, with some orders extending beyond a year.
Honor Seiki said its order backlog stands at about NT$1.7 billion to NT$1.8 billion, with new bookings mainly coming from the aerospace and basic processing industries in China and India. The company expects operations to improve in the third quarter and for the full year.
Shieh Yih reported a loss in its core business in the second quarter, partly because some customers postponed shipments until the third quarter due to higher freight costs. It expects its core operations to return to profitability in the third quarter.
Taiwan Takisawa Technology Co. said its bookings extend through the end of the year. Its orders mainly come from manufacturers of AI server cooling plates and liquid-cooling systems, as well as Chinese producers of robot reducers and components for robotic hands.
Looking ahead, global supply chain shifts and emerging markets are reshaping Taiwan’s machine tool industry. Growth is expected to come from new markets and higher-value applications, according to the Industrial Economics & Knowledge Center.
Semiconductor equipment, aerospace, AI servers, drones, and humanoid robot components are emerging as potential growth areas. Manufacturers are also shifting toward integrated solutions that combine automation, AI, digital monitoring, and multiple machining processes.
Taiwanese machine tool makers including Anderson Industrial Corp., Awea Mechantronic Co., Goodway Machine Corp., Kao Fong Machinery Co., Tongtai, and Shieh Yih are diversifying their businesses to capture new growth opportunities.

Workers in China worry over being replaced as they adapt to the growing impact of AI on jobs

Unknown Publisher

Workers in China worry over being replaced as they adapt to the growing impact of AI on jobs
HONG KONG (AP) — Computer programmer Fei Zhaojun’s boss asked him if artificial intelligence could soon replace humans in coding jobs. Two weeks later, he was laid off from his job in Beijing, together with about 160 of his colleagues.
It’s an increasingly common scenario as artificial intelligence, supported by government policies, reshapes China’s massive job market. Some economists believe that might eventually undermine the overall strength of the world’s second largest economy.
Rapid adoption of AI in many fields, from computer programmers to script writing and physical tasks, is pushing people out of their jobs or leaving them afraid that it might. China is at the vanguard of AI adoption as government policies encourage people and businesses to use AI applications and robotics in all aspects of life, so people like Fei are figuring out how to adapt.
“There appears to be far less anti-AI sentiment in China (than elsewhere). Most people seem either positive, neutral, or mildly interested in AI,” said Shujing He, a Beijing-based senior analyst at advisory and research firm Plenum.
“Individuals who worry about being replaced, as well as those who have already left traditional workplaces, are often eager to experiment with AI-enabled businesses and independent ventures,” she said. “The level of interest is striking.”
Until recently, Fei had doubted AI could do programming work perfectly, even though his bosses thought it was close enough.
“Mid-level coders’ job are essentially replaceable in most of the cases,” said Fei, 40. “Even if it is a disaster that leads to replacing all humans, at this stage, you just have to use it as everyone else is using it.”
Now he’s making vlog-style short videos during a career break while figuring out what he wants to do next. He’s not making a living off of his videos, which are about ordinary people’s lives, but hopes that they might help others.
If you can’t beat them, join them
Du Qinchun, a part-time translator, has been helping to train an AI model to do translations. That’s brought him more work, at least temporarily.
“But it’s true that the pay in the industry has been cut by more than half compared to what it was years ago,” said Du, who is based in southwestern China’s Chengdu city.
The trend is so evident that popular college programs in foreign languages have increasingly fallen out of favor as AI-powered translation tools have become more widespread.
The share of Chinese industrial enterprises saying they use AI models and “agents” jumped to 47.5% last year from 9.6% in 2024, according to the market intelligence firm IDC.
“China’s vibrant open-source model ecosystem fosters greater AI application innovation in industrial settings, gradually closing the gap between foundational model capabilities and real-world enterprise value creation,” said Yanze Du, an IDC senior research manager in Beijing.
Humanoid robots can now, for example, sort parcels in postal centers, although still on a small-scale basis, and are pushing the boundaries in performing more human tasks such as directing traffic and making coffee. Food delivery robots are also gaining ground across the country, potentially threatening the livelihoods of millions of Chinese food delivery workers.
Generative AI increasingly is used for creation, production and distribution in China’s short drama industry. The number of live-action short and vertical video series designed for mobile phones fell about 75% in the first quarter of this year from a year earlier, according to Chinese media reports.
“Tasks that once required specialized training can now be performed by almost anyone with access to AI tools. This is particularly evident in software development and multimedia creation,” said Plenum’s He. “As a result, workers whose roles are narrowly concentrated in these areas may face greater displacement risk.”
A report from International Labor Organization, meanwhile, found that women face higher risks of losing employment due to use of AI than men, as they tend to work in areas more suitable for automation, such as assembling electronics, and remain underrepresented in science and technology.
AI has mixed effects on the slowing economy
Under China’s “AI Plus” initiative and its five-year plan through 2030, the government is pushing to infuse AI across many industries, aiming to gain an edge in China’s technology rivalry with the U.S.
“What is specific to China is that the government is really into diffusing AI across the economy, so AI may get into different domains more quickly comparing to other countries,” said Zilan Qian, a research associate at Oxford China Policy Lab.
China’s economic growth has already been slowing. Consumer spending has lagged partly due to people becoming reluctant to spend because they’re worried about losing their jobs. It’s added to problems stemming from a prolonged downturn in the housing market that has undermined household wealth.
China’s tech industries may be innovative with high productivity, but they may not generate many new jobs, said Eswar Prasad, a professor of economics and trade policy at Cornell University.
“AI is likely to lift productivity across the board but could have a severe disruptive effect on employment, worsening the employment growth problem and resulting in a detrimental effect on social stability,” he said.
Similar to their U.S. rivals, Chinese tech giants have cut or restructured tens of thousands of jobs, partly due to AI. The outlook for the broader jobs market remains uncertain: China’s overall urban unemployment rate hovers around 5%, but unemployment for people aged 16 to 24, excluding students, is roughly triple that.
That said, in the longer run, some experts say unemployment rates could fall, since China’s population of 1.4 billion is rapidly aging and shrinking.
By 2050, China is projected to have fewer than two working-age adults to support each retiree, compared with more than 2.5 in the U.S., said Xuenan Cao, a professor at San Francisco Bay University whose focus includes technology and society.
“Automation could partially offset a shrinking workforce rather than being purely a threat to it,” Cao said.
Some embrace AI to find new ways to make a living
Wang Zhicheng, 32, often used AI for brainstorming and fact-checking in his previous job as a scriptwriter for a company that produces 3D animated educational videos and interactive exercises for children.
After its parent company laid off roughly half of its 13 script writers, he chose to resign and work independently, making illustrated children’s books.
While AI sometimes saved time the scripts it generated, they often felt strange, Wang said. Episodes tended to be repetitive and formulaic and the level of detail devoted to knowledge varied widely.
“You can treat AI as a tool just like (Microsoft) Word,” said Wang, who has started his own studio making picture books and other creative works. “Humans are still the decision makers on which one to pick or pursue among all that AI generates.”
High school chemistry teacher Yang Zheng said he doesn’t consider AI as a threat to his job even though students use AI for help with their homework.
“Teachers cannot be there all the time,” he said. “It is a good thing for students as it generates in real-time so that students can ask follow-up questions,” said Yang, 29. “It often gets things wrong, but it improves over time.”
____
Fu Ting reported from Washington. AP video producer Wu Jia in Beijing contributed to this story.

Why Singapore’s Growing Political Diversity Matters
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
03:53:00 UTC
12:53:00 KST

Since the watershed election of 2011, one major trend in Singapore politics has been the growth of alternative political forces to the long-dominant People’s Action Party (PAP). General elections now resemble those in democracies, with all seats contested, rallies well attended, and election coverage widely followed across a range of media platforms. While the PAP remains dominant, since the 2020 election it has become expected that the opposition will match or beat its previous seat performance, currently at 10 elected parliamentary seats.
Civil society has also grown in size and significance since 2011, and “activist” is now less of a dirty word. A plethora of advocacy groups, many led by a new generation of activists, now actively champion and gain support for numerous causes such as political literacy, climate justice, death penalty abolition, media freedom, LGBTQ+ rights, workers’ rights, women’s rights, and justice for Palestine. As a prominent recent example, the work of environmental activists has helped increase public opposition to the government’s proposed developments at Maju Forest and Gillman Barracks in the name of environmental protection. These developments have all occurred despite a more challenging legislative environment over the last several years.
There is, however, a related second trend in Singapore politics that demands equal if not more attention than the first. This is the fact that the growth in size and significance of political alternatives to the PAP has come alongside the pluralization of these alternatives. While the opposition parties used to be discussed primarily in terms of their common goal of providing a check on the PAP, they now have more distinguishable ideological positions as well as perceived levels of competence and credibility amongst Singaporeans.
Alongside its growth, civil society has also experienced pluralization in a variety of ways. Besides the diversity of issues tackled, there is now a distinct division between formal registered civil society organizations and informal groups whose main form of institutionalization is their social media presence. This difference also somewhat overlaps with divergent views on the best way to engage in activism in Singapore. While formalized groups are more likely to utilize the more cautious path of “pragmatic resistance,” which involves strategic engagement with the state, informal groups are often more willing to treat the state as its adversary and confront it with sharper language and civil disobedience.
Discourses within civil society have also noticeably diversified. Communitarian ideas about the good of society and liberal rights-based framing remain prevalent, but younger activists are now much more comfortable adopting leftist frameworks and proposals. There are also clear differences of opinion in terms of what democracy really entails and, in turn, how much more democracy Singapore needs.
In some states in the region, like China and Thailand, there is a fear that the people have been “getting old before getting rich,” with aging populations potentially putting the countries at risk of stalling into a middle-income trap. Singapore, of course, faces no such concern about its standard of living. However, for proponents of a more politically open and competitive Singapore, there is a potential concern that the country may be “getting plural before getting democratic.” Paradoxically, greater political pluralization may make it more difficult to coordinate and build the type of broad coalitions required to pressure the ruling party into adopting political reforms.
Real disputes have indeed already emerged between civil society activists over these differences, including on how to protest the Singapore government’s ties with Israel in light of the genocidal massacres in Gaza. This debate is but one example of how diverse perspectives have also become more commonly expressed on matters of foreign policy. Recent anonymized interview research that I conducted with 12 Singaporean activists suggests that there is also significant diversity when it comes to civil society’s views on Singapore’s relations with other countries as well as global affairs more generally.
As countries across the globe look to Southeast Asia for new partnerships amidst the breakdown of the old international order led by the United States, it is important to get a sense of what these emerging voices think of foreign engagement with their countries. This includes their views on foreign support for the pro-democratic and rights-based work of civil society, a matter that remains highly sensitive to Singapore’s PAP government.
The PAP has always been averse to foreign “lecturing” and has long held the position that any foreign engagement with its domestic politics is “an absolute no.” In a July 2025 statement that is becoming increasingly commonplace in regional political parlance, the PAP was firm in its suggestion that “politics should stop at the water’s edge.”
In the interviews I conducted, it was unsurprising that Singapore’s civil society activists, who were selected for their pro-democratic and reformist orientations, have a different view from the PAP when it comes to foreign engagement on matters of human rights, social and environmental justice, and democracy. In fact, 10 out of 12 interviewees suggested that there is some role for foreign states to support their work on these issues. Only two participants took a firm line of completely rejecting foreign engagement on these matters, a position resembling the Singapore government’s own.
What was more revealing was the diversity of views on the ways in which foreign states can legitimately engage with Singapore on these issues. The responses of the 10 interviewees clearly fell along a spectrum between strong cosmopolitan or internationalist views on the one hand and more self-determination or anti-colonial positions on the other.
The three participants at the self-determination end of the spectrum strongly disagreed with foreign states bilaterally pressuring the Singapore government on matters of human rights and democracy. Western states in particular were singled out for their hypocritical stances on these matters considering their own human rights issues and polarization within their political systems. That said, these respondents still saw value in foreign states providing support to Singapore civil society through grants to attend overseas conferences and workshops for knowledge-sharing and capacity-building. They also encouraged foreign embassies to provide a space for civil society actors to gather, discuss, and meet with potential collaborators.
In the middle of the spectrum, four interviewees also argued against foreign states “naming and shaming” Singapore, albeit for different reasons. While the self-determination group argued against bilateral pressure in principle, the middle group of participants argued that such an approach would simply not work with the PAP in power.
Instead, foreign governments would find more success working constructively with the Singapore government, exchanging alternative policy proposals with evidence of effectiveness and making their own commitments to upholding human rights and environmental standards when investing. In terms of engagement with the ground, this group suggested that foreign states ought to go further, providing funding to civil society for specific projects and meeting with activists directly for information-sharing purposes.
The three participants on the internationalist side of the spectrum countered the PAP’s position on bilateral pressure most squarely, stating that foreign governments not voicing their concerns about rights and democracy legitimizes authoritarian structures, emboldens autocratic behavior, and gives a green light to human rights abuses. In addition to backing the aforementioned ways that foreign states can support Singaporean activists and advocates, this group argued that foreign embassies ought to vocally and visibly defend the already limited space for civil society when it is threatened by new repressive legislation or the embassies are pressured to cancel their events.
With such diversity in the political alternatives to the PAP, the next major breakthrough in Singapore’s political evolution may well depend on the extent to which these diverse actors are able to suture a common front capable of providing an effective counterweight to the PAP’s dominance. Part of this process will depend on finding sufficient commonalities, and perhaps even a common program, beyond the low baseline of wanting change.
One interesting point of convergence, at least within civil society, may be shared ideas regarding Singapore’s own foreign policy, including its relations both with its closest neighbors and the wider world. Remarkably, all 12 interviewees, including those who took a firm self-determination line regarding foreign engagement with Singapore, suggested that their own government must aim to be a better neighbor to its regional peers and a more principled actor on the world stage.
For the former, many interviewees called into question destructive sand-mining practices in Indonesia and Cambodia driven by Singaporean demand as well as Singaporean investment into a Myanmar economy dominated by the brutal military regime. For the latter, almost all participants wished to see a much stronger stance on Israel for its military actions in Gaza and beyond. One interviewee went as far as to state that: “I’m starting to get the sense that besides just pure economics and trade deals, there is a growing appetite for Singapore to have a spine and for Singapore to be on the right side of history.”
The Singapore government has already taken note of this shift. In response to Singaporeans’ reactions to events in the Middle East, Foreign Minister Vivian Balakrishnan admitted that “foreign policy now has domestic salience.” Should this salience increase, the desire for a more principled foreign policy may well be one of many threads that stitch together the more vibrant, plural civil society and political alternatives to the PAP.

South Australia reports 2nd suspected mammal bird flu case in seal

12:43:40 KST

CANBERRA, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- South Australian authorities on Monday reported a second suspected case of H5N1 bird flu in a seal, one day after the state reported Australia's first case in a mammal.
South Australia's Department of Primary Industries and Regions said on Monday that the long-nosed fur seal was found at the Pages Conservation Park, a protected area consisting of the North Page and South Page islands located about 18 km off the state's south coast.
The department said that samples have been sent to the Australian Center for Disease Preparedness for confirmatory testing.
It comes after the federal government on Sunday announced that Australia's first confirmed case of the highly pathogenic H5N1 avian influenza strain in a mammal had been confirmed in a long-nosed fur seal found dead in mainland South Australia on Wednesday.
South Australian Minister for Climate, Environment and Water Emily Bourke said that the two cases were incredibly concerning. The state government on Thursday said that over 1,000 birds had been found dead in suspected H5N1 mass mortality events on three islands, including North Page and South Page.
"We've seen devastation in seals around the world when it comes to bird flu," Bourke told Australian Broadcasting Corporation (ABC) radio on Monday.
According to the National Parks and Wildlife Service, the Page islands are home to one of three large colonies of endangered Australian sea lions in South Australia. The Invasive Species Council has warned that the H5N1 outbreak could be an extinction-level event for the species.
Bourke said that the strain circulating in South Australia potentially arrived in the state from Heard Island, a remote sub-Antarctic Australian territory.
The Australian Antarctic Program said in June that around 13,000 of the estimated 17,000 elephant seal pups on Heard Island had died from H5N1 avian influenza.
Federal Minister for the Environment and Water Murray Watt told ABC television on Monday that the cases in seals were not unexpected and authorities expect to see more mass mortality events. ■

Feature: On the Gobi, western China's oil city Karamay serves up tennis dreams
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:43:36 CST
12:43:36 KST

by sportswriter Sun Zhe
URUMQI, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- Karamay's name, derived from the Uygur language, means "black oil," reflecting the resource that shaped the city's development.
Rising from a remote stretch of the vast Gobi Desert, the city grew around its oil fields and developed into a modern industrial hub.
Beneath the vast skies of this once-isolated city, another passion has taken root. Over the decades, tennis has grown from a pastime for a small circle of enthusiasts into an established part of local sporting culture, turning Karamay into an unlikely center for the sport in inland China.
SEED TAKES ROOT
Karamay, in northwest China's Xinjiang Uygur Autonomous Region, is one of modern China's most important energy bases. With a population of fewer than 500,000, the city is home to Xinjiang Oilfield, which has maintained annual crude oil production of more than 10 million tonnes for 24 consecutive years.
Like many of his peers, Alipjan Awut grew up in a family connected to the oil industry.
Inspired by the teamwork and determination of the oil workers around him, he found joy in pursuing a common goal on the football pitch. As a midfielder, he led attacks and captained his primary school team.
"Football is a team sport. It tests cooperation and brings different people together," said the 36-year-old. "But nothing can surpass tennis in my heart."
As oil workers from across China settled in the Gobi city, they brought with them their lifestyles and hobbies. Since the 1980s, tennis has gradually taken root in Karamay, growing from a pastime among a small group of enthusiasts into a sport embraced by the wider community.
At 12, Alipjan got his first taste of tennis when a PE teacher spotted his athletic ability and invited him to pick up a racket for Karamay's first citywide school tennis competition.
"At that time, we didn't even have our own rackets. The school provided them. I just thought it was fun," Alipjan recalled.
After just over a month of training, he finished fifth in the city competition, turning his initial curiosity into a lifelong passion.
With few professional coaches available, Alipjan found his own ways to improve. Whenever a tennis tournament was broadcast on television, he would sit in front of the screen, studying every detail of the players' movements, footwork and technique.
The sport also took him beyond his hometown. During school holidays, coaches brought young players from Karamay to eastern Chinese cities with stronger tennis programs, where the team often drew curious looks.
"They were often surprised to see players from Xinjiang on the tennis court," Alipjan said. "We knew there was a gap, but we wanted to change that perception."
GROWING UNDER SUN
After graduating from university, Alipjan returned to his hometown and became a tennis coach at an amateur sports school.
As part of efforts to make tennis more accessible, Karamay expanded its facilities. A sport once constrained by a lack of courts now has nearly 40 venues across parks, communities and schools, some capable of hosting national competitions.
Alipjan has become busier than ever. More than 100 young players now train at his school, many of whom discovered tennis through short tennis programs offered at local schools.
"Those with potential will be selected into our elite training group, and they do not need to pay any fees," he said.
Among the young players he coaches, one stands out: Alfudin Hasimjan, his younger cousin. Before turning seven, Alfudin had never seriously played any sport, but he quickly fell in love with tennis.
"I don't know why, but I feel like I have some talent for tennis," the youngster said with a smile.
At 14, Alfudin is already over 1.8 meters tall and has won titles in his age group in Xinjiang. He spends almost every summer day on the court, where the intense Gobi sun has left him deeply tanned, but his passion remains undiminished.
"It is a sport under the sun," Alipjan said. "Whether they play for fun or dream of going further, we hope children can stay active. That is what we want to achieve."
As more young players picked up rackets, tennis became increasingly embedded in Karamay's sporting identity. The city has since been recognized by Chinese tennis media as one of the places with the greatest potential for the sport's growth.
BEYOND THE GOBI
At the ongoing 15th Xinjiang Games, nine regions sent under-18 players across two age groups, marking a record turnout. Karamay remains a strong force, but its dominance is facing growing challenges.
Once numbering fewer than 50 players, Xinjiang's youth tennis community has now grown to about 500, with specialized clubs emerging to provide greater support for the next generation.
"Urumqi, the regional capital, is developing quickly, with more courts, coaches and families embracing tennis," Alipjan said. "I'm not worried. The more people play, the stronger Xinjiang tennis will become."
Still, Alipjan knows Karamay has a long way to go to reach the level of the world's leading tennis regions. For him, that gap has always been motivation to improve.
In 2024, Alipjan became a senior coach certified by the Chinese Tennis Association. For him, building a tennis ecosystem in Karamay remains a long-term endeavor.
"Honestly, it is a long process," he said. "But one day, I hope players from my team can also step out of Xinjiang and represent this region on a bigger stage." ■

China, Kuwait hold tea culture exchange event
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
11:43:20 CST
12:43:20 KST

People participate in the Chinese & Kuwaiti Tea Art and Treats Tasting event at the China Cultural Center in Kuwait in Hawalli Governorate, Kuwait, Aug. 23, 2026. (Photo by Asad/Xinhua)
KUWAIT CITY, Aug. 24 (Xinhua) -- More than 150 people gathered Sunday evening at the China Cultural Center in Kuwait for the Chinese & Kuwaiti Tea Art and Treats Tasting event, where they savored teas and sweets and learned about tea-making traditions in both countries.
Jointly organized by the China Cultural Center in Kuwait and Kuwait's National Council for Culture, Arts and Letters (NCCAL), the event was part of Kuwait's 18th Summer Cultural Festival. It aimed to introduce Chinese and Kuwaiti tea traditions and promote cultural and people-to-people exchanges between the two countries.
Attendees sampled Chinese green, black, white and oolong teas, accompanied by Chinese sweets. A separate tasting area featured Kuwaiti and Arab beverages, including karak tea, loomi tea and Moroccan mint tea, along with local and Arab sweets.
In his speech, Chinese Ambassador to Kuwait Yang Xin noted that this year marks the 55th anniversary of the establishment of diplomatic relations between the two countries, and cultural exchanges constitute "a bridge connecting the hearts of the two peoples."
Speaking to Xinhua at the end of the event, Yang said the occasion represented "a window into China's time-honored culture and a means of promoting cultural exchanges and friendship between China, Kuwait and the Arab world."
NCCAL Secretary-General Mohammad Al-Jassar noted that presenting Kuwaiti and Arab tea traditions alongside Chinese tea reflects the links between cultures and shared daily customs.
The Chinese tea ceremony opens a window into an authentic aspect of Chinese culture and showcases rituals and values passed down through generations, Al-Jassar said.
Liu Jinhong, director of the China Cultural Center in Kuwait, said the center was pleased to see "tea as a bridge to introduce the rich tea cultures of China and Kuwait," noting that the tradition of welcoming guests by serving tea represents a shared value between the two cultures.
Kuwaiti tea cultural expert Sarah Maher AlMajed, a certified tea sommelier and tea master, gave a presentation on Arab tea culture, beginning with an overview of the trade and cultural routes through which tea spread from China to the Arab world.
Nasser Alsaqer, a Kuwaiti enthusiast of Chinese tea culture, shared his experience of studying tea-making in China. He explained the process of Chinese tea production, from picking fresh leaves through processing and manufacturing.
The event also featured a tourism booth showcasing routes and resources related to tea culture in China. It was part of the Tea for Harmony program organized by the China Cultural Center in Kuwait throughout 2026. ■

Shin Bet must protect Eisenkot before political violence brings Israel another tragedy - editorial
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
03:20:51 UTC
12:20:51 KST

Israel knows the devastating effects that incitement and political violence can wreak on the fabric of a taut society. It can tear it in two.
One only has to look back to November 4, 1995, when prime minister Yitzhak Rabin, the target of vicious incitement campaigns over his support of the Oslo Accords, was gunned down by far-right ultranationalist Yigal Amir. Israel has not been the same ever since.
Although the country has not experienced another political assassination, the specter remains always just under the surface. Security for elected officials was heightened, and warnings from Israel’s security services about the threat of political violence have accompanied every election campaign since that dark day in November 1995.
That’s why the decision, as reported by N12 on Saturday night, by Shin Bet (Israel Security Agency) chief David Zini not to provide Yashar Party head Gadi Eisenkot with a security detail is so perplexing and worrisome.
Eisenkot has emerged as Benjamin Netanyahu’s leading challenger in the October 27 poll. The decision was reportedly made despite regular threats directed at Eisenkot on social media and warnings from the defense sector that Iran and other hostile actors may attempt to target current and former senior officials.
Eisenkot’s campaign field director wrote to Zini and other security officials in June saying the Yashar leader had been forced to hire a private security firm because he was not receiving state protection.
According to the N12 report, Zini’s representatives told Eisenkot’s staff that while the Shin Bet would not provide him with a security detail, the agency would assign a liaison and gather intelligence if concerns emerged about an exceptionally serious incident. However, the request for permanent protection was denied.
Netanyahu, Lapid, leading candidates in 2022 election, both received full security detail
In the last election campaign in 2022, both leading candidates, Yair Lapid and Netanyahu, were provided with full security details - Lapid as sitting prime minister and Netanyahu as a former leader as part of the lifelong package for past heads of government.
Following Zini’s decision, Eisenkot’s campaign submitted its objections in writing to the Shin Bet, Israel Police, and the attorney-general, warning that physical threats against the former IDF chief of staff were escalating, and he called for the decision to be reversed.
“The atmosphere on the Israeli street, as well as on social media, is becoming increasingly heated, and threats are emerging and multiplying,” the letter said.
Just last week, N12 reported that Zini was considering providing Eisenkot with an armed detail amid indications that Iran was increasing efforts to harm Israeli leaders as elections drew close.
The decision not to grant Eisenkot state protection during the campaign is playing with fire. One only has to scroll on social media or watch one of the TV news talk shows to see that the level of vitriol on all sides of the political fence is reaching alarming proportions.
Zini's decision politically motivated?
The suggestion has been raised by the Eisenkot team that Zini’s decision was politically motivated. The letter sent by his team in protest alleged that the government, the Ministerial Committee on Shin Bet Affairs, and the committee’s chairman “are failing to fulfill their personal responsibility for political and ulterior motives and are avoiding carrying out their duties.”
Eisenkot’s campaign further alleged that a consideration in denying the security detail was a desire to avoid images of Eisenkot looking “prime ministerial” by appearing in public surrounded by security personnel – images which could boost his stature in the public eye.
Although that sounds somewhat conspiratorial, it’s worth noting that the chairman of the Ministerial Committee on Shin Bet Affairs is Netanyahu, and its members consist of Defense Minister Israel Katz, Justice Minister Yair Levin, National Security Minister Itamar Ben-Gvir, and Education Minister Yoav Kisch.
Zini has already faced claims that he’s a Netanyahu appointee who has pledged allegiance to the prime minister. Now is the time to smother those charges and demonstrate that the decisions of the Shin Bet are being made with solely professional considerations in mind, and not according to political alliances.
Granting Gadi Eisenkot a state security detail leading up to the October 27 election is the surest way to clear the air. And more importantly, doing so will help ensure that another devastating national tragedy has less of a chance of taking place.

Taiwan labor insurance rate to rise to 13% in 2027
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
03:13:12 UTC
12:13:12 KST

TAIPEI (Taiwan News) — The labor insurance contribution rate will rise by 0.5 percentage point to 13% in 2027, reaching the statutory ceiling under the Labor Insurance Act.
The increase will raise insurance costs for employers and workers nationwide, with nearly 626,000 businesses expected to incur an additional NT$13.147 billion (US$413 million) in costs next year, while more than 10.51 million workers will see higher rates, per UDN.
Under the current system, the 13% rate includes a 1% employment insurance component, meaning the ordinary labor insurance rate itself will rise to 12% next year. Labor insurance premiums are shared among employers (70%), workers (20%), and the government (10%).
Premiums are calculated according to an insured salary scale rather than directly on an employee's actual salary. The maximum monthly insured salary for labor and employment insurance is NT$45,800.
With the average insured salary of NT$36,511, the 0.5% increase will raise an employer's monthly contribution by an estimated NT$127.79 per worker. Workers will pay an additional NT$36.51 per month, or about NT$438.14 annually.
The increase is expected to generate approximately NT$23.021 billion in additional labor insurance revenue annually.
Employers are also preparing for a possible minimum wage increase next year. Businesses have argued that mandatory labor-related contributions already represent a significant financial burden.
Labor insurance provides social security coverage for insured workers, including eligible foreign and migrant workers. Benefits include payments for ordinary injury or sickness, disability, old age, and death, per a Bureau of Labor Insurance press release.
For ordinary injury or sickness, eligible workers can receive benefits equal to 50% of their average monthly insured salary for up to six months, with an additional six months available under certain conditions.
Occupational injury and disease benefits are now administered separately under the Labor Occupational Accident Insurance and Protection Act. Eligible workers can receive compensation equal to 70% of their average monthly insured salary, subject to statutory limits and conditions.
Labor insurance also provides old-age benefits, including monthly pension payments or lump-sum benefits for eligible workers. Disability and survivor benefits are available to qualifying insured workers and their families.

Scientists discover a real-life “dragon” and name it after Syrax
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
03:11:22 UTC
12:11:22 KST

Scientists discover a real-life “dragon” and name it after Syrax
- Date:
- August 23, 2026
- Source:
- Pensoft Publishers
- Summary:
- Scientists discovered a small, yellowish mountain horned dragon in Thailand and named it Acanthosaura syrax after a dragon from House of the Dragon. Found only in a narrow band of high-elevation forest, the distinctive new species could become a flagship for protecting its rare mountain habitat.
- Share:
Scientists have identified a new species of lizard living in the high mountain forests of western Thailand. The species, Acanthosaura syrax, takes its name from Syrax, the dragon ridden by Queen Rhaenyra Targaryen in House of the Dragon.
Acanthosaura syrax belongs to a group of agamid lizards known as mountain horned dragons, which are distinguished by the spiny crests that extend along the neck and back.
Researchers found the species in an evergreen forest within Mae Wong National Park, in Tak-Kamphaeng Phet Province, at elevations above 1,300 meters. So far, it has not been found anywhere else. Its discovery increases the number of recognized species in the genus Acanthosaura to 23.
The research was led by Poramad Trivalairat and colleagues from Chulabhorn Royal Academy and Kasetsart University. The team intentionally chose the name Syrax because several traits of the fictional dragon are reflected in the newly described lizard.
Why Scientists Chose the Name Syrax
In the fantasy series, Syrax is known for her striking yellow coloration, relatively small size compared with other dragons, and unusually high egg production.
The researchers saw similar characteristics in A. syrax. The lizard has yellowish-green coloration, ranks among the smallest species in its genus, and produces relatively large clutches of eggs for its body size. The scientists have proposed "Syrax mountain horned dragon" as its English common name, along with a Thai name that carries the same meaning.
The species is distinctive for more than its fantasy-inspired name. It has the smallest neck and back crest scales yet documented in the genus, as well as a generally small body size. Unlike several closely related species, it does not have a black patch around the eye. Instead, it has a characteristic dark collar marking.
DNA Confirms a Distinct Species
Genetic testing supported the physical differences observed by the researchers. An analysis of two genes showed that A. syrax is genetically distinct from its closest known relative, A. lepidogaster, as well as from every other recognized species in the group.
The newly identified lizard appears to occupy only a narrow zone of high-altitude forest. According to the researchers, the rugged landscape naturally separates its populations across the mountain range, which could make the species especially vulnerable if its habitat faces additional pressure.
The team is urging stronger protection for the high-elevation forests of Mae Wong. They suggest that A. syrax could become a flagship species for conservation in the region, joining other rare animals found there, including the Asian forest tortoise, Oldham's leaf turtle and the Indochinese tiger.
The study is published in the open-access journal ZooKeys.
Story Source:
Materials provided by Pensoft Publishers. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.
Journal Reference:
- Poramad Trivalairat, Krittiya Trivalairat, Nawee Moungkhaek, Simon Caponov, Benchapol Lorsunyaluck. Acanthosaura syrax sp. nov., a new species of mountain horned dragon from high-elevation habitats of western Thailand (Squamata, Agamidae). ZooKeys, 2026; 1287: 47 DOI: 10.3897/zookeys.1287.186636

Enes Kanter Freedom ejected from Fever-Sky game after he was confronted by Sky’s Cloud
Unknown

Enes Kanter Freedom ejected from Fever-Sky game after he was confronted by Sky’s Cloud
CHICAGO (AP) — Former NBA center Enes Kanter Freedom was ejected from Sunday night’s Indiana-Chicago WNBA game after he was confronted by Sky guard Natasha Cloud late in the third quarter.
Freedom was sitting along the baseline. He had on a black shirt that read “WOMAN noun. adult human female.”
The Fever called for a timeout after Cloud scored inside with 1:22 left in the third. Cloud then did a chest bump with teammate Aicha Coulibaly before turning around and walking in Kanter’s direction.
Cloud, 34, started yelling and pointing at Kanter, 34, as she approached him. A standing Kanter held his arms out and took one step on the court as security and a handful of Sky players moved in between the two.
“There was just a fan incident and the security handled it, and we’re just going to focus on the game,” Chicago forward Azura Stevens said after the Sky’s 113-90 loss.
Chicago coach Tyler Marsh said Cloud was concerned about being a distraction for the team.
“I told her she wasn’t,” Marsh said. “I told her that we all embrace her as someone that protects our team and protects people that need to be protected and so Tash is always going to stand on that, and we stand for Tash.”
Freedom stopped near the basket to plead his case to security as he was escorted from the court area. He spun around while holding his shirt out and encouraged the crowd to respond as he walked toward the front lobby.
He had a conversation with a group of police officers before departing Wintrust Arena.
“I didn’t see it, we were talking about the next play in our huddle,” Indiana star Caitlin Clark said, “so I think that’s probably a question for Chicago.”
Cloud met with team and league security after the game. She did not speak with the media.
The WNBA has been the subject of recent debates on whether transgender women — people assigned male at birth who transition to align with their gender identity — should be allowed to participate in the league. There has never been such a player in the WNBA.
Although the league’s collective bargaining agreement says the WNBA is restricted to women, it contains no more specific language about gender identity or sex assigned at birth.
Fever guard Sophie Cunningham said in an ESPN profile published last month that she was opposed to transgender girls and women competing in girls’ and women’s sports. Freedom and Royce White, another former NBA player, have declared themselves eligible for the WNBA draft, saying they identify as women.
Kanter joined a small rally in support of Cunningham outside the arena before the game.
Asked if he had a message for Kanter, Marsh praised the league and its players.
“If you come to a game you should probably come to enjoy the basketball,” he said, “and that seems pretty simple to me. I think these players deserve that and have earned that. Being a former basketball player, you should probably understand and feel that too.”

Aston Villa was thrashed 4-0 away to Brighton in a game that was effectively over after half an hour.
Victor Lindelof's own goal put Brighton ahead after just eight minutes. Maxim De Cuyper doubled Brighton's lead in the 18th minute before two goals from Jack Hinshelwood in the space of two minutes made it 4-0.
Things went from bad to worse for Aston Villa before halftime when Joao Gomes was sent off. ■

Taiwan tracks 9 Chinese ships, 2 military aircraft
