Brahma Chellaney On Taiwan: Taiwan is becoming a harder target for China
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
16:38:09 UTC
01:38:09 KST

The Iran and Ukraine wars are rewriting modern military strategy. These conflicts are demonstrating that a less conventionally powerful state, by leveraging asymmetric capabilities, can impose major costs on an aggressor and fundamentally reshape the outcome of conflict. Taiwan is not only drawing lessons from those conflicts, but also translating them into practice.
Far from seeking to match China ship for ship, missile for missile or aircraft for aircraft, Taiwan needs to make Chinese aggression so costly, problematic and uncertain that Beijing is deterred from launching an attack. Taiwan cannot become a bigger wolf than China, but it can ensure that no predator seeks to swallow it without getting badly wounded.
That is the logic driving Taiwan’s long-overdue pivot toward asymmetric capabilities — aerial drones, autonomous attack boats, land-based anti-ship missiles, mobile air defenses and other relatively inexpensive, distributed weapons.
The shift has been accelerated by developments in two very different wars: Ukraine’s growing capability to target energy and other strategic sites deep inside Russia and Iran’s refusal to bend to American coercion, leaving US President Donald Trump struggling for a face-saving way to exit the war he initiated. Both conflicts have shown that, despite sophisticated and expensive weapons remaining important, large numbers of cheap, mobile and expendable systems can impose disproportionate costs on a stronger opponent.
Ukraine has been the more important model for Taipei, given how Kyiv has stalled Russia’s advances on the battlefield by taking the war to the enemy’s heartland. Ukraine has shown that drones can transform the battlefield by providing surveillance, targeting and strike capabilities at a fraction of the cost of conventional aircraft. Taiwan’s defense planners are also studying Iran’s use of drones and missiles to impose regional costs on the US by striking American bases and facilities in the Middle East.
Nothing matters more for Taipei than deterring Chinese aggression.
For Beijing, invading Taiwan would be an exceptionally difficult amphibious operation for several reasons: the Taiwan Strait is about 130 kilometers wide at the narrowest point; weather is favorable for a major crossing only during a few windows each year; Taiwan has relatively few beaches suitable for large-scale amphibious landings; and many of those beach approaches lead into mountainous or urban terrain. Above all, China would have to move enormous quantities of troops, equipment, ammunition and supplies across the Strait while under attack.
That is exactly where Taiwan’s asymmetric strategy can impose significant costs on its foe. To turn the Strait and the approaches to Taiwan’s coastline into a killing zone, land-based anti-ship missiles can attack Chinese vessels while autonomous attack boats can swarm larger naval ships and landing craft. Drones, for their part, can provide constant surveillance and strike targets without putting Taiwanese pilots at risk. Mobile air defenses can frustrate China’s effort to establish air superiority.
In such a scenario, the objective will not be to win a traditional naval battle, but to prevent Beijing from achieving the quick victory on which its invasion strategy would depend.
Taiwan, learning the right lessons from conflicts elsewhere, is already making substantial progress. It is on track to produce more than 1,000 Hsiung Feng II and III anti-ship missiles by this year-end. Its heavy investment in layered air defenses combines expensive Patriot interceptors with much cheaper and more widely distributable Stinger missiles.
What stands out, however, is the scale of Taiwan’s drone-manufacturing goal, which is aimed at creating deterrence against China while also building export leverage abroad. It plans to produce 100,000 drones a month within four and a half years, with roughly half intended for export, while its military is likely to acquire more than 210,000 aerial and sea-based drones.
To plug a potential vulnerability, Taiwan has formed a new “Littoral Combat Command” to help integrate drones, mobile missiles and artillery so that these separate systems become components of a unified coastal-defense architecture. This is a wise step.
Reducing its traditional reliance on imported big-ticket platforms in favor of relatively cheap, distributed asymmetric systems is making Taiwan a harder target for China.
Taiwan, of course, still needs fighter aircraft, submarines, sophisticated air defenses and other high-end capabilities. But big-ticket systems should form the upper layer of a broader defense architecture rather than constitute its foundation. The foundation should be survivability, dispersion and punitive response.
That is especially important because China may choose to begin a war not with an amphibious invasion, but by seeking to isolate and slowly strangle Taiwan.
A blockade or quarantine could be used to disrupt shipping, intimidate commercial traffic, restrict energy supplies and even sever Taiwan’s communications with the outside world. Taiwan’s dependence on subsea cables makes this a particularly acute vulnerability. Without a single Chinese soldier setting foot on Taiwan, a communications blackout could create confusion and panic, disrupting financial markets, government operations, emergency services, logistics, military command-and-control, and the flow of information to the outside world.
Seen in this light, Taiwan’s recent exercise simulating an internet disruption was more than just a civil-defense drill. By deliberately throttling mobile data across parts of the island, Taiwan tested how citizens, businesses and institutions would function if communications were degraded during a crisis.
Such preparations are pivotal to an asymmetric strategy. Overwhelming an invading force with asymmetric capabilities depends on resilient networks so that drones and unmanned attack boats can detect targets, sensors can transmit information, missile batteries can receive targeting data, military commanders can communicate with dispersed units, and civilian authorities can coordinate emergency responses. If China were to sever Taiwan’s communications before the Taiwanese military could respond to an invasion, even an impressive arsenal of drones, missiles, artillery and autonomous attack boats would not be able to repulse aggression.
If resilience is to define national defense, Taiwan needs to invest not only in redundant communications and alternative satellite links, but also in hardened command networks, distributed data centers, backup power, and communications systems that can function when conventional internet access is cut. Taiwanese society should be able to operate under degraded communications conditions for weeks. And even when portions of the communications network are destroyed or jammed, Taiwan’s drones, missiles, sensors and command centers must remain operational.
Taiwan is rightly seeking to leverage its extraordinary technological and manufacturing base to build a defense-industrial ecosystem capable of mass-producing drones, autonomous systems, sensors, communications equipment and other expendable technologies. In fact, Taiwan has already begun to emerge as a significant drone exporter.
The ultimate purpose of the pivot from prestige weapons to asymmetric capabilities is not to prepare Taiwan to fight a war indefinitely. Rather, it is to make Beijing realize that starting a war would be a disastrous gamble.
Making Taiwan too hard to blind, too hard to blockade, too hard to invade and ultimately too painful to conquer would establish enduring deterrence.
Brahma Chellaney, professor emeritus of strategic studies at the independent Center for Policy Research in New Delhi, is the author of nine books, including the award-winning Water: Asia’s New Battleground (Georgetown University Press).

Leveraging mapping data and artificial intelligence (AI) models developed in cooperation with China, it has built a comprehensive retail and consumer ecosystem. When seen from Beijing’s perspective, the flaw in this logic becomes apparent. The Chinese Communist Party (CCP) relies heavily on positive messaging and tightly managed information to maintain political stability. Taiwan simply cannot beat an authoritarian state at its own

Industrial PC maker Neousys Technology Inc (宸曜科技) expects strong growth in its edge artificial intelligence (AI) business from this year, driven by rising demand across manufacturing, transportation, semiconductors, defense and healthcare.
Edge AI computers account for about 40 percent of its product mix, said Neousys, whose edge AI portfolio includes fanless industrial computers, graphics processing unit (GPU)-enabled AI systems and mission computers designed for harsh environments.
The company expects edge AI-related revenue to grow 10 to 20 percent year-on-year this year, Neousys vice president Bryan Lan (藍林忠) said in an interview with the Taipei Times on Thursday.
Photo: Meryl Kao, Taipei Times
“This year, we’ve seen growing demand for computers with AI computing or expansion capabilities, even for applications that previously required only data collection or human-machine interaction,” he said.
High-performance AI systems are used mainly in autonomous driving and defense applications, but customers are increasingly demanding basic AI inference capabilities even in smaller industrial computers, Lan said.
In view of growing demand for edge AI, Neousys is preparing products based on Intel Corp’s next-generation Nova Lake platform, with a launch possible as early as the first quarter of next year, he said.
The platform’s integrated neural processing unit would allow smaller, task-specific AI models to run at the edge without significantly increasing system costs, he added.
The company’s edge AI products are largely deployed in factory safety control, traffic enforcement and semiconductor optical inspection, Lan said.
At the Taiwan Automation Intelligence and Robot Show in Taipei last week, Neousys and its partners demonstrated its latest factory safety-monitoring system based on Nvidia Corp’s Jetson platform that can detect workers who have entered hazardous areas and issue real-time alerts.
The company is seeing growing demand from the semiconductor sector, with products used in wafer fabrication equipment accounting for about 10 percent of its total revenue, Lan said.
Neoysys counts the world’s two largest foundries among its customers, he added.
“AI data center expansion is also creating new opportunities,” Lan said. “For example, our POC-700 series compact industrial computers are being used by server makers as controllers for coolant distribution units, monitoring temperature, water pressure, and flow in in-rack and in-row systems.”
The company is also expanding into smart manufacturing by tapping into autonomous mobile robot and automated guided vehicle projects, he said.
In Asia, Neousys has participated in outdoor delivery projects using automated guided vehicles and other autonomous vehicles, Lan said.
As markets such as South Korea establish regulations for autonomous delivery vehicles, demand is expected to grow, he said, adding that Neousys is involved in autonomous vehicle applications for law enforcement, suspect tracking and agriculture.
Neousys expects the defense-related business to be a key growth driver over the next two years, as products for the sector carry higher margins, Lan said.
The company supplies products to drone makers and system integrators for uncrewed ground military vehicles, he said.
The defense-related business accounts for about 20 percent of its total revenue and is expected to rise to 25 percent by the end of this year, he added.
Neousys plans to expand into healthcare next year, targeting AI medical imaging, patient monitoring and care applications amid healthcare labor shortages, Lan said.
“We plan to enter the market through image processing, AI computing and rugged edge computing technologies, as healthcare tends to have longer product cycles and is less sensitive to economic fluctuations,” he said.
Neousys reported revenue of NT$1.14 billion (US$35.80 million) in the first half of this year, up 36 percent year-on-year.
The company expects revenue this year to grow 40 percent from NT$1.64 billion last year, and is targeting double-digit revenue growth next year, driven by edge AI, defense, smart manufacturing and demand in the US market, Lan said.

Breadcrumb
Syria 'arrests 70% of Assad-era pilots' involved in bombing
Syrian authorities have arrested around 70 percent of the pilots who took part in bombing civilian areas of the country under the former Assad regime, a transitional justice official has said.
Radif Mustafa, director of the Accountability and Oversight Department at Syria's National Commission for Transitional Justice, said efforts were continuing to pursue those implicated in violations and crimes committed during Assad's rule.
Speaking to Syria's official Al-Ikhbariya television channel, Mustafa said uncovering the truth about crimes involving the use of chemical weapons was a right owed to victims and a responsibility of the National Commission for Transitional Justice.
He said accountability for such crimes represented "a national obligation borne by state institutions".
Mustafa added that reparations and compensation for victims were primarily the responsibility of the government, while stressing the need to build an inclusive national narrative around crimes and violations committed by the former regime that preserves victims' rights.
He said Syria's transitional justice process remained at an early stage and required greater efforts and resources to achieve its goals of uncovering facts, ensuring accountability and providing reparations.
Mustafa's comments came as Syrian Interior Minister Anas Khattab said authorities were continuing to pursue those involved in the chemical weapons massacre in Eastern Ghouta 13 years ago.
Khattab said a number of people who participated in the attack had already been arrested.
In a post on X on Friday, the minister said images of the victims and the suffering of their families remained present in Syrians' memories, stressing that their right to justice remained intact.
He said authorities would continue pursuing the remaining suspects, adding that "no criminal will escape punishment, no matter how much time passes".
Syrian authorities have announced several arrests in recent months linked to the former regime's chemical weapons programme.
On 29 April, the Interior Ministry announced the arrest of Major General Adnan Abboud Halwa, whom Khattab described at the time as one of the most prominent officers accused of involvement in the Eastern Ghouta chemical weapons massacre.
In May, Syria's mission to the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons announced the arrest of 18 people, including former officers and experts from the Scientific Studies and Research Centre, as part of investigations into the former regime's chemical weapons programme.
The Interior Ministry also announced on 15 July the arrest of Colonel Ahmed Habib Ali, saying he was a chemical weapons specialist who had supervised the manufacture of bombs loaded with sarin gas while working for the former regime.

ICAR registers 16 new breeds of indigenous animals including four cattle
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
16:31:33 UTC
01:31:33 KST

Umarda, a newly registered indigenous cattle breed from Maharashtra. Photo Credit: ICAR-NBAGR
NEW DELHI: Expanding the list of well-documented and scientifically recognised animal breeds in the country, the Indian Council of Agricultural Research (ICAR) has registered 16 more new breeds of indigenous animals including cattle and buffalo, taking the total number of such breeds in India to 262. The move will help in conservation and sustainable utilisation of India’s diverse and climate-resilient animal genetic resources at a time when rising temperature due to global warming is posing grave risk to animal productivity and the overall food security.The new indigenous breeds include four each of cattle (Umarda, Periyar, Koppal and Mahakaushali) and Sheep (Madgyal, Seemanchali, Kow Debar and Asomi); two goats (Totapuri and Battisi); and one each of buffalo (Gomanchali), dog (Kombai), pig (Nagal), horse/pony (Kashmiri), donkey (Braj) and yak (Sikkimese yak).These breeds, registered early this month, represent diverse agro-ecological regions spreading across 13 states -- Karnataka, Madhya Pradesh, Kerala, Maharashtra, Goa, Rajasthan, Uttar Pradesh, Assam, Uttarakhand, Bihar, Nagaland, Sikkim and Tamil Nadu -- and UT of Jammu & Kashmir. Goat breed Battisi is distributed across Rajasthan and Uttar Pradesh whereas the sheep breed Madgyal is found in Maharashtra and Karnataka.
"Indigenous breeds have evolved under diverse production environments and possess locally adapted characteristics that can be valuable for climate resilience, disease adaptation, low-input production, livelihood support and sustainable livestock farming. Their conservation is therefore important not only for maintaining genetic diversity but also for ensuring the availability of adaptive livestock resources for future generations," N H Mohan, directorof the ICAR's National Bureau of Animal Genetic Resources (NBAGR), told TOI.
Newly registered indigenous livestock and dog breeds. Photo credit: ICAR-NBAGR
Karnal-based ICAR-NBAGR is the nodal institute for registration of livestock and poultry breeds in India. With the new addition, the indigenous animal breeds now include 59 for cattle (Sahiwal, Gir, Red Kandhari and Hallikar etc.) 23 for buffalo (Murrah, Nili Ravi, Bhadawari and Mehsana etc.), 45 for goat, 50 for sheep, 16 for pigs, nine each for horses & ponies, camel and duck; five for donkey; six for dog and three for yak among others."The new registrations strengthen the national effort to reduce the proportion of nondescript livestock populations through systematic breed identification and documentation. This approach is particularly important for ensuring that valuable locally adapted populations are scientifically recognized and brought within appropriate conservation and sustainable utilization programmes," said Mohan.
He said, "ICAR-NBAGR's efforts are aligned with the broader national objective of strengthening India's livestock genetic base and supporting food and nutritional security, sustainable livelihoods and climate-resilient livestock production."
Vishwa Mohan is Senior Editor at The Times of India. He writes on environment, climate change, agriculture, water resources and clean energy, tracking policy issues and climate diplomacy. He has been covering Parliament since 2003 to see how politics shaped up domestic policy and India’s position at global platform. Before switching over to explore sustainable development issues, Vishwa had covered internal security and investigative agencies for more than a decade.

Global Alliance for Palestine to launch worldwide Day of Action in October
The Global Alliance for Palestine (GAFP), a recently launched international coalition of pro-Palestine groups, has announced a worldwide day of action on 10 October, calling for an arms embargo, sanctions and what it describes as an end to international complicity with Israel.
The organisation’s Executive Director has stressed the importance of campaigning for Palestinian rights as the devastating war in Gaza approaches its third year.
Speaking to The New Arab, GAFP head Robert Andrews highlighted the potential of “the power of synchronised global action” as the organisation prepares a major campaign for the weekend of 9–11 October 2026, with the Global Day of Action taking place on Saturday, 10 October.
According to GAFP, hundreds of organisations worldwide are expected to participate, with the initiative seeking to coordinate actions across cities in several countries.
The Alliance said the 10 October mobilisation aims to put Israel’s ongoing genocide and its war crimes back on the media agenda amid continuing hostilities between the US and Iran.
Andrews said the coordinated actions planned for 10 October would call for an arms embargo, Boycott, Divestment and Sanctions (BDS), and greater accountability over Gaza and the West Bank.
“In terms of policy changes, we are pushing for policies that adhere to international law and that essentially move away from the racist discourse or any discourses vis-à-vis the Palestinians that we see across multiple different contexts,” he told The New Arab.
“So it's not that we are hoping that this mobilization will suddenly lead to an arms embargo against Israel or enhanced BDS measures, but we are looking to contribute to the variety of efforts taking place within the solidarity movement to try and push for these things to happen.”
Citing activist efforts such as Gaza-bound aid flotillas seeking to challenge the decades-long illegal Israeli blockade of the territory, Andrews said the Alliance aims to amplify opposition to political silence, as Israeli attacks continue in Gaza despite an October 2025 ceasefire.
“We see this particular action in particular as one cog in the huge machinery that the movement is building in order to pressure the occupation state in the international context,” he said.
“We're hoping that success for us means widespread mobilization in different corners of the world and in different contexts where the Israeli government is seeking to gain more of an influence,” Andrews added.
“So we're really hoping for strong mobilization, for example, in the Latin America region, amidst the the the backdrop of the Abraham Accords and the growing relations between Israel and countries in Latin America.”
Andrews said the Alliance would help coordinate a range of protest activities across continents, bringing together grassroots movements, student protests, workplace actions, rallies and civil disobedience across the world.
“I think for us to have to have coordinated action is important because it allows for synchronized visibility,” Andrews told The New Arab.
“So the idea is instead of each organization working in their own space at their own time, it's to bring organizations together on one day under one clear message.”
He said that the action would take place on one weekend "with a number of organizations pushing the same message, which is 'End the Genocide, Defend the Land'.”
Andrews also said the Alliance had put measures in place amid governments disproportionately restricting and penalising expressions of solidarity with Palestinians.
“We have a team where we offer advice, and we can offer control. We have specialists that work with specific regions, so we have public relations offices that are specific to certain regions,” he told The New Arab.
“So we offer guidance and we offer support in the case that any organization is unclear about the the legal standing when it comes to protests- when it comes to actually organizing physical activities.”
He continued: “In terms of restrictions, we've obviously seen a huge attempt by by state institutions to minimize the visibility of pro-Palestine demonstrations. A big part of the crackdown has been a result of the efficiency of the pro-Israel lobby in pushing decision makers to restrict Palestine demonstrations, often on dubious grounds.”
Andrews also noted that in parts of the Middle East, “physical mobilization is simply impossible due to authoritarianism, government crackdown and the fear of violence.”
“Where their local circumstances are completely inhibiting them from organizing protests, we encourage them to do other actions on the day as as part of the mobilization,” Andrews added.
Prominent figures including former UK Labour leader Jeremy Corbyn, Palestinian activist and politician Mustafa Barghouti, and Greek economist and former finance minister Yanis Varoufakis are also said to be contributing members of the Alliance’s Steering Committee.
Andrews said that, particularly in the period preceding the Day of Action, the committee would participate through “national and international media engagements, the creation of key campaign broadcasts, and the orchestration of widespread digital outreach”.
He said the upcoming mobilisation would demonstrate the scale of the campaign to governments, institutions and the Israeli government itself.
“We want the Israeli government to understand that there is huge support for Palestine rights campaigns and for the rights of Palestinians, and that will not change,” he told The New Arab.
“It's far too long now that we have not seen real accountability against the state of Israel for its genocide against the people of Gaza, and at the same time, simultaneously, we've seen the huge double standard when it comes to imposing measures against other countries, such as Russia that are deemed to be committing human rights violations, so that is the message.”
Israel has killed over 73,000 people in Gaza since October 2023, 1,286 of them since the ceasefire came into effect in October 2025, according to Gaza’s health ministry.
Meanwhile, the West Bank, home to around three million Palestinians and some 500,000 settlers, has witnessed an increase in settler violence and seizures of land and resources.

Tunisia says recovered 12 migrants' bodies

Breadcrumb
Tunisia says recovered 12 migrants' bodies
The Tunisian national guard said Sunday it recovered 12 bodies from the sea after a boat carrying irregular migrants capsized off the country's southeastern coast, with six people still missing.
The boat was carrying 15 people, only one of whom was rescued after it sank some 14 nautical miles off the shore of Zarzis on Friday night.
"Search operations resulted in the recovery of three bodies yesterday and nine bodies today, bringing the total to 12," the national guard said in a statement.
Searches for the remaining missing passengers were still ongoing, it added.
On Saturday night, residents in Ben Guerdane - the city bordering Libya where 14 of the migrants were from - staged protests, blocking roads and setting tires on fire.
Tunisia, whose coast is some 145 kilometres (90 miles) from the Italian island of Lampedusa, is a key departure point for migrants seeking to make the perilous journey across the Mediterranean in search of better lives in Europe.
The central Mediterranean crossing is the deadliest migration route in the world, according to the International Organization for Migration (IOM).
The IOM said earlier this month that the number of migrant deaths on the central Mediterranean route had more than doubled in the first four months of 2026 compared to the same period last year.
At least 914 migrants have died or gone missing along the route this year, according to the IOM.
In 2023, Tunisia signed a 255-million-euro ($290 million) deal with the European Union, nearly half of which was earmarked for tackling irregular migration.
The deal, strongly supported by Italy's hard-right government, aimed to bolster Tunisia's capacity to prevent boats leaving its shore.
(AFP)

US envoy Tom Barrack’s Israel criticism tests his credibility as a mediator - analysis
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
16:10:55 UTC
01:10:55 KST

A statement Defense Minister Israel Katz put out via X/Twitter was unusual on two counts.
First, it was posted on Shabbat afternoon – something generally done only in emergency or especially unusual situations. Second, it included a frontal critique of an influential US administration figure: Washington’s ambassador to Turkey and special envoy to Syria and Iraq, Tom Barrack.
On Friday, Barrack was hosted on Mario Nawfal’s podcast and, while discussing last Tuesday’s IDF bombing of the Abu al-Duhur airbase in northern Syria, made several remarks that – and this is an understatement – raised eyebrows in Jerusalem.
First, he contradicted US policy and said that Israel was occupying the Golan Heights in contravention of UN resolutions and the “international order.” In 2019, US President Donald Trump issued a presidential proclamation recognizing Israeli sovereignty over the Golan.
Second, he said that Israel’s attack may have been an attempt to “bait” the Turks before the October 27 election, something he said would play well with Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu’s base.
Third, he said that the US checked into intelligence Israel provided showing that Turkey was planning to move troops and equipment into the site and found that it was incorrect.
And, fourth, he said that Turkey, including its president, Recep Tayyip Erdogan, was not interested in “attacking” or in any kind of “adversarial” relationship with Israel. Ironically, this statement came just as Turkey called for Interpol to issue a request to law enforcement agencies worldwide to arrest Netanyahu and a number of other Israeli officials on various charges, including genocide.
Barrack’s version of what happened last Tuesday is pretty significant. It goes beyond the boilerplate complaint that Israel often hears from Washington after carrying out a strike: that it was done without sufficient coordination with the US. Here you have a senior US official publicly disputing Israel’s threat assessment and floating an electoral motive for the attack.
Katz responds to Barrack’s comments
Apparently, Katz thought Barrack’s comments serious enough to warrant a swift response – even on Shabbat.
He wrote that Israel had clear intelligence indicating that Turkey planned to take actions at the site that would endanger Israeli security, and that the IAF attack was taken only after Israel delivered a direct warning to the Syrian regime and provided the necessary intel to the relevant US authorities.
“When the Syrian regime did not heed the warning, the strike was authorized and successfully carried out,” Katz wrote. “Erdogan was caught with his hand in the cookie jar and was forced to back down.”
Katz said that Barrack’s comments were “full of inaccuracies” and that his position on the Golan contradicts Trump’s own policy. He also said that efforts by opposition leaders and some in the media to paint the operation in Syria in “political colors” stem from “a combination of ignorance, a lack of understanding of Israel’s security interests, and a constant desire to attack the government – and it is deserving of every condemnation.”
Though he prefaced that comment by directly addressing it to opposition politicians and media figures, it is difficult to believe – since Barrack made the same speculation – that he was not also included in this group.
The brickbats come at a particularly sensitive time, as Barrack is trying to reduce the temperature between Israel and Turkey. The problem is that with comments such as these – clearly siding with Turkey’s explanation and interpretation of the events, perhaps as a result of his job as ambassador to Turkey – Barrack is harming his ability to play a constructive role.
Barack may have undermined his credibility as a mediator between Syria, Israel
Barrack’s dual role as ambassador to Turkey and special envoy to Syria matters. As ambassador to Turkey, he is responsible for reassuring Ankara; as Syria envoy, he is supposed to mediate a potential Israel-Syria security arrangement. By publicly appearing to credit the Turkish-Syrian account over Israel’s, he may have undermined his standing in Jerusalem as a trusted intermediary.
Barrack, in other words, is now becoming part of the dispute he is meant to manage – hardly the ideal position for a mediator.
By publicly questioning Israel’s intelligence, suggesting an electoral motive behind the strike, whitewashing Erdogan’s antipathy toward Israel, and contradicting Trump on the Golan Heights, Barrack may have reassured Ankara – where he temporarily lives and works – but at the cost of losing Israeli confidence in his ability to play the role of mediator.
Doubts about Barrack’s objectivity predate this particular incident.
Differences between Barrack and Israel surfaced over Lebanon earlier this year, with disagreements about how to deal with Hezbollah and its Iranian patron.
Following the June 26 trilateral Framework Agreement brokered in Washington, Israel expected a policy aimed at isolating Hezbollah, restoring Lebanese sovereignty and keeping Iran out of Lebanon’s political and military future. From Jerusalem’s perspective, all that was essential to secure the northern border.
Barrack, however, argued that no lasting settlement can be reached without involving Hezbollah and Iran. Because Lebanon is caught up in the wider conflict between Israel and Iran, he said, both must be part of any serious effort to resolve it. “How is it going to go away if you don’t have Hezbollah and Iran involved?” he asked, describing Lebanon as a “very complicated Rubik’s cube where removing one piece moves three others.”
Jerusalem viewed that approach as legitimizing Hezbollah and giving Iran a continuing say over Lebanon’s future.
Trusted mediator must understand both parties’ concerns
This does not mean that Barrack must accept Israel’s position on every issue. A mediator is not an advocate for either side. But to be effective, he must convince both sides that he understands their concerns, takes their intelligence seriously, and is not publicly embracing the other side’s version of events.
That is what makes Katz’s unusual Shabbat statement significant. It was more than a rebuttal of a few inaccurate comments. It was a public warning that Israel’s confidence in the man Washington has chosen to manage some of the region’s most delicate disputes is beginning to erode.
Barrack wants to lower the temperature between Israel and Turkey. To do that, however, he will first have to restore a measure of trust with Jerusalem. A mediator whom one side increasingly sees as speaking for the other will have a difficult time mediating anything.

Israel, Syria disagree on threat of Turkish military presence
Two sources told the Post on Saturday that the strike was intended to prevent the placement of a Turkish radar and air defense system.
Shabaini emphasized to Reuters that the Abu al-Duhur was not at risk of becoming a Turkish base and said he believed Israel carried out the strike even after that message was conveyed.

Israel says backchannels to Turkey remain after Syria strike

Breadcrumb
Israel says 'secret channels' to Turkey remain after Syria strike
An Israeli security official has said Israel has "no intention of turning Turkey into an enemy" despite striking a Syrian airbase over alleged plans by Ankara to deploy radar and air defence systems there.
The official told Israel's Kan Reshet Bet radio on Sunday that "secret channels" remained open between Israel and Turkey to exchange messages and prevent direct conflict, amid heightened tensions following the Israeli attack on Abu al-Duhur military airport in northern Syria.
However, the official warned that "when messages do not work, Israel is forced to act".
According to Kan, Israel has drawn "red lines" around any Turkish military reinforcement in Syria, particularly the deployment of air defence systems, drones or missiles that could restrict the Israeli air force's ability to operate over the country.
Israeli aircraft struck buildings and runways at Abu al-Duhur airport in eastern Idlib province last week "before the Turkish military equipment reached its destination", Kan reported.
The broadcaster said Israel had sought to send a message to Damascus that it "will not allow a new threat to be established near its borders", while stressing that Israel does not oppose the rebuilding of the Syrian army itself.
Turkey denied that it had any military presence at the airbase at the time of the attack.
"There was no Turkish military mission at the Syrian air force base before or during the Israeli attacks," Ankara said in a statement following the strike.
Kan reported on Saturday that Israeli security officials had informed the US that Turkey was preparing to install radar equipment at Abu al-Duhur, with plans for Turkish-operated air defence systems to follow.
Israeli officials claimed such a deployment could alter the regional balance of power by limiting Israel's ability to carry out air operations over Syria.
Abu al-Duhur lies around 70 kilometres from the Turkish border.
Israeli Defence Minister Israel Katz said on Saturday that the military had repeatedly recommended striking the base after receiving what he described as "clear intelligence" about Turkey's plans.
"The army recommended several times carrying out the strike at Abu al-Duhur airport, in light of clear intelligence obtained regarding Turkey's intention to undertake activities there that would endanger the security of the State of Israel," Katz said.
Katz said Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and senior security officials had agreed to warn Damascus before authorising the attack.
"It was agreed that before approval was granted, a direct warning would be sent to the Syrian regime at the highest levels, in an attempt to prevent this move, and that is indeed what happened," he said.
He added that the intelligence had also been shared with Washington.
According to Katz, Damascus failed to act on the warning, prompting Israel to approve the strike.
"Erdogan was caught with his hand in the cookie jar and was forced to back down," Katz said, referring to Turkish President Recep Tayyip Erdogan.
Israeli officials quoted by Ynet said Ankara had been preparing to install radar at the base before deploying air defence systems and a Turkish commando unit to operate them.
The officials said Israel believes Turkey could attempt a similar deployment elsewhere in Syria in the future.
They also claimed that Turkish-operated air defences in Syria could make any future Israeli strike on Iran more difficult by restricting Israeli aircraft operating in Syrian airspace.
Under international law, Israel has no general right to strike Syrian territory or dictate Damascus's foreign and security relationships. Syria's decision to establish military or political ties with Turkey is a matter of its sovereignty and self-determination, subject to its own international obligations.
The attack comes amid renewed tensions between Israel and Syria despite recent efforts to reach a security arrangement between the two countries.
Syrian President Ahmed al-Sharaa said last month that Damascus wanted an agreement with Israel that could "pave the way for a comprehensive peace", while insisting Syria would not abandon its claim to the occupied Golan Heights, which is considered illegally occupied and annexed under international law.
Israel also carried out another strike in Syria on Saturday, targeting a vehicle in the town of Beit Jinn in the Damascus countryside.
The Israeli military said it had fired on a person who posed "an immediate threat" to its forces and threatened further attacks against perceived threats.
Reserve Israeli officer Eyal Dror told Ynet that recent developments suggested relations with Syria were moving away from stability.
"In the absence of an attempt to reach some kind of arrangement or settlement, we may see these events with greater frequency," Dror said.

Multi-ancestry study explores how DNA and trauma affect smoking habits
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
16:00:13 UTC
01:00:13 KST

New research reveals how a person’s genetics and trauma symptoms combine to affect their tobacco use after a distressing event. The findings suggest that people with a lower genetic predisposition for tobacco use might actually be more vulnerable to smoking when experiencing specific trauma symptoms. The large study was published in Translational Psychiatry.
About 70 percent of people experience a traumatic event during their lifetime. Roughly 10 percent of those individuals go on to develop post-traumatic stress disorder, or PTSD. People with PTSD frequently struggle with substance use, including tobacco and alcohol consumption. Both PTSD and substance use behaviors are influenced by a mix of life experiences and biological factors.
Past research has linked PTSD to higher rates of smoking and drinking. What is less understood is how trauma symptoms interact with a person’s underlying genetic risk for substance use. Substance use behavior is heavily influenced by genetics, with many small variations in a person’s DNA contributing to their overall risk.
Researchers calculate this cumulative biological vulnerability using a mathematical tool called a polygenic risk score. A polygenic risk score works by scanning thousands of genetic variations across a person’s genome. Researchers assign a weight to each variation based on how strongly it links to a trait, and then they add those weights together to create a single score.
Most previous studies looking at how genes and the environment interact have focused on isolated genetic markers or populations of entirely European descent. Henri M. Garrison-Desany, a researcher at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health, led a team to investigate how overall genetic risk and trauma interact in a diverse group of people. The researchers wanted to see if specific elements of PTSD had distinct relationships with substance use when factoring in genetic risk.
The team analyzed data from 2,973 adults who had recently experienced a traumatic event. The participants were recruited within 72 hours of visiting an emergency department. The most common traumatic event reported was a motor vehicle collision, followed by physical or sexual assaults. The participants provided blood samples, which the team used to extract DNA and calculate polygenic risk scores for tobacco and alcohol use.
Because genetic research has historically overrepresented people of European descent, standard genetic risk scores often perform poorly in diverse populations. To address this bias, the researchers used a specialized statistical method designed to estimate genetic risk across multiple ancestries. The study group included individuals of predominantly African, European, and admixed American ancestries.
The participants completed surveys to track their mental health and behavior over the following months. The researchers measured PTSD symptoms at eight weeks after the initial trauma. They then looked at how often and how much the participants smoked or drank alcohol at six months after the event. The team divided PTSD symptoms into four categories: avoidance, hyperarousal, negative cognition and mood, and re-experiencing the trauma.
When looking at the genetic scores alone, the researchers found that higher polygenic risk scores for tobacco were associated with an increase in the risk of using tobacco at the six-month mark. The genetic scores for alcohol use did not show consistent associations with drinking behavior across the entire diverse cohort. The alcohol genetic score only reliably predicted drinking behavior in the subgroup of participants with European ancestry.
Next, the researchers examined how PTSD symptoms and genetic risk interacted. They found that trauma symptoms and genetic predisposition did not simply add together to create a massive risk for tobacco use. Instead, they observed an antagonistic effect. The association between trauma symptoms and subsequent tobacco use was weaker for individuals who already had a high genetic risk for tobacco use.
Conversely, people with a lower genetic risk for tobacco use showed a stronger association between their trauma symptoms and their smoking habits. If a person was not biologically predisposed to use tobacco, experiencing high levels of post-traumatic stress was linked to a noticeable increase in smoking. This suggests that people with a lower baseline risk might be highly sensitive to the environmental stress of a trauma.
This pattern was particularly apparent for two specific types of PTSD symptoms. Re-experiencing symptoms, such as flashbacks or nightmares, interacted strongly with the genetic scores. A similar interaction appeared for negative alterations in cognition and mood, which involves persistent negative emotions or distorted beliefs about oneself. For both of these symptom categories, the participants with the lowest genetic risk showed the sharpest increase in tobacco use in response to the symptoms.
The researchers did not find this type of interaction between PTSD symptoms and the genetic risk for alcohol consumption. Alcohol use was highly prevalent among the participants before the trauma occurred, which might have masked any changes related to the traumatic event itself. In addition, the genetic scores for alcohol were not consistently associated with drinking when adjusting for prior mental health conditions.
The study relies on self-reported survey data to measure substance use, which can introduce errors if participants underreport their habits. The types of trauma experienced by the participants were also heavily skewed toward car accidents. Other types of trauma, such as combat exposure or chronic abuse, often result in different symptom profiles that might interact differently with genetic risk.
While the researchers used advanced methods to account for diverse ancestries, the underlying genetic reference data still largely stems from European populations. As a result, the genetic risk scores remained most accurate for participants of European descent and underperformed in individuals of African and Indigenous American ancestries. Building more diverse genetic databases is a necessary step for making polygenic risk scores accurate for the general public.
These results point toward a threshold effect for substance use risk among trauma survivors. If a person already possesses a high biological risk for smoking, the added stress of a trauma might not elevate their risk much further. In contrast, those without a high genetic risk are more visibly affected by the onset of trauma symptoms. Identifying the specific symptoms that drive people to use substances could eventually help clinicians tailor treatments for trauma survivors based on their unique symptom profiles.
The study, “Post-traumatic stress and genetic interactions affect tobacco and alcohol use after trauma: findings from a multi-ancestry cohort,” was authored by Henri M. Garrison-Desany, Cecilia A. Hinojosa, Justin D. Tubbs, Jacquelyn L. Meyers, Sarah D. Linnstaedt, Stacey L. House, Francesca L. Beaudoin, Xinming An, Jennifer S. Stevens, Thomas C. Neylan, Gari D. Clifford, Laura T. Germine, Scott L. Rauch, John P. Haran, Alan B. Storrow, Paul I. Musey Jr, Phyllis L. Hendry, Sophia Sheikh, Christopher W. Jones, Brittany E. Punches, Jose L. Pascual, Mark J. Seamon, Erica Harris, Claire Pearson, David A. Peak, Roland C. Merchant, Robert M. Domeier, Brian J. O’Neil, Paulina Sergot, Leon D. Sanchez, Steven E. Bruce, Steven E. Harte, Samuel A. McLean, Kerry J. Ressler, Karestan C. Koenen, and Christy A. Denckla.

US tanker aircraft leave Bulgaria as Iran war raises doubts over NATO protection
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
15:55:00 UTC
00:55:00 KST

US tanker aircraft leave Bulgaria as Iran war raises doubts over NATO protection
TEHRAN — Two US Air Force KC-135 tanker aircraft, originally deployed to support US military operations involving Iran, have departed Bulgaria’s Bezmer Air Base. The withdrawal was confirmed on Friday by Bulgaria’s Defense Minister, Dimitar Stoyanov.
The temporary deployment was requested by the United States—which launched a joint military campaign with Israel against Iran on February 28—under a bilateral agreement governing the joint use of military facilities.
On July 22, Bulgaria’s parliament officially authorized the use of Bezmer Air Base as a refueling site, permitting roughly 250 US military personnel to be stationed at the facility until October. However, the decision immediately sparked protests among residents who voiced fears that the presence of the American planes could make the area a target for Iranian missile and drone strikes.
The deployment also triggered swift diplomatic warnings from Tehran. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi spoke to his Bulgarian counterpart shortly after the authorization, reminding her that "any party that participates in any way in carrying out a military attack against Iran will certainly have to accept responsibility for its consequences." Earlier in July, Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baghaei issued a similar warning against hosting the American aircraft, stating that facilitating such operations would amount to "complicity in the crimes of aggression and war crimes."
Tensions mounted further following a recent report by the Financial Times alleging that Tehran had evaluated potential strikes against American military assets in southeastern Europe—specifically highlighting Bulgaria—if the US escalated the conflict. In response to the report, an unnamed NATO official asserted that the alliance was fully prepared to address any threats against US military targets on European soil.
Dr. Tania Glouhtcheva, PhD in Political Sciences and Head of the International Department at Bulgaria’s DUMA newspaper, shared her insights on the local mood following the departure of the US aircraft. “Of course, people are calm now, especially those living in Bezmer.”
Despite the temporary relief, she raised deeper questions regarding NATO’s security guarantees for the region. “The main concern for most Bulgarians and Europeans is that NATO won’t be able to protect us,” she stated. “Most people don’t believe NATO is as strong as it is portrayed. Although we are part of the EU, crises in recent years have shown that every country acts in its own interests and would rather protect itself than help another member state.”
Dr. Glouhtcheva also expressed skepticism regarding Washington's reliability as a partner for Sofia.
“Although there is a very pro-American party in the parliament, ready to do whatever Trump orders, I think most people retain their common sense,” she said.
Pointing to shiftable geopolitical stances under the US leadership, she added, “Donald Trump changes his mind constantly. Today he assures us he is our friend and ally; tomorrow, he decides the opposite.”
The departure of the KC-135 tankers from Bezmer Air Base has brought immediate relief to local communities that feared being drawn into the crossfire of the West Asia conflict. Yet the episode has exposed far deeper concerns about Europe’s security architecture. For many Bulgarians, the controversy has reinforced doubts over whether NATO can actually shield its members from the consequences of a wider conflict, particularly when US military operations turn European territory into a potential target. It also underscores the difficult position of smaller NATO members, caught between pressure to meet alliance commitments and the growing need to protect their own populations from the risks created by Washington’s military engagements. At the heart of the debate is a growing concern that NATO’s security guarantees may offer less protection than expected, while closer alignment with US military operations could instead leave European allies more exposed to the consequences of conflict.

Voting ends and counting begins in Kazakhstan elections
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

00:50:03 KST

Kanyshai Butun
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
Voting in Kazakhstan’s first elections for the new 145-seat unicameral legislature, the Kurultai, concluded on Sunday at 8 pm local time (0300GMT), with the election commission beginning to count ballots.
According to the Central Election Commission, 74.19% of those eligible voted.
 
Meanwhile, voting was still underway at polling stations abroad, with Kazakh citizens continuing to cast ballots at diplomatic missions in accordance with local time.
Voting was suspended in Iran and Ukraine for security reasons, while no polling station was opened at Kazakhstan’s embassy in Ethiopia because no citizens are registered there.
The election is being held under a new Constitution adopted this year that abolished the previous bicameral parliament and replaced it with a single-chamber legislature of 145 deputies.
Voters are choosing among seven parties — Adilet, Nationwide Social Democratic Party, Baitak, People’s Party of Kazakhstan, Auyl, Ak Zhol and Respublica — as well as a “none of the above” option.
The Kurultai will be elected entirely through party lists, replacing the previous system that combined party-list and single-mandate elections.
Parties must receive more than 5% of the vote to win seats in parliament.

“I understand that we have many problems in society now. We are doing our best so the people are not afflicted, but the enemy is doing its absolute best so we won’t succeed,” President Masoud Pezeshkian said during a speech on Sunday morning, alluding to the six-month US-Israel war on Iran.
After US President Donald Trump threatened to target Iran with the “most crushing economic operation” ever undertaken against any country, the Iranian rial hit a new all-time low of 2 million rials per the US dollar in Tehran’s open market on Sunday afternoon.
On Friday, Pezeshkian noted that the price of fuel in Iran is considerably lower than in most countries in the world.
He said his administration pays 1.3 million rials (65 US cents at the current rate) per litre of petrol produced by refineries. The lowest price tier offered to the population is 15,000 rials (less than 1 cent) per litre (0.26 gallons).
Two other price categories for personal vehicle use – one at 30,000 rials (1.5 cents) per litre and the third at 50,000 rials (2.5 cents) – are also eating into the government’s finances.
Meanwhile, Iranians with imported, free-zone or newly registered vehicles are liable for the highest-price tier.
Still, there are limits to the amount of subsidised fuel Iranians can purchase, with each category having its own monthly quota, and sales are only allowed with a fuel card.
Pump stations have their own cards that offer some extra fuel at the highest-price category, but with a single-use limit of 25 litres in Tehran.
The quota for the cheapest category is 60 litres. From the start of the current calendar year in late March, authorities cut the quota for the second category from 100 to 70 litres. After two weeks of fighting between Iran and the US erupted again in July over the Strait of Hormuz, this allowance was cut again to 50 litres.
Iranians now consume roughly 135 million litres per day of fuel, with authorities saying earlier this month that production was at about 121 million litres per day.
To compensate for these financial losses, the government has attempted to increase refinery production, used petrochemical products, and reduced the quality of fuel by diluting it. Fuel imports have also stopped due to the war.
Three undesirable options
The government’s head of energy optimisation, Esmail Saghab-Esfahani, told state television last week that there are three options – each with their own complexities.
One option, he explained, is a first-come, first-served mechanism whereby prices would remain unchanged, but pump stations would simply shut down after running out of their allocated petrol.
Another is to offer all Iranians – including those without a vehicle – roughly 30 litres of fuel per month at the lowest price tier. Those who don’t drive could sell their monthly quota if they choose.
The third option is to liberalise the price of fuel for all, with the government reportedly considering a price of 872,000 rials (about 44 cents) per litre. But the consequence of this would be to create another huge inflationary bubble, with the massive increase in transport and logistics costs for businesses being passed on to consumers.
This price is closer to the refinery production price tag, and was almost implemented in a pilot programme in Kerman, the country’s largest province, in southeastern Iran.
Local authorities, reportedly in conjunction with the government, announced the new prices would be enforced in 204 pump stations across the province overnight into August 13. But the government cancelled the pilot scheme at the last minute, and contradicted local officials by saying they were not consulted on the move.
Nevertheless, the government has signalled that a considerable price increase is in the works.
On Friday, First Vice President Mohammad-Reza Aref said that the cheapest price tier with the 60-litre quota must remain in place. But the second quota could gradually fall, and prices should ultimately be liberalised transparently with proceeds directed toward vulnerable people.
“The government keeps talking about how fuel prices don’t match other countries, but it doesn’t like to talk about how salaries don’t even begin to match other places, or other expenses,” Mostafa, who earns 300 million rials ($150) a month working at a clothing shop in western Tehran, told Al Jazeera.
He explained that while the cost of driving to work in his 15-year-old Iranian-made vehicle does not factor heavily in his monthly calculations, housing, food and other runaway expenses are a major challenge after months of war, blockade and intensified US sanctions, as well as domestic mismanagement and state-imposed internet shutdowns.
Figures released by the Statistical Center of Iran in July reported that prices were 88 percent higher compared to the same month last year, with food inflation standing at over 128 percent.
A 55-year-old man working as a driver for multiple online ride-hailing services told Al Jazeera that conversations with passengers often turn into expressions of anger and frustration about the deteriorating living conditions in Iran.
“Everything will get more expensive a little while after fuel gets more expensive,” he said. “We’re already getting crushed by the prices we have today.”

Six Nordic football associations said on Sunday that they have "lost confidence" in FIFA President Gianni Infantino following his failed plan to open World Cup-linked commercial interests to private investment.
The football associations of Denmark, Finland, Iceland, Norway, Sweden and the Faroe Islands issued a joint statement after a meeting in Helsinki, expressing “serious concerns” about FIFA’s governance and senior-level decision-making.
“The six Nordic football associations have lost confidence in the FIFA President and have serious concerns about the governance and high-level decision-making of the organisation,” the statement said.
The associations said they stood firmly with UEFA and measures proposed jointly by its national associations, while demanding safeguards against private ownership of FIFA’s governance or competitions.
“We expect that FIFA provides binding assurances that FIFA will never again open its governance or competitions to private ownership,” the statement said.
“We also support the demand put forward by AFC, CONCACAF and UEFA, for a fully third-party review of the events surrounding the FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal.”
The associations called on FIFA to commission a broader independent examination of its governance structure.
“We also call for FIFA to initiate a comprehensive independent review of whether FIFA’s governance framework provides the independence, checks and balances, transparency and accountability, that were intended when FIFA adopted its reform programme in 2016.”
UEFA, the Asian Football Confederation (AFC) and the Confederation of North, Central America and Caribbean Association Football (CONCACAF) earlier issued a joint statement criticizing Infantino’s handling of the proposal and calling for an independent third-party review.
The three confederations have also pressed Infantino to resign.
Separately, several national associations, including England’s Football Association, have withdrawn their support for Infantino ahead of the next FIFA presidential election in March 2027.
FIFA earlier apologized for errors in the process surrounding the FIFA Forward Enterprise proposal and withdrew the plan following widespread opposition.

Syria says contacts with Israel halted after airbase attack
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
15:25:25 UTC
00:25:25 KST

Laith Al-jnaidi and Rania Abushamala
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
Syrian Foreign Minister Asaad al-Shaibani said Sunday that contacts between Syria and Israel were suspended after Tel Aviv struck the Abu al-Duhur airbase in northern Syria, but expected negotiations on a security agreement to resume “soon.”
“We expect negotiations with Israel on a security agreement to resume soon, which we hope will lead to its withdrawal from Syrian territory,” Shaibani said in an interview with Western media, as cited by Syria Alikhbaria TV.
He urged Israel to seize a “historic opportunity,” stressing that “the door remains open to diplomacy.”
Shaibani said Syria’s immediate priority is to halt Israeli attacks and take confidence-building measures.
He said the negotiating track was suspended following the Iran-Israel war and expressed hope that talks would resume in the coming period.
The minister disclosed that direct contacts with Israel stopped after an Israeli airstrike targeted the Abu al-Duhur airbase in the northern Idlib province on Aug. 18.
“We do not trust Israel at present,” he said.
Shaibani said Israel bombed the facility despite Damascus having informed it that the site “would not become a Turkish base.”
He nevertheless affirmed that Syria would continue relying on Turkish assistance in military training and cooperation.
“We will not dispense with this support,” he said.
Shaibani described communication with Israel as “necessary, given that it is a party that constantly threatens Syria’s security,” but said Damascus did not want such contacts to continue without producing results.
Security agreement
The foreign minister said Damascus and Tel Aviv reached understandings earlier this year on most provisions of a proposed security agreement.
“Almost everything was agreed upon on paper,” he said.
According to Shaibani, the proposed agreement would require Israel to refrain from attacking Syria or interfering in its internal affairs, halt its military operations and withdraw from territories it seized following the fall of Bashar al-Assad’s regime.
It would also establish several security zones near the border, including “a buffer zone where only the United Nations would be present,” alongside other areas where Syrian forces would be deployed at varying levels, he added.
Shaibani accused Israel of seeking to avoid finalizing the agreement.
“We did not find that they had the motivation or genuine will to reach an agreement,” he said.
Regarding the occupied Golan Heights, Shaibani said Syria’s current priority is to stop Israeli attacks, even before reaching a security agreement. Discussions on the Golan Heights and peace could follow later, he added.
US role
Shaibani said the US is exerting continuous pressure on Israel to return to the negotiating table and conclude an agreement with Syria.
He also reiterated Damascus’ ambition to establish stable relations with its regional neighbors.
On July 26, Syrian President Ahmad al-Sharaa said his country was working with several states to conclude a security agreement with Israel, arguing that its success could pave the way for “comprehensive peace” without relinquishing Syria’s claim to the occupied Golan Heights.
Israel has occupied most of the Syrian Golan Heights since 1967.
Following the fall of the Assad regime in late 2024, Israel declared the 1974 disengagement agreement void and seized the Syrian buffer zone and other positions, including the Syrian side of Mount Hermon (Jabal Al-Sheikh).

Feature: Where Europe meets Asia, over 2,000 swimmers take the plunge
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
23:24:07 CST
00:24:07 KST

ISTANBUL, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- At 10 a.m., a whistle cut through the morning air on Istanbul's Bosphorus.
One after another, swimmers leapt from the floating platform into the water off Kanlica, on the Asian side of the strait. Within minutes, more than 2,000 swimmers were moving toward the European shore, their bright orange safety buoys forming a long, winding stream across the blue water.
The 38th Bosphorus Intercontinental Swimming Race, held on Sunday, drew participants from more than 60 countries and regions. The roughly 6.5-km course took them from Asia to Europe, turning the Bosphorus, the narrow waterway at the heart of Istanbul, into a unique open-water swimming arena.
Near the European side, another unexpected scene unfolded. A pod of dolphins surfaced and leapt through the water as the leading swimmers approached. For a moment, the race seemed to belong not only to the swimmers, but to the strait itself.
Turkish swimmers Su Inal and Selim Oguz won the women's and men's races respectively, finishing in 54 minutes 54 seconds, and 51 minutes 13 seconds.
Around half of this year's participants were from Türkiye, while more than 1,000 came from abroad. Swimmers from Russia, the United States, Britain and other countries and regions took part in the event, according to organizers.
For many of them, the appeal lies in something that few other sporting events can offer: the chance to cross a continental boundary with every stroke.
Yet the Bosphorus is more than a picturesque backdrop. Its currents and changing water conditions make open-water swimming here a demanding challenge. The strait is also one of Istanbul's busiest waterways, where ferries, sightseeing boats and other vessels normally move between the city's European and Asian shores.
That combination of natural and maritime conditions is part of what has made the race distinctive since it was first held in 1989.
Over the years, the event has grown into one of Türkiye's best-known international sporting competitions and a major open-water swimming event. It has previously been ranked first among the world's top 100 open-water swimming races.
Senol Gunes, chairman of the organizing committee, said the event is more than a sporting competition. It also helps promote sports tourism and raise Istanbul's international profile, showcasing the city's unique geography to participants and visitors from around the world.
The beauty of the course also comes with risks that cannot be overlooked. Last year's race was overshadowed by the disappearance of Russian swimmer Nikolai Svechnikov during the event. His body was found in waters near Istanbul in January this year.
This year, organizers strengthened safety measures. Every swimmer was provided with a safety buoy and required to wear a yellow swimming cap. Water safety teams were deployed along the course, while maritime rescue services, the coast guard, maritime traffic authorities and police took part in the security operation. Medical emergency teams were also stationed at the venue.
The measures were visible throughout the race, as safety personnel monitored the swimmers and the surrounding waters. After the race, Veli Ozan Cakir, president of the Turkish Olympic Committee, thanked all the swimmers and said their safety remained the organizers' top priority.
For a few hours on Sunday, the Bosphorus was transformed from a major transportation route into a giant swimming course. Parts of the strait were temporarily closed to maritime traffic, while some ferry services and long-distance Bosphorus sightseeing cruises operated by Istanbul's municipal ferry company were adjusted.
The disruption was temporary, but it illustrated how deeply the race is connected to the city's geography and everyday life.
Istanbul is one of the few major cities in the world physically divided between two continents. The Bosphorus is not simply a geographical boundary: it is a transportation artery, a tourist attraction and a defining feature of the city's identity. ■

China's tech city inspires youth discussions on Asia-Pacific's green future
China

2026-08-23

Guests visit the Chunhui Substation in downtown Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, Aug. 21, 2026.(Xinhua)
SHENZHEN, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Young experts and scholars from the Asia-Pacific region gathered in Shenzhen, a world-leading tech hub in south China's Guangdong Province, to explore how the green energy transition could shape the region's future and their role in this endeavor.
Themed "Asia-Pacific Youth Gathering: Building a Shared Future Through Energy," the event on Friday brought together over 60 experts, scholars and journalists from 13 countries and regions for dialogue and discussion panels.
"Building a clean, secure and efficient energy system constitutes a vital cornerstone for the common prosperity of the Asia-Pacific," said Yu Guanyi, head of the think tank office of the APEC Sustainable Energy Center, at the opening ceremony of the event.
Noting the importance of young voices in the green transition, Leo Barry, an Australian master's student at the Yenching Academy of Peking University, said that encouraging more young people to take part in such professional discussions is crucial to inspiring them to make real contributions to delivering a cleaner, greener and more prosperous future.
Young representatives also visited China's first zero-carbon interactive substation, the 110-kV Chunhui Substation in downtown Shenzhen, to learn how green energy can deliver dependable power to fuel the metropolis' bustling industrial and commercial activities.
With Shenzhen set to host the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders' Meeting in November, delegates paid extra attention to green-energy cooperation among countries in the region.
The power network in the Asia-Pacific still faces common challenges such as accessibility and mismatches in resource and demand, which make energy cooperation within the region even more important, said Chhoeun Raksmey of Cambodia's Ministry of Industry, Science, Technology and Innovation.
In response, Yang Bo, a project commercial specialist at China Southern Power Grid Co., Ltd., shared his insights. He has been involved in China's first 500-kV cross-border alternating-current power link in Laos, which came into operation in April.
Earlier this month, hydropower from northern Laos reached the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area for the first time via the link, and is expected to reach a total transmission volume of approximately 600 million kWh by the end of October.
"This bilateral power cooperation program allows Laos to translate its resource endowments into tangible economic gains for local communities, strengthening its role as a regional clean energy hub," Yang told Xinhua.
Laos' green power arriving in Shenzhen comes as China deepens its green transition cooperation with regional partners. Under frameworks including the Belt and Road Initiative and the Lancang-Mekong Cooperation mechanism, China has actively participated in cross-border construction of clean energy projects in wind, solar, hydropower and energy storage, propelling the region's green development.
Such cooperation also introduces leading photovoltaic technology, power-grid equipment, intelligent dispatching systems and energy-management solutions, helping advance power supply reliability and energy efficiency, said Chisa Jermwarayukorn, secretary-general of the Asia-Pacific Think Tank.
She added that this approach will enable countries in the region to stay more closely connected and become long-term partners.
"As neighbors with different resources, it's time for us to share our advantages, enhance bilateral and multilateral cooperation, and bring more tangible projects to the Asia-Pacific region, so as to achieve a green and sustainable future together," stressed Chhoeun Raksmey. ■

Feature: Repairing what survives, a fading copper craft endures in S. Lebanon
China
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
23:23:55 CST
00:23:55 KST

BEIRUT, Aug. 23 (Xinhua) -- Before the first copper pot arrives, Tarek Jeshi carefully lays out his tools in the eastern corner of the main square in Kfar Remmen, southern Lebanon.
In his 60s, Jeshi has spent decades retinning copper cookware, a craft that has steadily disappeared as modern utensils replaced the old vessels. But war has given his fading profession an unexpected new purpose: he is now restoring copper pots salvaged from homes flattened by Israeli strikes.
As Jeshi sets up his makeshift workshop and blares his arrival over a loudspeaker, residents begin to approach with blackened, battered vessels -- often among the few household items to survive the devastation.
"The craft of retinning copper is more than 100 years old," Jeshi told reporters. "Until a few decades ago, it was part of everyday life in southern villages."
Jeshi works alongside fellow craftsmen Riad Daher and Samir Khalil, traveling between villages and towns to keep alive a profession that was once a familiar part of rural life.
"In the past, a retinner would stay in one town for a month, two months, or even three because there was so much demand," said Daher.
Copper pots, large cooking vessels, dough bowls, trays, plates and spoons were once household essentials. Families regularly brought them to retinners to maintain their surfaces and extend their useful lives.
Jeshi said the spread of modern cookware, however, pushed the profession into decline.
Now, soaring prices and shrinking purchasing power are pushing families to repair rather than replace. War has added another dimension to that revival. For those who lost everything, a salvaged copper pot is a rare thing that can still be saved.
Among them is Samira Azzam, whose home in the Nabatieh area was destroyed in an Israeli airstrike.
After the rubble was cleared, she found three copper pieces -- battered and blackened, yet intact. A retinner restored them to working order.
"The old copper proved its durability. While most of the other household items were destroyed, the copper pieces could still be repaired and used," said Azzam.
For 60-year-old Fatima Sbaiti from the village of Kfar Sir, a large copper cooking pot also survived the destruction of her home before. Displaced to the Chouf region, she now uses the restored vessel to cook for her family.
"Old copper is extremely durable. It survived the bombing and needed only retinning to become usable again," Sbaiti said.
Retinning a vessel takes between one and three hours and costs between 10 and 30 U.S. dollars, depending on size and condition. The process removes oxidation and rust, returning the cookware to its original shine.
Khalil calls the job physically demanding and involves exposure to pungent materials such as tin and ammonia.
Demand increases during religious occasions, particularly Ashoura, when large copper vessels are used to prepare hareesa, a savory wheat-and-meat porridge, although it remains far below levels seen decades ago, he added.
Forged to resist heat and impacts, old vessels often survive collapsing homes, battered but restorable. While the copper is durable, the craft proves far more fragile.
With fewer retinners left, younger generations shy away from the grueling work and limited pay. The once-common sight of a craftsman settling into the village square as women gather with their cookware is becoming a memory fast.
Yet Jeshi continues to prepare his tools, set up his work area, and wait for customers.
For families across southern Lebanon, the copper vessels they bring to him are no longer simply old kitchenware, but possessions that survived when much else was lost. ■
