23:17:18 KST

PM Tarique Rahman’s trip stalled: What it means for Bangladesh-India ties
New Delhi and Dhaka have not been able to move past the contentious question of Sheikh Hasina, the ousted Bangladeshi leader now living in exile in India.
New Delhi, India – Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Tarique Rahman’s first trip to India has been put on hold, highlighting the strained ties between the two South Asian neighbours since the July 2024 student-led uprising that forced Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina to flee the country.
Since coming to power in February, Rahman – the son of Hasina’s archrival, the late Khaleda Zia – has aimed to improve ties with India. But a press conference conducted by Hasina, who lives in India in exile, has riled Bangladesh.
Dhaka says that the August 5 press conference has “vitiated” the atmosphere, adding that “a propitious environment needs to be created for the visit” of Prime Minister Rahman.
For now, Rahman’s trip looks uncertain, as Bangladesh’s Foreign Ministry said officials from both countries have been engaged in talks for “several weeks” to work out a possible solution.
Here is everything you need to know about the latest diplomatic turbulence between the South Asian neighbours.
What’s up with Rahman’s India visit?
New Delhi had extended an invitation to Rahman for a stand-alone visit to India this month, ahead of next month’s scheduled BRICS summit. BRICS is a grouping of major emerging economies, currently chaired by India.
Since Rahman took office, there have been several exchanges between top ministers and diplomats from both sides. India appointed Dinesh Trivedi, a former minister and member of Prime Minister Narendra Modi’s Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP), as its envoy to Dhaka in a rare political appointment to the key post.
Last Tuesday, Trivedi appealed to Rahman’s government, arguing that the Indian mission is not asking Dhaka “to forget the past”, in an apparent reference to Hasina’s exile in India. “Keep the past and sort out the differences of the past. But move on. Don’t get stagnant,” he added.
At a reception hosted by the Indian High Commission in Dhaka, Trivedi said that Modi wanted Rahman’s visit to be “memorable”.
But those plans for a visit were already derailed after Dhaka took offence to Hasina virtually addressing a presser at the Foreign Correspondents’ Club in New Delhi on August 5, marking two years of her ouster.
India clarified that it had nothing to do with the event, but to no avail.
What have both countries said?
Both capitals have been tight-lipped about Rahman’s visit. “I have nothing to say right now,” said India’s Foreign Ministry spokesperson Randhir Jaiswal, responding to a question about Rahman’s visit.
Speaking at an event on Saturday, India’s Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar said India and Bangladesh’s bilateral ties must meet the “test of mutual interest”.
“It has to work for them, it has to work for us,” he said.
“There has to be a reasonable degree of my recognising and respecting what is their interest, just as I expect them also to do so,” Jaishankar said.
Rahman’s foreign affairs adviser, Humayun Kabir, told a Bangladeshi news agency that there is “no rush” in Dhaka to facilitate the prime minister’s visit to India.
Kabir added that Dhaka is still ascertaining what kind of relationship India wants with the newly elected government in Bangladesh.
“The neighbouring country must properly understand the reality of Bangladesh’s July Mass Uprising, which took place through the sacrifices of more than 1,500 people,” he said, referring to India sitting on the request for Hasina’s extradition.
Earlier this month, New Delhi had said that it was considering Hasina’s extradition request based on the established procedure. Both countries have an extradition treaty, but with an exception for political cases.
What are the points of tension?
Bangladesh has made Hasina’s extradition a major issue. Hasina’s government was seen as especially close to India, and New Delhi’s backing of her authoritarian rule also angered Bangladeshis.
Dhaka has been seeking the extradition of Hasina, who was handed a death sentence in absentia in November 2025. Some analysts have accused New Delhi of using it as a diplomatic bargaining chip.
Bangladesh has expressed its displeasure with India for hosting Hasina and sees Hasina’s political speeches as an interference in its internal affairs. During the August 5 presser, Hasina said she would return to Bangladesh.
“We have requested Indian authorities to expeditiously act on our request to extradite Sheikh Hasina and other fugitive criminals,” the Bangladesh Foreign Ministry said in an X post on August 16.
“We reiterate that we will continue to pursue our ‘Bangladesh First’ policy to promote friendly bilateral relations with other countries, including our neighbours, on the basis of sovereign equality, national dignity, non-interference in each other’s internal affairs and mutual benefit.”
For New Delhi, Dhaka inching closer to Pakistan after decades of strained ties is a major diplomatic setback. India played a major role in the formation of Bangladesh from Pakistan in 1971.
Shakil Ahmed, an assistant professor of government and politics at Dhaka’s Jahangirnagar University, noted that domestic politics tends to influence foreign policy at times.
“Relations between India and Bangladesh are constrained by their domestic politics, especially in Dhaka,” he said.
“People in Bangladesh want that any relation with India should be based on self-respect and mutual interests,” he said, adding that Rahman’s government has been diversifying its friendships with foreign countries, including the US, China, and Pakistan.
“New Delhi saw Bangladesh as one of India’s foreign policy followers,” Ahmed said, noting that that is not the case anymore. “Hasina gave India a blank cheque in foreign relations, which is not happening anymore.”
India’s Hindu nationalist government’s push to fence the 4,096km-long (2,545-mile) border with Bangladesh has also strained ties. Anti-Bangladesh rhetoric by ruling party officials has further antagonised Dhaka.
India has been deporting what it calls undocumented Bangladeshi immigrants across its borders. Dhaka has accused New Delhi of pushing people extrajudicially into Bangladesh without diplomatic verification.
What’s ahead for India-Bangladesh ties?
Sanjay Bhardwaj, a professor of South Asian studies at the Jawaharlal Nehru University in Delhi, told Al Jazeera that Bangladesh’s Prime Minister Rahman is playing to the gallery by stalling his maiden India visit.
Hasina’s case is one of political persecution, said Bhardwaj, pointing out that the previous government led by Hasina also targeted the opposition. Rahman lived in exile for more than 17 years in London, the United Kingdom, including all of Hasina’s years in power, after he was slapped with several criminal cases. He was convicted in absentia on money laundering charges and in a case linked to an alleged plot to assassinate Hasina.
“India has been positive to cultivate and have a developmental partnership with Bangladesh, with no reluctance to develop the economic participation,” he added. “But Rahman is interested in politics and not thinking about the development of Bangladesh.”
Hasina’s extradition is a contentious issue, he said, adding that both capitals must move beyond this to maintain a productive bilateral relationship.
Sreeradha Datta, a professor specialising in South Asian studies at India’s OP Jindal Global University, said that both countries need to talk, since “there is no alternative”.
As neighbours, “they do not have a choice to disengage”, she said, adding that merely the passage of time will not repair the relations.
“How can one have any control when there is no dialogue and engagement?” Datta asked.
“The initial warmth diluted in nationalistic noise on both sides,” Datta said, referring to initial interactions, including an Indian delegation led by Jaishankar visiting Dhaka last year for the funeral of Rahman’s mother, Khaleda Zia.
Datta argued that New Delhi needs to come to terms with a new reality that the government of Bangladesh may not share the same warmth as the one under Hasina did.
“But that doesn’t matter,” she said. “These are neighbours, and a relationship based on objectives or interests is what will take it forward.”

Ilkhanid-era stone inscription discovered in central Iran
Unknown
Unknown Publisher

Ilkhanid-era stone inscription discovered in central Iran
TEHRAN – A stone inscription dating to the Ilkhanid period has been discovered during restoration work at the eastern entrance of the Jameh Mosque in Nimvar, a historic city in central Iran.
The white travertine stone measures approximately 85 by 34 centimeters and is 10 centimeters thick. It bears eight lines of carved writing, ISNA reported on Sunday.
Preliminary examinations suggest that the inscription may be a stone endowment deed, a local official said, adding that a definitive assessment of its content and exact nature will require further specialist studies by epigraphists and researchers.
The date recorded on the inscription is 764 AH, corresponding to 742 in the Iranian calendar, placing the artifact in the Ilkhanid period, the official said.
The inscription could provide researchers with further information about Nimvar's historical, cultural, religious and architectural development, the official added.
Nimvar is a city in Mahallat county of Markazi province. It is regarded as one of Iran's ancient settlements, with historical links to the Parthian and Sasanian periods. In antiquity, the city was also an important center of Zoroastrianism.

Hamedan Day: Herbal medicine festival opens near Avicenna’s tomb

Hamedan Day: Herbal medicine festival opens near Avicenna’s tomb
TEHRAN – A herbal medicine festival and sales exhibition, named after Avicenna, opened next to the renowned Persian polymath’s tomb in Hamadan on Sunday, coinciding with Hamadan Day and commemorations honoring the celebrated scholar.
The event, titled the “First Festival and Exhibition of Herbal Medicines and Herbal Products of the Millennium Sage,” will run through August 28, according to Mohsen Masoum-Alizadeh, director general of Hamadan’s Cultural Heritage, Tourism and Handicrafts Department.
Speaking at the opening ceremony, Masoum-Alizadeh said the event provides an opportunity to showcase Hamadan province’s capacities, expertise and products in the field of medicinal plants.
The festival is being held in cooperation with relevant government bodies and organizations and features a range of programs, including the introduction of different medicinal plant species found in the province, the presentation of herbal products and derivatives, and the promotion of the sector’s production and economic potential.
Visitors will also be introduced to the properties and applications of medicinal plants, while specialized sessions are scheduled with university professors, researchers, experts and professionals working in herbal medicine and traditional medicine.
Masoum-Alizadeh said the development of health tourism is among Hamadan’s key tourism priorities, adding that promoting the province’s medicinal plants, traditional medicine and indigenous knowledge could help strengthen the sector and create new economic and tourism opportunities.
The festival is being held adjacent to the tomb of Avicenna, whose influential works in medicine shaped medical scholarship for centuries and remain closely associated with Hamadan’s cultural identity.

Bam Khatoon qualify for AFC Women’s Champions League 2026/27
TEHRAN - Sara Didar netted twice as Bam Khatoon came from behind to beat Jordan’s Etihad Club 3-1 on Sunday and qualify for the Group Stage of the AFC Women’s Champions League 2026/27.
The side of Iran topped Group E with seven points to earn their third consecutive Group Stage appearance while Etihad Club, who were in with a chance coming into the match, closed three points adrift.
Leen Al-btoush, taking advantage of shoddy defending, put Etihad Club ahead in the 10th minute when she stole in from the back, picked up a cutback from Carrie Consolino and curled the ball past a rooted Raha Yazdani, the-afc.com reported.

The custodian, however, failed to detect a lurking Didar in the 32nd minute, with the striker latching on to Melika Motevalli’s cross and guiding a looping header beyond Al Shalabe and into the bottom left corner.
Shaban outpaced defender Alanoud Al Zabrey on the left and steered her shot beyond Al Shalabe into the right corner.
Didar then sealed the match with her second goal in the 76th minute after she collected a pass from Dini and, running parallel to the goal, chipped past the lunging custodian. The game ended on a low note in the dying minutes when Al Zabrey and Lana Feras of Etihad Club and Bam Khatoon’s Tamrian and Shaban were yellow-carded for a fracas.

Survival of the wittiest: How humor and cleverness shaped human evolution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
14:00:05 UTC
23:00:05 KST

A new theoretical paper suggests that human cognitive and linguistic evolution was driven by early humans’ ability to be clever and humorous, an idea dubbed the “survival of the wittiest.” The analysis argues that the earliest stages of grammar provided a platform for verbal competition and sexual selection, gradually replacing physical violence with verbal agility. The research was published in PNAS Nexus.
For decades, discussions of human evolution have revolved around two dominant ideas. The first is Charles Darwin’s original concept of the survival of the fittest, which is often narrowly interpreted as physical strength or health. The second is the more recent hypothesis of the survival of the friendliest. This newer idea proposes that humans evolved primarily through selection for prosocial behavior and cooperation, which allowed early humans to form alliances and outcompete other groups.
Wayne State University linguist Ljiljana Progovac authored the new paper to offer an alternative viewpoint. Progovac argues that physical fitness and friendliness fail to capture the unique role that language played in human development. Being physically strong or socially cooperative are traits shared with many other animals, including bonobos and other primates. These traits alone do not explain the rapid and unique expansion of human cognition.
According to Progovac, focusing entirely on friendliness misses the competitive nature of human interaction. Evolution involves both cooperation and ruthless competition. To fully understand how our ancestors evolved into modern humans, researchers must account for the biological advantage of eloquence, imagination, and the ability to outwit rivals. This perspective centers on sexual selection, where traits that make an individual attractive to mates are passed down through successive generations.
To build this argument, Progovac analyzed linguistic structures that represent the earliest stages of grammar. Language leaves no physical bones behind, so researchers must rely on a process called reverse engineering. By peeling back the complex layers of modern syntax, linguists can reconstruct the most foundational building blocks of language. These foundational structures are referred to as living fossils.
In modern languages, these fossils appear as simple two-word combinations consisting of one verb and one noun. Examples in English include words like “killjoy,” “crybaby,” “pickpocket,” and “scatterbrain.” These basic compounds do not rely on complex grammatical rules. They lack the structural layers required to distinguish between subjects and objects or to establish tense.
These simple word pairs are remarkably consistent across entirely different language families. Progovac notes that similar verb-noun compounds exist in languages ranging from Serbian to Berber to Twi. Historically, these basic constructions have been used to create highly vivid, metaphorical nicknames. Often, these nicknames are derogatory or humorous, describing a person based on a prominent action or physical trait.
Progovac proposes that as early humans developed these two-word abilities, a new form of social competition emerged. Individuals who could quickly invent clever, insulting, or amusing names had a distinct social advantage. They could demean rivals and impress potential mates without resorting to physical combat. This quick-wittedness represented an enormous cognitive leap, showing that early language was not just for sharing information but for social maneuvering.
The biological benefits of this verbal agility are still visible in human populations today. In many traditional oral societies across the globe, the most eloquent speakers hold the highest social status. Individuals who can manipulate words effectively gain access to political power and better reproductive success. The ability to charm a mate through humor and metaphorical language proved to be highly adaptive over time.
The paper also reviews experimental evidence from neuroimaging to support this evolutionary timeline. In a prior functional magnetic resonance imaging experiment, researchers tracked brain activity while participants read ancient verb-noun combinations compared to more modern, complex words. The older compounds evoked a more visceral reaction in the brain than modern words.
The experimenters found that processing the older, fossil-like compounds activated the right side of the fusiform gyrus in the brain. This specific brain region is directly involved in face perception and face recognition. Finding that the same brain area handles both face recognition and basic verb-noun processing supports the idea that the earliest grammar was closely tied to naming individuals and attaching linguistic labels to faces.
A related brain imaging experiment looked at how the brain processes simple sentences compared to hierarchical, modern sentences. The simpler sentences resulted in less activity in the Broca’s area and the basal ganglia. The basal ganglia are deep brain structures involved in motor control and learning.
Over the course of human evolution, the connections between the Broca’s area and the basal ganglia became much denser. The gradual mastery of more complex language likely drove the physical evolution of these brain networks. This aligns with genetic changes unique to humans and Neanderthals, including variations in the FOXP2 gene, which is associated with speech and language development.
By replacing physical fighting with verbal dueling, quick-wittedness played a direct role in reducing physical aggression among early humans. Humor and laughter act as natural stress antagonists, lowering cortisol levels in the body. This biological response connects the survival of the wittiest with the concept of human self-domestication. Over time, societies selected for individuals who could use words to defuse tension or assert dominance, leading to a species that prizes cognitive contests over lethal battles.
While this perspective offers a robust framework for understanding language origins, measuring the evolutionary impact of humor and wit relies heavily on reconstructing the past. Researchers must reverse-engineer modern languages and rely on brain imaging proxies, which cannot definitively prove how ancient ancestors behaved in their daily lives. Brain scans of modern humans only provide an approximation of ancient cognitive processes.
Future studies could test this hypothesis by examining how individual variations in cognitive conditions process these fossil grammars. By observing how brains with different neurological setups handle early grammatical structures, scientists can better map the exact neural pathways that allowed language to flourish.
The study, “Survival of the wittiest (not friendliest): The art and science behind human linguistic and cognitive evolution,” was authored by Ljiljana Progovac.

Putin admits fuel market problems in Russia not yet fully resolved after Ukraine's strikes
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
13:56:16 UTC
22:56:16 KST

Elena Teslova
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
Russian President Vladimir Putin admitted on Sunday that fuel market problems in Russia due to Ukrainian strikes had not yet been fully resolved.
Speaking in an interview with the Russian broadcast company VGTRK, Putin said Prime Minister Mikhail Mishustin was dealing with the aftermath of Ukrainian strikes on energy infrastructure.
"Just the day before yesterday, we met and discussed this issue with the prime minister. Yes, not all issues have been resolved yet, but they are being resolved. The prime minister is keeping these issues under control. A special commission has been established," he said.
Putin also admitted that the strikes cause damage to the energy infrastructure. "Yes, of course, there are certain inconveniences for people, but the government must, of course, keep this under control," he said.
The president said he understood Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk’s position on the Nord Stream 2 gas pipeline, who said Germany should not prosecute those accused of blowing it up, noting that Poland had lost potential transit revenue after the project’s route was moved from Polish territory to the Baltic Sea.
According to him, the original plan had been to build the second gas route through Poland, alongside the existing Yamal-Europe pipeline.
The Russian president said that even infrastructure for the planned route was built on Poland's territory but then the decision was made to lay Nord Stream 2 under the Baltic Sea to reduce risks.
As a result, he said, Poland lost potential revenue from the transit of Russian hydrocarbons.
Putin accused Ukrainian authorities of making “neo-Nazi ideology” a foundation of the state and that this was among the reasons for Russia’s military operation in Ukraine.
He said Russia would not accept the “glorification of Nazism” in Ukraine, arguing that the country's authorities honor figures who participated "in mass killings of Poles, Jews and Russians."
Putin also pointed to Poland as an example of a country that, despite its strained relations with Moscow, has raised concerns about the glorification of Nazism in Ukraine.
“Despite the well-known Russophobia in Polish politics, the Polish authorities are paying serious attention to the fundamental foundations of today’s Ukrainian statehood,” he said.
He said Polish authorities had taken a firm position on the issue in response to public concerns.
Separately, Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak told VGTRK that Russia was not experiencing problems with supplies of diesel fuel or kerosene, with shortages affecting only gasoline.
“Russia has no problems with the supply of diesel fuel and kerosene. Difficulties remain only with gasoline,” he said.

HAIKOU, China (AP) — China said on Sunday it was postponing its planned ambitious Chang’e-7 lunar mission, which was set to carry out explorations including searching for water ice on the moon.
The Chang’e-7 spacecraft was originally set to lift off in the coming days from the Wenchang Space Launch Site on China’s southern Hainan island.
The mission does not meet the launch conditions, said the China Manned Space Agency in a brief statement, and “cannot take place during the planned window this year.”
The decision was made following a “comprehensive assessment,” the agency added, and was based on the principles of “prudence, reliability and absolute mission success.” It did not further elaborate on the reasons behind the decision.
Preparations have been carried out at the Wenchang launch site for the Chang’e-7 mission over the past weeks, the seventh in the Chang’e moon exploration program. It aimed at making breakthroughs in key technologies, the official Xinhua news agency previously reported.
It was set to explore permanently shadowed craters on the moon and conduct environmental and resource surveys of the lunar south pole, the Xinhua report said, citing the space agency.
Chang’e refers to a Chinese moon goddess. The Chang’e-6 probe returned to Earth in 2024 with rock and soil samples from the far side of the moon in a world first.

Over 8.2 million voters cast ballots in Kazakhstan's first election under new Constitution
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-23
13:49:52 UTC
22:49:52 KST

Elena Teslova
23 August 2026•Update: 23 August 2026
Turnout in Kazakhstan’s first elections to the new unicameral parliament, the Kurultai, reached 65.37% by 4 pm local time (1100 GMT) on Sunday, surpassing the turnout recorded in the last parliamentary elections in 2023, the Central Election Commission said.
CEC member Assel Zhanabilova said 8,240,336 (8.2 million) voters cast their ballots, representing 65.37% of those registered to vote.
Turnout varied significantly across the country, she noted.
Almaty, the country's largest city, recorded the lowest rate at 36.65%, while the highest turnout was reported in the Kyzylorda region at 81.38%.
In the capital Astana, 46.38% of registered voters cast ballots, according to CEC data.
Turnout in the 2023 elections to Kazakhstan’s lower house, the Mazhilis, was 54.21%.
The Aug. 23 vote is the first parliamentary election held under the new Constitution, adopted in a referendum earlier this year.
The new document abolished the previous bicameral parliament and replaced it with a 145-member unicameral Kurultai.
All 145 seats are being contested through party lists, with voters choosing among seven registered political parties.
There is no minimum turnout threshold for parliamentary elections, meaning the vote is considered valid regardless of the number of voters who participate.

Defence Secretary champions innovation on visit to largest Navy base in Western Europe
United Kingdom
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
14:30:01 BST
22:30:01 KST

Defence Secretary champions innovation on visit to largest Navy base in Western Europe
Defence Secretary visits Devonport Naval Base to see some of the latest equipment used by the Royal Marines and UK Commando Force.
- Defence Secretary Wes Streeting’s visits HMNB Devonport to see Navy innovation in action.
- Devonport is the largest naval base in Western Europe and pivotal to UK and NATO security.
- £7 billion investment in HMNB Devonport part of the largest naval infrastructure programme since the end of the Cold War.
Billions of pounds of investment is supporting skilled jobs and driving modernisation of the UK’s maritime forces, as the Defence Secretary saw firsthand during his visit to HMNB Devonport.
Accompanied by Luke Pollard, MP for Plymouth Sutton and Devonport and Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, the visit highlighted the unique and vital capabilities based at Western Europe’s largest naval base.
Plymouth is home to Royal Marines and UK Commando Forces and will become home to the Royal Navy’s new Type 26 frigates, cementing its position at the centre of the UK’s naval power for decades to come.
Devonport is the only facility in the UK responsible for the deep maintenance and defueling of the Royal Navy’s nuclear submarine fleet. Its maintenance work underpins the UK’s continuous at-sea deterrent by keeping the submarine fleet available and operational, while its defueling capability supports the decommissioning of older submarines at the end of their service life.
During the visit, the Defence Secretary met Royal Navy personnel and industry partners who deliver the engineering, maintenance and support that keeps the Royal Navy’s fleet operational and saw the facilities under construction that will support submarines in the years ahead.
Defence Secretary Wes Streeting MP, said:
  The work done here at Devonport is critical to keeping our country safe. From our Commando Forces ready to deploy at a moment’s notice, to our Navy personnel and industry who maintain our submarines – Plymouth is a city where defence runs in the blood.
As we bring the Type 26 fleet to Devonport in the coming years, we’re investing in this base and our forces, ensuring it will remain at the heart of our naval power for generations to come, and continuing to push the frontier of defence innovation.
Around £500 million was committed as part of the Defence Investment Plan to continue the transformation of the UK Commando Forces, including equipping personnel with new high-speed boats and the latest drone and autonomous technology.
Plymouth Sutton and Devonport MP, and Minister for Defence Readiness and Industry, Luke Pollard said:
  Devonport is the beating heart of Plymouth, and it was fantastic to welcome the Secretary of State here today to see for himself what our Commando Forces, submariners, and dockyard workers do for our national security.
This is a base with a proud history and an even brighter future. The Type 26 fleet and the continued investment in our submarine capability means Devonport will remain vital to the defence of this country, and vital to jobs and skills here in Plymouth.
As one of the Royal Navy’s three main naval bases, Devonport is set to be a major beneficiary of Royal Oak, a £26 billion ten-year programme to modernise UK naval infrastructure, confirmed as part of the Government’s Defence Investment Plan and the largest such programme since the end of the Cold War.
Royal Oak includes £7.1 billion to deliver major upgrades and new infrastructure across the Naval Base and Dockyard. The investment will bolster Devonport as a warfighting-ready facility, directly improving Royal Navy readiness, availability and lethality, while supporting thousands of skilled jobs in the Southwest of England.
£50 million defence investment is being put into Plymouth and the South West, making it easier for defence businesses to innovate, creating skilled jobs in the region and boosting UK national security through the Plymouth Growth Deal.
It will help create hundreds of new jobs and increase investment in the region. The investment reinforces Plymouth as a leader in maritime autonomy, developing the technology that helps keep the UK safe at sea. Plymouth was named the UK’s National Centre for Marine Autonomy, recognising the city’s growing role in developing autonomous maritime technology alongside the Royal Navy and industry partners, including work supporting the Navy’s Hybrid Navy programme.

France faces lowest potato yield in over 30 years as drought hits crops
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:32:52 UTC
22:32:52 KST

Necva Taştan Sevinç
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
France’s potato production is expected to fall at least 23% from last year as heat waves and severe drought hit crops, potentially resulting in the lowest yield in more than three decades, local media reported Monday.
France experienced five consecutive heat waves this summer, along with a severe rainfall deficit since late May and historically dry soils, significantly affecting potato crops.
“Last year, we were at just over 43.5 tonnes per hectare in 2025. And this year, for the moment, the projection is around 34.5 tonnes,” said Geoffroy D’Evry, president of the National Union of French Potato Producers.
“That’s even less than in 2022, when we were already at a historically low yield,” he added.
The anticipated decline comes after potato-growing areas were reduced by 10% in France and 11% across northwestern Europe following overproduction in 2025, French broadcaster RFI reported.
The French potato industry estimates that it has suffered nearly €400 million (about $466 million) in economic losses.
“The financial burden of climate change cannot be borne solely by the farmer. All of our buyers and customers need to understand that producing potatoes is expensive and risky,” D’Evry said.
He warned that the losses could also affect consumer prices.
Agriculture Minister Annie Genevard announced on Aug. 5 that the government was preparing a “comprehensive plan” to assist farmers affected by repeated heat waves in France and elsewhere in Europe.
The proposed measures include emergency support for farm cash flow, relief on social security contributions, regulatory exemptions and assistance to help the hardest-hit farms resume production.
The government has yet to specify the amount of aid.
Arnaud Rousseau, president of France’s largest agricultural union, FNSEA, said on Aug. 8 that the farming sector would need “billions of euros” to recover from what he described as a climate crisis unprecedented in scale and duration.
Genevard said decisions on the allocation of assistance would have to wait until a meeting of prefects scheduled for Aug. 27.
The French Federation of Commerce and Distribution also announced measures to support farmers, including relaxing standards concerning the size and appearance of fruit and vegetables and prioritizing French-grown products.

Poland signs $2.2B deal for domestically made Piorun air defense missiles

Şeyma Erkul Dayanç
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
Poland has signed an 8 billion zloty ($2.2 billion) framework agreement for several thousand domestically produced Piorun air defense missile launchers and missiles, Polskie Radio reported Monday.
The agreement was signed at the MESKO plant in Skarzysko-Kamienna in south-central Poland and covers several thousand launchers and missiles, along with training and logistics packages.
More than 80% of the order will be supplied to Poland’s armed forces, while the remainder will go to Lithuania, Latvia and Norway under the EU’s Security Action for Europe (SAFE) program, a loan instrument for joint defense procurement.
Defense Minister Wladyslaw Kosiniak-Kamysz said the agreement demonstrated Poland’s growing role as a defense producer and exporter.
“Poland can be an exporter of military equipment and can be a leader not only in defense spending but also in production,” he said.
Kosiniak-Kamysz added that the agreement was the first of its kind in which the consortium consisted of allied governments rather than companies.
The contract was signed between Poland’s state Armaments Agency and MESKO SA, a Polish defense manufacturer.
The Piorun is a very short-range air defense system designed to counter low-flying threats, including aircraft, helicopters, cruise missiles and drones.

The disaster diplomacy behind Israel's return to Venezuela
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:38:31 UTC
22:38:31 KST

Breadcrumb
The disaster diplomacy behind Israel's return to Venezuela
On 11 August, Delcy Rodríguez’s de facto government announced the re-establishment of diplomatic relations with Israel.
Venezuela, like Bolivia, had severed diplomatic relations with Israel in January 2009 in response to Operation Cast Lead, Israel’s military aggression that killed over 1,400 Palestinians in Gaza.
In a similar vein to the re-establishment of diplomatic relations with Peru, Chile, and the Dominican Republic over the past month, Venezuela began the process of re-establishing diplomatic relations with Israel at the consular level.
The move followed intense public relations efforts by Netanyahu and Delcy Rodríguez in the wake of the twin earthquakes that struck northern Venezuela in June, during which ZAKA and Israeli army operatives were deployed in Caracas and La Guaira.
The disaster, with a provisional death toll of over 6,300 and tens of thousands injured, was used by Delcy Rodríguez to argue that humanitarian cooperation would “open new paths and doors” for the re-establishment of diplomatic relations, whilst Netanyahu spoke of rebuilding “ruins and relations (…) proving how good it is to have relations with Israel”.
The reorientation of Venezuelan foreign policy from its alliances with Russia, China, Iran, and Cuba to its alignment with the US is part of a broader shift to the right across the region.
In most cases, this change has been imposed through the ballot box, with significant US interference and overt pressure.
In the case of Venezuela, it is primarily a consequence of US armed intervention on 3 January, which accelerated a political decline that had been underway for over a decade, culminating in total capitulation to the US, including major legal reforms at the service of US oil and mining corporations and the authorisation of military exercises and bombings on Venezuelan territory.
It is not surprising that the Israeli government declared that 2026 would be the year of Latin America. Besides Venezuela, Bolivia and Colombia also re-established relations with Israel. Honduras and Chile, meanwhile, have reappointed ambassadors who had been absent for years in protest against the Israeli genocide in Gaza.
Javier Milei, who calls himself the ‘world’s most Zionist president’, hosted legislators from 12 other Latin American countries in Buenos Aires in April to promote what he dubbed the ‘Isaac Accords’, parodying the ‘Abraham Accords’ between Israel and various Arab states.
It was slated as a forum to promote support for Israel and the adoption of the IHRA’s definition of antisemitism, which includes criticism of Israel as an instance of antisemitism.
Venezuela's post-Maduro political direction
In 2017-2018, whilst Delcy Rodríguez was Foreign Minister, there had already been an attempt to re-establish relations with Israel, as part of which Isaac Cohen, a leading rabbi of the Israeli Association of Venezuela, was awarded the Order of the Liberators.
Cohen would resume this role this year by mediating between Delcy Rodríguez and Netanyahu for the deployment of Israeli army officers and ZAKA agents in July to assess the damage to infrastructure caused by the twin earthquakes, and subsequently to re-establish diplomatic relations.
In addition to the conspicuous Israeli military presence following the earthquakes, in July, Caracas received delegations of Christian Zionists from the US National Faith Advisory Board and Republicans Brian Mast, Randy Fine, and Kat Cammack, Florida representatives in the US Congress linked to the pro-Israel lobby group AIPAC, who were received by Delcy Rodríguez.
In an interview in late July, when asked about what she considered Maduro’s greatest mistake, Delcy Rodríguez stated: “We should have been more open geopolitically (…) we are moving towards a new relationship with the US, and I believe that Venezuela’s international relations should be more open and diversified”.
Beyond its anti-imperialist rhetoric, the very structure of the Venezuelan regime has, from its inception, included elements of Christian Zionism.
It has cultivated its relationship with the Protestant right for years, through funding programmes such as ‘My Well-Equipped Church’, a monthly stipend for evangelical pastors, and the creation of an official Evangelical Pastors’ Day.
Nicolás Maduro Guerra, son of the former head of state and a member of the National Assembly, as well as Vice-President for Religious Affairs of the United Socialist Party of Venezuela, was the first senior official to call for resuming relations with Israel on 16 January, barely two weeks after US forces killed 81 people and kidnapped his father in Caracas.
Christian Zionists, Trump, and a right-wing shift
According to reports in the Israeli press, in the weeks leading up to the re-establishment of diplomatic relations, the Israeli Minister for Energy and Infrastructure and security cabinet member Eli Cohen discussed with his Venezuelan counterpart potential cooperation in energy, trade, and technology, with the diversification of its energy suppliers being one of the priorities for Israel.
Omar Vázquez Heredia, sociology professor at the Central University of Venezuela, considers the re-establishment of relations with Israel as “part of a foreign policy aligned with the Trump administration,” which he says has its precedent in the Venezuelan state’s withdrawal from the ICC amidst the State Department’s campaign to dismantle it.
“Rebuilding relations whilst Israel continues to commit genocide stirs widespread condemnation and demonstrates that the sole objective of the Chavista leaders is to prolong their control of the state, even if it implies subordination to Trump and Rubio,” Vázquez Heredia told The New Arab.
Ilan Pappé, professor at the University of Exeter and co-director of the European Centre for Palestine Studies, told The New Arab that Israel seeks to strengthen “an international coalition to sustain its current policies against the Palestinians, the Lebanese, the Syrians and the Iranians”.
According to Pappé, this coalition “has dwindled over the years, with the departure of social-democratic governments that used to support Israel but refused to remain in such a coalition given the nature of Israeli policies in recent years”.
The Israeli historian warns that “Israel can still rely on right-wing politics wherever they are found: Christian Zionists, some Jewish communities, the military, the security sector, and high-tech industries. But it needs to rely on a future in which there is no chance of the Left returning to power where there is currently a right-wing party in power”.
According to Alexander Aviña, a professor of history at Arizona State University, Israel views the current right-wing transition in Latin America as an opportunity to strengthen its position and influence political developments in the region, particularly given its growing international isolation over the genocide in Gaza.
Christian Zionism, following the spread of Pentecostalism since the early 2000s, has also laid the ideological groundwork for deeper relations with Israel.
“The right wing in Latin America has been using the Israeli flag as part of the symbolism of their political movement; for example, Bolsonaro in Brazil,” Aviña told The New Arab.
“One way to interpret the right-left divide in Latin America, at least at grassroots level, is to look at who is pro-Israel and who is pro-Palestine. It’s a bit murkier at state level, as always. For example, Mexico’s centre-left government has been unable to stop buying Israeli weapons.”
Trump’s presence in the White House presents, in some respects, an even more favourable situation for Israel in Latin America than in the 1970s and 1980s, when it was the main market for its weapons exports.
“The justification for Israel’s heightened role in Central America was that the Carter administration stopped sending weapons and money to these death squad regimes run by the military dictatorships in Latin America, which opened up the space for Israel to start arming the Salvadorans, the Guatemalans, and Nicaragua until the Sandinista revolution,” Aviña told The New Arab.
“Even Reagan, due to the US Congress and the Boland Amendment, was unable to openly align himself with what Israel was doing in Central America. Now, with Trump in power, there is no need to pretend that they are not aligned with Israel’s economic and political goals in Latin America.”
However, Latin America’s rightward shift and subsequent political opening for relations with Israel is not necessarily permanent.
“If you look at the polls, Israel’s reputation is, quite rightly, at rock bottom. In countries where there is an electoral option for the Left to return to power, those favourable conditions for Israel might recede,” Aviña says.
Simón Rodríguez is a Venezuelan journalist, researcher, and editor at Venezuelanvoices.org.

Israeli aid group to open Gaza clinic serving 10,000 children
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:31:06 UTC
22:31:06 KST

An Israeli humanitarian organization is set to open a medical clinic in southern Gaza next week, with the facility expected to serve around 10,000 children living in a displacement camp in the Mawasi area.
The clinic, scheduled to open Sept. 1 in the Al-Qarara area, was established by the Israeli aid organization Natan as part of the Gaza Children Village initiative, which already provides children with education, hot meals and other forms of support.
The facility was built with several hundred thousand dollars in donations from Israelis and American Jews. Palestinian medical staff in Gaza will examine and treat the children, while Natan will provide medical equipment and arrange remote consultations with Israeli doctors.
The project is being led by Natan CEO Alice Miller, an aeronautical engineer and civilian pilot best known in Israel for the landmark Supreme Court petition that led to the opening of the Israeli Air Force pilots’ course to women. The clinic was developed in cooperation with Dr. David Hasan, founder of Gaza Children Village.
NATAN Worldwide Disaster Relief, named after Israeli peace activist Abie Nathan, has operated for years in disaster zones around the world, providing humanitarian and medical assistance. Miller said restrictions on Israeli organizations operating directly inside Gaza mean much of Natan’s work there is conducted remotely through local and international partners.
According to the organization, Natan has a network of more than 1,800 staff members and volunteers, including doctors, nurses, psychologists, social workers and dentists. The new clinic is intended to add medical care to the services already provided through Gaza Children Village.
“Every child deserves access to basic medical care, no matter where they were born or what circumstances surround them,” Miller said. “This clinic is a direct response to a need we saw with our own eyes at the children’s village in Gaza.”
Dr. Hasan said the clinic would complete the support system already being built around the children. “These children need a place where they can gather and learn, a meal so they don’t have to remain hungry, and physical care for bodies suffering under extreme humanitarian conditions,” he said. “This clinic gives us that final piece: the physical care they can receive.”
‘Imagine your daughter getting her first period in a tent’
Miller spoke to ynet in December about the humanitarian work she had begun promoting inside Gaza. At the time, Natan was also helping women and girls by distributing reusable sanitary pads through its cooperation with Gaza Children Village. Miller said the organization maintained direct contact with women inside Gaza through an American partner.
She recalled the case of a 14-year-old girl who got her first period while living in a tent and had no suitable menstrual products. Her family, Miller said, was forced to use pieces of fabric from the tent. “Imagine your daughter getting her first period in a tent and having nothing to use,” Miller said at the time.
Miller also addressed criticism she received in Israel over assisting Gaza residents. “I don’t deal with politics. That’s not what I do. We are a humanitarian organization,” she said. “My heart cannot remain closed in the face of other people’s suffering.”
She added that even during wartime, showing compassion toward children and civilians matters. “Part of the public diplomacy we need to do is show the world acts of compassion,” she said.
Since then, Gaza Children Village has expanded considerably. According to the organization, it now operates educational programs across Gaza where children receive schooling, meals, medical assistance and psychological support.
The group says its longer-term goal is to build a stable support system that can continue accompanying children beyond the immediate humanitarian emergency. The opening of the Al-Qarara clinic is the latest stage in that effort.

World's oceans hit hottest temperature ever recorded in August as El Niño takes hold
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:42:14 UTC
22:42:14 KST

The average global sea surface temperature outside polar regions reached 21.1°C on Saturday.
The world's oceans have reached their highest daily temperature on record, with global sea surface temperatures hitting 21.1°C on 22 August - a new high made particularly striking by the time of year, according to the European Union's climate change data.
The reading, recorded by the EU's Copernicus Climate Change Service, narrowly surpassed the previous daily record of 21.09°C, set in March 2024.
Ocean temperatures typically reach their global peak in March and April, following the southern hemisphere summer, Copernicus explains. This new record being set in August, when temperatures would normally be declining, highlights the persistent warmth spreading across the world's oceans.
The latest figure also beats the previous August record of 20.98°C, set in 2023.
While swimmers may like warmer oceans, the consequences are devastating and wide reaching for both humans and animals.
What is the link between El Niño and warmer oceans?
The record comes as a strong El Niño develops in the tropical Pacific, adding further heat to an ocean that has already warmed significantly over decades because of human-driven climate change.
El Niño is expected to strengthen in the coming months, with the World Meteorological Organization forecasting a strong event. Copernicus seasonal forecasts suggest it could reach levels not seen for several decades.
But scientists caution against viewing El Niño as the sole explanation for the record.
“This record is another clear signal of an ocean under growing stress,” says Samantha Burgess, strategic lead for climate at the European Centre for Medium-Range Weather Forecasts.
“El Niño is adding heat to the system, but it is doing so on top of decades of human-driven warming,” she says.
What is the problem with warmer oceans?
"From the Atlantic waters off Ireland to the Mediterranean Sea, Europe's seas are experiencing an alarming surge in temperatures," Thomas Frolicher, an environmental physicist at the University of Bern, Switzerland, said in a study published last week.
"Our research shows clearly that this is being driven by climate change, in particular by the continued burning of fossil fuels," he adds.
The consequences of warmer oceans stretch from marine ecosystems to coastal communities.
Higher sea temperatures increase the likelihood and intensity of marine heatwaves, which can damage coral reefs and seagrass meadows and disrupt marine food webs.
Fisheries and aquaculture industries can also be affected as marine species move in response to changing conditions.
The global ocean has already experienced a sharp increase in marine heatwaves, with the number of marine heatwave days more than tripling since the early 1990s, according to Copernicus.
Warmer seas also contribute to rising sea levels because water expands as it heats. At the same time, a warmer ocean can transfer more heat and moisture into the atmosphere, potentially increasing the intensity of some rainfall and storm systems.
Another concern is that the ocean absorbs a large share of the carbon dioxide produced by human activity, but warmer water is less efficient at taking up CO2, Copernicus data revealed, noting that continued warming could weaken one of the planet's important carbon sinks against climate change.
Scientists are now watching to see whether the latest record proves to be a short-lived spike or becomes part of a more persistent period of extreme ocean warmth.

Police have arrested four suspects in an investigation into the deaths of 18 elephants in Kenya’s Amboseli ecosystem, where authorities also seized assorted substances including chemicals, the tourism and wildlife ministry has said.
A Kenya Wildlife Service (KWS) spokesperson told Reuters on Monday that the four had since been released on bail.

The ministry said investigators were also pursuing a fifth individual believed to have information relevant to the case. Glacier retreat could increase disease risk for bees: Study
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:42:42 UTC
22:42:42 KST

Aysu Biçer
24 August 2026•Update: 24 August 2026
Melting glaciers could increase the risk of disease spreading between wild bees and honeybees, according to a new study led by researchers at the University of Lausanne in Switzerland.
Scientists from the Universities of Lausanne and Milan and Italy’s Crea research organization studied bee populations around the Mont-Mine Glacier in the Val d’Herens. They investigated three viruses and two parasites, according to a report from SWI on Monday.
Normally, wild bees and honeybees tend to forage on different plant species. This natural separation reduces the chances of bees picking up pathogens from one another.
But as glaciers retreat, changing vegetation is bringing the insects together to feed on the same plants. Flowers can become sites of infection when infected bees leave pathogens behind that are then picked up by other bees.
Researchers found all five pathogens in honeybees in areas that had only recently become ice-free. Only two were detected in wild bees in those areas.
In older ice-free zones, where vegetation changed more significantly, the wing-deforming virus became much more common among wild bees.
The study highlights a less visible consequence of climate change, showing how glacier retreat can alter relationships between species as well as landscapes.

Israeli occupiers using violence, intimidation to drive Palestinians from West Bank homes: Ynet
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:38:51 UTC
22:38:51 KST

Israeli occupiers are increasingly using siege tactics, violence and intimidation to expel Palestinians from their homes and land in the occupied West Bank, Israel’s Ynet news portal reported Monday.
The recent siege of a Palestinian home in the West Bank town of Qusra -- which drew international attention -- was “far from an isolated case,” Ynet reported, adding that Israeli youths from illegal settlement outposts regularly block access to Palestinian villages and pressure residents to leave.
Within the past two weeks, Israeli occupiers, often protected by Israeli military personnel, have surrounded three Palestinian homes in Qusra, into which they have prevented the delivery of basic necessities, according to Ynet.
In the village of Jalud near Nablus, Mahmoud and Aida Tubasi said they had left their homes after months of threats, arson, stone-throwing and roadblocks by Israeli occupiers.
“No water, no flour, no rice [was allowed into the village],” Mahmoud Tubasi told Ynet. “We knew it was over, and we left.”
According to the report, the Tubasi family can still see their homes from the nearby residence to which they were forced to flee.
Tubasi said the occupiers had doused the doors of their homes with fuel before setting them alight, erected a structure nearby, threw stones, played loud music at night and threatened the family.
“They told us, ‘We will burn you like the Dawabshe family,’” he said, referring to a 2015 arson attack in the West Bank village of Duma that killed an 18-month-old Palestinian child and seriously injured his parents and four-year-brother.
Both parents later died of their injuries, while the surviving child suffered burns on 60 percent of his body and is now living under the care of relatives.
According to Ynet, the case is part of a wider pattern of violence by Israeli occupiers, who set up outposts inside areas nominally under Palestinian administration before waging campaigns of intimidation and violence against local Palestinians with the aim of driving them from their homes and land.
Peace Now, an Israeli anti-settlement group, said 26 occupier outposts had been established in Areas A and B of the occupied West Bank, where occupiers have seized control of approximately 100,000 dunams (roughly 25,000 acres) of land.
Yesh Din, another Israeli rights group, said more than 60 percent of the occupier violence it had documented in the first half of 2026 occurred in Areas A and B. Last year, it added, roughly one third of all documented incidents were concentrated in Area C.
“The deeper the settlement, the deeper the violence,” Yesh Din research director Yonatan Kanonich told Ynet.
Documented incidents include beatings, stone-throwing, Molotov cocktails, gunfire, and arson attacks on homes, vehicles and agricultural crops.
US Ambassador to Israel Mike Huckabee recently used unusually strong language to describe such attacks, saying: “When you engage in activity designed to create fear in an individual, a society or a community, that is the dictionary definition of terrorism.”
Ynet said similar accounts had emerged from other Palestinian communities, including Jaljulia north of Ramallah, where residents said the establishment of a settlement outpost 10 months ago had turned a previously quiet area into the scene of repeated attacks by occupiers.
Jaljulia residents said armed occupiers had trespassed on farmland, damaged crops and threatened agricultural workers with violence.
The West Bank was divided into Areas A, B and C under the 1995 Oslo II Accord.
Area A is under Palestinian administrative and security control, Area B is under Palestinian administrative and Israeli security control, and Area C -- which accounts for roughly 60 percent of the entire West Bank -- is under full Israeli control.

China and Jordan call for Strait of Hormuz to get back to normal after US-Iran conflict

Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:48:26 UTC
22:48:26 KST

China and Jordan call for Strait of Hormuz to get back to normal after US-Iran conflict
The two sides also criticised Israel’s ‘dangerous escalatory actions’ following King Abdullah’s meeting with Xi Jinping in Beijing
China and Jordan have called for the reopening of the Strait of Hormuz to shipping and called for the ceasefire between the United States and Iran to be maintained in a joint statement issued during King Abdullah’s visit to Beijing.
They also said they wanted to see “a comprehensive solution addressing the root causes of tension … through dialogue and negotiation, ensuring full respect for the sovereignty, security and territorial integrity of regional countries”.
Peace talks between the US and Iran have stalled and the strait, which was described in the statement as a “vital channel for international commerce and the energy trade”, remains closed to most shipping.
The statement, issued after the king’s meeting with President Xi Jinping and other top officials on Monday, called for the “restoration of normal transit through the strait”.
The two sides also criticised Israel’s “dangerous escalatory actions” in the West Bank and East Jerusalem, according to state news agency Xinhua.
They expressed “deep concern” over Israeli activities that included “land confiscation, the construction and expansion of settlements, and attempts to alter the historic and legal status quo of Islamic and Christian holy sites in Jerusalem”.

Saints and Stars gym chain fined €300k for breaching work rules
Unknown
Unknown Publisher
2026-08-24
13:50:51 UTC
22:50:51 KST

Saints and Stars gym chain fined €300k for breaching work rules
See more DutchNews articles in your Google search results
Amsterdam gym chain Saints and Stars has been hit with more than €300,000 in fines for breaching Dutch employment laws.
The biggest fine of €234,000 after labour inspectors found it hired 25 non-EU nationals without permits and had failed to check the identity of three staff.
The gym was at the centre of controversy last year when city newspaper Het Parool reported that it forced cleaners from Indonesia and the Philippines to work 17 hours a day and share beds with strangers while working in its four branches.
The exposée prompted several trainers and influencers to cancel their memberships at the €139-a-month gym. Last December a judge awarded five Filipino cleaners €15,000 each in compensation.
The latest fines also included €60,000 for failing to comply with the laws on minimum wage and holiday pay, after inspectors were unable to determine how many hours employees had worked and whether they had received the minimum wage.
The chain was also fined €22,500 for not observing mandatory break times.
The inspectors also issued two official warnings to Saints and Stars, meaning the gyms could be temporarily closed if they breach the rules a third time in the next five years.
The company said it would not appeal against the fines. “This should not have happened,” owner Tom Moos said in a press statement.
